The practical implication is that a bad stretch is not only a bad stretch. It changes the shape of what comes next, and recovering standing takes longer than losing it. If you want a career that goes somewhere, treat the relationship read-outs as a leading indicator rather than a scoreboard.

## Off the court

Between games there is a second game: training camp, attribute upgrades, signature moves, goals and rewards, contracts, brand deals and lifestyle purchases.

All of it runs on fictional in-game currency with no real-world value — worth saying clearly, because the presence of contracts and brand deals in a sports title invites the wrong assumption. Nothing here is money, and nothing here predicts, tracks or relates to any real athlete's earnings.

Real money does enter in one place, and it is separate from all of the above: Basketball Career Sim is free to download on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases and an Everyone content rating. [Basketball Draft GM Franchise](/apps/pro-basketball-draft-gm-mode/), the front-office companion, is on the same terms.

As a progression system, the off-court layer is where you convert results into capability. The strategic question is the same one that governs any upgrade economy: do you deepen your existing strength or patch your weakness? For a career sim, deepening usually wins earlier than instinct suggests, because being conspicuously good at one thing generates opportunities in a way that being unremarkable at everything does not.

## What the simulation assumes

A career sim is a model, and it is honest to say what kind.

The game is not calculating physics or reproducing real basketball outcomes. It takes your player's attributes, the choices you make on key possessions, and the state of the systems around you, and it resolves each situation according to its own internal rules. Stats, awards, records and the legacy score are all outputs of that model.

Three things follow. It does not describe any real player, team, school or league — every element is fictional and generated inside the game. It cannot tell you anything about how a real basketball career would go, because it was never modelling one. And the results it produces are meaningful only relative to itself, which is precisely why comparing your own careers against each other is the interesting comparison and the only one available.

## Practical advice for a first career

**Commit to an identity in the first ten minutes.** The archetype you pick at creation should still be recognisable in season eight.

**Be consistent on possessions rather than clever.** A predictable player is one the surrounding systems can reward. A player who alternates between hero ball and deference is one they cannot read.

**Check the relationship read-outs before you check the box score.** The box score tells you what happened. The relationships tell you what you will be allowed to do next.

**Spend the off-court economy on your strength first.** Patch weaknesses when they start actively costing you possessions, not before.

**Play a whole career before starting a second.** The stage-to-stage structure only reveals itself in retrospect, and a career abandoned at the draft has shown you about a third of the game.

## If the career is not the part you want

Some people want the possessions; other people want the board. If reading this made you want to build the roster instead of play in it, [Basketball Draft GM Franchise](/apps/pro-basketball-draft-gm-mode/) is the front-office version of the same sport, and the same drafting logic applied elsewhere is in the [football draft guide](/blog/football-draft-gm-guide/), the [baseball draft guide](/blog/baseball-draft-gm-guide/) and the [soccer draft XI guide](/blog/soccer-draft-xi-guide/). Everything the studio makes in this space is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: How a Basketball Draft Simulator Works — and How to Draft Better in One
metaTitle: Basketball Draft Simulator App: How to Draft Better
body:
Pick six of a salary cap draft, and the best player left on the board plays a position you have already filled twice. The next name down is worse on every visible number and covers a hole you have not touched. Take the higher rating and you have spent a pick on a backup. Take the lower one and you have, on paper, made your team worse.

That four-second decision is the game. The 82 games that follow are just the scoreboard reading back what you already decided.

## What the genre is actually about

Strip the jerseys off and a draft simulator is a constrained optimisation puzzle. You get a fixed number of picks. You do not control the pool. There is a scoring function that converts your finished roster into a result, and you can only ever infer its shape from the results it gives you.

That last part is what makes it worth playing more than once. If the model were visible you would solve it in an afternoon. Because it is not, the loop is: form a theory, draft to it, read the record, revise the theory. That is a genuinely different activity from playing a sports game, and it is why people who have no interest in tapping through a match will happily spend twenty minutes on a draft board.

It is also why the genre lives comfortably on a phone. A draft is a sequence of discrete decisions with a clean stopping point. There is nothing to twitch, nothing to time, nothing you lose by being interrupted.

## Three ideas that separate good drafters from lucky ones

Most bad drafts are not bad luck. They are one of these three mistakes, repeated.

### Value is relative to your own bench, not to the field

The number next to a player's name tells you how good they are. It does not tell you what drafting them is worth to *you*.

If you already have a strong player at a position, the second one you draft there does not add their full rating to your team. They add the difference between themselves and the player they displace, and if they displace nobody, they add close to nothing. Meanwhile the position you left empty is not costing you a small amount — it is costing you the entire gap between a real starter and whatever the roster puts there instead.

This is the single most useful reframe in the whole genre. Stop asking "who is the best player left" and start asking "which pick moves my worst slot the furthest".

### Positional scarcity decides your order, not your preferences

Some positions are deep in a given pool and some are thin. If you can reliably find a competent option at a position in the late rounds, you should not spend an early pick there, even if the early option is genuinely better. If a position dries up quickly, you take it before it does — and you accept a small loss in raw quality to avoid a large loss later.

Scarcity is a property of the board, not of the sport, and it changes from run to run. Reading it is a skill. The tell is usually the shape of the drop-off: a position where the third-best and the tenth-best options look similar is one you can wait on. A position where quality falls off a cliff after two names is one you cannot.

### Every pick is an opportunity cost

There is no such thing as a free pick. Taking a player is simultaneously deciding not to take every other player, and in a format with a budget it is also deciding not to spend that money elsewhere.

This sounds obvious and it is routinely ignored, because rating numbers are visible and opportunity costs are not. The discipline is to make yourself name the alternative before you confirm a selection. If you cannot say what you gave up, you did not make a decision — you clicked the top of a list.

## Formats are the difficulty setting

[Basketball Draft GM Franchise](/apps/pro-basketball-draft-gm-mode/) ships eight draft formats: Unlimited Draft, Quick Draft, Blind Draft, Franchise Draft, Salary Cap Draft, VS Computer, Battle Mode and a Daily Challenge. The important thing about that list is not its length. It is that a roster which dominates one format can fall apart in the next, because each one changes the constraint you are optimising under.

Consider what a budget does to drafting. Without one, the board is a ranking problem — take the best available thing that helps you. Add a cap and it becomes an allocation problem, where a merely good player at a low price can be a better pick than a great player at a high one. The same board, the same players, a completely different correct answer.

Competitive formats change it again. Drafting against an opponent introduces a resource you were not tracking before: what they can still take. Now a pick can be defensive — you take a player earlier than their value justifies because losing them to the other side costs you twice.

If you are new to the genre, the honest advice is to spend your first several runs in an unconstrained format learning what the board looks like, and only then add constraints. Learning the pool and learning the rules at the same time means you cannot tell which one beat you.

## Reading the season result without over-reading it

This part matters, so it is worth being blunt about it.

When the season simulation returns a record, that record is the output of a model. It is a function of the roster you built, evaluated against whatever the game weighs — quality, positional coverage, balance, and the depth you did or did not leave yourself. It is a **score for your drafting**. It is not a prediction, it does not describe anything that happened in the real world, and it has no bearing on any actual game, team or player anywhere.

Two practical consequences follow.

**First, judge yourself on the process, not on one result.** A single season is one sample of a model you cannot see. If you want to know whether a drafting approach is better, run it several times and compare the distribution, not the best run you got out of it.

**Second, use the record diagnostically.** A disappointing record after a draft you were proud of is information, and it is usually pointing at exactly one of two things: an uncovered position you talked yourself out of caring about, or a roster stacked in one area at the expense of everything else. The catalogue description of the game is explicit that balance and depth carry more weight than a single marquee pick, and the simulation is where that shows up.

## GM Mode is where a good draft gets wasted

Drafting well and then abandoning the roster is the most common failure in franchise play. Draft day sets your ceiling; the front office decides how much of it you reach.

The GM side of the game covers contracts, trades and rotations. Each of those is a different kind of decision from drafting:

- **Rotations** are a distribution problem. You have a fixed amount of playing time and a roster that is not uniformly good. Concentrating minutes on your best players raises your average but thins you out; spreading them protects you against a weak spot but dilutes your strengths.
- **Trades** are the only tool that can fix a structural mistake. If the draft left you long at one position and short at another, that is precisely the imbalance a trade exists to correct — you are converting surplus you cannot use into coverage you need.
- **Contracts** are drafting with a time dimension. The question is no longer only what a player is worth, but what they are worth for how long, and what committing to them stops you doing later.

Franchise play across multiple seasons compounds all of this. A team built to peak immediately and a team built to stay strong are different teams, and choosing between them before the draft rather than during it is most of the skill.

## A routine that reliably improves results

If you want a concrete method rather than principles:

1. **Scan the whole board before the first pick.** Find where each position falls off. That map, not your favourite player, decides your order.
2. **Name your alternative out loud on every pick.** If you cannot, you are not choosing.
3. **Fill your worst slot, not your best one.** The team is only as good as the position you neglected.
4. **Leave one pick's worth of flexibility if the format allows it.** Boards develop; a plan with no slack cannot respond.
5. **After the season, write down one sentence about why the record came out where it did.** This is the whole learning loop, and skipping it is why people plateau.

## Where to go from here

The drafting principles above port cleanly across sports, but the *shape* of the problem does not. Football has the deepest roster and the widest spread of positional value, which is covered in the [football draft simulator guide](/blog/football-draft-gm-guide/). Baseball is the most statistically explicit, and the [baseball draft guide](/blog/baseball-draft-gm-guide/) goes into what those numbers mean before you draft on them. Hockey is the tightest puzzle of all — six players and a coach, where a single weak slot has nowhere to hide, as the [hockey draft guide](/blog/hockey-draft-gm-guide/) explains.

If the front office is not what appeals and you would rather live inside one player's career than run the organisation, that is a genuinely different game; the [basketball career sim guide](/blog/basketball-career-sim-guide/) covers it. The rest of the studio's management and drafting titles sit in the [sports GM category](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Basketball Positions Explained: What the Five Numbers Mean
metaTitle: Basketball Positions Explained (1 Through 5)
secondaryKeywords: what does a point guard do
difference between power forward and center
body:
Here is the thing nobody mentions when they teach you the five positions: they are not in the rulebook. FIBA, which publishes the Official Basketball Rules recognised internationally, governs how many players a team may have on the playing court and how the game is conducted. It does not say what any of them is called or what any of them is for.

Positions are a vocabulary that grew up around the sport to describe recurring jobs. That is why they can shift over a decade without a single rule changing, and why arguments about whether a player "is" a four or a five are arguments about description, not about legality.

Understanding them is still worth your time — you cannot talk about basketball without them — but understanding what kind of thing they are is what stops you being confused later.

## Why the numbers run 1 to 5

The numbering is not arbitrary and it is much easier to remember than the names once you see the logic: **it runs from the player who operates furthest from the basket to the player who operates closest to it.**

1. Point guard — furthest out, brings the ball up
2. Shooting guard — perimeter, primarily a scorer
3. Small forward — the middle, on the wing
4. Power forward — inside the arc, works the interior
5. Centre — closest to the rim

That single organising idea also explains the groupings you hear constantly: 1 and 2 are the **guards**, 3 and sometimes 2 and 4 are the **wings**, 4 and 5 are the **bigs**.

## The five, one at a time

### 1 — Point guard

The point guard's job is decision-making. They bring the ball up against pressure, organise the offence, choose which action the team runs, and are usually the last person to touch the ball before a shot goes up.

**Core skills:** ball-handling under pressure, court vision, passing accuracy and timing, decision speed.

**Typical build:** traditionally the smallest player on the floor, because the job rewards handling and agility over size.

**How the job goes wrong:** turnovers under pressure, and — more subtly — a point guard who dominates the ball so much that four teammates stand still.

### 2 — Shooting guard

The two is a perimeter scorer. Where the point guard creates opportunities, the shooting guard is usually the one converting them: coming off screens, spotting up, attacking a closeout.

**Core skills:** shooting from range, movement without the ball, finishing after the catch, and — often overlooked — defending the opponent's best perimeter scorer.

**Typical build:** taller than the point guard, still built for speed rather than strength.

**How the job goes wrong:** a two who only functions with the ball in their hands is doing the one job while occupying a slot designed for the other.

### 3 — Small forward

The three is the sport's generalist. The role sits between the perimeter and the interior and is usually asked to do a little of everything: score inside and out, defend multiple positions, rebound without being a primary rebounder.

**Core skills:** versatility above all, plus the physical range to guard both smaller and larger opponents.

**Typical build:** the balance point of the roster — big enough to hold up inside, quick enough to survive on the perimeter.

**How the job goes wrong:** a three with no defined strength ends up merely adequate at everything, which is different from being versatile.

### 4 — Power forward

The four works inside the arc. Rebounding on both ends, defending in the paint, setting screens, and scoring in the mid-range and around the rim.

**Core skills:** rebounding, physical strength, screening, interior finishing — and increasingly, shooting from range.

**Typical build:** large and strong, built for contact.

**How the job goes wrong:** a four who cannot function away from the basket shrinks the floor, because the defender guarding them has no reason to leave the paint.

### 5 — Centre

The five is the anchor. Defensively they protect the rim and are the last line when a drive gets past everyone else. Offensively they finish close to the basket, screen, and collect offensive rebounds.

**Core skills:** rim protection, positioning, rebounding, finishing in traffic.

**Typical build:** usually the tallest and longest player on the roster.

**How the job goes wrong:** a five who cannot move laterally becomes a target the moment the opposition forces them to defend away from the basket.

## The three groupings that actually organise a roster

If you take one structural idea away from this article, make it this one. Most modern thinking about lineups uses three bands rather than five slots:

- **Guards** — handle the ball, create advantages, initiate.
- **Wings** — score and defend across the perimeter and the space just inside it.
- **Bigs** — protect the rim, rebound, screen, finish inside.

The bands are useful because they describe what a lineup *needs* rather than what players are called. A five-player unit has to be able to bring the ball up against pressure, space the floor so the paint is not congested, and protect the rim. If a lineup cannot do all three, it does not matter what positions are listed next to the names.

## Positionless basketball, accurately described

The phrase gets used to mean "positions no longer exist", which is not what happened.

What happened is that the sport got better at recognising that these responsibilities can be distributed differently. A tall player who can handle the ball can initiate offence. A big who can shoot from range drags a rim protector away from the rim. A team can switch every screen if all five players can defend across a wide range of opponents.

The vocabulary followed: **combo guard** for a player between the one and the two, **point forward** for a forward who initiates, **stretch four** for a power forward who shoots from range, **small-ball five** for a team playing a forward at centre to gain speed at the cost of size.

Notice that every one of those terms is defined *by reference to the traditional positions*. That is the clearest evidence the framework has not been discarded. It has been demoted from an identity to a description — a shorthand for what a player is doing in a given possession rather than what they are.

There is also a genuine cost to the flexible approach, which usually goes unmentioned: a lineup where everyone can do a bit of everything can end up with nobody who does any one thing well enough to build around. Versatility is a strategy with trade-offs, not a free upgrade.

## Position, role and assignment are three different things

Worth separating, because they get conflated:

- **Position** is the label on the roster.
- **Role** is what the team asks this player to do — primary scorer, defensive stopper, floor spacer, connector.
- **Assignment** is who they are guarding on this possession, which can change several times within one trip down the floor.

A player can be listed at one position, occupy an entirely different role, and take assignments that match neither. When you hear that a team "plays two point guards", this is the distinction being described: two players whose *position* is the one, sharing a *role* usually held by a single player.

## What this means inside a career simulation

Position is the first decision in [Basketball Career Sim](/apps/pro-basketball-my-career-sim/), and it does more work than it appears to. You choose a position, then set name, height, weight, wingspan, age, jersey number and playing style, and pick the archetype and attributes you want to build on.

That combination is the reason the choice matters. A build only means something against a job. Length and lateral movement point in one direction; handling and vision point in another; the game then asks you to actually make those decisions during Live Sim possessions — shoot or move it on, lock down your matchup or call for help, play it safe or take the risk — with the court view showing score, stats, momentum and positioning as it resolves.

The career then runs through youth basketball, high school, recruiting and college, the draft and the pro years, with coach trust, team chemistry, reputation and the reactions of teammates, rivals, media and fans all responding to what you do. Position is the frame all of that happens inside.

If you are starting a first career, the practical advice is to pick the position whose *decisions* sound interesting rather than the one whose highlights do. You will spend the career making those choices repeatedly.

## What it means when you are building a roster instead

From the front-office side, positions stop being identities and become **coverage**. The question is not "do I have a small forward" but "can this lineup bring the ball up, space the floor and protect the rim". That is the subject of [how to build a balanced basketball roster](/blog/how-to-build-a-balanced-basketball-roster/), and it is the reason drafting five high-rated players at overlapping positions produces a worse team than drafting four and a specialist.

## Further reading

The roster-construction side is covered in [building a balanced basketball roster](/blog/how-to-build-a-balanced-basketball-roster/), and the drafting principles that sit underneath it are in [how fantasy draft strategy works](/blog/how-fantasy-draft-strategy-works/). For the career game specifically, see the [basketball career sim guide](/blog/basketball-career-sim-guide/); for the front-office game, the [basketball draft simulator guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/).

Both sit alongside the studio's other management titles in the [sports GM category](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Offline Arcade Games on Android: What "Offline" Actually Means, and How to Test It
metaTitle: Offline Arcade Games on Android: What to Check
secondaryKeywords: android games that work without internet
how to test if a game works offline
do free games need internet for ads
body:
The moment that makes people care about this is always the same. Underground, on a plane, in a hospital waiting room, somewhere in the countryside with one bar — you open the game you installed specifically for this, and it shows you a spinner.

The frustrating part is that the game itself does not need the network. Almost none of them do. What needs the network is the scaffolding around the game, and whether that scaffolding is polite about being unable to reach the internet is entirely down to how the developer wired it up.

## "Offline" is four claims, not one

People use the word to mean four different things, and a game can honestly satisfy some of them while failing others.

1. **It plays without a connection.** The core loop runs on your device with no round trip to a server.
2. **It ships with all its content.** Nothing is downloaded on demand — no level packs, no asset bundles fetched the first time you reach a new area.
3. **It needs no account.** You are not blocked at a sign-in wall before you can start.
4. **It does not sync.** Your progress lives on the device rather than in a profile that has to reconcile.

These are independent. A game can play perfectly offline and still refuse to start until it has verified a sign-in. Another can need no account at all and still stall the first time you reach a stage whose assets it never downloaded. When a store listing or a review says "works offline," find out which of the four is being claimed.

Notice too that the fourth one cuts both ways. A game that keeps everything on your device is the most reliably offline kind there is — and it also means an uninstall, or a new phone, takes your progress with it. That is a real trade, not a flaw.

## What actually reaches for the network in an arcade game

Six things, in rough order of how often they cause the problem.

**Ads.** An ad request is a network call. A well-built game treats a failed request as "no ad available" and continues immediately. A badly built one blocks on the request until it times out, which can be several seconds of nothing at exactly the moment you wanted to play. This single difference accounts for most of the "it says offline but it hangs" complaints about ad-supported games.

**Rewarded video specifically.** Any feature that trades watching an advert for an unlock genuinely cannot work without a connection, because there is nothing to show. This one is not a bug. It is a feature that is simply unavailable, and the honest design is to grey it out rather than let you tap it and fail.

**Leaderboards and achievements.** Games that use Google Play Games Services for scoreboards, achievements or saved games are talking to Google's servers, and that layer generally expects a signed-in player. Achievements can often be earned offline and pushed later, but the sign-in flow at launch is a common blocking point.

**Cloud save.** Same category, different consequence. If the game's authoritative save lives remotely, it has to decide what to do when it cannot read it, and the safe engineering answer — refuse to start rather than risk overwriting your progress with a stale local copy — is the one that ruins your flight.

**Remote configuration and live events.** Modern free-to-play games change events, offers and balance without shipping an update, which means fetching a config file at launch. If that fetch is on the critical path, no config means no game.

**Purchase verification and crash reporting.** Both need the network and neither should block start-up. Occasionally one does.

None of these six is the arcade game. All six are attached to it.

## The Play listing tells you less than you would like

There is no standard "works offline" field on Google Play. That is the root of the problem — the label most people want does not exist, so you are reading proxies.

What you *can* read:

- **Contains ads** and **In-app purchases** badges. These tell you two of the six network dependencies above are present. Ads in particular are worth noting: their presence does not mean the game fails offline, but it does mean there is a network call in the launch path somewhere.
- **The Data safety section.** Developers must declare what data the app collects and shares and how it is handled. A game that declares no collection at all is very unlikely to be phoning home during start-up. A game declaring account information and identifiers is doing something remote.
- **The developer's own description.** Plain text like "play offline" or "no internet required" is a statement the developer chose to make on a store listing, which makes it a more meaningful claim than silence.
- **Permissions.** The `INTERNET` permission is the one people fixate on, and it is close to meaningless as a positive signal — almost every app declares it, because almost every app shows an advert or reports a crash. It is useful only in reverse. An app that does not declare it cannot be reaching the network at all.

What you cannot read is the thing that matters: whether the developer put a network call on the critical path to the main menu. Nothing on the listing answers that.

## The airplane-mode test

Which is why the only reliable method is empirical. It takes about as long as making a cup of tea and it settles the question permanently.

1. **Install and launch once with a connection.** This is important. Many games download assets, fetch a config or complete first-run setup on the very first launch. Testing before that step tells you about installation, not about play.
2. **Play for a few minutes.** Get past the tutorial, start an actual run, let it finish. You want the game to have done whatever it does on a normal session.
3. **Force-stop it.** In Android settings, under Apps, find the game and force-stop it. Do not just background it — a warm start can reuse cached data and a resident process, which is exactly the state you are trying to avoid.
4. **Turn on airplane mode.** Wi-Fi off as well. You want a genuine no-network condition, not a slow one.
5. **Cold-launch the game and time the difference.** This is the whole test. Does it reach the main menu at roughly the same speed as before, or does it sit on a splash screen? A blocking network call announces itself as a pause of several seconds followed by either a resigned continue or an error.
6. **Start a run and finish it.** Then check whether anything you earned is still there after another force-stop.

Grade it on three things: does it start, does it play, and does it keep what you earned. A game that clears all three is offline in every way that matters to you on a train.

### What "failing gracefully" looks like

There is a meaningful quality difference between two games that both technically work offline.

The good one notices there is no network almost instantly, shows the menu, greys out anything that genuinely needs a connection, and never mentions it again. The mediocre one waits out a timeout on every screen transition, pops a dialogue asking you to check your connection, and offers you a rewarded-ad button that fails when you tap it.

Same offline capability. Completely different experience. This is worth checking because you will feel it every session, not just on the plane.

## Some arcade formats are naturally offline-friendly

Genre is a decent predictor before you install anything.

**Naturally self-contained:** run-based single-player games — score attack, wave survival, roguelike runs, endless modes. Everything the game needs to evaluate you happens locally, the run has a defined end, and there is no second player whose state has to be reconciled. This is one of the quiet advantages of the arcade format: it was designed for a cabinet with no network at all.

**Naturally network-bound:** anything with matchmaking, real-time or asynchronous multiplayer, timed live events, seasonal passes, a shared economy, or a marketplace. None of those can be authoritative on your device without inviting people to edit it.

**In between:** games with meta-progression that the developer wants backed up. The gameplay is local; the account is not.

If you are specifically shopping for something to play without signal, the arcade shelf is the right shelf. Its whole structure predates the assumption of connectivity.

## Our own two, stated plainly

We make two games in this category, and the honest description of them is narrower than the marketing sentence you were probably expecting.

[Space Shooter - Galaxy Arcade](/apps/space-shooter-classic-arcade/) is a wave-based shooter with four abilities, readable projectile patterns, an upgrade path fed by the rewards you earn during a run, and an Endless Mode with no finish line. It is free to download on Google Play, supported by ads, offers optional in-app purchases and carries an Everyone content rating. [Our guide to reading enemy fire](/blog/space-shooter-arcade-guide/) covers how to actually play it.

[Zombie Survival: Last Survivor](/apps/zombie-survival-last-survivor/) is a horde survival game where your weapons fire automatically and movement is the entire input, with mid-run level-ups that hand you an upgrade choice on the spot. It is free to download, supported by ads, has no in-app purchases at all, and carries an Everyone content rating. [The build guide](/blog/zombie-survival-roguelike-guide/) covers how the upgrade decisions work.

Neither listing describes multiplayer, matchmaking or online leaderboards, and both are structured as single-player runs whose progression comes out of the run itself. What we are deliberately *not* doing is telling you they are certified offline games, because that is not a claim our store listings make, and a claim about your specific device and Android version is not one we can make from here. Install one, run the airplane-mode test above, and hold us to the result. Both sit with the rest of our [Action & Arcade Games](/apps/category/action-arcade/).

The same reasoning applies to media rather than games, incidentally: a local video player is the other obvious thing to load up before a long journey, and [why a video file plays on one device and not another](/blog/android-video-player-guide/) is worth knowing before you find out mid-flight.

## The short version

There is no offline badge on Google Play, so stop looking for one. Read the ads and in-app purchase labels and the Data safety section to work out what the game is likely to be talking to, then settle it with a cold start in airplane mode after a normal first session.

The gameplay is almost never the problem. Ads, sign-in, cloud save and remote config are, and whether they are handled well is a craftsmanship question you can answer in one test.

title: Offline Sports Games on Android: How to Tell Which Ones Actually Work
metaTitle: Offline Sports Games on Android: What to Check
secondaryKeywords: sports games that work without wifi
how to test if an app works offline
body:
The moment you find out whether a game really works offline is almost always the worst possible moment: doors closed, phone in hand, several hours ahead of you, watching a spinner.

The frustrating part is that this is checkable in advance. It just is not checkable by reading the word "offline" in a store listing, because that word is doing at least four different jobs.

## Four things "offline" can mean

Android's own architecture guidance defines an offline-first app as one that can perform all — or a critical subset — of its core functionality without access to the internet. That "critical subset" is where all the ambiguity lives, and it produces a spectrum rather than a yes or no:

1. **Fully playable offline.** The entire loop runs locally. Nothing degrades.
2. **Playable but degraded.** The game runs, but something peripheral stops: a leaderboard, a cloud save, a daily reward, an ad-gated bonus.
3. **Playable after setup.** The first launch downloads assets or creates a profile. After that it is fine, but the very first run needs a connection.
4. **Not playable.** Live opponents, server-authoritative state, or a login on every launch.

Categories 2 and 3 are the ones that catch people out, because a game in either of them is honestly described as working offline and still fails at the moment you needed it.

## Why management and simulation games are the genre to look at

If you specifically want sport on a phone with no signal, you are far more likely to find it in the front office than on the pitch.

A draft, a roster decision and a simulated season are all **turn-based and self-contained**. There is no opponent whose input has to arrive, no clock that has to stay synchronised, and — critically — no live data feed. A simulator that produces a record from the roster you built needs a model and your inputs. Both can sit on the device.

Compare that with anything built around real-time competition, live sports data, or a shared persistent world. Those are not offline problems that developers have failed to solve; they are designs where the connection *is* the product.

This is a statement about what a genre makes possible, not a guarantee about any particular app. Plenty of management games are built server-side for entirely good reasons. But if you are scanning a category and want to know where to look first, turn-based simulation is the right place.

## What to read on the listing before you install

**Look for an explicit statement.** Developers who have built for offline play generally say so in the description, because it is a selling point. Absence of the claim is weak evidence, but presence of it is reasonably strong.

**Check whether an account is required.** An app that needs you to sign in has, by definition, something on a server. An app that starts playing the moment you open it does not necessarily keep everything local, but it is a much better sign.

**Read the Data safety section.** Every Play listing carries one. It is a standardised declaration of what the app collects, what it shares, how data is protected and whether you can request deletion. Google requires developers to complete it and makes them responsible for its accuracy. It will not tell you about offline capability directly, but it tells you how much of the app's life happens somewhere else — and an app that collects nothing has very little reason to phone home.

**Note whether it contains ads.** Ads are fetched over a network. That does not make an app online-only, but it does mean the no-connection behaviour is a specific thing the developer had to decide, and different developers decided differently.

**Ignore the download size.** A large app is not more offline-capable than a small one. Assets tell you nothing about where the game logic runs.

## The airplane-mode test

Two minutes, and it settles the question for good.

1. **Install and open once with a connection.** This lets any first-run download complete, so you are testing steady-state behaviour rather than setup.
2. **Turn on airplane mode.** Confirm Wi-Fi is genuinely off too — on many devices Wi-Fi can be re-enabled independently while airplane mode stays on, which quietly invalidates the test.
3. **Force-stop the app and reopen it.** Relaunching from cold is where login checks and asset fetches show up. An app that survives being backgrounded may still fail a cold start.
4. **Play a complete unit of the game.** Not thirty seconds — a whole draft, a whole match, a whole session including whatever screen normally shows an ad. Failures cluster at transitions.
5. **Check that progress persisted.** Reconnect, reopen, and confirm the offline session is still there. A game that plays offline and discards the result is worse than one that refused to start.

Do this on the ground, before the flight.

## The things that quietly need a connection

Even in a well-built local game, these are the usual suspects:

- **Ad delivery**, including rewarded ads attached to a bonus.
- **Purchase validation**, if you buy something while disconnected.
- **Cloud save and sync**, which usually queues and resolves later.
- **Leaderboards and achievements**, which need a server to compare against.
- **Daily or timed content**, if the game checks the date against a server rather than the device clock.
- **Remote configuration**, where the developer can adjust settings without an update.

None of these has to break the core loop. All of them can, if the app was not designed with a disconnected path.

## Where our own sports games stand

We should be exact here rather than convenient, because a vague claim is worse than no claim.

**[Basketball Career Sim](/apps/pro-basketball-my-career-sim/)** is the one we state plainly: it supports offline play, and no account is required to start a career. The design suits it — you create a player, work through youth basketball, high school, recruiting and college, the draft and the pro years, and the key possessions are resolved through Live Sim decisions on the device. Contracts, brand deals and lifestyle purchases all run on fictional in-game currency.

**[162-0 Baseball Draft & GM Team](/apps/baseball-draft-gm-team/)** has no online multiplayer and does not use live results. Every record it produces is a projection from the roster you drafted. That removes the two biggest structural reasons a sports game would need a server, though it is not itself a statement that every screen works disconnected.

**[20-0 Football Draft & GM Mode](/apps/football-draft-gm-mode/)** is built around drafting a roster position by position and handing it to a season simulator, with Franchise and GM Mode past draft day, plus VS Computer, Battle, Tournament, a Daily Challenge and Gridiron IQ. Its competitive modes are against the computer rather than a live human opponent.

All three are free to download, contain ads, and offer optional in-app purchases. Where a listing does not explicitly promise offline play, run the airplane-mode test above — on ours as readily as on anyone else's. We would rather you verified it than trusted a paragraph.

## What offline actually costs you

Worth saying, because "offline" is often treated as strictly better.

A game that keeps everything on your device also keeps your progress on your device. No cloud save means a lost or wiped phone takes the save with it. No account means no way to restore. That is a genuine trade, and it is the same trade in every locally-stored app: you gain independence from a server and you accept sole custody of your data.

There is also no live element by definition. If part of what you want from a sports game is a season that moves with the real calendar, a local simulator is not that and never will be. What it is instead is a model you can run at three in the morning with no signal, which is the whole point.

## Related reading

If you want to understand what a simulator is doing while you have no connection, [how sports simulation engines work](/blog/how-sports-simulation-engines-work/) covers the model behind the record. For the drafting side, [what makes a good draft board](/blog/what-makes-a-good-draft-board/) is the preparation half, and the [football draft simulator guide](/blog/football-draft-gm-guide/) walks through one game end to end. The career-mode alternative is covered in the [basketball career sim guide](/blog/basketball-career-sim-guide/).

Everything in the studio's management and simulation range is listed in the [sports GM category](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Sports Manager Games for Short Sessions: What Makes One Work on a Phone
metaTitle: Sports Manager Games for Phone: Short Session Guide
body:
The problem with playing a management game on a phone is not the screen. It is that you get interrupted, and most management games are built on the assumption that you will not be.

That assumption shows up in a specific way: the game's smallest unit of progress is larger than the window you actually have. You open it, spend four minutes loading context back into your head, make one decision, and put it away. Do that five times and you have played twenty minutes and achieved nothing you can point at.

This article is about which properties fix that. It is not a ranking, because "best" depends entirely on how long your windows are and what you enjoy deciding.

## The property that matters: a closed loop

A session feels worthwhile when it **ends with a verdict rather than a checkpoint.**

That is the whole thing. If you started something, finished it, and found out how it went, the session was complete regardless of whether it took three minutes or thirty. If you merely advanced a state, you have to remember where you were, and remembering is the tax that eventually stops you opening the app.

Draft-and-simulate is the shortest closed loop the genre has produced. You face a roster problem, make a sequence of decisions, hand the result to a simulator and receive a record. Problem, decision, verdict — with no season to administer in between.

## The three supporting properties

A closed loop is necessary and not sufficient. Three more things determine whether a game survives real life.

**Save-anywhere.** Can you stop mid-draft and come back? Games that only checkpoint at large boundaries force you to either finish or lose the thread. This is the single most common failure and the easiest to test.

**No real-time timers.** Energy meters, build timers and countdowns are session-schedulers: they decide when you play rather than letting you decide. In a genre whose appeal is deliberate decision-making, being told to come back in four hours is a poor fit.

**Legible decisions.** On a small screen you need to be able to compare two options without a spreadsheet. A game that shows you the two or three attributes that actually differ is a game you can play while standing up. Side-by-side comparison tools exist precisely for this.

## Matching a mode to the window you have

Different amounts of time suit genuinely different modes.

| You have | What fits | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A couple of minutes | A single decision — one possession, one comparison, one quiz | Complete in itself, no context to reload |
| Five to ten minutes | A no-refresh or limited draft | Fixed number of decisions, ends with a result |
| Fifteen to thirty minutes | An open draft, or a block of front-office work | Room to compare options or handle several tasks |
| An evening | Franchise or club management across seasons | The payoff needs continuity |

The important row is the second one, because it is the most common window and the one most management games serve worst. A limited draft is quicker than an open one not because there is less to do but because the *comparison* step is removed — you are deciding rather than searching.

## What to check before you commit to any manager game

These questions apply to any product in the genre, ours or anyone else's.

1. **How long from cold start to first result?** Time it once. If the answer is "I have not got one yet", the game is not built for your commute.
2. **Can you stop halfway through a task?** Try it deliberately. Back out mid-draft, close the app, reopen it.
3. **Is anything gated behind a real-time wait?** Look for energy, cooldowns or timed events before you invest.
4. **Can you compare two options without leaving the screen?** If every comparison needs three taps and a memory test, short sessions will be frustrating.
5. **What does it cost, and when does it start asking?** Free-to-install and free-to-play-properly are different claims.
6. **Where does your progress live?** Local saves mean nothing to log into and nothing to recover. [Sports GM games without internet](/blog/sports-gm-games-without-internet/) goes through this and the offline question properly.

## How the studio's sports titles are shaped

Not a league table — a description of session shape, so you can match one to your routine.

### Soccer: a draft that fits a gap, and a save that does not have to

[38-0 Football Draft XI Soccer](/apps/soccer-draft-gm-xi/) is explicit about running at two speeds. A draft and simulation fits comfortably into a short session, while club management and season progress are there when you want a longer save.

The short-session version is a complete loop: draft across every position on the pitch, weighing position fit and playing style rather than stacking ratings, then run the 38-game campaign and read the wins, draws and losses. Limited drafts and budget challenges shorten it further by constraining the search. The longer version — formations, squad depth, transfers, contracts, fitness and season progress — is the evening game, and quizzes, player guessing and daily challenges sit in between as single-decision filler. The [soccer draft XI guide](/blog/soccer-draft-xi-guide/) covers the squad-building side, and [formations explained](/blog/soccer-formations-explained/) covers the shape you are drafting into.

### Football: four rulesets, one clear verdict

[20-0 Football Draft & GM Mode](/apps/football-draft-gm-mode/) is built for sessions that end with a result. Unlimited, Limited with no refreshes, Salary Cap and Playoff Mode each change what a good pick looks like, so the same short loop poses a different question depending on which you pick. The Daily Challenge sets a target to hit, and Gridiron IQ tests how well you read a team sheet — both single-sitting things. Franchise Mode and GM Mode are the longer game behind them.

### Hockey: the smallest roster in the genre

[84-0 Hockey Draft & GM Manager](/apps/hockey-draft-gm-manager/) asks for six slots and a coach, which makes it the fastest draft here by decision count. Limited Draft gives you one pass with zero refreshes; Unlimited lets you keep searching. Either way the session ends with a projected 84-game record. Franchise GM Mode extends it across seasons for anyone who wants the longer version.

### Baseball: depth in small pieces

162-0 Baseball Draft & GM Team is stat-led — pitchers and hitters compared on ERA, WHIP, home runs, on-base ability, fielding, speed and WAR — which sounds like the least phone-friendly option and is not, because the comparisons are explicit rather than hidden. The ten-pick Limited Refresh Draft with no rerolls is a tightly bounded session, and Baseball IQ and the Daily Challenge are single sittings. Franchise GM Mode handles the batting order, rotation, bullpen and payroll when you have longer.

### Basketball: two different shapes

Basketball Draft GM Franchise carries eight draft formats, and two of them exist specifically for short play — Quick Draft and Blind Draft — alongside Unlimited, Franchise and Salary Cap drafting, VS Computer, Battle Mode and a Daily Challenge, with a full 82-game season behind them.

Basketball Career Sim goes the other way and produces the shortest unit in the whole catalogue: Live Sim hands you a single possession and asks what your player does. One decision is a complete interaction. It also supports offline play and needs no account, which makes it the least demanding of a bad connection.

### Combat sports: brackets and single bouts

40-0 MMA & Boxing Fight Draft offers Unlimited Fight Draft, Limited Draft, Tournament, VS Computer, Draft Battle Royale and single-sport MMA and boxing drafts. The single-sport drafts are the quickest entry point, and the Fighter Explorer, comparisons, quizzes and daily challenges are all one-sitting items. It is free with no in-app purchases at all.

## Habits that make a five-minute session worth something

Short play can be shallow or it can compound. Three habits decide which.

**Change one thing per run.** If you alter three decisions and the record moves, you have learned nothing. Alter one and you have learned something small and real.

**Name the pick you would take back.** Before you start the next draft, say which single decision the result is disagreeing with. This is the difference between playing a lot and getting better at it.

**Use the constrained formats deliberately.** No-refresh and budgeted drafts are not harder versions of open ones — they are a different exercise, testing judgement rather than search. They also happen to be shorter, which is a convenient coincidence.

## What the simulators are and are not doing

Every record these games return is produced by internal rules acting on players the game generated.

They are scoring roster construction, not reproducing sport. Nothing in a result describes, forecasts or relates to any real league, club, team or athlete, and none of it is a prediction or guidance of any kind. The perfect records the games are named for are deliberately hard to reach rather than the expected outcome of competent play, and no approach guarantees one.

That is what makes the short loop worth repeating. The only meaningful comparison is against your own previous attempts, and a five-minute session is enough to run exactly one of those.

## Where to read next

If connection rather than time is your constraint, [sports GM games without internet](/blog/sports-gm-games-without-internet/) covers what offline actually means and how to test it. If you are still deciding what kind of sports game you want, [career mode versus franchise mode](/blog/career-mode-vs-franchise-mode/) sets out the two shapes and who each suits.

Every drafting and management title the studio makes is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/), and the rest of the writing on them is under [sports and GM articles](/blog/category/sports-gm/).

title: How Boxing Scoring Works: The 10-Point Must System, Round by Round
metaTitle: How Boxing Scoring Works: The 10-Point Must System
secondaryKeywords: what is a 10-8 round in boxing

sources.p: Association of Boxing Commissions and Combative Sports
Association of Boxing Commissions and Combative Sports
Association of Boxing Commissions and Combative Sports

body:
Three people watch the same twelve rounds and hand in three different scorecards. To most viewers that looks like incompetence. It is not — it is a direct consequence of how the scoring system is designed, and once you know what judges are actually being asked to do, the disagreements become predictable rather than mysterious.

The system is public. The Association of Boxing Commissions and Combative Sports publishes the unified rules and a manual for judges, and state regulators adopt them; Nevada's administrative code for unarmed combat contains provisions on the method of judging a contest. None of what follows is inside knowledge.

## The system in one paragraph

Under the unified rules, a bout is evaluated and scored by three judges, and the **10 Point Must System** is the standard method. The winner of a round *must* be awarded 10 points, and the loser gets nine or fewer. An even round is scored 10-10 and is treated as rare.

That word "must" is the part people misread. It does not mean the winner must be obvious. It means the arithmetic is anchored: the judge is never deciding whether to give the round winner 10, only how far below 10 the other boxer falls.

## What separates a 10-9 from a 10-8

The ABC's judge manual sets out a rule of thumb for each score.

| Score | When it applies |
| --- | --- |
| 10-9 | One boxer routinely won the round |
| 10-8 | One knockdown, or one boxer wins the round in an extremely decisive manner including hurting their opponent |
| 10-7 | Two knockdowns, or one boxer clearly dominates and has knocked their opponent down at least once |
| 10-6 | More than two knockdowns, and the score can go lower if more occur |
| 10-10 | The round ends with no clear winner — should rarely happen |

Two details in that table matter more than they look.

**A 10-8 does not require a knockdown.** A round can reach 10-8 on dominance alone, and the manual is specific that this is particularly true where one boxer has done nothing offensively — running, or simply surviving in a defensive posture for the whole round.

**A 10-7 essentially does require one.** The guidance says that to reach that score you should always have at least one knockdown. It is available with a single knockdown if the boxer who scored it also wins the balance of the round decisively and dominantly and hurts their opponent.

### The knockdown is not the whole round

This is the single most misunderstood point in boxing scoring, and the manual addresses it head on.

If Boxer A scores a knockdown, the round should normally be 10-8 for A. But if Boxer B decisively and dominantly wins the rest of the round and actually hurts A while doing it, the round may be scored 10-9 for A. Scoring that situation 10-10 is described as not advisable.

The instruction underneath is blunt: do not assume a knockdown gives an automatic 10-8, especially if it happens early in the round — you still have to score the entire round. And a landed punch, including a knockdown, counts the same whenever in the round it occurs.

## The four factors

Judges are directed to weigh four things.

**Clean and effective punching.** The manual's framing is that fights are won by clean, effective punches landing, and that not all punches are equal — the effect of the punch matters, hard punches count, and so does the number of them. There is no formula that converts one into the other, and judges are told to be fair to both. They are also warned not to concentrate on head shots and forget effective body work.

Where a punch lands matters too. Punches landing directly on the arms are generally not scoring punches unless they are high up, near or on the front of the shoulders — which is worth knowing before you are certain a boxer "landed" a flurry against a high guard.

**Effective aggressiveness.** The boxer taking the fight to their opponent and getting positive results from it. The qualifier is doing real work: if the aggressive boxer is being beaten to the punch by a counterpuncher, that is *not* effective aggressiveness. Moving forward is not the same as winning.

**Ring generalship, or ring control.** The thinking boxer — the one controlling the action, using feints, slips and footwork to keep an opponent off balance and to put themselves in position to score without being scored upon. The manual states plainly that running and simply avoiding action should not be rewarded.

**Defence.** Punching while not being punched: slipping, countering, working off the ropes. Again with a qualifier — good defence is not holding or clinching to avoid contact.

The order is not decorative. Clean and effective punching is the primary consideration, and the later factors do most of their work in rounds where the punching is close.

## Independence, and why cards diverge

Each round is scored on its own merits. The manual is explicit: do not let actions in a previous round affect your score in a later one. A six-round bout produces six independent judgements.

That design has a consequence people find counter-intuitive. **A boxer cannot bank a lead.** Winning a round overwhelmingly is worth the same as winning it narrowly unless the margin was large enough to reach 10-8. A fighter who wins three rounds by a street and loses four narrowly is behind.

It also explains the divergent cards. In a genuinely close round, two judges applying the same four factors in good faith can favour different boxers — one weighing a countering, defensive performance, the other weighing forward pressure that mostly landed. Neither is cheating. The manual even warns against the opposite temptation: do not award rounds simply to make your scorecard look closer.

### The arithmetic of a shutout

If one boxer wins every round 10-9 with no knockdowns, the totals are just multiplication. Twelve rounds at 10 points is 120; twelve rounds at 9 points is 108. That is where the familiar championship shutout card of **120-108** comes from, and the judge manual uses exactly that figure as its illustration — noting that if one fighter wins every round by the slimmest of margins, this is the card you should hand in.

## Beyond the rounds: knockdowns, fouls and partial rounds

A few unified-rules provisions shape scoring at the edges.

- The **mandatory eight count** after a knockdown is standard procedure in all bouts, and a boxer who has been knocked down cannot be saved by the bell in any round.
- **Point deductions for intentional fouls are mandatory.** Where an intentional foul causes an injury and the bout is allowed to continue, the referee notifies the authorities and deducts two points from the boxer who caused it. Where an intentional foul causes an injury severe enough to terminate the bout immediately, the boxer who caused it loses by disqualification.
- **Partial rounds are scored** if four rounds or more have been completed — which is why judges are advised to keep a running score in mind at all times, so that an early stoppage does not leave them guessing.

Point deductions land on the final tally after the rounds are added, which is how a boxer can win more rounds than their opponent and still not win the bout.

## How three cards become one result

Each judge's card is totalled separately, and the result describes how those three totals agree:

- **Unanimous** — all three judges scored for the same boxer.
- **Split** — two judges scored for one boxer, one for the other.
- **Majority** — two judges scored for one boxer and one scored the bout even.
- **Draw** — depending on how the three cards fall, a bout can be drawn unanimously, by majority, or by three differing cards that total to a draw.

Nothing about this system is a measurement in the way a stopwatch is. It is three trained people applying published criteria to a fast, ambiguous event, and the unified rules are an attempt to make their disagreements narrow and explicable rather than to eliminate them.

## Scoring inside a simulation

[40-0 MMA & Boxing Fight Draft](/apps/mma-boxing-fight-draft/) simulates boxing separately from mixed martial arts, and the difference is precisely the scorecard. The MMA simulator resolves bouts by knockout, technical knockout, submission or decision; the boxing simulator adds draws and judges' scorecards, and weighs hand speed, power, defence, footwork and ring control.

That attribute list maps onto the four factors reasonably closely, which is why the boxing side of the game rewards a different kind of drafting. Style advantages shape results — a stylistic edge can outweigh a ratings edge, so the higher-rated fighter does not always get the nod. Anyone who wants only this half of the game can use the Boxing Only Draft rather than mixing both pools.

### What the model is doing

The simulator applies the game's own internal rules to fighters the game generated. It is not reproducing judging, it is not describing any real bout, athlete or promotion, and nothing it produces is a prediction, a forecast or guidance of any kind. It is a scoring model for a drafting puzzle.

The honest framing of a decision loss in the game is the same as the honest framing of a close card in reality: a result produced by criteria applied to an ambiguous contest, where reasonable models disagree. That the game can return a draw at all is a sign it is modelling the right thing.

## Where to read next

The companion article is [MMA weight classes explained](/blog/mma-weight-classes-explained/), which covers the unified-rules division table and how catch weight works. For the drafting side of combat sports, see the [MMA and boxing fight draft guide](/blog/mma-boxing-fight-draft-guide/), and for how running a stable differs from following one competitor, see [career mode versus franchise mode](/blog/career-mode-vs-franchise-mode/).

Everything the studio makes in this genre is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Bullet Hell vs Classic Shmup: Two Genres That Look Identical and Test Opposite Skills
metaTitle: Bullet Hell vs Classic Shmup: What Changed

sources.p: The Strong National Museum of Play

body:
Put a screenshot of a classic arcade shooter next to a screenshot of a danmaku game and the second one looks like the first one turned up. More bullets, more colours, more chaos. The obvious conclusion is that bullet hell is the hard version.

It is not. It is a different game wearing the same clothes, and the thing that separates them is not on the screen at all — it is the size of the part of your ship that can be hit.

## The hitbox is the whole argument

In a classic shoot 'em up, the vulnerable area is roughly the ship you can see. Clip a bullet with a wingtip and you die. That places a hard ceiling on how many projectiles the designer can put in front of you, because a large target needs a large gap, and large gaps need a sparse screen.

In danmaku, the vulnerable area is a small point near the ship's centre — often a few pixels across, and frequently drawn on screen so you can see exactly where it is. Everything else is decoration that bullets pass straight through.

Change that one number and the entire design space changes with it:

| | Classic shmup | Bullet hell (danmaku) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vulnerable area | The visible ship | A point near its centre |
| Bullets on screen | Few | Many |
| Bullet speed | Fast | Usually slower |
| Gap width | Ship-sized | Point-sized |
| Time to decide | Fractions of a second | Longer, but with more to process |
| Core skill | Reaction | Route planning |

Read that table as cause and effect rather than as two lists. Slow bullets exist in danmaku *because* small gaps are usable; small gaps are usable *because* the hitbox is a point; the hitbox is a point *because* the designer wanted hundreds of bullets. Pull on any one of them and the rest come with it.

## Density is information, not difficulty

Here is the part that surprises people who have only watched the genre rather than played it.

Four fast bullets fired directly at your current position are, moment for moment, harder than a hundred slow ones in a rotating spiral. The four give you almost no time and almost no information — they arrive at the speed of your reflexes and there is nothing to read. The hundred are moving slowly enough that the shape of the pattern is visible while it develops, the gaps are geometric and repeatable, and you can decide where you intend to be two seconds from now.

Density is closer to a legibility tool than a cruelty tool. A dense pattern makes its own structure obvious. That is why experienced players describe danmaku screens as calm, and why a beginner watching the same screen sees noise: the structure is there, and reading it is the skill being taught.

Classic shooters do the opposite. They take away information deliberately. A sparse screen of fast, aimed shots gives you nothing to plan with, so you are being tested on how quickly you can respond to something you did not see coming.

## The two techniques that do not transfer

Because the tests are different, the techniques are different, and each one is close to useless in the other subgenre.

### Streaming (danmaku)

Most danmaku enemies fire *aimed* shots — projectiles launched at wherever you were standing at the moment of firing. If you sit still, they converge on you. If you sprint across the screen, they spread out into a wall.

The answer is to move in a steady sequence of small steps in one direction. Each shot is aimed at where you just were, so they gather into a trailing line behind you rather than a spread around you. You travel slowly across the screen, dragging a stream of dead bullets, and when you run out of room you make a single sharp turn through the gap the stream created.

Streaming is patient, unglamorous and the single highest-value habit in the subgenre. It also does very little in a classic shooter, where projectiles are fast enough that they have already arrived by the time a stream would have formed.

### Micro-adjustment under time pressure (classic)

Classic shooters reward a completely different motor habit: staying loose, keeping your ship in open space, and making a single small correction the instant something changes. There is rarely a route to plan, because the threat resolves faster than planning takes. What matters is that you were not already committed to a movement when it appeared.

Players who come to a classic shooter from danmaku tend to over-plan and get hit while executing a route that was already invalid. Players who go the other way tend to twitch, and twitching in a dense field means crossing bullets you had already avoided.

## Macro-dodging and micro-dodging

There is a useful vocabulary here that applies to both subgenres and gets used mostly in danmaku circles.

**Macro-dodging** is choosing which region of the screen to be in before a pattern develops — reading a boss's wind-up and moving to the half of the arena the attack will not cover. It is decided seconds ahead and it is where most of the survival comes from.

**Micro-dodging** is the small corrections inside a pattern once you are already committed to a region. It is what everyone thinks the genre is, and it is the less important of the two.

The general rule is that a player who dies during micro-dodging usually made the mistake during macro-dodging. Being in a bad third of the screen when a pattern starts cannot be fixed by good hands afterwards. This is exactly the lesson [our guide to reading enemy fire](/blog/space-shooter-arcade-guide/) works through in practical terms, and it is the one that carries across every version of the genre.

## Resources: the other structural difference

Classic shooters generally treat your life bar as the resource. You have some number of chances, and a mistake costs one.

Danmaku typically adds a second, spendable resource — a screen-clearing panic option that also usually cancels the bullets currently in flight. The presence of that option restructures the whole risk calculation, because a mistake is no longer necessarily fatal; it is expensive. Play then becomes a question of whether the current situation is worth the spend, which is a decision the classic subgenre mostly does not offer.

There is a well-documented psychological trap attached to any charged resource: you save it for a moment worthy of it, and the moment that finally qualifies is the one that already killed you. Whatever a given game calls its defensive option, it is worth nothing while it sits unused.

[Space Shooter - Galaxy Arcade](/apps/space-shooter-classic-arcade/) puts four distinct answers on the screen rather than one — FIRE for the main weapons, ALT for a secondary attack, a charged Ultimate, and a Shield that protects you while it holds. That structure sits closer to the classic side of the divide in feel, with the modern habit of making resource timing an explicit skill rather than an afterthought.

## Scoring: where both subgenres get strange

Once a player can survive a game reliably, the game stops being about survival, and both traditions responded by building an optional second game on top.

Chain scoring — destroying enemies in quick enough succession to hold a multiplier — is the common form. Its important property is that the safe route through a wave and the high-scoring route through it are deliberately different, so players set their own difficulty by choosing how greedy to be.

Some designs pushed this into the pattern itself. Ikaruga, released by Treasure in 2001, gives the player a ship that switches between two polarities: it absorbs bullets of its own colour, does extra damage to the opposite one, and scores by destroying enemies in same-colour groups of three. The bullets are simultaneously the threat and the ammunition, and a screen full of them can be a resource rather than a problem depending on which polarity you are currently in.

Danmaku added grazing, which awards score for passing close to a bullet without touching it. That is only possible because the hitbox is a point — with a ship-sized hitbox there is no meaningful gap between "near" and "hit". It is the clearest illustration of how one design decision propagates through everything.

## So which should you play?

The honest framing is that neither is the advanced version of the other, so pick by what you want the game to demand.

**Choose classic if** you want short decisions, immediate feedback, and a game you can play badly and still enjoy. It is more forgiving of divided attention, which matters on a phone.

**Choose danmaku if** you like the idea of a screen you learn to read like a map, and you are willing to spend the first several hours being genuinely bad at it. The payoff is a specific and unusual feeling — calm inside something that looks like chaos — and nothing else in games produces it in quite the same way.

**Choose either if** what you actually want is patterns that reward learning. That property is not owned by a subgenre. It comes from three things: a pattern telegraphs before it arrives, it behaves the same way every time, and a survivable route existed before the shot was fired. A game with those three is worth your time at any density.

Our own take keeps the readable-pattern contract and the arcade run length. Enemy models move and attack in their own ways, bosses ask you to learn a rotation rather than out-gun it, and Endless Mode strips out the finish line so the only measure left is how long your positioning holds. It is free to download on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases and an Everyone content rating, and it sits with the rest of our [Action & Arcade Games](/apps/category/action-arcade/). If you would rather have positioning without any aiming at all, [Zombie Survival: Last Survivor](/apps/zombie-survival-last-survivor/) removes the firing input entirely and makes movement the only thing you control.

The games named in this article belong to the companies that made them. Reign Creative LLC is an independent studio with no connection to any of them.

## The short version

The subgenres differ by one number, and that number is how much of your ship can be hit. Everything visible on the screen — bullet count, bullet speed, gap width, how long you have to think — is downstream of it.

Classic shooters take information away from you and test how fast you respond. Danmaku gives you more information than you can process at once and tests how well you read it. Both are about where you are standing. They just disagree about how long you get to decide.

title: Cantonese Tones Explained: Six Tones, One Structure, and How to Practise Them
metaTitle: Cantonese Tones Explained: A Practical Guide
secondaryKeywords: how many tones does cantonese have

sources.p: The Linguistic Society of Hong Kong
U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Most explanations of Cantonese tones hand you a numbered list of six pitch descriptions and leave you to it. The list is accurate and almost useless, because it presents six independent facts to memorise when what is actually there is one small structure with six positions in it.

Learn the structure and the list stops being a list.

## What tone is doing

In English, pitch belongs to the sentence. You raise your voice at the end of a question, you drop it at the end of a statement, and you can say the word "cat" on any pitch you like without it becoming a different animal.

In Cantonese, pitch belongs to the word. The same string of consonants and vowels said on a different pitch pattern is a different word — not an emphasised version of the same one, not a regional accent, a different entry in the dictionary. Tone is a property of the word in exactly the way the vowel is.

That has one immediate consequence for how you study: **you cannot learn vocabulary now and add tones later.** A word stored without its tone is stored wrong, and the correction is harder than the original learning would have been.

## The six tones, as a structure

Jyutping numbers the tones 1 to 6 and writes the number after the syllable: *si1*, *si2*, *si3*. Here is the usual description.

| Jyutping | Usual description |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | high level |
| 2 | rising |
| 3 | mid level |
| 4 | low falling |
| 5 | low rising |
| 6 | low level |

Now the part that makes it memorable. Those six are not six unrelated shapes. They are:

- **Three level tones at three heights** — 1 high, 3 mid, 6 low. Same flat shape, stacked.
- **Two rising tones** — 2 and 5. Same rising shape, starting from different heights.
- **One low falling tone** — 4, the lowest thing in the system, often described as creaky in ordinary speech.

Six tones, three shapes. Once you hear the system that way, "which tone was that?" becomes two smaller questions — *what shape* and *how high* — and both are easier to answer than the original.

A caution that belongs here rather than in a footnote: descriptions differ between references. Some transcribe tone 1 as high falling for certain speakers or in certain positions, and exact pitch heights vary by region, by individual and by how carefully someone is speaking. Some linguistic descriptions use Chao's five-point pitch scale to write these values numerically. Treat any tone table, including this one, as a map rather than a measurement.

### Tone is relative, which is why perfect pitch is beside the point

The single most discouraging myth about tonal languages is that you need a musical ear.

Cantonese tone is defined relative to the speaker's own range. A child, a woman with a high voice and a man with a low one all produce recognisable tone 1 at completely different absolute frequencies. What identifies the tone is where it sits *within that speaker's range* and what shape it traces.

So you are not learning notes. You are learning a small set of patterns that get rescaled to whoever is talking — which is a normal perceptual skill, not a talent.

## The classic demonstration

The standard teaching example is the syllable *si*, which supports all six tones with six unrelated meanings:

| Jyutping | Character | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| si1 | 詩 | poem |
| si2 | 史 | history |
| si3 | 試 | to try, to test |
| si4 | 時 | time |
| si5 | 市 | market, city |
| si6 | 是 | to be |

One note on the last row: 是 is the formal and written word. In spoken Cantonese, "to be" is 係 (*hai6*) — same tone, different word — and you will meet 是 mostly when reading Standard Written Chinese aloud. That distinction between spoken and written registers is one of the things beginners meet earlier than they expect, and it is covered in our [beginner's guide to Cantonese](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/).

The set is not a party trick. It is the proof that tone is lexical: nothing else about these six syllables differs.

## Why some sources say nine

You will see Cantonese described as having nine tones, and the disagreement is not about the facts.

Cantonese syllables can end in **-p, -t or -k**. Those endings stop the syllable short — the vowel is cut off rather than allowed to run. An older analytical tradition, inherited from classical Chinese phonology, counts these "entering tone" syllables as their own category, and since they occur at three pitch levels, that adds three to the count. Six plus three is nine.

Modern descriptions do not add them, because the three pitch levels involved are the ones already used by tones 1, 3 and 6. Nothing new is being distinguished. Jyutping therefore writes checked syllables with the same numbers:

- 一 (*jat1*) — "one", checked, at the tone 1 level
- 百 (*baak3*) — "hundred", checked, at the tone 3 level
- 十 (*sap6*) — "ten", checked, at the tone 6 level

Six and nine are two ways of counting one system. If a course teaches you nine, you are not being misled; you are being taught with older terminology.

Checked syllables are worth practising deliberately for a different reason: they are short. There is less time for the pitch to be audible, so the contrast has to be caught quickly. A useful minimal pair here is 識 (*sik1*, "to know") against 食 (*sik6*, "to eat") — identical apart from tone, both cut off by the same final consonant, and both extremely common.

## The contrasts that actually cause errors

Not all fifteen possible pairs are equally hard. Practice time is better spent on the three that generate most beginner mistakes.
