**Tone 2 against tone 5.** Both rise. The difference is where the rise starts and finishes, not the shape. This is comfortably the hardest pair for most learners, and it matters because tone 5 carries a large share of the most common words in the language — 我 (*ngo5*, "I"), 你 (*nei5*, "you"), 佢 (*keoi5*, "he/she") are all tone 5.

**Tone 3 against tone 6.** Both level. The difference is purely height, with no shape cue to fall back on. Height differences are harder to judge than shape differences, especially across speakers.

**Tone 4 against tone 6.** Both low. Tone 4 falls and tone 6 stays flat, but at the bottom of a speaker's range the difference is small and often blurred by creak.

By contrast, **tone 1** is usually the easiest tone to identify, because it sits clearly above everything else in the system. If you can reliably hear tone 1 versus everything, you have already solved a fifth of the problem.

The practical instruction is unglamorous: drill the confusable pairs, not the whole set. Six-way identification exercises spread your attention evenly across contrasts you have already mastered and contrasts you have not.

## One complication worth knowing about early

Cantonese has a phenomenon usually called **changed tone**, where a syllable in certain words and certain contexts is pronounced with a different pitch from its dictionary tone — commonly a rising one. It turns up in familiar or derived vocabulary, in some compounds, and in some ways of naming people and things.

There is no simple rule you can apply on sight, and it is not a mistake or sloppiness. The honest advice for a beginner is: learn that it exists so you are not confused when a word you know comes out differently, and learn the individual cases as vocabulary rather than trying to derive them. A course that flags these words as they arrive saves you the experience of concluding your ear is broken.

## How to practise tone without a teacher in the room

Five things that work, in the order they pay off.

**Learn tone with the word, always.** Never write down a Cantonese word without its Jyutping number. A vocabulary list of bare syllables is a list of words you will have to relearn.

**Drill in pairs, not in sets of six.** Take one confusable pair — 2 and 5, say — and work only on that until identification is fast. Then take the next pair. Six-way drills feel more advanced and teach less.

**Separate perception from production.** These are two skills and they improve at different rates. Being able to hear that two recordings differ does not mean you can produce the difference, and being told your production is wrong does not tell you what to change. Work on identification first; it is the one you can verify alone.

**Record yourself and leave a gap.** Listening back immediately, you hear what you intended. Listening back the next day, you hear what you said. That delay is doing real work.

**Use the words in sentences early.** Tone in isolation is a laboratory exercise. Tone at conversational speed, inside a phrase, with your attention on meaning rather than pitch, is the actual skill — and it is noticeably harder than the isolated version, which is why doing only isolated drills produces a plateau.

[Learn Cantonese for Beginners](/apps/learn-cantonese/) is sequenced around the first two of those. Initials, finals and syllables come first, then tone contrasts, before conversation starts, so pronunciation is a foundation rather than a later correction. Where your device provides a Cantonese voice the app uses it and falls back clearly when it does not. Review modes — Daily Review, Speed Run Review, Mistake Rescue, Listening Blitz and Dictation Mode among them — pull from material you have already covered, and a missed-questions list collects what you keep getting wrong, which is exactly where a confusable tone pair ends up.

Two limits stated plainly. No app can hear you the way a fluent speaker can, so it cannot tell you which of six tones you actually produced. And recognising a contrast in a quiet room is easier than producing one mid-sentence, which is easier than either in a noisy restaurant. This is foundation work, not a substitute for a teacher or a conversation partner.

## Is this the hardest part of Cantonese?

It is the part that frightens people most, which is not the same thing.

The US Foreign Service Institute places Cantonese in **Category IV**, its hardest group, at **88 weeks of full-time instruction (2,200 class hours)** for its own students — a figure that describes intensive classroom training for diplomats, not app study, and that covers the whole language rather than its tone system. Tone is one component of that, and it is a component with an unusual property: it front-loads.

Tones are hardest in weeks one to eight, when every word is new and nothing is automatic. They get quietly easier after that, not because your ear improves dramatically but because context starts doing more of the work and because the words you use most often become fixed. The learners who struggle longest are usually the ones who postponed tone in month one and are now carrying a few hundred words that need repairing.

Which is the entire argument for doing this first. Tones are not the hard part of Cantonese if you learn them with the vocabulary. They become the hard part if you do not.

If you are weighing Cantonese against other tonal languages before committing, [the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) takes a completely different approach — five tones that are calculated from spelling rather than memorised per word — and the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) include options with no tones at all.

title: Cantonese vs Mandarin: The Differences That Actually Change Your Study Plan
metaTitle: Cantonese vs Mandarin: The Differences That Matter
secondaryKeywords: is cantonese a dialect of mandarin
should i learn cantonese or mandarin

sources.p: The Linguistic Society of Hong Kong
U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
The question people usually ask is "which one should I learn". The question that determines whether you waste six months is "how much of one gets me the other", and the answer is: much less than the shared writing system makes it look.

Both are varieties within the Chinese language family. Neither descends from the other. In conversation they are not mutually intelligible — a monolingual speaker of one does not follow the other. Everything below is an attempt to say precisely where the difference sits, because "they're different languages" is true and not actionable.

## Sound: the part with no useful overlap

If you take away one thing, take this. The two languages do not share a syllable inventory, a tone system, or a set of possible word endings. Nothing about Mandarin pronunciation carries across.

### Different tone systems, not different tone counts

Mandarin is normally described as having four tones plus a neutral tone. Cantonese is normally described with six contrasting tones, which Jyutping numbers 1 to 6.

It is tempting to read that as "Cantonese has two more", as though the four Mandarin tones sit inside the Cantonese six. They do not. The pitch shapes are defined differently, the contrasts a learner has to hear are different, and there is no mapping from one to the other.

The two systems also behave differently in connected speech. Mandarin has a well-known rule where two consecutive third-tone syllables shift, so 你好 (*nǐ hǎo*) is not said with two identical falling-rising tones. Cantonese has its own tone-change behaviour, which works on different principles and has to be learned as part of the words it affects.

The Cantonese six are worth meeting properly rather than in passing; our [beginner's guide to Cantonese](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/) sets them out alongside the "nine tones" figure you will also see quoted.

### Cantonese kept endings Mandarin lost

This is the difference that surprises people who assumed the two were close.

Cantonese syllables can end in **-p, -t, -k, -m, -n or -ng**. Mandarin syllables can end in **-n or -ng** and nothing else, aside from the *r* suffix common in northern speech.

That is not a small phonetic footnote. It means a large number of Cantonese syllables have no Mandarin equivalent at all, and it is why Cantonese poetry rhymes in places Mandarin does not. It also means the very common Cantonese word 唔 (*m4*, "not") is a syllable made entirely of a nasal consonant, with no vowel — a shape Mandarin does not use.

Running the other way, Mandarin has a set of retroflex initials — the sounds written **zh, ch, sh** and **r** in Pinyin — that Cantonese does not have. Each language has sounds the other simply lacks.

## Two romanisations, and you cannot swap them

**Pinyin** is a Mandarin romanisation. It was designed for Mandarin sounds and it encodes Mandarin tones with diacritics: *nǐ*, *hǎo*, *shì*. Applied to Cantonese, it is not inaccurate so much as inapplicable — there is no Pinyin spelling for a syllable ending in -p, and no Pinyin tone mark for Cantonese tone 5.

**Jyutping** is a Cantonese romanisation published by the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong. It writes tone as a digit after the syllable: *nei5*, *hou2*, *hai6*. That makes it typeable on any keyboard and unambiguous to read aloud.

The clearest way to see the gap is a word both languages write identically. 你好 is "hello" in both, with the same two characters:

| | Written | Romanised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mandarin | 你好 | nǐ hǎo |
| Cantonese | 你好 | nei5 hou2 |

Same page, different language. This is exactly why a Cantonese course has to be built as a Cantonese course rather than adapted from Mandarin material, and it is the design premise behind [Learn Cantonese for Beginners](/apps/learn-cantonese/), which teaches traditional characters and Jyutping together from the first lesson.

One more romanisation note, because it causes real confusion in libraries and catalogues: the Library of Congress ALA-LC tables exist to transliterate Chinese consistently for cataloguing, not to be pronounced from. If you meet a romanised name that matches neither Pinyin nor Jyutping, that is often what you are looking at.

## The same characters, in two different situations

Here the languages genuinely do overlap — and the overlap is more complicated than "they share a script".

### Traditional and simplified are about place, not about language

Character standards follow jurisdictions rather than spoken varieties. Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan use **traditional** characters. Mainland China uses **simplified** characters, and that includes Guangdong province, where Cantonese is widely spoken.

So there is no such thing as "the Cantonese character set". A Cantonese speaker in Hong Kong reads traditional; a Cantonese speaker in Guangzhou reads simplified. The Unicode Standard encodes both, which is why your phone renders either without being told which language it is looking at.

For a learner the decision is practical: pick the set that matches where you intend to use the language. Learn Cantonese for Beginners teaches traditional characters, which matches Hong Kong and Macau usage.

### Written Cantonese is a third thing

Most formal writing in Hong Kong — newspapers, contracts, textbooks, government notices — is **Standard Written Chinese**, whose grammar and vocabulary are closer to Mandarin. A Cantonese speaker reads it aloud using Cantonese pronunciations, which means the sentence on the page is not the sentence they would have said.

**Written Cantonese** is the other register: spoken Cantonese committed to the page, used in messaging, social media, advertising, comics and fiction dialogue. It uses characters that do not appear in Standard Written Chinese at all — 係 (*hai6*), 唔 (*m4*), 佢 (*keoi5*), 嘅 (*ge3*).

A Mandarin reader can usually handle the first register and is stopped by the second. That asymmetry is the single best illustration of how the two languages relate: close in the formal written channel, genuinely separate in the spoken one.

## Everyday words that are simply different words

The character overlap hides this, so it is worth showing directly. These are not different pronunciations of one word. They are different words that happen to be written in the same script.

| English | Mandarin | Cantonese |
| --- | --- | --- |
| to be | 是 (shì) | 係 (hai6) |
| not | 不 (bù) | 唔 (m4) |
| he / she | 他 · 她 (tā) | 佢 (keoi5) |
| to eat | 吃 (chī) | 食 (sik6) |
| to drink | 喝 (hē) | 飲 (jam2) |
| to look at | 看 (kàn) | 睇 (tai2) |

Six rows, and between them they cover a large share of any ordinary sentence. A learner who assumes Mandarin vocabulary transfers will produce Cantonese that is comprehensible in the way that word-for-word translated English is comprehensible — decipherable, and clearly not the language.

Politeness diverges too, in a way English speakers find genuinely useful once it clicks. Mandarin uses 謝謝 (*xièxie*) broadly for "thank you". Cantonese splits the job: **唔該 (*m4 goi1*)** thanks someone for an action or a service and also does duty as "excuse me" and "please", while **多謝 (*do1 ze6*)** thanks someone for a gift or a compliment. Using *do1 ze6* for a refilled teacup is one of the most audible beginner errors there is.

Numbers, at least, behave. 一, 二, 三 are *jat1, ji6, saam1* in Cantonese and *yī, èr, sān* in Mandarin — same characters, same logic, different sounds, and both build larger numbers on the same regular pattern.

## Where each one is spoken

This tends to be the deciding factor, and it is worth stating without hype.

**Mandarin** is the standard spoken variety of the People's Republic of China and of Taiwan, and one of the official languages of Singapore. It is the language of national broadcasting and education across mainland China, and it has by far the larger volume of teaching material, dictionaries and classroom availability outside Asia.

**Cantonese** is the everyday spoken language of Hong Kong and Macau — where the official languages are Chinese and English — and of Guangzhou and much of the surrounding province, along with long-established communities overseas. It carries a century of film, television and popular music that exists in Cantonese and is not the same body of work in Mandarin.

Neither is "more useful" in the abstract. They are useful in different places, for different things.

## The difficulty question, answered carefully

The most defensible public benchmark is the US Foreign Service Institute's training categories, which group the languages FSI teaches by how long its own students typically need to reach Professional Working Proficiency — a score of Speaking-3/Reading-3 on the Interagency Language Roundtable scale. FSI places **both** Cantonese and Mandarin in **Category IV**, its hardest group, at **88 weeks of full-time instruction (2,200 class hours)**, alongside Japanese, Korean and Arabic.

Two things follow. First, the published institutional guidance does not rank one above the other, so anyone telling you Cantonese is "twice as hard" is not working from that source. Second, those figures describe intensive, full-time, small-group classroom training for diplomats — 2,200 hours across 88 weeks is about 25 class hours a week, before homework. They are not a prediction about phone study and should never be read as one.

What FSI is genuinely good for is relative scale. Both languages sit at the demanding end, which is a reason to choose deliberately rather than a reason not to start.

## How to actually choose

Four questions, in the order that matters.

**Where will you use it?** This settles it more often than anything else. Hong Kong, Macau, Guangzhou or a Cantonese-speaking family points one way. Mainland China outside Guangdong, Taiwan or Singapore points the other.

**Whose voice do you want to understand?** If a specific person, a body of film, or a set of songs is the reason you are learning, learn the language they are actually in.

**How much material do you need around you?** Mandarin has more of everything: courses, tutors, dictionaries, graded readers. Cantonese material is thinner but sufficient, and thin is not the same as absent.

**Are you optimising for the least effort?** Then neither is the answer. Both sit in FSI's hardest category, and if breadth of conversation per hour invested is the goal, [Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/) sits two full categories lower and starts in the Latin alphabet.

The one strategy that reliably fails is starting both at once. The character sets overlap enough to feel efficient and the sound systems conflict enough to guarantee interference — you end up with a Cantonese accent full of Mandarin finals, or Mandarin tones bent toward Cantonese shapes. Finish a foundation in one before you open the other.

## If you have already learned one

The transfer is real and lopsided.

**Reading transfers well.** If you read traditional characters for Mandarin, a large part of Hong Kong signage, menus and formal writing is immediately available to you. You will still be stopped by written Cantonese, which is worth treating as a small separate vocabulary project rather than as a mystery.

**Speaking transfers badly.** You are learning a new tone system, new syllable endings, and a new romanisation. The most common failure among Mandarin speakers moving to Cantonese is assuming the tones will settle by themselves. They do not, because the habit already in place actively competes.

**Grammar mostly transfers, with edits.** Word order is broadly similar, classifiers exist in both, neither conjugates verbs for tense. But the specific grammar words differ, aspect marking differs, and Cantonese carries a large inventory of sentence-final particles that Mandarin does not match. Learn Cantonese for Beginners teaches that layer explicitly — word order, pronouns, classifiers, possession, negation, aspect markers, questions, comparisons, adjective placement and sentence-final particles — rather than assuming a Mandarin-shaped starting point.

## The short version

They share a script and a family. They do not share sounds, romanisation, everyday grammar words, or the ability to be understood by each other's speakers. Choose on geography and on whose voice you want to follow, pick one romanisation and one character set, and give it a year before you consider the second.

If you are still comparing options across languages rather than within Chinese, the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) sit at very different points on the same scale: [the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) front-loads almost all of its difficulty into the writing system, and [Cyrillic](/blog/learn-russian-cyrillic-beginners-guide/) is the shortest hard part of a hard language.

title: Career Mode vs Franchise Mode: Two Sports Games Wearing the Same Jersey
metaTitle: Career Mode vs Franchise Mode: Which One Suits You
secondaryKeywords: what is career mode in sports games
body:
Two sports games sit next to each other on a store page. Both promise seasons, drafts, contracts and championships. One of them will absorb you for months and the other will bore you inside an hour, and which is which depends entirely on a question the store page never asks: **do you want to be a person, or an institution?**

That is the whole distinction. Everything else — session length, decision density, what failure feels like — falls out of it.

## The camera position

A **career mode** puts the camera behind one player. You create them, develop them, and answer for them. The game's questions are personal: take this shot or move it, sign here or hold out, spend this off-season on your weakness or on your strength.

A **franchise mode** raises the camera above an organisation. You are not any of the people on the field. The game's questions are structural: which player do you take with this pick, can you afford this contract, is this rotation getting the minutes to the right places.

Both are legitimately "sports management". They are managing different things.

## What you actually decide

The number of decisions differs by an order of magnitude, and so does their weight.

A franchise season hands you dozens of small calls, most of them recoverable. A bad signing can be traded. A poor draft pick is one of several. The mode is forgiving in the specific sense that there is nearly always another lever.

A career season hands you a handful of decisions that cannot be undone. You cannot trade away a reputation. You cannot restructure a relationship with a coach the way you restructure a contract. Attribute development compounds, so a choice made early keeps paying — or keeps costing — for seasons.

That difference produces two very different feelings. Franchise play feels like tuning. Career play feels like committing.

## What failure looks like

Ask what going badly wrong actually means in each, and the modes separate cleanly.

- **Franchise failure** is a badly constructed team: an unbalanced roster, a cap situation you cannot escape, a season that ends early. It is legible. You can point at the decisions that caused it, and there is a next draft.
- **Career failure** is more personal and less legible: a player who never became anything in particular. Nothing dramatic happened. The opportunities just narrowed, quietly, over a long time.

People who like diagnosing systems tend to prefer the first. People who like consequences tend to prefer the second.

## How time behaves

A **career has an arc.** It starts somewhere and ends somewhere, and the shape of that arc is the content. The mental shift halfway through — from *improving* to *accumulating*, from becoming good to leaving a record — is a real part of playing one well.

A **franchise is open-ended.** There is no natural stopping point, and the interesting tension is that the roster which maximises this season and the roster that leaves you flexible next season are frequently not the same. Deciding which one you are building for, before the draft board tempts you, is the discipline the mode asks for.

This has a practical consequence people underestimate. A career abandoned partway through has shown you a fraction of what it is; a franchise abandoned after two seasons has shown you most of the loop.

## Session shape

Franchise work is naturally chunked. A draft, a set of contracts, a rotation change — each is a task with an end, and you can put the phone down between them without losing the thread.

Career decisions are less separable. They arrive in sequence and each one is context for the next, so the mode reads better in slightly longer sittings. The exception is games that hand you individual moments rather than whole matches: when the unit of play is one possession, a career mode chunks about as well as a franchise does.

| | Career mode | Franchise mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| You are | One player | The organisation |
| Decisions per session | Few, heavy | Many, light |
| Reversibility | Low | High |
| Time structure | An arc with an ending | Open-ended |
| Failure state | A player who never became anything | A badly built team |
| Natural session | Longer, sequential | Chunked, interruptible |
| Replay comes from | A different kind of player | A different construction problem |

## Where these two shapes show up

The studio publishes both patterns, which makes them convenient examples of the split.

### The career shape

[Basketball Career Sim](/apps/pro-basketball-my-career-sim/) is the career pattern in its clearest form. You create a player — position, build, jersey number, playing style, archetype and attributes — and run through youth basketball, high school, recruiting and college, the draft, and the professional years.

Its Live Sim system is what makes the mode work in short bursts: rather than playing whole matches, you step into key possessions and choose what your player does — take the shot or move it on, defend the matchup alone or call for help, play safe or take the risk — with the court view showing score, stats, momentum and positioning as the choice resolves.

Around that sit the systems that make a career a career: coach trust, team chemistry, rivals, teammates, media and fans all react to what you do and change the opportunities you are offered, while training camp, attribute upgrades, signature moves, contracts, brand deals and lifestyle purchases handle off-court progression. All of the money involved is fictional in-game currency with no real-world value. The game supports offline play and needs no account. The [career sim guide](/blog/basketball-career-sim-guide/) goes into how to play one well.

### The franchise shape

[Basketball Draft GM Franchise](/apps/pro-basketball-draft-gm-mode/) is the other pattern. Every run begins on the draft board, the roster then plays a full 82-game season and a playoff race, and contracts, trades and rotations are yours. Eight draft formats — Unlimited, Quick, Blind, Franchise and Salary Cap drafts, plus VS Computer, Battle Mode and a Daily Challenge — change the constraints, so a roster that dominates one format can fall apart in another.

The same shape recurs across the other sports with different vocabulary. Football has Franchise Mode and GM Mode extending control past draft day to the wider organisation. Hockey has Franchise GM Mode for organising forwards, defenders and goaltending across seasons. Baseball has Franchise GM Mode covering the batting order, rotation, bullpen and payroll. Soccer calls it club management and includes formations, squad depth, transfers, contracts, fitness and season progress. Combat sports has GM Mode, where you sign fighters, manage contracts and move contenders toward title shots with your decisions feeding the rankings.

## The third shape nobody names

There is a pattern between the two that gets filed under franchise and is really its own thing: **draft-and-simulate**.

You build a roster, hand it to a simulator, and get a record back. That is a complete session — problem, decision, verdict — usually in a few minutes, with no season to administer. It is the shortest closed loop in the genre, which is why it survives on a phone better than either of the other two.

Most of the studio's sports titles are built on this loop with a franchise mode attached behind it, which is a sensible arrangement: the draft is the entry point and the management is the depth. The [basketball draft and GM guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/) covers how the two connect.

## What both kinds of simulation are assuming

Whichever shape you play, the model underneath deserves stating plainly.

These games take fictional players, apply internal rules to your decisions, and return an outcome. They are not reproducing the physics of the sport, and they are not describing, forecasting or relating to any real league, team, school or athlete. Nothing they produce is a prediction or guidance of any kind, and no approach guarantees a result — the perfect records these games are named for are deliberately hard to reach rather than the expected outcome of competent play.

What that leaves is a comparison against yourself. In a franchise, change one construction decision and see whether the model agrees. In a career, commit to an identity and see how far the surrounding systems let it go. Both are honest uses of a model; neither tells you anything about the real sport.

## Which one do you want?

Three questions settle it faster than any feature list.

1. **When something goes wrong, do you want to fix it or live with it?** Fixing is franchise. Living with it is career.
2. **Do you enjoy a spreadsheet-shaped problem, or a story-shaped one?** The first has a right answer you are searching for; the second has an identity you are defending.
3. **How long are your sessions really?** If the honest answer is a few minutes at a time, start with a draft-and-sim loop or a career built on individual possessions rather than a full-season franchise.

Getting this choice wrong is the most common reason people conclude they do not like sports sims. Usually they just tried the wrong camera position.

## Where to read next

If short sessions are the constraint, [manager games for short sessions](/blog/best-sports-manager-games-for-short-sessions/) works through what actually makes a management game survive a five-minute window. If a patchy connection is the constraint, [sports GM games without internet](/blog/sports-gm-games-without-internet/) covers what to check before you rely on one. And for the two modes in depth, see the [career sim guide](/blog/basketball-career-sim-guide/) and the [draft and GM guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/).

Everything the studio makes in this genre is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Color Theory for Beginners: The Part That Actually Changes Your Pictures
metaTitle: Color Theory for Beginners: A Practical Guide
secondaryKeywords: how to choose a color palette

sources.p: National Eye Institute, U.S. National Institutes of Health
National Eye Institute, U.S. National Institutes of Health

body:
The single most useful idea in colour theory is not about colour. It is that a picture is mostly built out of light and dark, and the hues are painted on top of a structure that would still work in grey.

That is unintuitive enough that most people spend a long time solving the wrong problem — trying different hues when the actual issue is that everything in the image is the same brightness. So this is where to start, and everything else in this article hangs off it.

## Three properties, and one of them does the heavy lifting

Any colour can be described by three independent properties. Getting them separated in your head is most of the battle.

**Hue** is the name — red, orange, teal, violet. It is what people mean when they say "colour", and it is the property that changes as you travel around a colour wheel.

**Saturation** (also called chroma) is how pure the hue is versus how grey. Full saturation is the most intense version available; zero saturation is a neutral grey with no identifiable hue at all.

**Value** (also called lightness) is how light or dark the colour is, independent of hue. A pale yellow and a pale blue can have identical value even though they look nothing alike.

This three-part structure is not something a design blog invented. Albert Munsell built a colour ordering system on exactly these axes — hue, value and chroma — in the early twentieth century, arranging colours in a solid so that equal steps looked equal to the eye. Nearly every modern colour picker you have ever used is a descendant of that idea.

### The grayscale test

Here is the practical consequence. Convert an image to grayscale, or just squint at it until the detail disappears, and you are looking at value alone.

If the shapes still read as separate objects, the picture works. If they merge into one grey mass, no amount of hue variation will fix it, because the human visual system uses lightness edges to find the boundaries of things.

Almost every "my colours look muddy" problem is a value problem in disguise. A picture where the hair, the clothing and the background all sit at similar lightness will look flat and confusing regardless of how carefully the hues were chosen. Spread the values out and the same hues suddenly look intentional.

## Why the primaries you were taught are wrong

Two different physical processes get called "mixing", and they have different primaries because they work in opposite directions.

**Additive mixing** is what light does. A display emits red, green and blue light, and where those overlap the result is brighter — all three at full intensity gives white. This is why screen colours are specified as RGB, and why each channel in a standard image runs across an eight-bit range from none to full intensity.

**Subtractive mixing** is what ink and paint do. A pigment works by absorbing some wavelengths and reflecting the rest, so every pigment you add removes more light. The primaries here are cyan, magenta and yellow, and stacking them all approaches black rather than white.

The red-yellow-blue wheel taught in most schools is a traditional approximation of the subtractive system, and it is a poor one — mixing red and blue paint in practice gives a dull purple rather than a vivid one, because the actual subtractive primary is magenta.

None of this changes how you colour a picture. It does explain two things that otherwise seem arbitrary: why a colour that glowed on screen looks dull in print, and why "mix the opposite of what you want to darken it" produces grey rather than a richer version of the colour.

The formal side of this — how colour is measured rather than mixed — sits with the International Commission on Illumination, whose colour spaces underpin essentially every digital colour standard in use.

## The colour wheel maps one property only

A colour wheel arranges hues in a circle so that similar ones sit near each other and opposites sit across from each other. That is all it does. It says nothing about value or saturation, which is why a wheel alone cannot tell you whether a combination will work.

What it is genuinely good for is naming relationships:

| Scheme | What it is | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monochromatic | One hue, varied in value and saturation | Guaranteed harmony, risks being dull |
| Analogous | Neighbouring hues | Calm and coherent, low contrast |
| Complementary | Two opposite hues | Maximum hue contrast, tiring at full strength |
| Split-complementary | One hue plus the two neighbours of its opposite | Most of the contrast, less of the harshness |
| Triadic | Three hues evenly spaced | Lively, hard to balance |

The reason these are useful is not that they are magic ratios. It is that each one **restricts** your choices, and restriction is what makes a set of colours look chosen rather than collected. Give someone an unlimited picker and each region gets decided in isolation; give them four related hues and every region relates to every other one whether or not they understand why.

The working method that follows: pick a scheme, let one hue dominate most of the surface at moderate saturation, give a second hue a supporting role, and reserve your highest saturation for the smallest area. Focal points are made by *contrast against the rest of the picture*, so the loudest colour has to be rare or it stops being loud.

## Colour is contextual, which is why swatches lie

The same colour looks different depending on what is next to it. A mid grey on a dark background appears lighter; the identical grey on a pale background appears darker. This is simultaneous contrast, and it is a property of how vision processes edges rather than a trick.

The practical rule is simple and constantly ignored: **judge colours in place, not in the picker.** A swatch that looked perfect against the neutral background of a palette can be completely wrong once it is surrounded by the rest of the image, and the fix is often to change the neighbours rather than the colour you were unhappy with.

This is also why fixing one region at a time rarely converges. Colour decisions are relational, so adjusting a region changes the apparent value of everything touching it.

## Temperature does depth for free

Hues are loosely sorted into warm — reds, oranges, yellows — and cool — blues, greens, violets. The division is cultural as much as physical, but it produces a reliable perceptual effect: warm colours tend to advance toward the viewer and cool colours tend to recede.

That gives you a depth cue that costs nothing. Push background elements slightly cooler and less saturated, keep foreground elements warmer and more saturated, and a flat image acquires space without a single line being drawn.

It also gives you the most common way to wreck one. A character coloured warm against a cold background looks pasted on, because the temperature relationship contradicts the depth relationship. Decide the overall temperature of an image before you commit to anything large, because reversing it later means recolouring the biggest area you have.

## Limited palettes, and why constraint helps

Give ten people the same drawing and an unlimited colour picker, and most of the results will be muddy. Give them the same drawing and eight colours, and most of the results will look deliberate.

The constraint does the work. When every colour in the image is drawn from one small set, everything harmonises structurally — the relationships are built in. Unlimited choice invites picking each colour at the moment you reach the region, with no reference to what came before, and the accumulation of locally reasonable decisions is what produces a globally incoherent picture.

If you are choosing a palette from scratch, a reliable starting shape is: one dominant hue occupying most of the area, one supporting hue at similar or lower saturation, one accent used sparingly at high saturation, and a neutral. Then vary value freely within those. Almost every palette you admire decomposes into something close to that.

## Do not let hue carry meaning on its own

One accessibility rule is worth internalising early because it also makes pictures better.

Colour vision deficiency is common, and the most frequent forms affect discrimination between reds and greens. If the only thing distinguishing two elements in an image is their hue, those elements may be indistinguishable to a substantial number of viewers.

The fix is the same discipline that makes images read well anyway: **pair every hue difference with a value difference.** If red and green are doing different jobs in your picture, make one of them lighter as well. You get accessibility and a stronger grayscale structure from the same decision, which is a rare case of a constraint that costs nothing.

## Practising this without having to draw

The obstacle to learning colour is usually not the theory. It is that testing an idea normally requires producing a whole picture first, and most people cannot.

Colouring existing line art removes that entirely. Composition, proportion and perspective are settled, so every decision left is a colour decision, and you can run the same drawing three times under three different schemes and compare them directly — which is a genuine experiment rather than a guess.

[Anime Coloring Book: Paint Art](/apps/anime-coloring-book/) is set up for that kind of practice. The palettes span soft pastels, vibrant tones, classic shades, warm and cool sets, glow-inspired colours, chalk and glass-like textures, gradients and mosaics, and a Recently Used row keeps whatever you are actually working with within reach — which matters more than it sounds, because a limited working set is exactly the constraint described above. Fill covers large regions in a tap, so trying a value structure costs seconds rather than an evening. Two erasers, one for the artwork and one for the background, mean an experiment that fails costs nothing. Continue Coloring brings back unfinished pages, kept on your device, so a palette experiment can sit half-finished for a week.

Three exercises worth doing in that setting:

1. **The value run.** Colour one picture using a single hue at four clearly different lightnesses. It will look better than you expect, and it demonstrates the grayscale point faster than any explanation.
2. **The temperature swap.** Colour the same drawing twice, once with a warm set and once with a cool one, changing nothing else. The difference in mood is the whole lesson about temperature.
3. **The accent test.** Colour a picture in analogous hues, then add one small area of the complementary hue at full saturation. Watch where your eye goes.

If you want what the style specifically asks for rather than the general theory, [our guide to colouring anime line art](/blog/anime-coloring-app-guide/) covers hair, eyes and skin conventions in detail. The rest of what we make in this area is in [Anime & Creative Games](/apps/category/anime-creative/).

## The short version

Colour has three properties and value is the one that decides whether a picture reads. Screens add light and pigments subtract it, which is why their primaries differ and why the wheel from school is an approximation of one of them.

Schemes work by restricting hue. Restriction is the actual mechanism, not the specific scheme you picked. Judge colours in place rather than in the picker, spread your values before you fuss over hues, keep the highest saturation for the smallest area, and never make hue the only thing distinguishing two elements.

title: Digital Coloring Techniques: Halos, Flats, Shading Order and Rescuing a Muddy Page
metaTitle: Digital Coloring Techniques That Actually Help
secondaryKeywords: why does fill leave a white outline
body:
Knowing which colour to use and getting it cleanly onto the page are different skills, and the second one has a short list of specific problems that everybody hits in the same order. Pale seams around every fill. A bucket that floods the entire image. Shading that looks correct in isolation and wrong in place. A finished page that somehow reads as grey.

All four have concrete causes. None of them require talent to fix.

## The pale halo is anti-aliasing, and it is not a bug

Tap fill inside a region and you will often see a thin light line surviving between your colour and the black outline. It looks like sloppy work. It is a direct and unavoidable consequence of how the line art was drawn.

A perfectly hard black line on a pixel grid produces visible stair-stepping on every diagonal. To avoid that, drawing tools use **anti-aliasing**: the pixels along the edge of a line are rendered as partial blends between the line colour and whatever is behind it, so a diagonal reads as smooth at normal viewing distance.

Those blend pixels are neither line nor background. They are somewhere in between.

A **flood fill** works by starting where you tapped and spreading outward across pixels that match, stopping when it reaches something that does not. The semi-transparent blend pixels do not match, so the fill stops just short of them — leaving a ring of the original blend colour, which against your new fill reads as a pale halo.

Three responses, in order of how often they are the right one:

1. **Ignore it.** At the size the picture will actually be looked at, a one-pixel seam is invisible. Zooming to five times normal size and being annoyed by something nobody will ever see is a way of not finishing pictures.
2. **Brush the seam.** Zoom in, take the same colour, and run the brush along the inside of the outline. This is the reliable fix and it takes seconds per region.
3. **Choose darker fills near the lines.** A seam between black line art and a dark fill is far less visible than a seam between black line art and a pale one. If you know a region will show its edges, biasing it darker hides the problem for free.

### And when the fill floods everything

Same mechanism, opposite failure. A flood fill spreads until it hits a boundary, so if there is a single-pixel gap anywhere in the outline of a region, the fill escapes through it and keeps going.

Undo, then follow the outline of the region at high zoom looking for the break. The usual suspects are hair tips, fingers, the point where two lines nearly touch, and anywhere the artist deliberately left a line open for style. Close the gap with the brush and fill again.

## Flats first, always

The most consequential habit in the whole activity is boring: **put down every flat base colour before you shade anything.**

The reason is that colour decisions are relational. A shadow tone that looks right against a white background will look wrong once the region next to it is filled, because how light something appears depends on what surrounds it. Shading an isolated region is therefore judging a decision with most of its information missing, and the near-universal result is that the shading gets redone.

A flats pass also gives you the single most useful checkpoint available: with the whole picture blocked in and nothing else, you can see the value structure. Squint at it. If everything merges into one mass, fix that now — while it costs one fill per region — rather than after you have shaded every individual area.

## Cel shading and soft shading are different decisions

They are usually presented as a skill ladder, with cel shading as the beginner option. They are not. They are two different questions.

**Cel shading** asks *what shape is the shadow?* You pick a small number of tones — often just a base and one darker partner — and draw the shadow as a deliberate region with a hard edge. Everything inside the edge is one flat tone. Because the edge is drawn rather than calculated, the shading carries information about form the way a line drawing does, and a confidently drawn shadow shape reads as more solid than a hesitant gradient.

**Soft shading** asks *how fast does the light fall off?* Instead of an edge, there is a transition, which means you need a way of laying colour at partial strength.

That second requirement is worth being blunt about. A toolset built around solid fills and a hard brush naturally does cel shading well and soft shading badly, and fighting it produces a page that looks like neither. Anime and manga styling has always been built on flat tones with clear edges, so leaning into cel shading on a hard-edged toolset is not a compromise. It is the style working with the tool.

### A workable cel shading pass

1. **Decide the light direction and say it out loud.** "Light from the upper left." Every shadow after this answers to that sentence, and consistency in lighting is most of what makes a picture look deliberate.
2. **One partner tone per region.** For each major area, pick a second colour in the same hue family that is clearly darker. Same family, different value — not a different hue.
3. **Draw the shadow shape on the side away from the light.** Under the chin. Beneath the fringe. On the underside of a sleeve. Along the lower edge of each hair clump.
4. **Keep the edges confident.** A hard edge drawn in one stroke reads better than one nibbled at repeatedly.

Two tones plus consistent direction will carry an entire picture. A third tone is a refinement, not a requirement.

## Contact shadows earn more than cast shadows

If you only add one thing beyond flats, make it the dark line where two objects touch.

Where a collar meets a neck, where hair rests on a shoulder, where a sleeve meets a wrist, light is blocked from almost every direction, so those seams are the darkest part of the picture by a wide margin. Adding a narrow darker band exactly at the contact does more for a sense of solidity than a large, carefully rendered cast shadow anywhere else.

It is also cheap. These are small areas, they follow existing lines, and they cannot really be got wrong — if two things are touching, there is a shadow there.

## Rim light: the trick worth learning early

A thin strip of a lighter, often warmer colour along the edge of a subject on the side facing away from the main light. It reads as light spilling around the form from behind.

Rim light does something no amount of shading does: it **separates the subject from the background** along a hard edge, which makes a character sit in a scene rather than on it. It works especially well when the background is dark and the rim is bright, and it is a single thin stroke per edge.

Use it sparingly and only along edges the light could actually reach. A rim on every silhouette makes the figure look like it is glowing, which is fine as a deliberate effect and distracting as an accident.

## Gradients and textures are surface, not colour

Gradient and textured colour sets — chalk, glass-like, mosaic — change how a surface behaves rather than what hue it is, and they solve one specific problem: a large flat region that looks empty.

Skies, walls, dresses and open backgrounds are the natural candidates. A single texture across one large area gives the eye something to rest on without adding a decision to the picture.

The failure mode is obvious once stated. Two textured regions compete; three make the picture look like a collage. One textured area per image, used on the biggest empty shape, is almost always the correct dose.

## Zoom discipline

The mistake is working zoomed in and judging zoomed in.

Detail passes require magnification, but a picture is looked at whole. Every so often, snap back to full view and look at what you have. Half the time the thing you spent five minutes perfecting is invisible, and the thing that is actually wrong is a large shape you have not been looking at.

The rhythm that works: block in at full view, refine at zoom, judge at full view. Never make a decision about a colour while looking at it magnified, because at that size you are seeing a swatch rather than a picture.

## Rescuing a muddy page

When a finished page looks flat and grey, run these three checks in this order. The order matters, because the first one fixes the most cases and the third one fixes almost none.

**1. Check the value spread.** Squint until detail disappears. If the hair, clothing and background all read as the same grey, that is your problem, and no hue change will solve it. Push the largest region clearly lighter or clearly darker and the whole image will resolve.

**2. Check for opposing hues at similar saturation.** Colours from opposite sides of the wheel neutralise each other toward grey when they meet at similar intensity. If two large adjacent regions are doing that, drop the saturation of one and let the other be the loud one.

**3. Only then change hues.** By this point you rarely need to. Most pictures described as having "the wrong colours" turn out to have acceptable colours in the wrong value arrangement, and swapping hues without fixing that just produces a differently muddy picture.

## Doing this with a small toolset

None of the above requires an elaborate application. It requires a fill, a brush, an eraser and the patience to lay flats before shading.

[Anime Coloring Book: Paint Art](/apps/anime-coloring-book/) has exactly that shape. Fill covers large areas in a tap, which makes a full flats pass fast enough to be worth doing properly. The brush handles the seam cleanup, the shadow shapes and the rim strokes. Two erasers — one for the artwork and one for the background — mean an experiment that fails costs nothing, and the ability to fail cheaply is what makes people try the more interesting option. Zoom, move and center handle the detail pass, with center snapping the view back when you lose your place.

For colour selection, the palettes run from soft pastels and classic shades through vibrant tones, warm and cool sets, glow-inspired colours, chalk and glass-like textures, gradients and mosaics, and the Recently Used row keeps your working set close — which is what makes a two-tone cel pass practical, since you are moving between a base and its darker partner constantly.

Continue Coloring brings back unfinished artwork with your work in place, stored on your device with no account required, so a flats pass and a shading pass can happen days apart. And Get Random Artwork unlocks a surprise canvas in exchange for watching a rewarded ad, which is genuinely useful for practice — the drawing you would not have chosen is the one that makes you solve a problem you have been avoiding.

More on what anime line art specifically asks for is in [our guide to coloring anime art on a phone](/blog/anime-coloring-app-guide/), and the rest of what we make sits in [Anime & Creative Games](/apps/category/anime-creative/).

## The short version

The pale ring around a fill is anti-aliasing and either brush it out or ignore it. A fill that escapes means a gap in the line art. Lay all your flats before shading anything, because shading judged against white gets redone.

Cel shading is drawing a shadow shape and soft shading is drawing a falloff; a hard-edged tool does the first well, and the style you are colouring was built for it anyway. Add contact shadows where things touch, one rim light where it separates the subject, one texture on the biggest empty area. Then judge the whole thing at full size, and when it looks muddy, fix the values before you touch a hue.

title: The Football Draft Simulator, Explained: Units, Budgets and the Cost of a Refresh
metaTitle: Football Draft Simulator App: A Drafting Guide
body:
The screen shows you a set of options for one position. There are no refreshes. Whatever you pick here is what you have, and you will not find out whether it was the right call for another dozen picks, by which point you cannot do anything about it.

This is the moment the football draft genre is built around, and it is a more interesting problem than it looks. You are not being asked which player is best. You are being asked to commit under uncertainty, with a partial view of a pool whose shape you can only guess at.

## Football rosters are a unit problem

Every drafting sport rewards balance. Football rewards it harder, and for a structural reason.

In a sport with a small lineup, a weak player is a weak player — costly, visible, and roughly proportional to their own contribution. Football groups its players into units that operate together, and a weak *group* does not fail proportionally. It fails as a group, and it takes the parts of the team that depend on it down with it. Excellence elsewhere does not compensate; it just gets stranded.

The game's own framing acknowledges this. Salary Cap Draft "rewards spending well and exposes the units you skimped on" — note that it is units, plural, that get exposed, not individual picks. That is the correct diagnosis of what goes wrong in football roster building.

The practical rule that falls out of it: **your team is capped by your worst unit, not averaged across all of them.** When you are deciding between upgrading something already good and repairing something bad, football pushes the answer toward repair more aggressively than the other draft sports do.

## Four rulesets, four different questions

[20-0 Football Draft & GM Mode](/apps/football-draft-gm-mode/) offers several draft rulesets, and they are not difficulty tiers stacked on one another. Each poses a distinct question.

| Ruleset | What it gives you | What it is actually testing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unlimited Draft | Refresh and compare options as long as you like | Whether you know what a good roster looks like when nothing stops you building one |
| Limited Draft | No refreshes at all | Whether you can commit on incomplete information |
| Salary Cap Draft | A budget as well as a board | Whether you can price value, not just rank it |
| Playoff Mode | The whole roster under pressure | Whether your build has a weak point that only shows up when it matters |

The reason to try all four is that they expose different failures. A drafter who is excellent in Unlimited and poor in Limited is not unlucky — they rely on search to substitute for judgement. A drafter who is fine in Limited and falls apart under a cap has never had to think about price. Those are two separate skills and the formats separate them cleanly.

## The cost of a refresh

Refreshing options feels free. It is not, and understanding why sharpens your drafting in both directions.

In an unlimited format, more searching genuinely does produce better picks — but with sharply diminishing returns, because you are sampling from the same pool and the ceiling is fixed. What extended searching mostly buys you is *confidence*, and confidence is not the same thing as roster quality. Plenty of long, satisfying Unlimited drafts produce rosters no better than a decisive one, with the time spent on validating a choice you had already made.

Remove the refresh and the calculation inverts. Now the value of a pick includes what it tells you about the rest of the draft. Every position you fill is a data point about the pool's quality level, and a good Limited drafter is updating a model of the board with every selection rather than evaluating each option in isolation.

Two habits follow from that:

- **Set a reference level early.** Your first few picks establish what "good" looks like in this run. Without one, you will either reject perfectly fine options waiting for something that is not coming, or accept a weak one because you have nothing to compare it against.
- **Take the scarce thing before the abundant thing.** If a position is generally deep, a late pick there costs you little. If it is thin, deferring it is how you end up with the hole that caps the roster.

## Spending well under a cap

A salary cap converts a ranking problem into an allocation problem, and that is a bigger change than it sounds.

Without a budget, the question is "who is the best player who helps me?" With one, it is "who is worth what they cost, given everything else I still have to buy?" Those questions have different answers often enough that cap drafting deserves its own approach.

The trap is the marquee signing. Concentrating budget into one exceptional player is emotionally satisfying and structurally dangerous, because in a sport built on units the money you did not spend shows up as an entire group that underperforms. Spending is not neutral — every unit you underfund is a fixed liability the rest of the team has to carry all season.

A defensible default is to buy competence everywhere first, then spend whatever is left on excellence. It rarely produces the most exciting roster on paper and it produces far fewer catastrophes.

## What the season simulator is doing

When you finalise a roster and the simulator returns a record, the record is a model's output. It reflects roster quality and how well the pieces fit together, evaluated by the game's own internal rules.

Three things are worth saying explicitly, because the genre attracts confusion on all three.

**It is not a prediction.** Nothing about the result describes, forecasts or relates to any real football game, team, player or season. The players in the pool are fictional and generated by the game.

**It is a score, and should be read like one.** Treat the record as feedback about your drafting, in the same way a puzzle game returns a score. The useful question is never "did I get lucky" but "which of my decisions is this record disagreeing with".

**The perfect record is meant to be hard.** A run of 20 games without a loss is the target the whole game is built around, not the expected outcome of a competent draft. If you finish short, that is the game working, and the gap between your record and perfection is precisely the information you drafted for.

None of this is betting guidance and none of it is a forecast. It is a scoring model for a roster puzzle, which is a more honest and more interesting thing to be.

## Past draft day

Franchise Mode and GM Mode extend control beyond the draft to the wider organisation, and they change what "a good roster" means.

A single draft is optimised for one season. A franchise is optimised for a sequence of them, and the two builds diverge quickly. The player who maximises this year's record and the player who leaves you flexible next year are frequently not the same person, and the discipline of franchise play is deciding which one you are building for *before* the board tempts you.

This is also where a draft-day mistake stops being fatal. Long play gives you the tools to convert a surplus at one position into coverage at another, which is the only real cure for an imbalanced draft. The drafting principles carry over from the other sports the studio simulates — the [basketball draft and GM guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/) covers the same ideas where lineups are small and the [baseball draft guide](/blog/baseball-draft-gm-guide/) covers them where the numbers are explicit.

## Gridiron IQ, and why a knowledge test belongs in a draft game

Sitting alongside the drafting are VS Computer, Battle, Tournament, a Daily Challenge, and Gridiron IQ, which tests how well you actually read a team sheet.

That last one is a better fit than it first appears. The core skill in this genre is not knowing football trivia — it is *reading a roster and seeing what it will do*. Being able to look at a filled-out team sheet and spot the group that will let it down is the same skill the draft board requires, isolated and tested directly. If your drafts keep coming back with records you did not expect, that is often where the gap is.

## A pre-draft checklist

1. **Decide the format's question before you start.** Unlimited asks what you know; Limited asks whether you can commit; Salary Cap asks whether you can price.
2. **Find your worst unit at every point in the draft.** That group, not your best one, is what the record will reflect.
3. **Set a reference level in the first few picks** so later options have something to be judged against.
4. **Buy competence before excellence** when a budget is in play.
5. **After the record comes back, name the one pick you would change.** Doing this after every run is the difference between playing a lot and getting better.

More drafting and management titles from the studio, across five sports and combat sports, are listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Football Positions Explained, and What Each One Is Worth on a Draft Board
metaTitle: Football Positions Explained: A Drafter's Guide
secondaryKeywords: what does a tight end do
positional value in a football draft
body:
The board offers you a slot marked **OT** and three names under it. You have already spent picks on the positions you understand, the ones whose contribution you could describe to somebody at a bus stop. Now you are being asked to pay for a player whose entire job is to make sure something does not happen.

This is the part of football drafting that separates people, and it is not really about football knowledge. It is about knowing what each slot on a team sheet is *for*, and therefore what it costs you to get it wrong.

## Football is three rosters wearing one uniform

Most team sports ask the same players to attack and defend. Football does not. The group that plays offence, the group that plays defence, and the group that plays on kicking downs are largely different people with different builds, different training and different skills.

That single structural fact explains almost everything else about the sport, including why the position list runs to twenty-odd names while other sports manage with five or six. It also explains why football roster building feels harder than it looks: you are not assembling a team, you are assembling three of them, and a surplus in one does nothing for the others.

### The arithmetic that never changes

Eleven players per side, always. What varies is how you distribute them.

A common offensive grouping looks like this:

> five offensive linemen + one quarterback + one running back + one tight end + three wide receivers = eleven

Swap a receiver for a second tight end and you get a heavier grouping better suited to running. Swap the running back out for a fourth receiver and you get a lighter one built to throw. The eleven is fixed; the mix is a decision, and it is a decision that tells the defence something.

Defences work the same way. One common arrangement:

> four defensive linemen + three linebackers + two cornerbacks + two safeties = eleven

Take a linebacker off and add a defensive back and you have traded run defence for coverage. Every defensive alignment you will ever hear named is some version of that trade.

## The offence, position by position

### The offensive line: centre, guards, tackles

Five players whose job is to control the space in front of the quarterback and open the space in front of the runner.

- **Centre** snaps the ball and typically identifies the defensive front, which makes it the position with the most thinking attached. A centre who reads a front wrongly gets four other linemen blocking the wrong people.
- **Guards** line up immediately either side of the centre. Their work happens in a crowd, at close quarters, against powerful interior linemen. Good guard play is mostly invisible; bad guard play arrives in the quarterback's lap almost instantly.
- **Tackles** play the outside edges of the line, and this is where the line gets exposed. A tackle is regularly left alone against the quickest pass rusher the opposition has, in open space, with nobody nearby to help. The tackle protecting the side the quarterback cannot see is the most demanding of the five.

The important thing about the line is that **it is graded as a unit and it fails as a unit.** Pressure only has to get through in one place. Four excellent linemen and one poor one do not average out to a good line; they produce a line with a known address that the defence will visit repeatedly.

### Quarterback

The quarterback touches the ball on essentially every offensive snap, which makes it the one position where a rating gap is felt continuously rather than situationally.

What the position actually requires is decision-making under a deadline: read what the defence is doing, decide where the ball goes, and deliver it before protection breaks down. Arm strength is the part that shows up in highlights; the reading is the part that decides seasons.

### Running back

Three jobs, and drafters usually only count the first. A back carries the ball, catches passes out of the backfield, and blocks blitzing defenders. That third job is the one that gets quarterbacks hurt when it is done badly.

Running back is also the position where the surrounding cast matters most. A back running behind a poor line and a back running behind a good one are being asked different questions, which is why production at this position travels less well than production anywhere else on the field.

### Tight end

The hybrid. A tight end lines up attached to the offensive line and is expected to block there, then run routes and catch passes like a receiver.

Its real value is ambiguity. When a genuinely two-way tight end is on the field, the defence cannot tell from the personnel grouping whether a run or a pass is coming, and has to prepare for both. A tight end who can only block, or only catch, hands that information back for free.

### Wide receivers

Receivers are usually split into outside and slot roles. Outside receivers work near the sideline against a defender with the boundary as an extra defender; the job rewards speed and the ability to win a contested ball. Slot receivers work in the congested middle, where the job rewards quickness, route craft and the willingness to catch in traffic.

Both get open. They get open differently, and a roster of three players who all get open the same way is easier to defend than the sum of their ratings suggests.

## The defence, position by position

### The defensive line

Split roughly into interior and edge.

**Interior linemen** occupy blockers. The best of them command two, which mathematically frees a teammate somewhere else. This is the clearest example in the sport of a contribution that never appears next to the player's own name.

**Edge defenders** rush the passer from outside. The reason they are prized is subtle: a front that generates pressure with four rushers lets the other seven defenders drop into coverage. A front that has to send extra rushers to generate the same pressure is playing coverage a man short. Pressure without blitzing is the single most valuable output a defensive front can produce.

### Linebackers

Linebackers sit behind the line and have to be good at contradictory things — filling running lanes, dropping into coverage, and occasionally blitzing.

The middle linebacker is usually the defensive equivalent of the centre: the one making the calls and setting the front. Outside linebackers vary enormously by scheme, which is why the label alone tells you less than any other on the team sheet.

### The secondary: cornerbacks and safeties

**Cornerbacks** cover receivers, either tracking a man or holding a zone. It is the most isolating job on the field. Every mistake is public, immediate and usually large.

**Safeties** play deepest and function as the error-correction layer. One is typically deployed as a free defender with responsibility for the deep middle; the other plays closer to the line and contributes against the run. A defence with only one of those two types is a defence that is either soft against the run or thin over the top.

## Special teams

Kicker, punter, long snapper, holder, returners and the coverage units that run down the field with them.

These positions have low volume and high leverage: they are involved rarely, and when they are involved the outcome swings a lot. Drafters ignore them because they are boring and because there is no way to make them exciting. They are also the cheapest place on a roster to lose games you had otherwise won.

## Turning all of that into draft-board behaviour

Knowing what a position does is step one. Knowing what it is *worth to you* is step two, and it is a different question.

**Importance and value are not the same thing.** Importance asks how much a position affects a play. Value asks how hard the slot is to fill from the pool in front of you. A position can be enormously important and still be poor value if competent options are everywhere, and a position can be modest in importance and expensive in value if the pool is thin.

**Find your worst unit, repeatedly.** Because the lines fail as groups, a football roster is capped by its weakest unit rather than lifted by its best one. Every time you are choosing between improving something already good and repairing something bad, football pushes the answer further towards repair than the other drafting sports do. The [football draft simulator guide](/blog/football-draft-gm-guide/) works through what that means under a salary cap and in a no-refresh format.

**Distrust lists sorted by production.** Counting statistics credit the player at the end of the sequence. The blocker, the double-teamed tackle and the safety who prevented the play from being called are all invisible on that list, and they are exactly the players a well-built roster is quietly full of.

**Take the scarce thing first.** If a position group is deep, waiting costs you very little. If it is thin, waiting is how you finish the draft with the hole that defines your season.

| Group | Positions | What you are really buying |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Offensive line | C, G, T | Time for the quarterback and space for the runner |
| Backfield | QB, RB | Decisions per snap, and carries plus protection |
| Receiving | WR, TE | Ways to get open, and ambiguity before the snap |
| Defensive front | DT, DE / edge | Pressure that does not cost you coverage |
| Second level | LB | Run fits, coverage underneath, disguise |
| Secondary | CB, S | Isolation coverage, and the error-correction layer |
| Kicking units | K, P, LS, returners | Rare events with outsized swing |

## What the simulator is doing with all this

When you finish a roster in [20-0 Football Draft & GM Mode](/apps/football-draft-gm-mode/) and the season simulator returns a record, that record is the game's own assessment of how well your eleven-by-three fits together. It is scoring roster construction under the model's internal rules.

Three limits are worth stating plainly. The players are fictional and generated inside the game, so nothing in the result describes or forecasts any real league, team or athlete. The record is a score, not a prediction, and the useful question after one arrives is which of your picks it is disagreeing with. And the perfect unbeaten run the game is named for is deliberately hard rather than the expected outcome of a competent draft — the gap between your record and perfection is the information you drafted for.

The game's Gridiron IQ challenges test the same skill from the other direction: reading a completed team sheet and spotting which group will let it down. If your drafts keep producing records you did not expect, that is usually where the gap lives.

## Where to go next

Positional thinking transfers across sports, and it changes shape as the lineups get smaller. Hockey compresses the same ideas into six slots, which the [hockey positions guide](/blog/hockey-positions-explained/) covers, and soccer expresses them as shape rather than personnel, which is the subject of the [soccer formations guide](/blog/soccer-formations-explained/). If what you want is a roster puzzle you can finish on a train, the [short-session manager games guide](/blog/best-sports-manager-games-for-short-sessions/) is the more practical read.

Everything the studio makes in this genre is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: A History of the Shoot 'em Up: How One Idea Kept Reinventing Itself
metaTitle: History of Shoot 'em Up Games: Arcade to Danmaku
primaryKeyword: history of shoot em up games

sources.p: The Strong National Museum of Play

body:
The shoot 'em up is one of the few video game genres old enough to have been declared dead several times and stubborn enough to have outlived each obituary. It has changed hardware three times, changed continents, changed business model, and changed its own difficulty philosophy twice — while asking the same question the whole way through.

That question is not *can you shoot the thing*. It is *where are you going to be standing when the thing shoots back*.

## Before the genre had a name

In 1962, a group of programmers at MIT wrote **Spacewar!** on a PDP-1, a room-sized minicomputer with a circular vector display. Two ships, a star with gravity, torpedoes, and a limited fuel supply. It was written to show off the machine, it was never sold, and it spread by being copied onto other PDP-1 installations by people who wanted to play it.

Two things about Spacewar! matter for everything that followed. It established that a screen could hold a hostile object with its own motion and its own agenda, and it established that the interesting part was manoeuvring rather than aiming. Both ideas went dormant for the better part of a decade while the technology to sell them caught up.

## Space Invaders turned it into a genre

**Space Invaders**, developed by Tomohiro Nishikado and released by Taito in Japan in 1978, is where the commercial genre starts. A single ship at the bottom of the screen. A grid of aliens descending. Four destructible shields, and a score.

The design is worth examining because so much of it became the default. The player cannot advance; the threat advances instead. The enemy formation moves as a unit, so its behaviour is legible. The shields degrade, which means safety is a consumable rather than a place. And the game cannot be won — only survived longer — which converts the entire experience into a score.

There is also a famous accident in it. The aliens accelerate as you destroy them, and the acceleration was not authored: with fewer sprites left to draw, the hardware simply had less work to do per frame and ran the remaining ones faster. The team kept it. Difficulty that rises as the player succeeds turned out to be exactly the pacing curve the format needed, and designers have been building it deliberately ever since.

## The early 1980s pulled the form in five directions at once

The years immediately after Space Invaders were the genre's most experimental period, and nearly every structural variant that still exists was invented in them.

- **Namco's Galaxian** (1979) broke the formation. Enemies peeled off the grid and dived at the player individually, which meant the threat was no longer a single legible block. **Galaga** (1981) extended that with capture-and-rescue and a bonus stage that rewarded pattern knowledge rather than survival.
- **Atari's Asteroids** (1979) removed the fixed axis altogether. Momentum-based movement in open space made positioning a physics problem, and the screen wrapped, so there was no edge to hide against.
- **Williams Electronics' Defender** (1980), designed by Eugene Jarvis, introduced horizontal scrolling and a radar strip showing the part of the world you were not looking at. It is the first widely played shooter where the play area was larger than the screen.
- **Atari's Tempest** (1981) projected the whole thing down a tube, so the enemies climbed toward the camera instead of across it.
- **Namco's Xevious** (1982) split threats into air and ground targets requiring different weapons, and scrolled vertically over what read as terrain rather than empty space.
- **Williams' Robotron: 2084** (1982), also from Jarvis with Larry DeMar, gave the player two joysticks: one to move, one to aim. Separating movement from firing is the design decision the entire twin-stick lineage rests on.

What all six share is that they took the survival problem and rotated it. None of them made shooting more interesting. They made *being somewhere* more interesting, which is a strong hint about where the genre's actual content lives.

### Why scrolling stuck

Automatic scrolling was not a technical inevitability — Asteroids and Robotron both prove that. It won because it hands pacing control to the designer.

When the camera advances at a fixed rate, the sequence and the timing of every encounter is guaranteed. That makes patterns learnable, makes difficulty curves precise, and makes a run comparable to every other run of the same game. The cost is exploration, and the genre decided very early that choreography was worth more.

## Power-ups turned a run into a build

By the mid-1980s the survival layer was well understood, and the next move was to put something on top of it.

**Konami's Gradius** (1985) is the clearest example. Destroying certain enemies dropped capsules that advanced a selector along a bar at the bottom of the screen — speed, missile, double, laser, option, shield — and you chose when to cash it in. That is a resource management game running underneath a shooter, and it introduced a genuinely painful decision: spend now on something small, or wait and risk dying before the good one.

**Irem's R-Type** (1987) went the other way and gave you one thing: a detachable pod that could be docked front or rear, absorbed fire, and fired independently. Instead of a shopping list, a single object whose placement was the whole tactical layer.

These two approaches — accumulate a build, or master one tool — still describe most of what modern arcade shooters do with progression. The lineage runs directly into contemporary phone games. [Space Shooter - Galaxy Arcade](/apps/space-shooter-classic-arcade/) sits on the accumulate side: rewards earned during a run go into weapons, unlocked upgrades, ship systems and bonuses you pick yourself, so the ship you launch with next time is a different ship.

## Scoring became a second game

Somewhere in the 1990s, top-level players stopped treating survival as the objective. If you can reliably finish a game, the only remaining challenge is how you finish it, and designers responded by building scoring systems complex enough to be worth studying on their own.

Chain scoring is the canonical example: destroy enemies in quick succession and a multiplier climbs, break the rhythm and it resets. This inverts the safety incentive.
