The safe route through a wave and the high-scoring route through it are deliberately different, and the player chooses their own difficulty by choosing how greedy to be.

**Treasure's Radiant Silvergun** (1998) built an elaborate weapon-and-chain system around destroying enemies in colour order. Its successor **Ikaruga** (2001) reduced the idea to something almost austere: your ship switches between two polarities, absorbs same-colour bullets, does extra damage to the opposite colour, and chains score by destroying enemies in groups of three matching colours. The result is a shooter where the bullets are simultaneously the threat and the ammunition.

The important structural point is that scoring layers are optional. A player can ignore them and still finish. That is a rare and useful piece of design: two audiences, one game, no difficulty setting.

## Danmaku: when density became the point

The style most people now call bullet hell — *danmaku*, meaning barrage or curtain of bullets — took shape in Japanese arcades through the 1990s as hardware finally allowed hundreds of sprites on screen at once.

Toaplan's **Batsugun** (1993) is commonly credited as the bridge between the older style and the new one, and when Toaplan closed, its staff scattered into several studios that went on to define the form. **Cave** was one of them, and its **DonPachi** (1995) and **DoDonPachi** (1997) set the template that most later danmaku follows.

The design innovation that made it work is counter-intuitive and easy to miss: the player's vulnerable area shrank. Rather than the whole ship sprite being lethal to touch, only a small point near its centre counts. Once that is true, a gap a few pixels wide is a real, usable route, and a screen that looks completely impassable becomes navigable. Density stopped being a difficulty multiplier and became a *readability* device — slower, denser patterns give you more information about where the gap is than a handful of fast shots ever did.

Several games in this lineage added grazing, which awards score for passing close to bullets without being hit, formalising the idea that proximity is a skill rather than a mistake.

The style also escaped commercial arcades entirely. **Touhou Project**, made largely by a single developer working as Team Shanghai Alice, moved to Windows in 2002 and built a large independent scene around games distributed outside the traditional publishing route.

## What happened when the arcade went away

The coin-operated arcade declined, and the genre lost the venue it was designed for. What it did not lose was its unit of play: a run that lasts a few minutes, ends decisively, and invites an immediate retry.

That unit turned out to be extremely well suited to a device you pull out of your pocket. Touch controls also changed the input in an interesting way — dragging a ship with one finger removes the deadzone and the digital-direction problem of a stick, at the cost of your thumb covering part of the screen. Most modern mobile shooters answer that by keeping the player's ship near the bottom of the display and moving the interesting information upward.

Our own entry keeps the arcade shape rather than the arcade hardware. Four abilities — FIRE for the main weapons, ALT for a secondary attack, a charged Ultimate, and a Shield — and waves that arrive in readable patterns, where movement and timing keep you alive more reliably than firepower. Endless Mode removes the finish line entirely, which is the same open-ended score contract Space Invaders wrote in 1978. If you want the tactical version rather than the historical one, [our guide to reading enemy fire](/blog/space-shooter-arcade-guide/) covers how the patterns actually break down, and [Action & Arcade Games](/apps/category/action-arcade/) has the rest of what we make in the genre.

Reign Creative LLC is an independent studio. The games named above belong to the companies that made them, and none of them are connected to us in any way — they are here because you cannot describe this genre honestly without them.

## What never changed

Five decades, four hardware generations, two continents and at least three complete rethinks of what difficulty means. Through all of it, the shoot 'em up has been a game about occupying the right square metre of screen at the right moment, with a gun attached mostly to give you something to do while you get there.

Everything else — the power meters, the chains, the polarities, the curtains of thousands of bullets — is elaboration on the moment in 1978 when a row of aliens got one step closer and you had to decide which way to move.

title: Seven Picks, Nowhere to Hide: How Hockey Draft Simulators Work
metaTitle: Hockey Draft Simulator App: Seven Picks, No Hiding
body:
Seven decisions. Six players and a coach, and the season is set.

That number is the whole design. In a sport where you draft dozens of players, a bad pick is absorbed — it becomes a small drag on a large system. Here, one poor slot is a substantial fraction of everything you own, and no amount of quality elsewhere hides it. [84-0 Hockey Draft & GM Manager](/apps/hockey-draft-gm-manager/) is built to reward balance between scoring and defence and to punish thin spots, and with a roster this small it does not have to try hard to do either.

## The smallest puzzle in the genre

It is worth seeing the roster sizes side by side, because they explain why the same drafting instincts produce different results across sports.

| Game | Picks that make the roster |
| --- | --- |
| 84-0 Hockey Draft & GM Manager | Six players and a coach |
| [162-0 Baseball Draft & GM Team](/apps/baseball-draft-gm-team/) | Nine players and a coach |
| [38-0 Football Draft XI Soccer](/apps/soccer-draft-gm-xi/) | A full starting XI |

As the roster shrinks, two things happen at once. Each individual pick matters more, and the number of ways to compensate for a mistake falls. A nine-player club has slack; a six-player roster does not. That is why a drafting habit that works perfectly well in the [baseball draft simulator](/blog/baseball-draft-gm-guide/) — taking a flyer on a slot you can fix later — is expensive here.

The corollary is more encouraging: with seven decisions, you can actually think about all of them. A hockey draft is short enough to plan properly, which makes it the best entry point in the genre for anyone who wants to learn drafting theory without managing a large board at the same time.

## Scoring and defence are not the same currency

The obvious way to draft is to take the best available player at each position and let the balance take care of itself. It does not take care of itself, and the reason is worth understanding rather than just accepting.

Scoring and defensive quality do different jobs. More scoring raises how many games you can win by outscoring the opponent. More defensive quality raises how many games stay winnable in the first place. A roster with excellent scoring and thin defence spends the season in high-variance games; a roster with the reverse spends it in tight ones it cannot always close out.

Neither is wrong. What is wrong is buying your fourth unit of a strength you already have while a genuine gap sits open, because the return on the strength is diminishing and the cost of the gap is not.

**A working rule:** at each pick, ask what the roster is currently worst at, and require a clear reason before you draft anything else. "This player is rated higher" is not a clear reason on its own — it is the input, not the argument.

## The goaltending problem

Every small-roster sport has one position that carries disproportionate weight, and in hockey it is the goaltender. It is also the position where drafters make the most self-inflicted errors, in both directions.

Under-spending is the common one. Goaltending is a single slot among seven, and it is easy to treat it as one-seventh of the decision. It is not, because nothing else on the roster substitutes for it — a skater who is having a poor run can be offset by the others, and there is no equivalent redundancy behind a weak goaltender.

Over-spending is the subtler one. Committing your best resources to that slot and then filling five skating positions with whatever is left produces exactly the lopsided roster the projection penalises. The game weighs defence and goaltending as inputs alongside everything else; it does not let one exceptional slot carry an otherwise hollow lineup.

The honest answer is that goaltending should be solved early and solved *properly* — not maximised, and never deferred.

## Search versus judgement

There are two rulesets, and they are not difficulty tiers.

**Unlimited Draft** keeps your options open. You can keep looking until you find the combination you want. What it tests is whether you know what a good roster looks like when nothing prevents you from building one — and the honest failure mode is spending a long time confirming a decision you had already made, then producing a roster no better than a decisive one.

**Limited Draft** gives you one pass at every position with zero refreshes. Search is off the table, and what replaces it is inference. Each option you see is evidence about the quality level of this run, and a good limited drafter is continuously updating a sense of what "good" means here rather than applying a fixed standard from previous games.

The classic limited-draft failure is holding out at an early position for a quality that was never in this pool, then accepting something genuinely poor at the end because there is nothing left. Calibrate on the first two or three slots, then decide quickly.

## The pick that is not a player

The coach completes the roster, and it is the pick most likely to be made carelessly after the effort of assembling six players.

Coaching is one of the factors the projection weighs. More usefully, it is the one decision you make with complete information about your own roster — by the time you get there, you know exactly what you built, where you compromised, and what the lineup will struggle with. Treating it as the final adjustment rather than a formality is free improvement.

## Reading an 84-game projection

The simulator turns the finished lineup into a complete regular-season record over 84 games.

Be clear about what that is. It is the output of a model, computed from the roster you assembled according to the game's own rules. It does not describe, predict or relate to any real hockey game, club, player or season — the entire pool is fictional and generated inside the game. It is not a forecast of anything, and it carries no information about any real-world event.

What it *is* is a score, and the most productive way to use it is comparatively. Most rosters land short of perfect, which is by design; the number to beat is not the perfect record but your own previous best. Replaying with a different approach and improving on your last result is how the game is meant to be played, and it also happens to be a decent experimental method: change one thing, run it again, see whether the projection moves.

That discipline — one variable at a time — is worth more than any individual piece of drafting advice, because it lets you learn the model rather than trusting somebody's rules of thumb about it.

## Franchise GM Mode

Beyond a single draft, Franchise GM Mode organises forwards, defenders and goaltending across multiple seasons, weighing strengths against weak positions and guiding the club forward.

The change this introduces is a time dimension. A one-off draft asks what is best now. A franchise asks what stays good, and the two answers differ. A roster optimised for a single projection can be a poor foundation, while a roster built to remain solid may never post the single best season you are capable of.

The other thing multi-season play gives you is a cure for a bad draft. In a one-shot format, an imbalanced roster is simply the roster. Across seasons, shoring up a weak position before it costs you is a move you can actually make — which is the same corrective role trades play in the larger-roster sports, covered in the [basketball draft and GM guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/).

## The supporting formats

Timed challenges, roster-building tasks, quizzes, achievements and side-by-side player comparisons fill in around the management.

The comparison tool deserves a mention, because it addresses the single hardest part of small-roster drafting: deciding between two players who are close. When each pick is roughly a seventh of your team, "close enough, take either" is not good advice, and looking at two profiles directly against each other is usually how you find the attribute that actually separates them.

## A drafting checklist

1. **Solve goaltending properly and early.** Not maximised, not deferred.
2. **At each pick, name the roster's current worst area** and require an argument to draft anywhere else.
3. **Calibrate in the first three picks** if refreshes are off, then commit without agonising.
4. **Make the coach a considered decision**, with the roster's known weakness in mind.
5. **Change one thing per run.** The projection is only informative if you can attribute the change to something.

84-0 Hockey Draft & GM Manager is free to download on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases and an Everyone content rating.

Drafting under different constraints — larger rosters and deeper boards, or style matchups rather than positions — is covered in the [football draft guide](/blog/football-draft-gm-guide/) and the [MMA and boxing fight draft guide](/blog/mma-boxing-fight-draft-guide/). The full set of the studio's management and drafting titles is under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Hockey Line Combinations Explained: Why Coaches Keep Shuffling Them
metaTitle: Hockey Line Combinations Explained: Why Lines Shuffle
secondaryKeywords: what is a forward line in hockey
body:
Watch a coach for two periods and you will see the same forwards appear beside three different partners. It looks like indecision. It is closer to the opposite: line combinations are the main lever a hockey coach holds once the puck has dropped, and pulling it is most of the job.

Understanding why is the difference between watching hockey as a series of individuals and watching it as what it actually is — a rotation of small units, each of which is either working or not.

## The unit is the thing, not the player

Hockey groups its skaters twice over. Forwards are grouped into **lines** of three: a centre with a left wing and a right wing. Defencemen are grouped into **pairs**. Those two groupings rotate independently, so the five skaters on the ice at any given moment are normally one forward line plus one defence pair, with the goaltender staying on throughout.

That is exactly the shape [84-0 Hockey Draft & GM Manager](/apps/hockey-draft-gm-manager/) asks you to build: a starting six of centre, left wing, right wing, two defence slots and a goaltender, plus the coach who ties it together. Six decisions, which sounds small until you notice that every one of them is load-bearing.

The consequence of playing in units is that individual quality stops being the interesting question. A forward who is excellent at retrieving pucks in the corner and terrible at finishing is a problem on one line and a solution on another. Nothing about the player changed; the combination did.

## Why lines exist at all

Other sports substitute at stoppages. Hockey substitutes while the play is running, and shifts are short — deliberately, brutally short — because skating at full effort has a hard ceiling measured in seconds rather than minutes.

That single fact restructures everything. A hockey roster is not a starting lineup with reserves behind it; it is a **rotation**, and every player in it will be on the ice. The usual arrangement across the sport is four forward lines and three defence pairs, which is internally tidy: four lines of three forwards accounts for twelve forwards, and three pairs of two accounts for six defencemen.

So the question a coach is answering is not "who are my best players" but "how do I divide the available minutes so that the ones I trust most get the situations that matter most, without any of them being exhausted when it counts".

## What a working line contains

The instinct of every new drafter is to put the three highest-rated forwards together. It is also the most reliable way to produce a line that underperforms its ratings.

Functioning lines tend to contain different jobs rather than three copies of the same one:

- **Someone who gets the puck back.** Forechecking, board battles, winning it in the corner. Unglamorous and non-negotiable, because a line that cannot recover possession spends its shifts defending.
- **Someone who moves it.** Vision, passing, and the willingness to give the puck up. Frequently the centre, though not always.
- **Someone who finishes.** The release and the instinct to be in the right place when the chance arrives.

Three finishers on one line will all drift to the same space and none of them will do the retrieval work. Three grinders will win every puck and have nothing to do with it. The combinations that stick are almost always the ones where the three jobs are genuinely covered.

### Handedness, and why it is not trivia

A left-handed shot playing on the right wing receives the puck on their forehand coming across the middle and shoots from a different angle than a right-handed shot in the same spot. Neither arrangement is correct in general; they produce different shot locations and different passing lanes.

The same applies on defence, where a pair with one left-shot and one right-shot defenceman can each play their natural side without turning their body away from the play. Coaches care about this more than casual viewers expect, and it is one reason a pair that looks unbalanced on ratings can still be the better arrangement.

## The hierarchy, and what each line is for

Lines are usually numbered by the minutes and the situations they get.

| Line | Typical job | What good looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Score, against the opposition's best | Producing while facing the hardest matchup |
| Second | Score, against softer matchups | Genuine secondary production rather than a diluted copy of the first |
| Third | Defensive assignments, checking, tough zone starts | Coming out even against a stronger line |
| Fourth | Short, energetic shifts; preserving the top lines | Not conceding, and changing the momentum of a period |

The bottom of that table is where most people misjudge a roster. A fourth line's contribution is largely negative in the arithmetic sense — it consists of goals that did not happen and minutes the first line did not have to play. That contribution is real and it never appears next to anybody's name.

Defence pairs follow the same logic in miniature. The pair that plays the most is not necessarily the one with the highest ratings; it is the one the coach trusts with a one-goal lead and a faceoff in their own end.

## The levers a coach actually has

Once play starts, a coach controls three things.

**Matchup.** Rulebooks generally give one side the final line change before a faceoff, so one coach can choose who faces whom and the other has to react. This is why a checking line exists in the first place: its purpose is to make the opposing coach's best option unattractive.

**Zone starts.** A faceoff in the attacking end and a faceoff in the defensive end are different assignments. Coaches routinely give offensive-minded lines the favourable draws and hand the awkward ones to a line built to survive them — which then makes the raw production numbers of both lines misleading.

**Minutes.** Shortening the bench late in a close game concentrates ice time in the lines a coach trusts, at the cost of running them tired. It is a trade, and coaches make it every night.

## Why lines get shuffled

Given how much value there is in combinations settling, constant shuffling looks self-defeating. There are four sound reasons for it and one bad one.

1. **Injury.** Somebody has to move, and moving one forward usually moves three.
2. **A line that is not working.** Not the same as a line that is not scoring. A line getting outplayed on possession is failing even if the scoreboard has not noticed yet.
3. **Reviving a struggling player.** Putting a forward who has lost confidence beside a playmaker is the cheapest available fix.
4. **Chasing or protecting.** Behind late, coaches load one line up deliberately. Ahead late, they shorten the bench and lean on the lines they trust defensively.

The bad reason is reacting to a single result. Combinations need shifts together before you know anything, and a coach who rebuilds the forward group after every defeat never accumulates the evidence that would tell them what is actually wrong.

## Special teams are a different roster

When a side is short a skater, the arithmetic changes: five skaters against four, instead of five against five.

That extra space means the units are not built like ordinary lines. A power-play unit is normally assembled from whoever moves and shoots the puck best rather than from an intact forward line, which often means loading it with forwards and carrying a single defenceman for the point. A penalty-killing unit is chosen on the opposite basis — players who deny passing lanes, block shots and get the puck out of the zone without needing to do anything clever with it.

The practical implication for roster building is that special-teams ability is a separate axis. A player who is unremarkable at even strength can be genuinely valuable on one of these units, and a lineup that ignores the distinction is leaving something on the table.

## Drafting for combination

All of which points at a specific drafting habit: **stop asking who is best available and start asking what this lineup is currently missing.**

The hockey draft asks for six slots and a coach, and the game's own framing is explicit that a lineup loaded up in one area can still fall short — position balance, coaching, defence and goaltending all feed the projection. The two rulesets pull in different directions. Unlimited Draft lets you keep searching for a combination that fits, which rewards knowing what you are looking for. Limited Draft gives you one pass with zero refreshes, which rewards deciding what the roster needs *before* you see the options.

Franchise GM Mode is where combination thinking earns most, because it extends past a single draft into organising forwards, defenders and goaltending across seasons and shoring up weak positions before they cost you. A one-off draft is a snapshot; a franchise is the same problem with the ability to fix it. The [hockey draft and GM guide](/blog/hockey-draft-gm-guide/) goes further into that side, and the game's side-by-side player comparisons are the fastest way to test whether two candidates actually differ in the way you think they do.

## What the projection is doing

When the last pick is in and the simulator returns a projected 84-game record, that number is the game's own assessment of the lineup you built, produced by its internal rules.

Three things are worth stating plainly. The players are fictional and generated inside the game, so nothing in the result relates to any real league, team or athlete. It is a score on a roster puzzle, not a prediction, a forecast or guidance of any kind. And the perfect record the game is named for is deliberately hard — most rosters land short, and the size of the shortfall is the feedback you drafted for.

The productive loop is comparative. Change one slot, draft again, and see whether the projection agrees with your reasoning about combinations. That tells you something real about how you evaluate a lineup, even though it tells you nothing about hockey outside the game.

## Where to read next

If the positions themselves are the part you want spelled out, the [hockey positions guide](/blog/hockey-positions-explained/) covers what each of the six slots actually does. The [football positions guide](/blog/football-positions-explained-for-drafting/) shows the same unit-versus-individual argument in a sport with far more slots to fill. And if you want to run a franchise on a train with patchy signal, [sports GM games without internet](/blog/sports-gm-games-without-internet/) covers what to check before you rely on one.

Everything the studio makes in this genre is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Hockey Positions Explained: What Each of the Six Slots Actually Does
metaTitle: Hockey Positions Explained: All Six on the Ice
secondaryKeywords: what does a centre do in hockey
left wing vs right wing hockey
body:
Six slots. Centre, left wing, right wing, two defencemen and a goaltender — that is the whole lineup a hockey draft asks you to fill, and it is the smallest set of decisions in any of the major drafting sports.

Small does not mean easy. With six slots, every one of them is load-bearing, and there is nowhere to hide a mistake.

## The labels describe where you start, not where you are allowed

Before going through the positions individually, one correction that saves a lot of confusion: hockey positions are not zones of responsibility in the way that soccer positions can be. Everybody defends and everybody attacks, and the play moves too fast for anything else to be possible.

What a position actually tells you is where a player lines up for a faceoff, which part of the ice they are primarily accountable for, and what the coach expects them to do first when possession changes hands. That last one is the useful definition.

## Centre

The most demanding forward slot, and it is not close.

A centre operates through the middle of the ice, which is the most congested area available and the one where the least time exists to make a decision. Three responsibilities define the position:

**Faceoffs.** Every stoppage restarts with one, and the centre takes it. Winning a draw in the attacking end hands your line a possession in a dangerous place; losing one in your own end hands the other side the same gift. It is a small, repeated advantage that accumulates over a game.

**The middle lane.** Centres carry the puck through the neutral zone and support both wingers, which means covering more ice than anyone else on the line. Vision matters here more than raw skill, because the centre is usually the player with the widest view of what is developing.

**First forward back.** When possession turns over, the centre is typically the forward responsible for the area in front of their own net — the highest-danger real estate on the ice. A centre who does not do this reliably creates a defensive problem that no amount of scoring compensates for.

That combination is why "two-way centre" is close to the highest compliment available in the sport, and why a centre who is excellent at only the offensive half of the job is a genuinely awkward player to build around.

## Left wing and right wing

Wingers work the outer lanes and, in most systems, live along the boards.

Their attacking job is straightforward to describe and hard to do: get the puck out of the corner, drive the net, and be in a position to finish. Board battles are the substance of the role, and a winger who loses them consistently makes their line's possession numbers collapse whatever their shot is like.

Their defensive job is the part casual viewers never watch. In most defensive structures the wingers are responsible for the opposition's defencemen at the blue line — the players receiving the puck at the point and shooting from distance. A winger who drifts off that assignment gives the other side free shooting lanes, and the goal that eventually results will be blamed on somebody else entirely.

### Types of winger

- **Power winger** — wins the boards, gets to the front of the net, hard to move. Generates chances by force.
- **Skill winger** — creates separation, finds space, finishes. Generates chances by geometry.
- **Checking winger** — reliable without the puck, wins the defensive assignment, kills penalties.

None of these is the correct answer. A line with three of the same kind is the wrong answer, which is the argument made at greater length in the [line combinations guide](/blog/hockey-line-combinations-explained/).

### Handedness and the off wing

A left-handed shot playing right wing takes passes on their forehand as they cut toward the middle and shoots from an angle a right-handed shot would not. Coaches use this deliberately. It is not better or worse in the abstract — it is a different set of shot locations and passing lanes, and it is one reason two wingers with similar ratings can produce very different results in the same slot.

## Defence

Two slots, and the job runs in both directions.

**Going backwards: gap control.** The core defensive skill is managing the distance between yourself and the attacker carrying the puck. Too much space and they can shoot or pass through you; too little and they can skate around you. Everything else a defenceman does defensively — angling attackers to the outside, clearing the front of the net, blocking shots — sits downstream of getting that distance right.

**Going forwards: the first pass.** The fastest way out of your own end is a clean, early pass to a forward. A defenceman who makes that pass turns defence into attack in one motion. A defenceman who cannot has to skate the puck out under pressure or fire it away and concede possession, and the difference between those two options across a whole game is enormous.

Beyond that, defencemen hold the offensive blue line, decide when to pinch in to keep a puck alive (the classic high-risk, high-reward hockey decision), and shoot from the point.

### The types, and how a pair fits together

A **stay-at-home** defenceman prioritises denial: position, gap, net front, safe clears. An **offensive** defenceman activates into the attack and accepts more risk to generate chances. A **two-way** defenceman does an acceptable amount of both.

Pairs generally work better when the two players complement each other, because both defencemen joining the attack at once is how odd-man rushes happen going the other way. It is the same logic as lines: a pair is a unit, and the question is fit rather than ranking.

## Goaltender

The only position in the sport where one player can decide a result on their own, in either direction.

What separates goaltenders is less about spectacular saves than about three quieter things:

**Positioning.** A goaltender who is in the right place makes hard shots look routine. Most of what looks like reflex is actually pre-positioning that removed the need for a reflex.

**Rebound control.** Stopping the puck is half the job; putting it somewhere safe is the other half. A save that drops into the slot is barely a save.

**Puck-handling.** A goaltender comfortable playing the puck behind the net relieves pressure on defencemen chasing dump-ins, which quietly improves the whole defensive group.

Goaltending is also the most volatile position to evaluate, because the workload varies so much with the team in front. That volatility is precisely why it is a bad place to economise: the downside of a poor goaltender is not a slightly worse result, it is losing games your skaters won.

## The coach is a roster slot too

[84-0 Hockey Draft & GM Manager](/apps/hockey-draft-gm-manager/) asks you to pick a coach alongside the six players, and it is not decoration — the game's projection weighs coaching along with position balance, defence and goaltending.

That is a fair representation of the sport. Coaching in hockey is largely about deployment: who plays against whom, who starts in which zone, and who is on the ice with a one-goal lead and two minutes left. Those decisions are made with the roster you handed over, and they are the reason two identical lineups can produce different outcomes.

## Judging each slot at a draft board

| Slot | Ask first | The failure mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Centre | Can they do the defensive half of the job? | An offensive centre who leaves the slot uncovered |
| Wings | Do they win the boards and hold the point assignment? | Three finishers who all want the same space |
| Defence | Gap control going back, first pass going forward | Two of the same type paired together |
| Goaltender | Positioning and rebound control before highlight saves | Treating it as the leftover slot |
| Coach | Does the deployment style match the roster you built? | Ignoring it entirely |

The two draft rulesets test different halves of this. Unlimited Draft lets you keep comparing until the combination fits, which rewards knowing what you are looking for. Limited Draft gives you one pass with zero refreshes, which rewards deciding what each slot must provide before you see who is available. Franchise GM Mode then extends the whole thing across seasons, where organising forwards, defenders and goaltending and repairing weak positions becomes an ongoing job rather than a single decision. The [hockey draft and GM guide](/blog/hockey-draft-gm-guide/) covers that longer game.

## What the simulator is actually doing

The projected 84-game record that comes back at the end of a draft is the game's own verdict on the lineup, produced by its internal rules acting on players it generated.

Worth stating explicitly: nothing in that result describes, forecasts or relates to any real league, team or athlete, and none of it is a prediction or guidance of any kind. It is a score on a roster puzzle. The perfect record the game is named for is deliberately hard to reach, so most lineups finish short — and the size of the shortfall is the feedback the exercise exists to produce.

The way to use it is comparative: change one slot, run it again, and find out whether the model agrees with your reasoning about what that slot was worth.

## Where to read next

The natural companion to this article is the [line combinations guide](/blog/hockey-line-combinations-explained/), which covers how these six slots get grouped, deployed and shuffled. For the same positional-value argument in a sport with three separate personnel groups, see [football positions explained](/blog/football-positions-explained-for-drafting/); for a sport that expresses positions as shape rather than as slots, see [soccer formations explained](/blog/soccer-formations-explained/).

title: How Fantasy Draft Strategy Actually Works
metaTitle: Fantasy Draft Strategy: How It Actually Works
secondaryKeywords: how to prepare for a draft
body:
Pick thirty-four of a twelve-round draft. The top name on your board is a shooting guard, and you have already taken two of those. The next name down is worse on every number on screen and plays the one position you have not touched.

Whatever you do in the next four seconds is your draft strategy. Not the plan you wrote before the draft opened — this.

## A draft is an allocation problem wearing a scouting costume

It looks like a talent evaluation exercise. It is a resource allocation exercise. You have a fixed number of picks, you do not control what is available when your turn arrives, and every selection permanently removes an option from the board for everyone including you.

That reframing does real work, because it changes what "good pick" means. A good pick is not the best player. It is the selection that improves your **finished** roster the most, accounting for everything you can still reasonably get later.

Almost every recognisable draft strategy is a different answer to one question: how do you decide what a pick is worth to you specifically, rather than what a player is worth in the abstract?

## Replacement level: the idea the rest sits on

The number beside a player tells you how good they are. It does not tell you what drafting them does for your team. For that you need the player they replace.

Say you are choosing between two candidates, using ratings out of 100:

- An **88-rated guard**, at a position where you already start an 85. Net improvement: **3**.
- A **79-rated centre**, at a position currently filled by a 61-rated bench body. Net improvement: **18**.

The lower-rated player is worth six times more to you. Nothing about that arithmetic is subtle, and people still take the 88, because the 88 is the bigger number and the bigger number feels like the better decision.

Two honest caveats. First, ratings rarely convert to results linearly — the distance from 85 to 88 is not necessarily the same amount of "team quality" as 61 to 79, in a real sport or in a simulation. Second, the fallback is not always as bad as you think; deep positions have decent fallbacks, which is exactly why they are deep. Replacement-level thinking is a direction, not a formula.

But the direction is right, and it dissolves the phoney argument between "best player available" and "draft for need". Those are not two philosophies. They are two situations. Best available is correct when the gap at the top of the board is enormous. Need is correct when the hole you are ignoring cannot be patched later. Both are the same calculation run on different boards.

## Tiers carry information that rankings throw away

A ranked list is a lie of uniform spacing. It presents the gap between the fourth and fifth names as equivalent to the gap between the twelfth and thirteenth, and it almost never is.

Tiers fix this. Group the board into bands where you would be genuinely content with any name in the band. Then the strategy falls out of the structure:

- **Your tier still has five names in it.** You can spend this pick elsewhere. You will very likely still get one of the five.
- **Your tier is down to one name.** This is the pick. Waiting costs you the whole drop to the next tier.
- **Two positions both have one name left.** Take the one whose next tier is further down.

### Building tiers without overthinking it

Sort each position by rating and read down the column looking for the cliffs — the places where the numbers stop declining gently and fall. Draw the line at the cliff. You do not need precision here. Five or six bands per position is plenty, and the exercise takes a couple of minutes.

The point of tiers is not accuracy. It is that they force you to notice the shape of the drop-off before you are under time pressure, when noticing is easy.

### Reading a run

A run is when several managers take the same position in consecutive picks. It happens because everyone is reading the same board and the same cliff, and it is the single most common way a draft plan gets destroyed.

The correct response is unglamorous: check whether your tier at that position survives the run. If four names remain and three picks separate you from your turn, you are fine — hold. If the run will empty the tier before you pick again, you either jump into the run now or you accept the next tier and plan around it. What you should not do is join a run out of anxiety when your tier is deep, because that is how you end up with three players at a position you had already solved.

## Your slot changes the plan, not the outcome

In a snake draft the order reverses each round, so your position determines the gap between your picks rather than their average quality.

Take ten teams. Round one runs picks 1 to 10 in order; round two runs 11 to 20 in reverse. The manager at slot 1 selects with picks **1 and 20**. The manager at slot 10 selects with picks **10 and 11**.

That is a 19-pick gap versus a 1-pick gap, and it has direct consequences:

- **Early slot.** You get the single best player in the draft and then watch nineteen names disappear. This rewards taking the one player you rate far above the field, because that surplus is the compensation for the wait. It punishes plans that depend on a specific second player being there.
- **Late slot.** You never get the top name, but you take two players back to back with nobody able to interrupt. This rewards taking a matched pair from the same tier, and it lets you cover two positions in one motion.
- **Middle slots.** Even gaps, no extremes, and the most sensitivity to runs, because there are always picks on both sides of you.

None of these is an advantage. They are different constraints, and the mistake is running an early-slot plan from a late slot.

## Four strategy families, and what each one is actually buying

Named strategies proliferate, but nearly all of them are one of these four trades.

**Balanced accumulation.** Take the largest available improvement at every pick, spread across positions. Buys: reliability and a high floor. Costs: you rarely end up with the single best unit in any one area.

**Concentration.** Spend early picks on a small number of very high-rated players and accept weak slots elsewhere. Buys: a genuine ceiling and units nobody can match. Costs: your weakest slot is very weak, and formats that weight depth punish this hard.

**Scarcity-first.** Take the thin positions early regardless of raw rating, and fill the deep ones from the leftovers. Buys: you never finish with an uncoverable hole. Costs: you pass on better players and can end up merely adequate everywhere.

**Deliberate waiting.** Identify a position where the tenth-best option is nearly as good as the third and refuse to spend an early pick there. Buys: extra early picks for scarce positions. Costs: it fails badly if you misread the depth, and you cannot know you misread it until it is too late to fix.

Every one of these is right sometimes. That is not a cop-out — it is the actual structure of the problem. The board is different every draft, the format changes what the roster is scored on, and the other managers move too.

## What strategy cannot do

It cannot guarantee a result. A draft has an irreducible amount of variance in it: which players are generated or available, where the runs happen, what the managers around you do. A well-reasoned draft can produce a mediocre roster and a careless one can fall into a good board.

That is not an argument for drafting carelessly. It is an argument for judging yourself on the decision rather than the outcome, and for evaluating any approach across many drafts instead of the one you remember.

In a simulation, there is a second limit worth stating plainly. When a game returns a record for the roster you drafted, that number is the output of a model scoring your team-building. It is not a prediction about anything in the real world, and it should never be read as one.

## Formats decide which strategy is even legal

The reason drafting stays interesting after fifty runs is that changing the rules changes the correct answer with the same players on the board.

[Basketball Draft GM Franchise](/apps/pro-basketball-draft-gm-mode/) includes eight draft formats — Unlimited Draft, Quick Draft, Blind Draft, Franchise Draft, Salary Cap Draft, VS Computer, Battle Mode and a Daily Challenge — and they pull in different directions:

- **Unlimited Draft** gives you room to compare, which is where you learn what a board looks like.
- **Quick Draft** removes deliberation time, so whatever tiers you built beforehand are the only structure you get.
- **Blind Draft** removes information, which makes scarcity-first reasoning more valuable than fine-grained rating comparisons.
- **Salary Cap Draft** attaches a price to every pick, converting the ranking problem into an allocation problem where a merely good player at a low cost can beat a great one at a high cost.
- **VS Computer** and **Battle Mode** add an opponent, which introduces a resource you were not tracking: what they can still take.

The catalogue description of the game is direct about what the season rewards — balance and depth carry more weight than any single marquee pick. That is a design decision, and it is exactly the kind of thing you can only learn by drafting differently and comparing.

[20-0 Football Draft & GM Mode](/apps/football-draft-gm-mode/) makes the same point from the other end with its Limited Draft, which removes refreshes entirely. Take away the ability to keep looking and every pick has to stand on its own, which is the purest test of whether your tiers were real or decorative.

## A practice loop that actually improves you

1. **Tier the board before your first pick**, not during. Under time pressure you will default to the ranking.
2. **Name what you gave up on every selection.** If you cannot say which player you passed on and why, you did not decide anything.
3. **Track your worst slot, not your best.** The roster is judged on the whole, and the position you keep not fixing is where the loss lives.
4. **Run the same plan several times.** One draft tells you about that board. Five tell you about the plan.
5. **Write one sentence afterwards** about why the result came out where it did. This is the only step that converts drafting into learning, and it is the one everybody skips.

## Where to read next

The two big format decisions each deserve their own treatment: [snake versus auction drafting](/blog/snake-draft-vs-auction-draft/) covers what changes when picks are bought instead of taken in order, and [salary cap basics](/blog/salary-cap-basics-for-gm-games/) covers budgets as a constraint. If the preparation side is what you want to improve, [building a draft board](/blog/what-makes-a-good-draft-board/) is the practical version of the tier work above, and the [basketball draft simulator guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/) applies all of it to one game end to end.

The rest of the studio's drafting and management titles sit in the [sports GM category](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: How Historians Date Events: The Methods Behind the Numbers on a Timeline
metaTitle: How Historians Date Events: The Methods Explained
secondaryKeywords: what does circa mean in history

sources.p: Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit, University of Oxford
Research Laboratory for Archaeology and the History of Art, University of Oxford
U.S. National Archives and Records Administration

body:
"How do they even know that?" is the right question to ask of any date attached to something that happened before living memory, and it has real answers. There are perhaps five families of method doing the work, each with a domain where it is strong and a domain where it produces confident nonsense. This is a tour of all five, including the failure mode of each.

## The question behind every date on a timeline

A timeline gives you a number and moves on. What it does not show is the chain of reasoning that produced the number — and that chain varies enormously in strength. Some dates are recorded in a document written at the time by someone present. Some are inferred from a chemical measurement on a fragment of charcoal, calibrated against a reference curve, and published as a range. Some are conventions that scholars agreed on in order to have something to point at.

All three appear on the same timeline in the same typeface. Knowing which kind you are looking at is most of the skill.

## Two families of method

Dating methods divide into two broad families, and understanding the split makes everything else easier.

**Relative dating** establishes *order* without producing numbers. If one layer of soil sits above another and neither has been disturbed, the lower one was deposited first. That is a real, defensible finding, and it carries no dates at all.

**Absolute dating** attaches an actual figure, almost always with a stated uncertainty. Radiocarbon measurement, tree-ring counting, and a document that names its own date all belong here.

In practice they are used together. Relative methods build the skeleton — this before that, this contemporary with that — and a comparatively small number of absolute dates pin the skeleton to the calendar. A site with a hundred stratified layers and four radiocarbon dates is not four-hundredths dated; the four dates constrain the whole sequence, because the layers between them are bracketed.

## Stratigraphy: the sequence in the ground

The oldest principle in the toolkit is also the simplest. In an undisturbed deposit, material accumulates from the bottom up, so lower is earlier. Archaeological excavation, as the National Park Service describes the discipline, records the position of everything it removes precisely because that position is itself evidence.

Two qualifications matter more than the principle:

- **"Undisturbed" is a claim, not a default.** Burrowing animals, later construction, ploughing, flooding and looting all move material between layers. Establishing that a deposit is intact is part of the work, not an assumption preceding it.
- **A layer dates the deposition, not the objects.** A coin in a layer tells you the layer formed no earlier than the coin was minted. It does not tell you the layer formed *when* the coin was minted — the coin could have circulated for decades first. This is why archaeologists speak of a *terminus post quem*: a date after which something must have happened.

That second point is a general one, and it recurs in every method below.

## Radiocarbon: what it measures, and what it does not

Radiocarbon dating is the method most people have heard of and the one most often described inaccurately.

The physical basis: living organisms continuously exchange carbon with their environment, including a small proportion of the unstable isotope carbon-14. When the organism dies, that exchange stops and the carbon-14 present begins to decay at a known rate. Measuring how much remains indicates how long ago the exchange stopped. Willard F. Libby was awarded the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in the Nobel Foundation's words, "for his method to use carbon-14 for age determination in archaeology, geology, geophysics, and other branches of science."

Three things about the method are routinely lost in summary.

**A raw measurement is not a calendar date.** The amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has not been constant through time, so a measured radiocarbon age has to be converted using a calibration curve built from independently dated material. The Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit distributes OxCal, the widely used calibration and chronological modelling program; its current release works with the IntCal20 curve, alongside SHCal20 for the Southern Hemisphere and Marine20 for marine samples. A date reported without saying whether it is calibrated is ambiguous, which is why publications mark the distinction explicitly.

**The output is a probability distribution.** Because the calibration relationship is wiggly rather than straight, one measurement can map onto more than one stretch of calendar time. Results are therefore published as ranges at a stated confidence level. When a popular article converts that range into a single crisp year, information has been discarded.

**It dates the death of the organism, not the event of interest.** A charcoal fragment dates the tree, and the tree may have been dead for a long time before it was burned — the "old wood" problem. Short-lived material such as a seed, a twig or a nutshell sits much closer to the event, which is why excavators prefer it. Bridging the gap between what was measured and what you want to know is an argument that has to be made, not a step that can be skipped.

The method also has a practical ceiling. Beyond roughly fifty thousand years there is too little carbon-14 remaining to measure reliably, so anything older requires an entirely different technique.

## Tree rings: the method that reaches single years

Dendrochronology is the highest-precision dating method available for the periods it covers. Trees in seasonal climates add one growth ring per year, and the pattern of wide and narrow rings — driven by shared climate — repeats across trees in a region. Match the pattern in an unknown sample against a regional master chronology built from overlapping known samples, and the sample's rings can be assigned to specific calendar years.

The Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research at the University of Arizona, founded in 1937 by A.E. Douglass, who originated the science of tree-ring dating, remains a central institution in the field.

The constraints are specific:

- You need enough rings to produce a distinctive pattern; a short sample can match many places by chance.
- You need a master chronology covering the right region and species.
- You need the outermost ring — ideally with bark still attached — to date the felling year rather than some earlier point in the tree's life.
- The tree must grow in a climate with a genuine annual cycle, which limits the method geographically.

Where all of that holds, dendrochronology can date a timber to the year and sometimes the season. That precision is also why tree-ring sequences are used to build and test radiocarbon calibration curves: one method with absolute annual resolution anchoring another with statistical resolution.

## Written records: the most direct and the most deceptive

A document that states its own date looks like the end of the problem. Frequently it is the beginning of one.

Records are dated within a system, and systems differ. Regnal years count from a ruler's accession, which requires knowing when the accession was and how the local convention handled partial years. Calendar reform shifted dates by days and moved the start of the year. Different regions adopted the same reform decades or centuries apart. None of that makes the records unreliable; it makes them require translation. Archives generally state which system a document uses — The National Archives in the United Kingdom and the U.S. National Archives both publish research guidance to their own holdings — and the translation is a solved problem once you know you have to do it.

We cover the calendar side of this in more depth in [how to actually learn something from a timeline](/blog/world-history-timeline-guide/), including why there is no year zero and why two sources can give different years for the same event without either being wrong.

The subtler problem with written records is that a text tells you what someone wrote, which is not automatically what happened. A chronicle compiled two centuries after the events it describes is a source about the compiler's period as much as the one it narrates. Historians handle this by asking when the text was produced, from what, and for whom — and by looking for independent corroboration.

**Synchronisms** are the practical tool here. If a record in one tradition mentions an event that appears in another tradition dated by a different system, the two chronologies can be locked together. Chains of these links are how ancient chronologies get built, and their weakness is that a single bad link propagates through everything downstream.

## Astronomical anchors

Some ancient records describe events in the sky — eclipses, planetary conjunctions, heliacal risings. Because celestial mechanics can be computed backwards, an unambiguous description can sometimes be matched to a specific computable date. The U.S. Naval Observatory's Astronomical Applications Department publishes the kind of positional data this depends on.

The catch is "unambiguous". Ancient descriptions are often brief, sometimes figurative, and frequently do not record the observing location — and eclipses recur. A proposed match is a hypothesis whose strength depends on how many candidate dates fit and how specific the description is. When it works, though, an astronomical tie-point is exceptionally strong, because the calculation does not depend on any human record being accurate.

## Physical remains and their limits

Beyond radiocarbon there are other physical approaches — luminescence methods for when mineral grains were last exposed to light, techniques based on other decay systems for geological timescales, and typological sequences built from how object styles change. Each has its own domain, its own error behaviour, and its own version of the same warning: the method dates a material property, and connecting that property to a human event is a separate inferential step.

Sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List frequently carry dates derived from several of these methods at once, cross-checked against each other. Agreement between independent methods is the strongest evidence available in the field, and disagreement is what drives the next round of work.

## Why dates change

Historical and archaeological dates get revised, and the revisions are sometimes large. Three ordinary reasons account for most of it:

1. **Calibration improves.** Radiocarbon calibration curves are periodically revised as more independently dated material is incorporated. A date published against an older curve may shift when recalculated.
2. **Better samples appear.** A date resting on charcoal from long-lived timber can be replaced by one resting on a seed from the same context, cutting out the old-wood gap.
3. **An inference is re-examined.** Many dates depend on chains — this layer relates to that structure, which relates to that record. Break or improve a link in the chain and everything attached to it moves.

A field that never revised its dates would not be more reliable. It would be one that had stopped checking.

## What this means when you read a timeline

Three habits are worth carrying:

- **Notice the phrasing.** "Circa", "conventionally dated to", "traditionally attributed to" and "no earlier than" all mean different things, and each is a signal about how much weight the number can take.
- **Ask what was actually measured.** For any scientific date, the useful question is what material was tested and how close that material sits to the event.
- **Prefer converging evidence.** A date supported by a document, a stratigraphic sequence and a radiocarbon range is in a different category from one supported by any single strand.

## Using a timeline app for this

[World History Timeline Sim](/apps/world-history-timeline-sim/) covers more than 2,000 events and lets you browse by year, era, region, country and category, alongside a world history map, quizzes, flashcards and timeline-ordering exercises. That format is genuinely useful for the thing it does: building the relative structure — what was happening alongside what — which is the scaffolding that dating methods hang on.

It is an orientation tool, not a citation apparatus. When a date matters for something you are writing or arguing, take it to an archive, a museum catalogue entry or a publication that states its evidence. The archives listed in our sources below are free and open.

More apps in this area are collected under [education and brain training](/apps/category/education-brain/), and our other writing on the subject sits under [education and brain training articles](/blog/category/education-brain/). If you want the period labels that sit above these dates — "Bronze Age", "medieval", "early modern" — and where they come from, see [how the major eras of world history are defined](/blog/major-eras-of-world-history/).

title: How Long Does It Take to Learn Russian? What the Published Figures Do and Do Not Say
metaTitle: How Long Does It Take to Learn Russian?
secondaryKeywords: how hard is russian to learn

sources.p: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Nobody can tell you how long Russian will take you, and anybody who does is selling something. What does exist is one published institutional figure, produced by an organisation that has taught the language to thousands of students under conditions it documents. Understanding exactly what that figure measures is more useful than any estimate someone could invent for your situation.

## The figure, and what it describes

The US Foreign Service Institute trains American diplomats in the languages they will work in, and it groups those languages by how long its students typically need to reach **Professional Working Proficiency** — a score of **Speaking-3/Reading-3** on the Interagency Language Roundtable scale.

Russian is in **Category III**, at approximately **44 weeks of full-time instruction**, published as **1,100 class hours**.

Every part of that sentence is load-bearing:

- **Full-time.** 1,100 hours across 44 weeks is about **25 class hours a week**, before any homework — a job, not an evening habit.
- **Class**, meaning small-group instruction with trained teachers, correcting you continuously.
- **Typically**, meaning an average across students who have been selected and are being paid to do this as their job.
- **Speaking-3/Reading-3**, a professional standard — using the language for work, not ordering coffee.

Where Russian sits relative to its neighbours is the genuinely useful part:

| Category | Weeks | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | shortest | Spanish, French, Italian, Dutch |
| II | 36 | German, Malay, Indonesian, Swahili |
| III | 44 | Russian, Polish, Thai, Khmer, Vietnamese |
| IV | 88 | Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic |

Russian is demanding, and it is a **full category below** the hardest group — the Category IV figure is exactly double. If your mental model was that Russian sits alongside Mandarin in difficulty, FSI's own accounting disagrees.

## Why you should not divide

The obvious next move is arithmetic. Take 1,100 hours, divide by your daily study time, and read off an answer. At 30 minutes a day every day, a year gives you about 182 hours, and the division suggests something in the region of six years.

That number is arithmetically correct and close to meaningless, for a reason worth being precise about: **FSI hours and app hours are not the same unit.**

An FSI hour is small-group instruction, with a trained teacher hearing every sentence you produce and correcting it immediately, inside a programme where the language is your full-time occupation for most of a year. A solo hour on a phone is genuinely valuable — retrieval practice, controlled listening, vocabulary that comes back — and it is a different thing. Neither is a fraction of the other in a way you can compute.

There is a second problem with the division: it assumes hours are the only variable. They are not. A learner who talks to Russian speakers weekly and a learner who never speaks aloud can log identical hours and end up in very different places.

So use the FSI figure the way it is genuinely reliable — as a **relative scale between languages** — and be sceptical of anyone converting it into a personal timeline, including yourself.

## Russian's curve has an unusual shape

More useful than a total is knowing where the effort lands, because Russian distributes it very unevenly.

### The alphabet is fast

Thirty-three letters. Most adults working consistently can read Russian slowly and accurately within about a fortnight, and can sound out signs and product names well before that. It is the fastest-completed stage of the whole language.

It also pays out immediately, because Russian carries a large stock of internationally recognisable vocabulary that becomes legible the moment you can decode the letters. That early win is worth engineering deliberately — it is the clearest possible evidence that the language is a solvable problem, and it arrives before the grammar has had a chance to discourage anyone.

The trap is treating the alphabet as the gate rather than the doorstep. Our guide to [the Russian Cyrillic alphabet](/blog/learn-russian-cyrillic-beginners-guide/) covers the letters worth over-practising, and the two things the alphabet does not give you: stress, which is unmarked in ordinary text, and vowel reduction, which means the spelling gets you to a word rather than to a pronunciation.

### The grammar is slow

This is where the time actually goes.

**Six cases**, marking the role each noun plays, with adjectives, pronouns and numerals agreeing. The endings are learnable in an afternoon and the *reflex* — choosing a form while you are mid-sentence, without stopping — takes months. That gap between knowing and using is the defining feature of the Russian curve, and it is the main reason honest time estimates for Russian run longer than the modest letter count suggests.

**Verb aspect**, which most English speakers find harder than the cases. Russian verbs largely come in pairs, and choosing between them is a decision about how you view an action rather than when it happened. There is no English structure to map it onto, so there is nothing to transfer and nothing to guess from.

**Three genders and agreement**, which means gender is not a label you can postpone; it determines which endings a noun takes.

### The vocabulary is moderate

Better than it looks. Russian shares almost no everyday vocabulary with English, which sounds bad — but the internationalism layer is large, word formation is highly regular once you know the prefixes and suffixes, and knowing one root frequently gives you a family of related words. Compared with an unrelated language that has no shared borrowings at all, Russian vocabulary is not the bottleneck.

### And some things are simply absent

**No articles.** Nothing corresponding to *a* or *the*, at all.

**No present tense of "to be".** It is normally just omitted, so a large number of sentences are shorter than their English equivalents.

**Free word order**, because the case endings carry the roles. You are rarely wrong for arranging a sentence unusually.

## Milestones as a sequence, not a schedule

The order in which things happen in Russian is predictable. The pace is not, and it depends on factors nobody can see from here — how much you already know about grammar, whether you have studied a Slavic language, how much contact you have with speakers, how consistently you show up.

So here is the sequence, with no times attached, because attaching times to it would be inventing them.

**You can decode the alphabet.** Signs, brand names, place names. Slow and accurate.

**You can read internationalisms without effort** and start recognising word shapes rather than spelling them out letter by letter.

**You can produce fixed phrases correctly**, including the polite words that are heavily reduced in ordinary speech and do not sound like their spelling.

**You can build a sentence with a subject and an object** and get the accusative right. This is the moment cases become real rather than theoretical.

**You can say where you are and where you are going**, which means you have the в/на motion-versus-location distinction working — arguably the single highest-value grammar point in early Russian.

**You can be understood while making case errors.** An underrated milestone. Russians are used to hearing the language spoken imperfectly and the errors are usually recoverable from context.

**You stop translating in your head for common situations.**

**You can read a paragraph of unmodified text** — a news lead, a product description — and get the gist without a dictionary.

**Aspect starts feeling like a choice rather than a coin flip.** This one arrives late and is the clearest sign that the grammar is becoming internal.

Progress in Russian is not linear, and the plateau between "I can build sentences" and "I can build them without stopping" is long enough that a lot of people conclude they have stopped improving. They usually have not; they have moved from acquiring rules to automating them, which produces much less visible change per week.

## What actually changes the rate

Four things, roughly in order of impact.

**Whether you speak aloud with people.** The single biggest divergence between learners with identical study hours. Production under real-time pressure is the skill; everything else supports it.

**Whether you learned stress with each word.** Russian stress is mobile and unmarked in ordinary text. Learners who treat it as optional accumulate hundreds of words stored with the wrong stress, and repairing those later is far more expensive than storing them correctly.

**Whether you reviewed, or only advanced.** Case endings, gender assignments and stress patterns are exactly the kind of material that decays quietly and then fails under speaking pressure. Review that pulls from your own history, rather than fresh lists, is what keeps that from happening.

**Prior languages.** Any previous experience with a case-marked language — German, Latin, Polish, Czech — reduces the conceptual load considerably, because the idea of a case is already there and only the specifics are new.

## A note on the other scale you will see

If you look into Russian courses you will meet **CEFR** levels — A1 through C2 — maintained by the Council of Europe. That framework describes what a learner can *do* at each level rather than how long it took, which makes it useful for a different purpose: judging whether a course, a textbook or a reader is pitched where you actually are.

FSI answers "how long for our students". CEFR answers "what does this level look like". Neither answers "how long for you", and mixing the two produces most of the confident timelines you will find online.

## Where an app fits, honestly

A course on your phone is good at a specific set of jobs: making the alphabet legible, introducing grammar in stages small enough to absorb, keeping vocabulary coming back instead of appearing once, and giving you something to do on the days when a lesson with a person is not going to happen.

[Regal - Learn Russian Language](/apps/learn-russian/) is built for those jobs. Cyrillic lessons come first so the script is a skill rather than an obstacle. Cases, gender, agreement and verb forms are introduced gradually, and the exercises explain why the correct answer is correct instead of only marking it. Vocabulary returns through listening, matching, sentence building and review rather than appearing once. Saved words and missed-question practice pull back exactly what you got wrong. And once the basics are in place there are stories, documents, roleplays, culture lessons and history to read, which is where practice stops being drills.

What it does not do — what nothing on a screen does — is hear you the way a fluent speaker can, or give you the experience of being misunderstood and having to repair it. That experience is where a lot of the actual learning happens, and it needs another person.

The app's own answer to the fluency question is the right one: no app can promise that. The realistic goal is a foundation — alphabet, working grammar, useful vocabulary, phrases for everyday situations — that makes the conversations you eventually have productive rather than baffling.

## The honest answer

Russian takes longer than Spanish and half as long as Mandarin, by the only public institutional accounting that exists. The alphabet takes a fortnight, the case system takes months to automate, and verb aspect takes longer than either. The FSI figure of 44 weeks and 1,100 class hours is real, it is checkable, and it describes full-time professional training rather than anything you are about to do.

The useful question is not "how long" but "how consistently". A learner doing twenty focused minutes daily for two years will pass a learner doing four-hour weekend sessions for the same period, and both will be passed by someone with a weekly conversation partner.

If you have not started, start with the letters — that piece is genuinely finishable this month. If you want to see how differently the same question plays out in another Category III language, our [guide to the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) covers a language with the same FSI rating and a completely different difficulty shape, and the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) span the range from Category II to Category IV.

title: How Much Protein Per Day? What the Published Reference Numbers Actually Answer
metaTitle: How Much Protein Per Day? The Published Numbers
secondaryKeywords: is there an upper limit for protein

sources.p: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine
MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine
U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Library
U.S. Departments of Agriculture and Health and Human Services
U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service

body:
Ask four different sources how much protein a person needs in a day and you get four different answers, all of them correct. That is not a contradiction in the science. It is four organisations answering four different questions and everybody afterwards quoting the answers as though they were one.

Sorting out which question each number answers takes about five minutes, and it is the difference between reading a nutrition label usefully and arguing with strangers about it.

## The four numbers, and what each one was built for

| Figure | Published by | The question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.8 g per kg body weight per day | National Academies (RDA) | How little can nearly all healthy adults eat without becoming deficient? |
| 10–35 percent of calories | National Academies (AMDR) | What share of energy from protein is associated with adequate nutrition overall? |
| 50 grams per day | FDA (Daily Value) | What common yardstick lets shoppers compare two packages? |
| 1.2–2.0 g per kg per day | Cited by NIH ODS for athletes | What does the training literature suggest for people doing serious athletic work? |

None of those rows is a recommendation for you. Three of them are population reference figures and the fourth is a labelling convention. What they are genuinely good for is orientation: knowing roughly where your intake sits relative to a published reference is a far more useful piece of information than a number you invented.

> This article is general information, not medical or dietary advice. Protein requirements shift with age, body composition, pregnancy, kidney function, illness and medication, and some conditions make higher intakes inappropriate. Talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before setting a figure you intend to eat to.

## The RDA: a floor with a precise definition

The Recommended Dietary Allowance for protein for adults is **0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day**, from the National Academies' Dietary Reference Intakes report.

The definition matters more than the number. An RDA is set at the level estimated to meet the requirements of *nearly all* healthy individuals in a life-stage and sex group — it is deliberately pitched above the average requirement so that almost nobody in the group falls short. The average requirement itself, the Estimated Average Requirement, sits lower, at 0.66 g/kg per day in the same report.

Two consequences follow, and both get lost in retelling.

**It is a floor.** The RDA answers "how little is safely enough", which is a completely different question from "how much supports the thing I am training for". Reading a floor as a ceiling is the single most common misuse of the figure.

**It scales with body weight**, so the gram figure is personal even though the ratio is not:

- 60 kg → 0.8 × 60 = **48 g/day**
- 70 kg → 0.8 × 70 = **56 g/day**
- 90 kg → 0.8 × 90 = **72 g/day**

If you think in pounds, divide by 2.2046 first. 154 lb is about 70 kg; 180 lb is about 81.6 kg, which puts the RDA arithmetic at roughly 65 g.

### The reference intakes also vary by life stage

The DRI tables do not stop at one adult figure. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, summarising the same reference framework, cites 0.8 g/kg/day for healthy adults and 0.85 g/kg/day for adolescents. Infants, children, pregnancy and lactation each carry their own reference values in the DRI tables, and USDA maintains a public DRI calculator that reports them for a given age, sex and life stage.

If you are in one of those groups, that is precisely the situation where a reference table stops being a shortcut and a professional conversation starts being the right move.

## The AMDR: a wide band, deliberately

The same report sets an **Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range** for protein of **10 to 35 percent of daily calories** for adults.

Convert it and the width becomes obvious. At a 2,000 calorie intake, and with protein carrying 4 calories per gram:

- 10 percent = 200 calories ÷ 4 = **50 g**
- 35 percent = 700 calories ÷ 4 = **175 g**

A range from 50 to 175 grams is not a target. It describes a span within which protein intake is compatible with getting enough of everything else — the range exists because pushing protein toward either extreme starts crowding out carbohydrate or fat.

The AMDR is also the reason percentage-based and gram-based targets keep talking past each other. A fixed gram target becomes a larger *percentage* as total calories fall, without you changing a thing about what you ate.

## The Daily Value: a shopping tool wearing a nutrition costume

The **50 grams** printed against protein on US Nutrition Facts labels is FDA's Daily Value, based on a 2,000 calorie reference diet. At 4 calories per gram that is 200 calories, or 10 percent of the reference diet — the bottom of the AMDR, which is a reasonable choice for a comparison scale and a poor choice for a personal goal.

FDA is explicit that the reference diet behind Daily Values may not match your own calorie needs. The DV exists so a shopper can put two packages side by side and read them on one scale. That is a real and useful job. It is not the job people usually assume it is doing.

One quirk worth knowing: a percent Daily Value for protein is not required on most Nutrition Facts panels. Manufacturers declare it when they make a protein claim, or for foods aimed at young children. A missing %DV for protein is normal, not an omission.

## The athlete range: where the number comes from

The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements' fact sheet on exercise and athletic performance states that since the Food and Nutrition Board developed the protein RDA, more recent data have suggested that athletes require a daily protein intake of **1.2 to 2.0 g/kg** to support metabolic adaptations, muscle repair and remodelling, and protein turnover. The same fact sheet reports a joint position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and the American College of Sports Medicine recommending that athletes consume 0.3 g/kg of high-quality protein — about 20 g for a person weighing 150 lb — within 0 to 2 hours after exercise and then every 3 to 5 hours.

For a 70 kg person, 1.2–2.0 g/kg is 84–140 grams a day. That is roughly one and a half to two and a half times the RDA arithmetic for the same person, which is why the two figures feel like they are in conflict when they are simply answering different questions about different people.

The important qualifier is who the range describes. It is drawn from research on athletes in training, and "I go to the gym" and "I am an athlete in a structured training programme" are not automatically the same population.

## What the references deliberately do not say

**There is no Tolerable Upper Intake Level for protein.** The Food and Nutrition Board did not set one. The ODS fact sheet explains why: the board judged the risk of adverse effects from excess protein *from food* to be very low. The same source advises caution for people whose high intakes come from foods plus supplements, because data on that combination is limited.
