A single Khmer syllable can carry a consonant, a second consonant tucked underneath it, a vowel sign to the left, another part of the same vowel sign to the right, and a diacritic on top — all of which are read in an order that has very little to do with the order they appear in on the page.

Once you know that the syllable is the unit, the whole system stops being arbitrary. This article is about how that unit is assembled.

## Khmer is an abugida, not an alphabet

In an alphabet, consonants and vowels are equal citizens on the same line. In an **abugida**, the consonant is the base and the vowel is attached to it — and if no vowel is written, the consonant is still read with a built-in vowel.

Khmer is an abugida, descended from the Pallava script of southern India, with inscriptions in Old Khmer going back to the seventh century CE. The same ancestry produced the Thai and Lao writing systems, which is why all three look like relatives despite Khmer belonging to a completely different language family. It is also used to write Pali in Cambodian Buddhist contexts.

The practical consequence is that "how do I read this letter" is the wrong question. The right question is "how do I read this cluster", and the cluster is where all the interesting machinery lives.

## Two series, one vowel sign, two readings

This is the feature that most distinguishes Khmer from its neighbours, and the one that punishes learners who skip it.

Each of the roughly **33 consonant letters** belongs to one of **two series** — the first and second series, or the a-series and o-series, depending on which textbook you have. The naming varies; the mechanism does not.

The series is not primarily about the consonant's own sound. It determines **how the vowel sign attached to that consonant is pronounced**. The same vowel symbol has two possible readings, and the base consonant selects between them.

Take **ក** and **គ**. Both are k-type consonants, and to an English ear they are close. But **ក** is first series and **គ** is second series, so if you attach the same vowel sign to each, you get two different vowels. The letter you are looking at tells you the consonant; the series of that letter tells you the vowel.

That is why a Khmer consonant learned without its series is not learned. You know a sound, but you cannot read a syllable. It is the closest Khmer equivalent to the Thai consonant classes described in our [guide to the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) — a second piece of information bundled invisibly into every letter, which has to be memorised from the first exposure rather than added later.

### The two diacritics that switch series

Because the series is fixed to the letter, Khmer needs an escape hatch for the cases where a word requires a consonant sound with the wrong series. There are two marks for this, and they are exact opposites:

- **៉** — often called *musikatoan*, sometimes translated as "mouse's teeth". It converts a second-series consonant into a first-series one.
- **៊** — often called *triisap*, sometimes translated as "snake's teeth". It converts a first-series consonant into a second-series one.

Two small marks that flip the vowel reading of the entire syllable. They are worth learning early, not because they are frequent, but because encountering one without knowing what it does makes an otherwise readable word unreadable.

## Vowel signs attach on four sides

Dependent vowel signs — the ones that hang off a consonant — do not sit in a fixed position. They attach wherever their shape dictates:

| Position | Example sign |
| --- | --- |
| To the right of the consonant | ា |
| To the left of the consonant | េ |
| Above the consonant | ិ |
| Below the consonant | ុ |

And some vowels occupy more than one position at once. **ោ** is written as a piece on the left and a piece on the right, wrapping the consonant on both sides.

The left-side vowels are the ones that catch people out, because they are **written before the consonant but read after it**. The visual order and the spoken order genuinely disagree. Anyone who has learned Thai or Devanagari has met this before; anyone coming straight from an alphabet has not, and it is the single most common source of early misreadings.

There is also **ំ**, a mark written above the consonant that adds a nasal to the syllable rather than replacing the vowel. It appears in some of the first words you will meet, including the name of the capital.

### Dependent versus independent vowels

Everything above describes **dependent** vowels, which need a consonant to attach to.

Khmer also has a separate set of **independent vowel letters** — full-size characters that stand alone and are used for syllables that begin with a vowel sound. They appear mostly in vocabulary of Sanskrit and Pali origin, along with a handful of common native words. There are not many of them, they are not needed on day one, and they are genuinely a separate memorisation job rather than variations on the dependent signs.

## Subscripts: the second consonant goes underneath

When a Khmer syllable begins with a consonant cluster, the second consonant is not written next to the first. It is written **beneath** it, in a reduced subscript form called **coeng** — the Khmer word for foot or leg, which is exactly what it looks like.

Every one of the 33 consonants has a subscript form. Some are recognisably shrunken versions of the full letter; several are not, and have to be learned as separate shapes. That effectively doubles the number of consonant forms a reader has to recognise.

Three words show the system doing real work:

| Written | Usually romanised | What is stacked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ខ្មែរ** | Khmer | subscript **ម** under **ខ**, with a left-side vowel sign |
| **កម្ពុជា** | Kampuchea | subscript **ព** under **ម**, with a vowel sign below it |
| **ភ្នំពេញ** | Phnom Penh | subscript **ន** under **ភ**, plus the nasal mark and a left-side vowel |

Look at **ខ្មែរ** carefully and you can see the whole problem in one word: the vowel sign sits to the left of a consonant that has another consonant hanging off its underside, and the final consonant closes the syllable on the right. Four components, four positions, one syllable.

This is why tracing practice matters more for Khmer than for most scripts. The letterforms are intricate enough that writing them out is a genuine aid to telling them apart — recognition and production reinforce each other in a way that pure flashcard drilling does not reproduce. [Learn Cambodian, Speak Khmer](/apps/learn-cambodian-khmer/) teaches consonants, vowels and numbers with tracing practice and pronunciation help for this reason, with romanised spelling shown alongside so that speaking is not held hostage to reading.

## The marks that shorten and silence

A few more diacritics do jobs that have no English parallel, and all of them are common enough to meet in the first month.

**់** shortens the vowel of the syllable it sits on. It is small, easy to miss, and changes the word.

**៍** marks a letter as **not pronounced**. Khmer spelling preserves the full written form of many Sanskrit and Pali loanwords even where modern pronunciation has dropped syllables, and this mark is how the script signals "this is here for etymology, do not say it".

**៌** is inherited from the Sanskrit *repha*, written above the consonant. In modern Khmer it is generally not pronounced as a separate sound.

Taken together, these three explain something beginners notice immediately and find discouraging: **Khmer words often look longer than they sound**. That is not a quirk of the script being inefficient. It is the script being conservative, holding the older Indic spelling steady while the spoken language moved on. Once you know that some letters are decoration with a mark to prove it, the mismatch stops feeling like a trap.

## Numerals, punctuation and the missing spaces

Khmer has its own digits — **០ ១ ២ ៣ ៤ ៥ ៦ ៧ ៨ ៩** for zero to nine — used alongside Arabic numerals on prices, documents and signage. They are the fastest-learned part of the entire writing system and pay for themselves in a market within about ten minutes.

Punctuation is short and worth knowing:

- **។** ends a sentence or section, doing roughly the job of a full stop.
- **៕** marks the end of a text or a major section.
- **៖** functions much like a colon, introducing what follows.
- **ៗ** is a repetition mark: it tells you to say the preceding word twice. Khmer, like Malay and Indonesian, uses reduplication for real grammatical work, and this mark is the shorthand for it.

And then the two absences. Khmer text runs **without spaces between words** — spaces separate phrases and clauses, and word boundaries are something the reader works out. There is also **no case distinction**, so nothing marks a proper noun or the start of a sentence.

Both absences point at the same study conclusion. Letter recognition is not reading. You can know all 33 consonants and still be unable to parse a sentence, because the skill of finding word boundaries only develops on continuous text. Practise on real sentences early, even short ones, rather than staying in the safety of isolated characters.

## What Unicode does underneath

If you are typing Khmer, or wondering why a word occasionally renders as a row of boxes, the encoding is worth thirty seconds of your attention.

Khmer lives in the Unicode block **U+1780–U+17FF**, with a second small block, **Khmer Symbols** at U+19E0–U+19FF, holding the lunar date symbols used in traditional calendars.

The important detail is that subscripts are **not separate characters**. Unicode encodes a stack as: base consonant, then an invisible combining character **U+17D2 KHMER SIGN COENG**, then the consonant that should be subscripted. The font works out the shape. That is why Khmer needs a properly featured font to display at all, why copy-pasted Khmer sometimes falls apart in older software, and why the character count of a Khmer string is not the number of shapes you can see on screen.

## A workable order for learning it

The script is not a single obstacle, it is a sequence of them, and they are best taken in this order:

1. **Numerals first.** ០ to ៩, done in a sitting, immediately useful. It is a genuine win at a stage when wins are scarce.
2. **Consonants with their series, never without.** Learn each letter as a pair of facts — sound plus series. Retrofitting the series later means relearning the whole inventory.
3. **The most common dependent vowels, one position at a time.** Get comfortable with right-side signs, then above and below, then the left-side ones, then the two-part ones. The left-side signs need dedicated practice precisely because the reading order inverts.
4. **Subscripts.** Only after full-size consonants are automatic. Start with the subscript forms that resemble their parent letters, then the ones that do not.
5. **The diacritics.** Series-switchers, the vowel shortener and the silencer. By this point you have enough context for each of them to make sense as a fix to a problem you have already run into.
6. **Continuous text, early and badly.** Signs, menus, app labels — anything real. The word-boundary skill has no shortcut.

Spacing this work out across weeks rather than compressing it into a single intensive fortnight is the difference between recognition that survives and recognition that evaporates. A script learned in a burst tends to fade in exactly the same shape it was crammed in.

## What the script does not give you

Two honest limits, because the script is often oversold as the key to the language.

It does not give you **word boundaries**, as covered above. And it does not fully give you **pronunciation**, because the series system plus the conservative Indic spellings mean that a written form points at a word rather than dictating exactly how to say it. You still need audio, and you still need to hear words at normal speed rather than only in careful isolation.

What the script does give you is a **stable form for every word**. That matters more in Khmer than in most languages, because romanisation is not standardised — *suosdei* and *sua sdei* and several other spellings are all attempts at the same greeting, **សួស្តី**, and none of them is authoritative. Once you can read even slowly, every word has exactly one spelling, and you can finally look things up.

For where the script fits into the language as a whole — the absence of tones, the counting system, the politeness registers and what a first month looks like — start with our [beginner's guide to Khmer](/blog/learn-khmer-beginners-guide/). If you are comparing scripts before committing, the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) span systems from the Latin alphabet through Cyrillic to Thai and Chinese characters, and the trade-offs are different in every case.

title: Language Learning Apps Compared: What to Do When Your Language Isn't One of the Big Ones
metaTitle: Best Language Learning App for Rarer Languages
primaryKeyword: best language learning app for less common languages
secondaryKeywords: app to learn khmer or malay
body:
Most language app comparisons assume the hard part is choosing between products. For anyone learning Spanish, that is true. For anyone learning Cantonese, Khmer or Malay, the hard part happens one step earlier: finding out which products cover the language at all, and what "cover" turns out to mean.

That single question eliminates more options than every feature comparison combined, and it is answerable in about five minutes.

**Disclosure:** this article is published by Reign Creative LLC. We publish Android courses for several of the languages discussed here, including the Cantonese course named below, so we have a direct commercial interest in you installing one. We have written this to be useful if you end up somewhere else, and the recommendations at the end genuinely point elsewhere in several cases.

Everything stated about another company's product was read on that company's own website on **9 August 2026** and is limited to what those pages said. Course catalogues change; check the current listing yourself before deciding.

## Check availability before you compare anything

Duolingo's own introduction to its catalogue states: "We offer over 100 courses teaching 40+ languages," and a separate post on its blog describes it as "the free language app that teaches more than 40 languages." Those numbers are the company's own, and they are the right frame for the decision.

Forty-plus is a lot of languages. It is also a tiny fraction of the languages people actually want to learn, and which forty-plus changes over time as courses are added. So the first thing to do is not read a comparison article — it is to open the platform's own course list and look for your language. If it is there, the case for using the biggest platform is strong: more content, more polish, more people to ask when you get stuck.

If it is not there, the rest of this article is for you.

## "Available" can mean two different things

This is the distinction that trips people up, and it is visible on vendors' own pages if you know to look for it.

When we read Memrise's pages for Cantonese, Khmer and Malay on 9 August 2026, each one described the offering the same way: Memrise teaches that language's vocabulary **"with word lists created by other users."** On the Cantonese page, Cantonese did not appear among the courses listed in the page's own navigation.

That is a description of a content model, not a criticism. Community-contributed word lists are how an enormous amount of rare-language study actually happens, and for a language with no commercial course anywhere they may be the best material in existence. But they are a different product from a sequenced course, and the difference shows up in practice:

- **A produced course** has decided what comes first. Someone chose the order of the grammar, the point at which the script is introduced, and what gets reviewed when.
- **A word list** gives you items. You are supplying the sequencing, the grammar and the judgement about what matters.

Neither is better in the abstract. But if you are a complete beginner in a language whose writing system you cannot yet read, "you supply the structure" is a much heavier ask than it sounds.

Memrise's own home page describes its produced-course method as built on native speaker videos with pronunciation practice, verb conjugation, sentence building and AI speaking practice, and states plainly: "You can start learning for free. Our paid plan unlocks extra features, but building confidence doesn't have to cost a thing." For the languages where that machinery exists, it is a serious product. The question is only whether it exists for yours.

## Four shapes of tool

Once you stop sorting by brand and start sorting by what the software actually is, there are roughly four shapes, and they fail and succeed for different reasons.

### The large course platform

Duolingo is the reference example. Its own blog describes a free app teaching more than 40 languages, with Duolingo Max subscribers getting unlimited access to its Video Call feature. Where a course exists, this shape gives you sequencing, habit mechanics and scale.

The trade is inherent to the shape rather than to any company: producing a course is expensive, so coverage concentrates where demand is largest. The languages named across Duolingo's own pages we read are Spanish, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Greek and English — which tells you where the production effort has gone, not what the full catalogue contains. Go and read the catalogue.

### The vocabulary platform with community contributions

Memrise, as described above. Enormous language coverage; two different content models underneath it. Check which one applies to your language on Memrise's own page for that language before you plan a study routine around it.

### The scheduling engine with no content

Anki is the odd one out and the most under-appreciated tool in this article. Its own site describes it as "a flashcard program that helps you spend more time on challenging material, and less on what you already know," scheduling each card's next review "for when you're most likely to forget the information."

Critically, **it ships with no study material at all.** You build decks or download shared ones through AnkiWeb. The computer version is free for all major platforms, AnkiDroid on Android is described on that page as "free and developed by contributors," and the iOS app is a paid purchase that funds development.

That combination — free on Android, no content, best-in-class scheduling — makes it the default answer for languages nothing else covers. If someone has published a shared deck for your language, you have a study tool. If nobody has, you can still build one from a textbook. Nothing else in this article degrades so gracefully as coverage disappears.

What it will not do is teach you. There is no syllabus, no grammar explanation and no pronunciation model. Many people run Anki alongside a course rather than instead of one.

### The audio method

Pimsleur publishes a Chinese (Cantonese) course. Its own page for that course describes audio-language instruction with supplemental learning tools, states that "each lesson takes just 30 minutes," and refers to Levels 1–5 steadily expanding speaking skills, with supplemental flashcards, quizzes, interactive exercises and a Voice Coach tool offering AI pronunciation feedback.

The page describes the course in terms of listening and speaking. If your goal is to talk to relatives or to get around a city, and reading is secondary or irrelevant, an audio-first method is a legitimate and well-established route, and for some learners it is a better fit than any screen-based course including ours. Check their site for how the course is sold and whether written Cantonese is covered anywhere in the product.

## What a tonal language and an unfamiliar script actually demand

Feature lists rarely capture this, and it is where beginner courses succeed or fail.

**Tone is not decoration.** In Cantonese, the same syllable carries different meanings at different pitches. Jyutping — the romanisation produced by the **Linguistic Society of Hong Kong**, whose own materials reference the original 1993 scheme — marks six tones. An app that teaches you vocabulary without first teaching you to hear and produce those contrasts is handing you words you will pronounce as something else. Whether the sound system comes before the conversation is the most consequential design decision a Cantonese course makes.

**A new script is a separate project from a new language.** Chinese characters live in Unicode's CJK Unified Ideographs block at U+4E00–U+9FFF; Khmer has its own block at U+1780–U+17FF. A learner of either is doing two things at once: learning to read, and learning to speak. Courses that acknowledge that split — teaching the script deliberately rather than assuming it — save you a month of confusion. Our [Khmer beginner's guide](/blog/learn-khmer-beginners-guide/) and [Thai script guide](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) go through what that costs in practice.

**And sometimes there is no script problem at all.** Malay is written in the Latin alphabet, which removes the reading barrier entirely and puts the whole difficulty into vocabulary, affixes and usage. That makes it one of the more approachable starting languages, and it changes what you should look for in a course — see the [Malay beginner's guide](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/).

## Where our Cantonese course sits

[Learn Cantonese for Beginners](/apps/learn-cantonese/) is the specialist shape: one language, one sequenced path, built on the assumption that Cantonese is its own spoken language rather than a variant of Mandarin.

Twelve units run from greetings and introductions out through family, food, shopping, numbers, money, dates and time, transport, work, school, health, emergencies and social situations. Pronunciation gets its own foundation first — initials, finals, syllables, then tone contrasts — before conversation. Traditional characters and Jyutping appear together from the first lesson, so reading and pronunciation are learned at the same time rather than one bolted on later. Grammar is taught on Cantonese terms: word order, pronouns, classifiers, possession, negation, aspect markers, questions, comparisons, adjective placement and sentence-final particles.

Review is the part that holds it together. Daily Review, Speed Run Review, Mistake Rescue, Listening Blitz, Sentence Builder, Match Blitz and Dictation Mode all draw on material you have already covered, and a missed-questions list collects what you keep getting wrong. There is no hearts or lives system, so a mistake never blocks you. Cantonese-from-English and English-from-Cantonese are separate courses with separate progress. Where your device provides a Cantonese voice the app uses it, and falls back clearly when it does not.

It is free on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases; some locked lessons can be opened with a rewarded ad when one is available.

The honest limits: **it teaches one language.** There is no community, no live tutoring and no video call. Our courses are written and edited by our own team, and we do not claim they were reviewed by native speakers or professional linguists — where you see no named reviewer on an article or an app, no such review took place. And no beginner course, ours included, produces fluency; it produces a foundation you then take to actual conversation.

We publish separate beginner courses for Khmer, Malay, Thai and Russian on the same model, listed under [language learning](/apps/category/language-learning/), and the [Cantonese beginner's guide](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/) covers the language itself rather than the software.

## Honest recommendations

**If your language is on a large platform's course list**, start there. Scale is a real advantage and free is a real price.

**If your language appears on a platform only as community word lists**, decide whether you want to supply the structure. If you are an experienced language learner, that is a fine trade. If this is your first language, it usually is not.

**If nothing covers your language**, use Anki with a shared deck, and find a grammar reference separately. It is free on Android and it does the one thing — scheduling review — that human willpower does worst.

**If you want to speak rather than read**, an audio method such as the Pimsleur course described above fits that goal more directly than a reading-and-writing course, ours included.

**If you specifically want Cantonese with tones and characters from the start**, that is what ours is built for, and it is why it exists.

**If you want a tutor**, none of these are that. Apps are a supplement to conversation, not a replacement for it.

## How we checked, and a note on names

Every statement above about Duolingo, Memrise, Anki and Pimsleur was read on those companies' own websites on 9 August 2026 and is reported as what those pages said. We did not state which languages any platform does or does not offer beyond what its own pages showed us, because catalogues change and an out-of-date absence claim is worse than no claim. We used no screenshots, icons or brand styling.

Duolingo, Memrise, Anki, AnkiDroid, Pimsleur and all other product names and trademarks mentioned are the property of their respective owners. Their use here is nominative — for identification of the products discussed — and implies no affiliation, sponsorship, partnership or endorsement in either direction.

title: Learn Cantonese for Beginners: What the First Month Actually Demands
metaTitle: Learn Cantonese for Beginners: An Honest Guide
secondaryKeywords: written cantonese vs standard written chinese

sources.p: The Linguistic Society of Hong Kong
U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Two things put people off Cantonese before they have written a single character. The first is being told it is "a dialect", which makes learning it sound like a detour off the main road. The second is the tone system, usually introduced in a way that suggests you need perfect pitch to order lunch.

Both deserve a straight answer, because the decision you are actually making — Cantonese or something else, now or never — is worth making on accurate information.

## "Dialect" is the wrong word for what you are choosing

Cantonese and Mandarin sit inside the same language family and share an enormous amount of written vocabulary. What they do not share is mutual intelligibility in speech. A monolingual Mandarin speaker dropped into a Cantonese conversation does not follow it, and the reverse is equally true.

That has one concrete consequence for you: **material written for Mandarin will not teach you Cantonese.** Pinyin does not encode Cantonese sounds. Mandarin's four-tone system is not Cantonese's six. Mandarin grammar words — the ones you use in every sentence for "is", "not", "he" and possession — are frequently different words in spoken Cantonese, not just different pronunciations of the same word.

This is the practical reason a Cantonese course has to be built as a Cantonese course rather than adapted from Mandarin, and it is the design decision behind [Learn Cantonese for Beginners](/apps/learn-cantonese/): the sound system, the grammar sequence and the character set are all built around Cantonese rather than borrowed and relabelled.

### Where Cantonese sits on the difficulty scale

The most defensible public benchmark for language difficulty is the US Foreign Service Institute's training categories, which group languages by how long its students typically need to reach Professional Working Proficiency — a score of Speaking-3/Reading-3 on the Interagency Language Roundtable scale. FSI places Chinese – Cantonese in **Category IV**, its hardest group, at **88 weeks of full-time instruction (2,200 class hours)**, alongside Arabic, Mandarin, Japanese and Korean.

Read that carefully before it discourages you. It describes intensive, full-time, small-group classroom training for diplomats — 2,200 hours across 88 weeks is about 25 class hours a week, before homework. It is not a statement about how long a phone app takes, and it is not a target for someone who wants to greet their partner's family properly. What it is good for is calibrating expectations: Cantonese is at the demanding end, so a course that promises speed is promising something the evidence does not support.

## The tone system, described honestly

Here is the part that gets over-dramatised.

Cantonese uses pitch to distinguish words. The same string of sounds, said with a different pitch pattern, is a different word — not a differently-emphasised version of the same one. Say the syllable *si* six ways and you get six unrelated meanings. Tone is not decoration you can add once your vocabulary is bigger; it is part of the word, in the same way that the vowel is.

Modern descriptions of Hong Kong Cantonese count **six contrasting tones**, and Jyutping numbers them 1 to 6:

| Jyutping number | Usual description |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | high level |
| 2 | rising |
| 3 | mid level |
| 4 | low falling |
| 5 | low rising |
| 6 | low level |

Descriptions differ slightly between references — some transcribe tone 1 as high falling in certain speakers, and the exact pitch heights vary by region and individual — so treat the table as a map rather than a measurement.

You will also see Cantonese described as having **nine tones**. That figure comes from an older tradition that counts syllables ending in **-p, -t or -k** as three extra "entering" tones. Those syllables are cut short by the final consonant, but their pitch levels are the same ones already used by tones 1, 3 and 6, which is why Jyutping writes them with those numbers instead of adding three more. Six and nine are two ways of counting the same system, not a disagreement about the facts.

### What this means for how you practise

The useful takeaway is not "tones are hard". It is that **tone has to be learned with the word, from the first exposure**, because relearning a word's tone later is much harder than learning it right the first time.

That is why a sensible Cantonese course front-loads pronunciation instead of treating it as polish. Learn Cantonese for Beginners works through initials, finals and syllables and then tone contrasts before conversation starts, and where your device provides a Cantonese voice the app uses it and falls back clearly when it does not. Hearing a contrast is the part you cannot get from a page.

Two honest caveats. Recognising a tone contrast in a quiet room is easier than producing one mid-sentence, and both are easier than either in a noisy restaurant. And no app can hear you the way a fluent speaker can — this article and the course are a foundation, not a substitute for a teacher or a conversation partner.

## Jyutping, and why you should pick one system and stay there

Jyutping is a romanisation scheme published by the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong. Its defining feature is that tone is a digit written after the syllable: *nei5*, *hou2*, *m4*. That makes it typeable on any keyboard and unambiguous to read aloud.

The main alternative you will meet is **Yale**, an older Cantonese system that marks tone with diacritics and spelling changes instead. Yale is not wrong; a lot of good older material uses it. The problem is mixing them. Half-learning two romanisations produces a learner who is confident about neither and who quietly mispronounces words that the two systems spell differently.

Pick one and commit. Learn Cantonese for Beginners uses Jyutping throughout, which is also the system you are most likely to meet in current Hong Kong teaching material and input methods.

## Three ways Cantonese gets written down

This is the part that surprises most beginners, and understanding it early saves a lot of confusion.

**Traditional characters** are the standard script in Hong Kong and Macau. Guangdong province in mainland China, where Cantonese is also widely spoken, uses simplified characters. The Unicode Standard encodes both, which is why your phone renders either without complaint, but a learner still has to choose which set to read fluently. Learn Cantonese for Beginners teaches traditional characters, which matches Hong Kong and Macau usage.

Beyond the character set, there are two written registers to be aware of:

- **Standard Written Chinese** is the formal written language used in newspapers, government documents, textbooks and business writing in Hong Kong. Its grammar and vocabulary are closer to Mandarin, and a Cantonese speaker reads it aloud using Cantonese pronunciations.
- **Written Cantonese** is spoken Cantonese committed to the page. You see it in messaging, social media, advertising, comics and dialogue in fiction. It uses characters that do not appear in Standard Written Chinese at all — 係 (*hai6*, "to be"), 唔 (*m4*, the common negator), 佢 (*keoi5*, "he/she"), 嘅 (*ge3*, the possessive and attributive particle).

A beginner meets both within weeks, usually without being told they are different things. Knowing that the formal notice on the wall and the message on your phone are written in two different registers is genuinely clarifying, and it is one of the things the course flags rather than glossing over.

## A small number of well-established phrases

Rather than a long list, here are three that repay learning precisely, with the character, the Jyutping and the register they belong to.

**你好 (nei5 hou2)** — "hello". Universally understood, and the standard opener in teaching material. Worth knowing that in casual Hong Kong speech people often reach for a time-of-day greeting such as **早晨 (zou2 san4)**, "good morning", or simply address the person directly, so *nei5 hou2* can sound slightly more formal in the street than it does in a textbook.

**唔該 (m4 goi1)** and **多謝 (do1 ze6)** are both translated "thank you" in English, and they are not interchangeable. *M4 goi1* thanks someone for a service or an action — the waiter who refilled your tea, the person who held the door. It also does duty as "excuse me" and "please". *Do1 ze6* thanks someone for a gift or a compliment, something given rather than done. English collapses this distinction; Cantonese does not, and getting it wrong is one of the most audible beginner errors there is.

Numbers behave the way you would hope. **一 (jat1)**, **二 (ji6)**, **三 (saam1)** — one, two, three — and they combine into larger numbers on a regular pattern, which makes prices, dates and phone numbers unusually good early practice.

## The grammar that actually catches English speakers

Cantonese grammar is often sold as "easy" because verbs do not conjugate for tense or person. That is true and it is only half the story. The work moves elsewhere.

**Classifiers** sit between a number and a noun, and which classifier you use depends on the noun. English has a trace of this — two *slices* of bread, three *head* of cattle — but Cantonese requires one every time you count. The general-purpose classifier 個 (*go3*) covers a lot, and getting a specific one wrong is understandable rather than incomprehensible, so this is a place where beginners should proceed and correct later.

**Aspect markers** replace tense. Instead of changing the verb, Cantonese attaches markers that say whether an action is completed, ongoing, experienced before, or habitual. English speakers reliably try to map these onto past and present, and reliably get tangled.

**Sentence-final particles** are the feature with no English equivalent at all. Cantonese carries a large inventory of them, and they carry meaning that English handles with intonation, extra clauses or facial expression — softening a request, marking surprise, signalling that something is obvious, turning a statement into a question. Beginners tend to omit them entirely, which is grammatical but sounds oddly flat.

These are exactly the areas Learn Cantonese for Beginners covers explicitly — word order, pronouns, classifiers, possession, negation, aspect markers, questions, comparisons, adjective placement and sentence-final particles — along with a section on the mistakes English speakers reliably make, which is more useful than it sounds.

## What the first month realistically looks like

**Week one is sounds, not sentences.** Initials, finals, syllables, then tone contrasts. It feels like a delay and it is not. Every word you learn afterwards is stored with whatever pronunciation you had when you learned it.

**Week two you start recognising characters inside words.** Not memorising a list of 200 in isolation — meeting high-frequency traditional characters inside phrases and sentences you are already saying, which is how the course introduces them.

**Week three the tones start colliding.** You knew a word yesterday and today it will not come out right. This is normal and it is the point at which most people quit. The structural answer is review that pulls from your own history rather than a fresh list: Daily Review, Mistake Rescue and the missed-questions list exist precisely for the words that will not stick.

**Week four you build sentences instead of reciting them.** Sentence Builder, Dictation Mode and Listening Blitz all attack the gap between recognising a phrase on a page and producing one out loud.

The twelve units of the course run from greetings and introductions out through family, food, shopping, numbers, money, dates and time, transport, work, school, health, emergencies and social situations. Working through them gives you a beginner foundation. It does not give you fluency, and the app does not claim it will.

## Who this language is actually for

Cantonese rewards a specific kind of learner. If you are heading to Hong Kong, Macau or Guangdong, if you are reconnecting with a family language, or if you want access to a century of Cantonese film and music on its own terms, the effort has an obvious payoff. If you want the largest possible number of conversation partners for the least effort, other languages answer that better — [Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/) sits two full FSI categories lower, for instance, and starts in the Latin alphabet.

There is no wrong answer there, only a mismatch between what a language costs and what you want from it. If you are still weighing options, the other beginner guides in our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) collection cover scripts with very different demands: [the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) asks you to learn tone through spelling rules, [Cyrillic](/blog/learn-russian-cyrillic-beginners-guide/) is the shortest hard part of a hard language, and [Khmer](/blog/learn-khmer-beginners-guide/) has a demanding script but no tones at all.

If Cantonese is the one you want, start with the sounds, keep Jyutping and traditional characters together from the first lesson, and judge your progress in months rather than days.

title: Learn Khmer for Beginners: No Tones, One Very Demanding Script
metaTitle: Learn Khmer for Beginners: Script and First Phrases

sources.p: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Most people arrive at Khmer expecting the same obstacle they were warned about for Thai and Vietnamese, and are relieved to find it is not there. Khmer is **not tonal**. Pitch does not change what a word means. The mental budget you were setting aside for tone drills can go somewhere else entirely.

Where it needs to go is the writing system, which is one of the more elaborate in daily use anywhere. That trade — no tones, hard script — defines what learning Khmer is actually like.

## Why "no tones" matters more than it sounds

In a tonal language, every word has to be stored with its pitch pattern, and getting it wrong does not produce an accent, it produces a different word. That is a real cognitive cost, and it is the reason so many people abandon [Cantonese](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/) or [Thai](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) in the first weeks.

Khmer removes that cost completely. You still have to pronounce a word correctly, but "correctly" means the right vowels and consonants, not the right melody, and if your intonation is off you sound foreign rather than unintelligible.

The pronunciation work does not vanish, it relocates. Khmer has a large vowel inventory with distinctions English does not make, including differences of vowel quality and length that carry meaning. Adults tend to find that easier than tone because it is a familiar kind of problem — you already distinguish vowels, you just have to distinguish more of them.

## The script is the price of entry

Khmer is written in an **abugida** descended from the Pallava script of southern India, with inscriptions in Old Khmer going back to the seventh century CE. The same lineage produced the Thai and Lao scripts, which is why they look like relatives even though the languages are unrelated in structure.

It is not a hard script for arbitrary reasons. It is hard because it encodes a lot of information, and three features do most of that work.

### Two series, and one vowel sign with two readings

Every Khmer consonant letter belongs to one of **two series**, usually called the first and second series, or the a-series and o-series depending on which textbook you have. Terminology varies; the mechanism does not.

The series is not really about the consonant's own sound. It determines **how the vowel attached to that consonant is pronounced**. The same vowel sign has two possible readings, and which one applies depends on the series of the consonant it is sitting on.

The consequence for a learner is unavoidable: a consonant learned without its series is not learned. You cannot read the syllable it appears in. This is the closest Khmer analogue to Thai's consonant classes — a piece of information bundled into the letter that has to be memorised alongside the sound from the first exposure, not bolted on later.

The modern consonant inventory is usually counted at 33 letters, split between the two series.

### Subscript consonants stack downward

Khmer writes consonant clusters by placing a **subscript form** of the second consonant beneath the first. The subscript form is called *coeng*, from the Khmer word for foot or leg, which describes exactly what it looks like on the page.

Each consonant has its own subscript shape, and some of those shapes are not obviously derived from the full-size letter. So a Khmer syllable can extend vertically as well as horizontally: a base consonant, a subscript beneath it, and vowel signs placed before, after, above or below. Reading Khmer means reading in more than one direction at once.

### No spaces, and no capitals

Like Thai, Khmer text runs without spaces between words. Spaces separate phrases and clauses instead, and word boundaries are something the reader infers. There are no capital letters, so nothing marks a proper noun or the start of a sentence.

Letter recognition therefore comes long before reading speed, and practising on real sentences matters far more than drilling isolated characters.

Khmer also has its own digits, ០ ១ ២ ៣ ៤ ៥ ៦ ៧ ៨ ៩ for zero to nine, used alongside Arabic numerals. They appear on prices, documents and signage, and they are among the fastest things in the whole script to learn.

## Romanisation is not standardised, and that is the argument for the script

Search for how to say hello in Khmer and you will find *suosdei*, *sua sdei*, *sursdey* and several other spellings, all attempts at the same word.

There is no single romanisation of Khmer in general use. There is a system used for geographic names, another used for library cataloguing — the Library of Congress maintains an ALA-LC table for exactly that purpose — and then there is whatever a given phrasebook author decided looked pronounceable. None of them is wrong, and none of them is authoritative in the way Pinyin is for Mandarin or Jyutping is for Cantonese.

This creates a practical problem that has nothing to do with purism. If every source spells a word differently, you have no stable written form to attach the word to, and you cannot look up something you heard. Even partial reading ability fixes this: the Khmer spelling is the one form that does not change between sources.

[Learn Cambodian, Speak Khmer](/apps/learn-cambodian-khmer/) handles the transition by showing romanised spelling alongside the script rather than choosing one, so you can start speaking while the alphabet is still settling in. Consonants, vowels and numbers are taught with pronunciation help and tracing practice, which matters more for Khmer than for most scripts — the letterforms are intricate enough that writing them is a genuine aid to telling them apart.

## Counting in fives

Khmer numbers are worth learning early, partly because you will use them constantly in markets and partly because the system is genuinely elegant.

One to five are individual words: **មួយ** (*muoy*), **ពីរ** (*pii*), **បី** (*bei*), **បួន** (*buon*), **ប្រាំ** (*pram*).

From six upward, the system builds on five. Six is *pram* plus one — **ប្រាំមួយ** (*pram muoy*). Seven, eight and nine follow the same pattern with two, three and four. It is a **bi-quinary** system, and once you have five numbers plus the pattern, you have nine.

Anyone who has bargained in a Cambodian market will confirm that numbers are the highest-value vocabulary a visitor can carry, well ahead of any set-piece phrase.

## Politeness is vocabulary, not tone of voice

Khmer marks respect through **word choice**, not through intonation or a single politeness suffix. The language carries distinct registers — everyday speech, polite speech, vocabulary reserved for addressing monks, and a separate royal vocabulary — and choosing the wrong register is not a grammatical error so much as a social one.

Beginners do not need the monastic or royal registers. What they do need is the everyday polite layer, and two words carry most of it:

**បាទ** (*baat*) and **ចាស** (*chaa*) function as "yes" and as a general polite acknowledgement. Which one you use depends on the speaker: **បាទ** for a male speaker, **ចាស** for a female speaker. They are used constantly, including simply to signal that you are listening, and omitting them makes otherwise correct Khmer sound curt.

The two phrases to learn precisely are **សួស្តី** (*suosdei*), "hello", and **អរគុណ** (*arkun*), "thank you", both of which sit comfortably in ordinary polite speech.

Alongside the words there is the **សំពះ** (*sampeah*), the greeting made with the palms pressed together. The height at which the hands are held varies according to who is being greeted, and it carries real meaning. It is the kind of thing that belongs in a culture lesson rather than a phrasebook, which is why the app runs culture material — history, landmarks, food, holidays, customs, proverbs and temple etiquette — alongside the language track rather than as an afterthought.

## The grammar is kinder than the script

After the writing system, Khmer grammar comes as relief.

Verbs do not conjugate for tense, person or number. Nouns do not decline. There is no grammatical gender and there are no articles. Basic word order is subject–verb–object, which matches English closely enough that early sentences feel natural.

What you learn instead is how Khmer expresses the things English handles with endings: time words placed around the verb rather than tense changes, particles that mark questions and attitude, and the register choices described above. The app's grammar track covers exactly this ground — sentence structure, pronouns, questions, negatives, polite speech, time expressions, particles and word order — in beginner-sized pieces.

Vocabulary carries a substantial Sanskrit and Pali layer, absorbed through Hinduism and Theravada Buddhism, alongside later borrowings including French from the colonial period. That layer is where words get long, and it is one reason Khmer written words can look more intimidating than they sound.

## Where Khmer sits on the difficulty scale

The US Foreign Service Institute groups the languages it teaches by how long its students typically need to reach Professional Working Proficiency — a score of Speaking-3/Reading-3 on the Interagency Language Roundtable scale. Khmer is in **Category III**, at approximately **44 weeks of full-time instruction (1,100 class hours)**, alongside Thai, Russian, Vietnamese and Polish.

That number describes intensive, full-time, small-group classroom training for diplomats — 1,100 hours across 44 weeks is about 25 class hours a week, before homework. It says nothing about what an app will do for you, and it should not be read as a timeline. Its value is comparative: Khmer is demanding, a category below Cantonese, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean and Arabic, and a category above [Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/).

## A first month before a trip

If you have a trip booked, the sequencing is different from a general study plan, because you have a deadline and a known set of situations.

**Week 1 — numbers and the polite layer.** Counting, prices, *baat* or *chaa*, hello and thank you. This is the highest-return vocabulary in the language for a visitor and it is a week's work at most.

**Week 2 — the situations you know you will be in.** Airport arrivals, hotels, tuk-tuks and taxis, ordering food, market bargaining, currency. The travel material in the app is grouped this way, with sections for Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, Angkor Wat, Battambang, Kampot, Kep and Sihanoukville, so you can revise only what your itinerary needs.

**Week 3 — start the alphabet properly.** Consonants with their series, then vowels, using tracing practice. You will not finish it in a week and you are not meant to. The goal is to stop seeing Khmer text as decoration.

**Week 4 — listening at real speed.** Tapping a phrase to hear it, slowing it down, then repeating it is the loop that closes the gap between reading a phrase and recognising one spoken at normal pace. Temple etiquette, pharmacies and emergency phrases are worth a pass here too — content you hope not to need is exactly the content you cannot look up in the moment.

Matching games, fill-in-the-blank questions, phrase building, flashcards you build and shuffle yourself, pronunciation lab exercises, speaking missions, stories, roleplays, daily challenges and speed rounds keep that month from settling into one shape, which matters over four weeks more than it does over four days.

## Is it worth it for two weeks in Cambodia?

Honestly: the language is not required. English is workable in the places most visitors go, and you will not be stranded without Khmer.

What a month of preparation buys is a different quality of trip. Numbers change how markets go. A greeting and a thank you in the right register change how people respond to you. And the script, even half-learned, turns a wall of unreadable signage into something you can partly decode, which is a surprisingly large shift in how a place feels.

If your motivation is family rather than travel, the calculation is different again and the answer is easier — a beginner course gives you a foundation to build on with people who can correct you, which is the only way anyone actually gets good.

Either way, treat this article and the course as a starting point rather than a substitute for speaking with fluent speakers. If you are still deciding between languages, the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) come with the same honest accounting: what the script costs, what the grammar costs, and what you get at the end of a month.

title: Learn Malay for Beginners: The Easy Start and the Part That Is Not Easy
metaTitle: Learn Malay for Beginners: An Honest Starter Guide

sources.p: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Malay is the language most often recommended to people who say they want to learn an Asian language but are put off by scripts and tones. That recommendation is basically sound, and it is usually made for slightly the wrong reasons.

What Malay actually gives a beginner is a very cheap first fortnight. What it does not give you is a cheap sixth month. Knowing where the change of gradient is makes the difference between a learner who keeps going and one who is quietly baffled about why progress stopped feeling free.

## What the difficulty scale says

The US Foreign Service Institute groups the languages it teaches by how long its students typically need to reach Professional Working Proficiency — a score of Speaking-3/Reading-3 on the Interagency Language Roundtable scale. Malay sits in **Category II**, at approximately **36 weeks of full-time instruction (900 class hours)**, in a small group with German, Indonesian, Haitian Creole and Swahili.

For comparison, Category III — Thai, Khmer, Russian, Polish, Vietnamese — runs to roughly 44 weeks, and Category IV, the group containing Cantonese, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean and Arabic, runs to 88 weeks. Malay is not in the easiest bracket, which is reserved for languages closely related to English, but it is comfortably the least demanding widely-spoken language of Southeast Asia for an English speaker to take up.

Those figures describe intensive, full-time, small-group classroom training for diplomats — 900 hours across 36 weeks works out at about 25 class hours a week, before any homework. They are not a prediction about what an app will do for you. They are useful precisely as a **relative** scale, and on that scale Malay is genuinely the gentlest entry point in the region.

## The part that really is easy

Four things are absent from Malay that consume a lot of beginner effort elsewhere.

**There is no new script.** Standard Malay is written in **Rumi**, the Latin alphabet. You can read a Malay sentence aloud on day one, badly but recognisably. Compare that with [the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/), where a month of work buys you the ability to sound out a word.

**There are no tones.** Pitch does not distinguish words. Say a word with the wrong intonation in Malay and you sound foreign; say a word with the wrong tone in Cantonese and you have said a different word.

**Verbs do not conjugate.** No person, no number, no tense endings. The same verb form serves "I eat", "she eats" and "they ate". Time is carried by separate words meaning *already*, *still*, *not yet* or *will*, or by context when context is enough.

**There is no grammatical gender and there are no articles.** Nouns are not masculine or feminine. There is no *a* or *the* to place. Even the third-person pronoun **dia** covers he and she without distinction, which quietly removes a whole class of error.

Add basic possession by word order — the possessor simply follows the thing possessed, so "my house" is literally *house I*, **rumah saya** — and you have a language where a beginner can assemble a true, comprehensible sentence in the first hour.

Greetings behave. **Selamat pagi** is "good morning", **terima kasih** is "thank you", **apa khabar?** is "how are you". Counting starts **satu, dua, tiga** — one, two, three — and follows a regular pattern upward. None of it requires a decoder.

## The part that is not easy: the affix system

Now the gradient changes.

Malay builds most of its vocabulary by attaching prefixes, suffixes and circumfixes to a root. One root generates a family of related words, and the affixes carry information that English carries with separate words or with word order. This is where Malay stops being a language you can guess at.

The standard illustration is the root **ajar**, "teach":

| Word | Rough meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ajar | the root idea of teaching |
| mengajar | to teach (someone something) |
| belajar | to study, to learn |
| pelajar | a student |
| pengajar | an instructor |
| pelajaran | a lesson, a subject of study |

Six words, one root, and the difference between "teach" and "learn" is carried entirely by the prefix. A learner who treats these as six unrelated vocabulary items is doing several times the necessary work. A learner who understands the pattern gets large parts of the dictionary at a discount.

Two other affix behaviours matter early:

**The passive.** Malay uses the passive far more readily than English does, and the **di-** prefix is one of the main ways of forming it. Sentences that an English speaker would instinctively make active are frequently passive in natural Malay, and this is one of the more common places where a beginner's grammatically correct sentence still sounds off.

**Reduplication.** Repeating a word can mark plurality — **buku** is "book", **buku-buku** is "books" — but reduplication also does other jobs depending on the word, including softening, marking variety, or forming a distinct word altogether. It is not a general-purpose plural marker to be applied at will, and plurality in Malay is often left to context or handled with a quantifier instead.

Then there are **classifiers**. When you count things, Malay puts a classifier between the number and the noun, chosen according to what kind of thing you are counting — one set for people, another for animals, another for objects. English speakers do this with *two slices of bread* and then forget the language ever required it.

This cluster — word order, pronouns, possession, questions, classifiers, reduplication, passive forms, comparison and the affix system — is exactly what [Learn Malay - Bahasa Melayu](/apps/learn-malay/) teaches as its grammar track, explained on Malay's own terms rather than by mapping onto English rules that do not fit.

## Malay and Indonesian: close, and not the same

This deserves its own section because getting it wrong wastes months.

Malay and Indonesian are closely related standardised varieties with a shared ancestor. A Malaysian and an Indonesian can hold a conversation with effort and goodwill. But they were standardised by different institutions under different colonial and national histories, and the differences are real:

- **Loanword sources differ.** Malaysian Malay has absorbed a great deal of English vocabulary. Indonesian carries a substantial Dutch-derived layer. Both draw on Sanskrit and Arabic from earlier periods, along with Portuguese, Chinese and Tamil.
- **Some words exist in both with different meanings.** *Kereta* is the everyday word for a car in Malaysia; in Indonesian it refers to a train. That kind of overlap is more dangerous than a word you simply do not know, because nothing signals that you have misunderstood.
- **Everyday vocabulary diverges.** Malaysian *wang* and Indonesian *uang* both mean money.
- **Pronunciation habits differ.** In much of Peninsular Malaysia a word-final *a* is commonly reduced toward a schwa; Indonesian keeps a fuller vowel there. Neither is a mistake — they are two conventions.

The two are close enough that a 1972 joint spelling reform aligned much of their orthography, which is why they look more similar on the page than they sound in a room.

The practical advice is simply to decide which one you are learning and use material that knows the difference. Learn Malay - Bahasa Melayu teaches **Standard Malay** and includes regional notes on how the language is used across different communities, and it deliberately does not present Indonesian as the same language.

## Rumi, Jawi, and what you actually need

You will occasionally see Malay written in **Jawi**, a script derived from the Arabic alphabet with additional letters for Malay sounds. Jawi has centuries of literary history behind it, retains an official role in Brunei, appears in religious and cultural contexts, and turns up on signage in parts of Malaysia.

For a beginner, the honest answer is that you do not need it. Rumi is the standard everyday script and is what a beginner course teaches. But knowing Jawi exists prevents the small shock of encountering it and assuming you have wandered into a different language.

## Pronunciation is predictable, with one wrinkle

Malay spelling is close to phonemic: letters generally correspond to a single sound, so a written word tells you how to say it. That makes it one of the more forgiving languages to read aloud.

The wrinkle is the letter **e**, which represents two different vowel sounds — a schwa and a clearer front vowel — and ordinary spelling does not distinguish them. Most learners absorb this through exposure rather than rules, and it is the one place where you genuinely need to hear a word rather than read it.

Beyond that, the work is in **rhythm** rather than in decoding. Malay syllables are relatively even, without the heavy stressed-and-reduced alternation of English, and beginners who import English stress patterns sound noticeably foreign even when every individual sound is right. This is why the pronunciation track in the app covers vowels, consonants, syllable rhythm and spelling-to-sound patterns together, using Malay speech support where your device provides it.

Recognising a rhythm and producing one are different skills, and neither this article nor an app substitutes for speaking with a fluent speaker.

## A realistic first month

**Week 1 — say true things immediately.** Greetings, introductions, numbers, family, daily routines. Because there is no script barrier, aim to produce sentences rather than to recognise words.

**Week 2 — situations, not lists.** Restaurants, shopping, directions, money, transport. Vocabulary learned inside a situation is retrieved inside that situation, which is the whole reason the app groups it that way rather than as alphabetical lists.

**Week 3 — meet the affixes.** This is where the language gets its shape. Take one root and learn its whole family rather than collecting isolated words. Expect this week to feel harder than the previous two; that is the gradient changing, not you failing.

**Week 4 — listen to dialogue at real speed.** The gap between reading a phrase and hearing one is where most beginners discover their comprehension is thinner than they thought. Dictation is unusually effective here because it forces you to commit to what you heard.

Learn Malay - Bahasa Melayu supports that shape with Daily Review, Speed Run Review, Mistake Rescue, Listening Blitz, Sentence Builder, Match Blitz and Dictation Mode drawing on material you have already covered, plus a missed-questions list. XP, daily goals, streaks and achievements track consistency, and there is no hearts or lives system, so a wrong answer never stops the lesson.

## An honest ceiling

A beginner course gives you a foundation: pronunciation, core vocabulary, working grammar, and enough structure to build your own sentences rather than recite memorised ones. It does not give you fluency, and no app can promise it.

What Malay offers that most of the region does not is a genuinely low cost of entry. You can be saying useful, correct things in week one, which matters more than it sounds — the languages people abandon are usually the ones where nothing works for a month.

If you want to compare that against the alternatives before committing, the other guides in our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) collection lay out what each one actually demands: [Cantonese](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/) sits two FSI categories higher, [Khmer](/blog/learn-khmer-beginners-guide/) has a demanding script but no tones, and [Russian](/blog/learn-russian-cyrillic-beginners-guide/) trades a new alphabet — learnable in days — for a grammar that does far more work than Malay's.

title: Learn the Russian Cyrillic Alphabet: The Shortest Hard Part of a Hard Language
metaTitle: Learn the Russian Cyrillic Alphabet: Beginner Guide
secondaryKeywords: how many letters in the russian alphabet

sources.p: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
The Cyrillic alphabet is the part of Russian that looks hardest from outside and turns out to be the smallest job in the whole language. Thirty-three letters, most of which behave, and an adult working at it consistently can be sounding out street signs inside a fortnight.

The trap is that people treat it as the gate rather than the doorstep. They stall on the alphabet, decide Russian is impossible, and never find out that the alphabet was the easy bit.

## Thirty-three letters, three piles

The modern Russian alphabet has **33 letters**: ten vowel letters, twenty-one consonant letters, and two signs — ь and ъ — that spell no sound of their own but change how the letters around them are pronounced.

Learning them as an alphabetical list is the slow way. Sorting them by how much trouble they will cause you is considerably faster.

### Pile one: the ones you already read

A handful of letters look like Latin letters and sound roughly like them: **А, К, М, О, Т**. You get these for free, and they are worth noticing early because they make your first Russian words legible before you have done any work at all.

### Pile two: the false friends

This is the pile that causes nearly all early errors, and it deserves disproportionate practice:

| Letter | Sounds like |
| --- | --- |
| В | v |
| Н | n |
| Р | r (rolled) |
| С | s |
| У | u, as in *boot* |
| Х | a rasping h, as in Scottish *loch* |

Every one of these looks like a Latin letter with a different value. Under time pressure — reading a sign from a moving bus, or a word you half-recognise — a learner who has only half-learned these will default to the Latin reading. The fix is not cleverness, it is over-practice: drill this pile harder than the genuinely new letters, because the new ones have nothing to interfere with them.

### Pile three: the genuinely new ones

Б, Г, Д, Ж, З, И, Й, Л, П, Ф, Ц, Ч, Ш, Щ, Ы, Э, Ю, Я, Ё, plus the two signs. These feel like the hard part and are usually not, because your brain has no competing habit to override. A new shape attached to a new sound is a clean association.

Three of them repay extra attention. **Ы** is a vowel with no close English equivalent and needs to be heard rather than described. **Ш and Щ** are a pair that beginners flatten into the same sound. And the two signs, **ь** and **ъ**, are not letters you pronounce — they modify the consonant before them, and the soft sign in particular is doing real grammatical work that will matter later.

### The reward arrives almost immediately

The alphabet pays out faster in Russian than in most languages, because Russian has absorbed a large stock of internationally recognisable vocabulary. Within a few days you can read **ресторан**, **метро**, **такси**, **банк**, **паспорт** and **футбол** off a sign and know exactly what they say, without having learned a single word of vocabulary deliberately.

That experience is worth engineering on purpose in your first week. It is the clearest early evidence that the script is a solvable problem, and it arrives before the grammar has had a chance to discourage anyone.

## What the alphabet does not give you

Here is the honest limitation, and it is the reason "I learned Cyrillic in a weekend" claims are only half true.

**Stress is not marked in ordinary text.** You will see stress marks in dictionaries, in books for children and in material written for learners, but normal Russian writing leaves them out because native readers do not need them. Russian stress is **mobile** — it can move between forms of the same word — and it is not predictable from spelling.

**Unstressed vowels reduce.** The most important case is the letter **о**: stressed, it is a clear *o*; unstressed, it shifts toward an *a*. So a word can be spelled with an о and pronounced with something much closer to an а, and nothing on the page tells you which syllable is stressed.

Put those together and the conclusion is uncomfortable but useful: **the alphabet gets you to a spelling, not to a pronunciation.** You have to learn each word's stress with the word, from audio, the way you would learn a gender or a tone.

There is a related habit worth knowing about early: common polite words are heavily reduced in ordinary speech. **Здравствуйте**, the formal "hello", is not pronounced the way its eleven letters suggest — the first **в** routinely disappears — and **пожалуйста** ("please", and also "you're welcome") is regularly compressed in casual speech. This is normal, it is not sloppiness, and a course that only ever plays words in careful isolation will leave you unprepared for it.

For less formal use, **привет** is the everyday "hi", and **спасибо** is "thank you". **Да** and **нет** are yes and no. Counting starts **один, два, три**.

## The second alphabet nobody mentions

You learn the printed forms. Then you meet a word in italics, or handwritten, and several letters have quietly become different shapes.

Italic and cursive Cyrillic diverge from the printed forms much more than italic Latin diverges from upright Latin. In italic, **т** takes a form that reads to an English eye like a Latin *m*, **д** looks like a *g*, **и** like a *u* and **п** like an *n*. Handwritten Russian goes further still, and a page of native handwriting is genuinely difficult for a beginner who has only ever seen print.

This is not an obscure edge case. Italics appear in ordinary books and websites, and handwriting appears on forms, notes and menus. It is best treated as a small second stage of the alphabet rather than as a nasty surprise six months in.

## Why romanisation is not a shortcut

There is no single agreed way to write Russian in Latin letters. The Library of Congress ALA-LC tables serve library cataloguing. Other schemes serve geographic naming, international standards work or academic linguistics, and each makes different choices. That is why the same composer's surname appears as Tchaikovsky, Chaikovsky and Čajkovskij depending on which system produced it.

For a learner, romanisation has the same defect in Russian that it has elsewhere: it is a lossy rendering aimed at readers who do not know the language. Since Cyrillic takes days rather than months, the cost-benefit is not close. Learn the letters and skip the intermediate step entirely.

It is also worth knowing that **Cyrillic is not one alphabet**. It is a script used for many languages, and their inventories differ — Ukrainian uses і, ї and є, which Russian does not; Serbian uses ј, љ, њ, ћ and џ. The Unicode Cyrillic block encodes the whole family, which is why your phone renders all of them, but knowing the Russian 33 does not automatically make you a reader of every Cyrillic language.

## A two-week plan for the alphabet

**Days 1–3 — piles one and two.** The free letters and the false friends together, because the contrast between them is the lesson. Read real signage and product names rather than letter charts.

**Days 4–8 — pile three, in small batches.** Five or six new letters at a time, immediately used inside whole words. A letter learned inside a word is retrievable; a letter learned in a grid is a quiz answer.

**Days 9–11 — internationalisms and place names.** Read words you can already verify. Being right builds speed, and speed is what turns recognition into reading.

**Days 12–14 — italics, then handwriting.** Meet the second set of shapes deliberately while the first set is still fresh.

Two weeks of that gets most adults to slow, accurate reading. Fluent reading takes months, and that is fine — you only need slow and accurate to start learning vocabulary from written material.

[Regal - Learn Russian Language](/apps/learn-russian/) is sequenced on exactly this assumption: alphabet lessons come first so you can recognise letters and sounds before vocabulary and grammar begin stacking up, and the rest of the course assumes you are meeting the script for the first time.

## What waits on the other side

Being straightforward about this is more useful than encouragement.

**Six cases.** Nouns, pronouns and adjectives change form according to their role in the sentence — nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, instrumental and prepositional. This is the feature that defines the Russian learning curve. It is not memorising six tables; it is developing the reflex to choose a form while you are speaking.

**Three genders and agreement.** Adjectives and past-tense verbs agree with the gender of the noun, so gender is not a label you can postpone.

**Verb aspect.** Most Russian verbs come in pairs — one form for an action viewed as ongoing or repeated, another for one viewed as complete. English handles this with tense and context; Russian handles it with a choice of verb. Aspect tends to be harder for English speakers than the cases, because there is no equivalent to map it onto.

**And some things get easier.** Russian has no articles at all — no *a*, no *the* — and the present tense of "to be" is normally simply omitted, so a great many sentences are shorter than their English equivalents.

The app's design responds to that curve directly: cases, gender, agreement and verb forms are introduced in stages, and exercises explain why the correct answer is correct rather than just marking it. Once the basics are in place, there are stories, documents, roleplays, culture lessons and history to read, which is where practice stops being drills. Saved words and missed-question practice pull back what you got wrong, with progress tracking, daily goals and achievements alongside.

## The honest scale

The US Foreign Service Institute groups the languages it teaches by how long its students typically need to reach Professional Working Proficiency — a score of Speaking-3/Reading-3 on the Interagency Language Roundtable scale. Russian sits in **Category III**, at approximately **44 weeks of full-time instruction (1,100 class hours)**, alongside Polish, Thai, Khmer and Vietnamese.

That describes intensive, full-time, small-group classroom training for diplomats — 1,100 hours across 44 weeks is about 25 class hours a week, before homework. It is not a claim about what an app achieves and it should not be read as one. What it does establish is where Russian sits relative to other options: harder than German or [Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/), and a full category easier than [Cantonese](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/), Mandarin, Japanese, Korean or Arabic.

A beginner course — this one included — is aimed at a foundation, not fluency: the alphabet, working grammar, useful vocabulary and phrases for everyday situations. That foundation is real, and Cyrillic is the first piece of it. It is also the piece you can finish this month.

For a sense of what other scripts ask by comparison, [the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) encodes tone through spelling rules rather than letters, and [Khmer](/blog/learn-khmer-beginners-guide/) writes vowels around the consonant with two different readings each. The rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) start from the same place: no prior study assumed.

title: How to Learn the Thai Script (and Why Romanisation Will Let You Down)
metaTitle: Learn Thai Script: A Beginner's Guide to Reading
secondaryKeywords: royal thai general system of transcription

sources.p: Office of the Royal Society, Thailand
U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
You can find the Thai for "thank you" written as *khop khun*, *kob khun*, *korb koon* and half a dozen other ways, and every one of them is a defensible attempt at the same word. None of them tells you what tone to say it on.

That single fact is the strongest argument for learning the script, and it is worth understanding before you decide how much effort to put in.

## The romanisation trap

Thailand's official transliteration standard is the Royal Thai General System of Transcription, maintained by the Office of the Royal Society. It is a good system for its actual purpose, which is putting Thai names and places into the Latin alphabet consistently — on road signs, in passports, in library catalogues.

It has one property that matters enormously to a learner: **it does not record tone, and it does not record vowel length.** Neither does the ad-hoc romanisation on a menu or in a phrasebook. Library cataloguing systems such as the ALA-LC romanization tables solve a different problem again and are not built to be pronounced from.

So a romanised Thai word is missing two of the four things you need to say it. You can memorise the missing information word by word, from audio, and plenty of people do. But you are then carrying in your head what the writing system would have carried for you, and you have no way to read a new word correctly on sight. The ceiling arrives sooner than people expect — usually at the point where two words you know look identical romanised and are obviously different to a Thai speaker.

Learning the script removes the problem at the root. It is not a prerequisite for saying "hello" on a beach holiday. It is a prerequisite for getting better after month two.

## What kind of writing system Thai is

Thai is not an alphabet in the European sense. It is an **abugida**: consonant letters carry a built-in vowel, and other vowels are written as signs attached to the consonant.

That distinction sounds academic until you see where the vowel signs go.

### Vowels do not sit in a line

In Latin script, letters run left to right and you read them in the order they appear. Thai vowel signs are placed **before, after, above or below** the consonant, and some are made of pieces that sit on more than one side of it at once.

The consequence is that **written order is not always spoken order**. A vowel sign written to the left of a consonant is pronounced after it. A beginner who reads Thai strictly left to right will produce syllables in the wrong order and conclude that the script is chaotic. It is not — it is consistent — but it is consistent according to a rule you have to be taught rather than one you can infer.

This is the single most common early stumble, and it is why alphabet practice that separates consonants, vowels, tone marks and syllables into stages works better than presenting a full chart on day one. It is how the alphabet section of [Regal - Learn Thai Language](/apps/learn-thai/) is organised: consonants, vowels, tone marks and syllables in sequence, with reading and writing basics, before sentences get long.

## Why 44 consonants for far fewer sounds

Here is the fact that makes Thai look harder than it is, and then makes it make sense.

The consonant inventory is usually counted at **44 letters**. Two of them, ฃ and ฅ, have dropped out of ordinary modern use. Those letters do not map to 44 different sounds — several letters are pronounced identically. Learners reasonably ask why the extra letters exist.

The answer is that Thai consonant letters do two jobs at once. They tell you the sound, **and** they tell you which of three **tone classes** the letter belongs to: high, mid or low. Two letters that sound the same can belong to different classes, and that difference changes the tone of the whole syllable.
