In other words, the redundancy is not redundancy. The tone information has to live somewhere, and Thai puts a large part of it in the choice of consonant letter. Once you see that, memorising the class alongside the sound stops feeling like arbitrary extra work and starts feeling like the point.

## Five tones, spelled rather than marked

Standard Thai distinguishes **five tones**: mid, low, falling, high and rising. There are **four tone marks**.

Four marks cannot label five tones, and that mismatch is the key to the whole system. The tone of a syllable is worked out from four things together:

1. The **class of the initial consonant** — high, mid or low.
2. The **length of the vowel** — long or short.
3. The **ending of the syllable** — whether it stops on a final consonant sound like -k, -t or -p, or ends openly.
4. The **tone mark**, if there is one.

The tone mark is one input among four, not the answer. This is why "just learn the four tone marks" is bad advice, and why learners who try to shortcut the consonant classes hit a wall a few weeks in.

The upside is real, though, and it is worth stating plainly: **the system is regular.** Once you know the rules, you can look at a Thai word you have never seen and derive its tone. That is something a romanised word can never give you, and it is the moment the script starts paying you back.

Recognising a tone and producing one are separate skills, and both are harder in conversation than in a quiet room. An app can give you controlled listening practice and prompt you to speak; it cannot hear you the way a fluent speaker can. Treat pronunciation work here as a foundation to bring to a real conversation, not a replacement for one.

## Three things nobody warns you about

**There are no spaces between words.** Thai runs continuously, and spaces mark the ends of clauses and sentences instead. Where a word ends is something you infer from context and from Thai syllable structure. Letter recognition comes fast; reading speed lags behind it for months, and this is why.

**There are no capital letters and no full stops.** Nothing on the page marks a proper noun or the start of a sentence. Punctuation exists but does less work than in English.

**Thai has its own digits.** ๐ ๑ ๒ ๓ ๔ ๕ ๖ ๗ ๘ ๙ run from zero to nine alongside the Arabic numerals you already read. You will meet them on official documents, temple signage and occasionally on price lists, and they take about an afternoon to learn — one of the highest returns on effort in the whole script.

## The handful of phrases worth getting exactly right

Kept deliberately short, because a phrase learned with the wrong tone is a phrase you will have to unlearn.

**สวัสดี** (*sawatdi* in RTGS, often written *sawasdee*) is the general greeting, usable at any time of day.

**ครับ** (*khrap*) and **ค่ะ** (*kha*) are politeness particles added to the end of a sentence, and which one you use depends on the speaker's gender rather than the listener's: **ครับ** for a male speaker, **ค่ะ** for a female speaker. They are not optional decoration. Thai marks politeness structurally, and leaving the particle off makes an otherwise correct sentence sound abrupt. The female form also shifts depending on whether you are making a statement or asking a question, which is a detail worth learning from a course rather than from a phrasebook.

**ขอบคุณ** (*khopkhun*) is "thank you", and it takes the same politeness particle on the end.

A note on which Thai you are learning: courses, including ours, teach **Standard Thai**, which is based on the Central Thai variety and is the language of education, broadcasting and government. Northern, Northeastern and Southern regions have their own varieties with real differences in vocabulary and pronunciation, and Northeastern Thai in particular is closely related to Lao. Standard Thai is understood everywhere; it is not the only Thai you will hear.

## Where Thai sits on the difficulty scale

The clearest public benchmark is the US Foreign Service Institute's training categories, which group languages by how long FSI students typically need to reach Professional Working Proficiency — a score of Speaking-3/Reading-3 on the Interagency Language Roundtable scale. Thai is in **Category III**, at approximately **44 weeks of full-time instruction (1,100 class hours)**, alongside Russian, Khmer, Polish and Vietnamese.

That figure describes intensive, full-time, small-group classroom training for diplomats — 1,100 hours across 44 weeks is about 25 class hours a week, before homework — so it is not a prediction about app study. Use it as a relative scale instead: Thai is demanding, but a full category easier than Cantonese, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean or Arabic. The script is front-loaded difficulty; the grammar behind it is considerably kinder than the writing system suggests.

## A four-week plan for the script

**Week 1 — mid-class consonants and short vowels.** A small set of letters and a small set of vowels, learned as syllables you can actually say. Resist the urge to learn all 44 consonants first; a chart you cannot pronounce is not knowledge.

**Week 2 — high and low classes.** Learn each new consonant with its class from the first exposure, the same way you would learn a German noun with its gender. Adding the class later is much harder than learning it at the same time.

**Week 3 — tone rules on real syllables.** Take the four inputs and start deriving tones for words you already know by ear. The goal is to make the rules produce something you can verify against audio, not to recite a table.

**Week 4 — read continuous text badly.** Slowly, out loud, getting word boundaries wrong. This is the stage most people skip and it is the one that converts letter recognition into reading. Dictation is unusually good practice here because it forces you to commit to a spelling, which forces you to commit to a tone.

Regal - Learn Thai Language is built around short daily lessons on a set path rather than open-ended word lists, which suits this kind of staged work — the alphabet section, pronunciation practice for tones and sounds, speaking practice, then grammar covering word order, polite particles, questions, negation, classifiers, numbers and time. Travel material is grouped by situation, so airports, hotels, restaurants, transport, directions, health and emergencies can be revised separately before a trip. Review modes, a sentence builder, dictation and a missed-questions list handle everything after the first pass.

## What is genuinely hard, and what is not

**Genuinely hard:** the tone rules, because they require holding four things in mind at once until they become automatic. Word segmentation in unspaced text. Producing tone contrasts reliably at conversational speed.

**Not as hard as advertised:** Thai grammar. No verb conjugation for tense or person, no grammatical gender, no articles, no plural inflection. Once the script is behind you, the sentence structures come faster than they do in most European languages.

That is the shape of the language, and it is why the script is worth the front-loaded effort. If you are still choosing, [Khmer](/blog/learn-khmer-beginners-guide/) shares the abugida structure and the no-spaces convention but has no tones at all, [Cantonese](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/) asks more of you on every axis, and [Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/) skips the script problem entirely. All of them, and the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/), start from the same assumption: you have never studied the language before.

title: Low-Carb Tracking Apps Compared: The Subtraction, the Extras and the Subscription
metaTitle: Best Keto App: Low-Carb Trackers Compared

sources.p: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine
U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service

body:
A general calorie counter and a low-carb tracker look almost identical on the surface. Both take a food, both give you macros back. The difference is one subtraction, performed dozens of times a week, and whether the app does it or you do.

That subtraction is also the reason low-carb comparisons go wrong. People compare feature lists when the thing that actually determines their daily experience is a counting convention buried three screens down.

**Disclosure:** this article is published by Reign Creative LLC. We make one of the four apps discussed below — Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb — so we have a direct commercial interest in you installing it. The comparison is written to remain useful if you choose one of the others, and we have set out below the cases where one of the others is the better fit.

Everything stated here about another company's product was read on that company's own website on **9 August 2026** and is limited to what those pages said. This category changes its packaging frequently; confirm current details with the vendor before deciding.

## The subtraction is the product

Net carbs is not a regulated measurement. A US Nutrition Facts panel declares Total Carbohydrate with Dietary Fiber, Total Sugars and Added Sugars beneath it — the net figure is arithmetic performed afterwards, by you or by software, according to a convention someone chose. We take that apart properly in [net carbs, explained](/blog/net-carbs-explained-keto-tracking/).

The practical consequence for choosing an app is this: **when a tracker shows you a net carb number, it is showing you the output of its own rule.** The rule usually starts from total carbohydrate and removes dietary fiber, and most low-carb conventions also remove sugar alcohols and some newer sweeteners. Which sweeteners, and whether all fibers are treated the same, is where apps diverge.

So the first question is not "does this app do net carbs" — nearly all of them do — but "does it do them the way I intend to count, and does it do them without me thinking about it."

[Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb](/apps/keto-diet-tracker/) subtracts fiber along with erythritol, allulose and monk fruit from total carbohydrate each time you log a food, and it can alert you when a day passes a limit you set yourself. That is a stated convention rather than a hidden one, which is the property that matters: a number you can reproduce beats a number that is theoretically purer.

## What each app is built around

### Carb Manager

Carb Manager's own site describes tracking net carbs, macros and micros, and going well beyond food: it names tracking for ketones, blood glucose and insulin, and for glycemic load and GKI, plus intermittent fasting. Its named sections include a Macros Tracker, Food Tracker, Meal Planner, Recipe Database, Keto Academy, Community, Exercise Portal, Advanced Insights and Health Integrations, with Fitbit and Garmin named among device syncs.

Two things stand out from that list as genuine differentiators. The **Recipe Database and Meal Planner** are positioned as a large part of the product rather than an accessory, and there is a **Community** and a **Keto Academy** — social and educational components that no purely mechanical logger has. If you want the app to also be where you get recipes and where you talk to other people doing the same thing, that is a real reason to pick it, and it is a reason we cannot match.

### Cronometer

Cronometer is not a keto app, and it is worth including precisely because of that. Its features page lists "Track Any Diet," describing customisation for keto among others, and its strength is the nutrient panel rather than the carb rule.

On its pricing page the free Basic tier includes custom macro *and micronutrient* targets, a barcode scanner, custom foods, meals and recipes, and device syncing, with reports and charts over a seven-day window. Gold adds photo and voice logging, a Recipe Importer, a Fasting Timer, a Macro Scheduler, custom charts, coaching and unlimited historical data.

If your interest in low-carb is partly a worry about what a restricted diet does to your micronutrient intake — a reasonable worry, given that MedlinePlus notes low-carb diets can limit daily fiber — a nutrient-depth tracker answers a question a carb-focused one does not.

### MyFitnessPal

MyFitnessPal is the general tracker most people already have. It logs macros and micronutrients and has the broadest set of entry routes, and it can be used for low-carb eating by treating carbohydrate as the number you watch.

The relevant detail for a low-carb reader is where its line falls. MyFitnessPal's own Premium page lists "Custom macros and goals" and an "Intermittent fasting tracker" among Premium features. Setting a specific carbohydrate target is the entire point of low-carb tracking, so which side of the paywall that sits on is not a minor packaging question. Read their current Premium page before assuming either way.

### Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb

Ours is built narrowly around the low-carb day. The net carb subtraction runs automatically on every entry, with an optional alert when a day passes the limit you chose. There is a low-carb food database and a barcode scanner for packaged items, custom foods and recipes for anything you cook, and a meal planner covering breakfast, lunch, dinner and desserts. A built-in macro calculator turns details you enter — age, height, weight, activity level — into starting fat, protein and net carb figures you are free to change.

Around the food sit the other logs: ketone readings you took yourself with blood, urine strips or a breath meter including GKI, an intermittent fasting timer, water, and sodium, potassium and magnesium. Body measurements, photo logs, charts and weekly and monthly summaries hold the history.

It is free to download on Google Play, supported by ads, and it has **no in-app purchases** — everything listed above is in that free download. No account is required, and logs are stored locally on your device rather than on our servers.

What it does not have: no wearable or device integrations, no community, no recipe marketplace or course content, and no full micronutrient panel beyond the electrolytes named above. Those are the trades we made to keep it a single-purpose log.

## The half of low-carb tracking that is not food

This is where these apps separate more than they do on food logging, and it is under-discussed.

**Ketone readings.** Blood meters, urine strips and breath meters each produce a number, and people who use them want that number next to the day it belongs to. Carb Manager names ketone, blood glucose, insulin and GKI tracking; ours records blood, urine strip and breath readings including GKI. Neither app measures anything — a phone cannot. It stores what you type in, and a reading is a data point you collected, not a medical result.

**Fasting windows.** Fasting timers appear across the category but not always in the free tier: Cronometer's pricing page lists its Fasting Timer under Gold, MyFitnessPal's Premium page lists an intermittent fasting tracker under Premium, Carb Manager names intermittent fasting on its site, and ours includes a fasting timer in the free app. If you fast, check this specifically.

**Water and electrolytes.** Sodium, potassium and magnesium get attention in low-carb circles that they do not get in general nutrition apps. Ours logs all three alongside water. We are not going to tell you what to do with those numbers — that is a conversation for a healthcare professional — but if you are tracking them, having them in the same record as the food is the difference between a habit and three apps.

## Where the money is

| App | What the vendor's own pages said on 9 August 2026 |
| --- | --- |
| Carb Manager | Their premium page lists a free Basic account and a paid Premium account, and highlights Premium extras including exclusive recipes, personalised meal plans and a video jumpstart course. The page's own comparison table did not clearly separate the tiers, so we have not stated which individual features are gated. |
| Cronometer | Free Basic tier including barcode scanner and custom macro and micronutrient targets, with a seven-day reporting window; paid Gold tier adding photo and voice logging, a fasting timer, coaching and unlimited history. |
| MyFitnessPal | Premium page lists ad-free logging, barcode and meal scan, voice and multi-day logging, custom macros and goals, an intermittent fasting tracker and downloadable progress reports; a Premium+ tier adds meal planning and grocery lists. |
| Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb | Free to download, supported by ads, no in-app purchases. |

The pattern is worth naming without judging it: the general-purpose trackers monetise through subscriptions and put some target-setting and automation behind them, while ours monetises through ads and puts everything in the download. Ads are not free either — they cost you attention and screen space. Which cost you would rather pay is a genuine preference, and people split on it.

## Who is better served elsewhere

**Pick Carb Manager if** you want recipes, meal plans, a community and course content in the same place as the log, and you are happy to evaluate its tier structure on its current pricing page.

**Pick Cronometer if** your real question is nutritional adequacy rather than carbohydrate specifically, you want micronutrient targets you can set for free, and you would use its biometric tracking.

**Pick MyFitnessPal if** you are already logging there, most of your food is packaged, and low-carb is one phase in a longer relationship with a general tracker.

**Pick [Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb](/apps/keto-diet-tracker/) if** you want the net carb subtraction handled with a stated rule, you log ketones or fasting windows or electrolytes, and you would rather have ads than a subscription.

**Pick a different tool entirely if** carbohydrate is not actually your constraint. If you are chasing a protein target rather than a carb ceiling, a general protein log is a better fit — [Protein Diet Tracker](/apps/protein-diet-tracker/) is ours, [how to track protein intake](/blog/how-to-track-protein-intake/) covers the habit, and the rest of the range sits under [health and nutrition](/apps/category/health-nutrition/).

## What none of these apps can do

None of them is a medical or diagnostic tool. They do not interpret a ketone reading, they do not assess whether a low-carb diet is appropriate for you, and they do not promise weight loss or any other outcome. MedlinePlus is direct on the point: a low-carbohydrate diet "can be safe, but you should talk to your health care provider before starting it."

They also cannot make an estimate exact. If you want to sanity-check what an app says about a generic food, USDA's **FoodData Central** is free to search and its data are in the public domain — comparing an app's entry against it takes a minute and occasionally changes your mind about the entry.

## How we checked, and a note on names

Every statement above about Carb Manager, Cronometer and MyFitnessPal was read on those companies' own websites on 9 August 2026 and is reported as what those pages said. Where a page was unclear — as Carb Manager's tier table was — we have said so rather than filled the gap with an assumption. We have not tested the other apps' interfaces, and we make no claims about their speed, accuracy or database contents. No screenshots, icons or brand styling appear here.

Carb Manager, Cronometer, MyFitnessPal and all other product names and trademarks mentioned are the property of their respective owners. Their use here is nominative — for identification of the products discussed — and implies no affiliation, sponsorship, partnership or endorsement in either direction.

title: The Major Eras of World History, and Why the Labels Are Arguments
metaTitle: Eras of World History Explained: The Labels
secondaryKeywords: when did the middle ages start and end

sources.p: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
U.S. National Archives and Records Administration
Lillian Goldman Law Library, Yale Law School

body:
Stone Age, Bronze Age, classical, medieval, early modern, modern. It is the sequence almost everyone absorbs at school, usually without being told where it came from or what it was built to describe. The labels are useful and they are also arguments — each one asserts that a stretch of time hangs together and that the stretches around it hang together differently. Here is what each one covers, and where each one stops working.

## Nobody has ever lived in an era

Start with the thing that makes the rest of this make sense: era labels were invented afterwards, by people looking back. No farmer in 1200 described the century as medieval. No one woke up in 1454 and noticed that antiquity had ended the previous year. Every period name in this article was applied retroactively by historians who needed a way to talk about large stretches of time without listing every year.

That does not make the labels useless. It makes them tools with a specific shape, and the shape is worth understanding before you rely on them. A period name is a claim that a stretch of time hangs together in some way — technologically, politically, culturally — and that the stretches on either side of it hang together differently. Sometimes that claim is well supported. Sometimes it is a habit inherited from nineteenth-century scholarship that nobody has bothered to dislodge.

## The very long run-up

Anatomically modern humans are a recent development on the scale of the fossil record. The Smithsonian's Human Origins Program dates *Homo sapiens* to "about 300,000 years ago to present", with the species evolving in Africa during a period of dramatic climate change.

Almost all of that span leaves no written trace of any kind. What survives is material: stone tools, hearths, worked bone, pigment, burials. The Smithsonian's summary of the behavioural evidence notes specifics that stone tools alone would not reveal — that by 164,000 years ago modern humans were collecting and cooking shellfish, and by 90,000 years ago had begun making specialised fishing tools.

The relevant point for periodisation is that this enormous stretch gets compressed into one or two labels while the last three thousand years get dozens. That imbalance reflects the density of surviving evidence, not the density of what happened.

## Prehistory and history: a line drawn by evidence

The conventional division between prehistory and history is the appearance of contemporary written records. Before writing, the evidence is archaeological — excavated, dated by physical methods, interpreted from context. After writing, documents join the record.

Two consequences follow, and both are regularly missed:

**The line moves.** Writing appears at very different times in different places. A region can be "prehistoric" in 1500 BCE and another region fully "historical" at the same moment. The label describes what we can read, not what stage anyone was at.

**It is not a quality judgement.** "Prehistoric" says that written sources are unavailable. It does not say that a society was simple, small, or lacking in organisation. Large-scale construction, long-distance trade and complex social structure all appear in the archaeological record without any accompanying text, which is exactly why archaeological method — as practised and described by bodies such as the National Park Service — is a discipline in its own right rather than a stopgap until documents arrive.

## The three-age scheme, and its biggest trap

Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age. It is the first sequence most people learn, and it is misused more than almost any other historical framing.

The sequence is **technological**, describing which materials dominated toolmaking. It is not a global calendar. The same label covers completely different absolute dates in different places, and the transitions happened over centuries rather than at a moment.

| Label | What it actually describes | The trap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stone Age | Tool traditions based on worked stone, spanning the overwhelming majority of the human past | Frequently treated as one short period rather than as hundreds of thousands of years containing enormous variation |
| Bronze Age | Periods in which copper alloys dominated metal tools and weapons in a given region | Dates differ by many centuries between regions; "the Bronze Age" with no region attached says almost nothing |
| Iron Age | Periods in which ironworking became the dominant metal technology in a given region | Overlaps heavily with the recorded history of neighbouring regions, so the same decades can be "Iron Age" in one place and "classical" next door |

There is a further problem: the sequence does not apply everywhere. Some regions did not follow a bronze-then-iron path at all, and applying the scheme to them imports assumptions that the evidence does not support. Regional specialists generally use regional periodisations for exactly this reason.

The practical rule: **a three-age label without a region is incomplete information.** If a source says "Bronze Age" and does not say where, it has not told you when.

## Classical antiquity

"Classical antiquity" conventionally refers to the Greek and Roman Mediterranean world and the societies it interacted with, roughly from the first millennium BCE to the middle of the first millennium CE. The label carries a value judgement in its own name — "classical" meaning exemplary — which is a reminder that it was coined by later Europeans who took that world as their model.

The contemporaneous world was very much larger than what the term covers. Powerful, literate, well-documented states existed across Asia, Africa and the Americas during the same centuries and do not appear in a period label built around the Mediterranean. This is not an argument against using the term; it is an argument for noticing what it excludes.

## The medieval problem

The term "Middle Ages" is the clearest illustration of periodisation as an argument rather than a discovery. It was coined to describe a middle stretch between antiquity and a later revival — that is, it was defined by what it sat between rather than by anything about itself. The framing built in a judgement before any evidence was consulted.

The boundary dates show the same character:

- **476 CE** — the deposition of the last western Roman emperor — is the most common conventional start. It is a defensible marker and also an odd one: contemporaries did not experience it as the end of an era, and the eastern Roman empire continued for roughly another thousand years.
- **1453** — the fall of Constantinople — is a common conventional end. So is 1492, so is 1517, and different traditions favour different ones.

That reasonable sources disagree here is not sloppiness. Each marker year emphasises a different kind of change: political, geographic, religious. The honest formulation is that the transition happened across a long stretch and that the single year is a filing convenience.

The term also travels badly. Applied outside Europe it usually imports a European chronology onto a region whose own historical divisions run differently, and specialists in those regions generally avoid it.

## Early modern

"Early modern" conventionally covers roughly the fifteenth or sixteenth century to the late eighteenth. It is a relatively recent addition to the scheme, created because the older two-part division could not accommodate several centuries of large-scale change — long-distance maritime empires, printing, religious fragmentation in Europe, and the beginnings of the political forms that would dominate later.

It is worth noticing that this era is defined largely by processes rather than events. That makes its boundaries fuzzier than the classical or medieval ones, and it is why you will see start dates anywhere across a hundred-year span depending on which process an author is tracking.

## The modern period, and framings that are openly arguments

For recent centuries the labelling becomes more explicitly interpretive, and several widely used framings are best read as claims:

- **The "long nineteenth century"**, running from the French Revolution in 1789 to the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, argues that the period between those two ruptures forms a coherent unit that the calendar century does not capture.
- **The "short twentieth century"**, running from 1914 to the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, makes the parallel argument at the other end.

Both are useful and both are contestable. They are propositions about what mattered most, not neutral divisions of the calendar, and they should be cited as interpretations rather than as facts. A student who writes "the twentieth century began in 1914" without that framing has stated somebody's argument as though it were a date.

The underlying events in these framings are, of course, documented in detail — the founding documents held by the U.S. National Archives, the holdings of The National Archives in the United Kingdom, and the treaty and constitutional texts collected in Yale Law School's Avalon Project are all freely consultable. The documents are firm. The brackets drawn around them are the interpretive layer.

## Periodisations that are not the European sequence

Plenty of well-established periodisations do not derive from the scheme above:

- **Dynastic periodisation**, used across much of East Asian historiography, divides time by ruling houses. It is precise, contemporaneous with the record-keeping it draws on, and organised around political continuity rather than technology.
- **Reign-era naming**, in which a period takes the name of an emperor's era rather than a number, produces dates that are exact within the system and require conversion to be compared with others.
- **Regional archaeological sequences**, developed independently for the Americas, Africa, Oceania and elsewhere, are built from local stratigraphy and material culture rather than imported from the Mediterranean.
- **Calendar-anchored systems**, such as dating from the Hijra in Islamic historiography, structure chronology around a different origin point entirely.

None of these is a variant of the European scheme. Treating them as translations of it — asking "which one is their Middle Ages?" — misdescribes how they work.

## What a period label is good for

Having spent this long on the caveats, the labels do genuine work:

- **They compress.** Saying "early modern" instead of listing three centuries of characteristics is efficient, and efficiency is why the vocabulary survives.
- **They flag context.** A label tells you roughly what kind of evidence to expect and what questions specialists in that area typically ask.
- **They make comparison possible.** Asking what was happening in two regions during overlapping stretches requires some shared vocabulary for the stretches.

What they are bad at is exactly what they are most often used for: implying that everything inside one label is similar, that the boundary years are real, and that the sequence is universal.

## Three habits worth keeping

1. **Always attach a region.** "Bronze Age" and "medieval" mean different times in different places, and often mean nothing at all outside the areas they were built for.
2. **Treat boundary years as filing conventions.** When two sources give different ones, ask what each is emphasising rather than which is right.
3. **Notice value-loaded names.** "Classical", "Middle Ages", "Dark Ages", "Renaissance" and "early modern" all encode a judgement in the label itself. Using them is fine; using them without noticing is not.

For the machinery that produces the underlying dates in the first place — stratigraphy, radiocarbon, tree rings, documents and astronomy — see [how historians date events](/blog/how-historians-date-events/). For separating documented record from interpretation while reading, see [how to actually learn something from a timeline](/blog/world-history-timeline-guide/).

## Seeing eras as filters rather than containers

[World History Timeline Sim](/apps/world-history-timeline-sim/) includes more than 2,000 events browsable by year, era, region, country and category, along with a world history map, daily quizzes, flashcards and timeline-ordering exercises. Era is one filter among several there, which is a more accurate reflection of how the labels actually work than a single fixed sequence would be.

Two exercises are worth doing with a tool like that. First, filter to one era and look at how much internal variety it contains. Second, filter to a single stretch of years and look across regions — the moment you see what different labels are being applied to the same decades, the conventional nature of the scheme stops being an abstraction.

Sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List are a useful reality check on the same point, since a single list spans societies that no single period scheme covers comfortably.

More in this area is collected under [education and brain training apps](/apps/category/education-brain/) and our [education and brain training articles](/blog/category/education-brain/).

title: A Malay Pronunciation Guide That Starts With What Actually Goes Wrong
metaTitle: Malay Pronunciation Guide for Beginners

sources.p: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Malay pronunciation has an unusual property for a language English speakers take on: the spelling mostly tells you the answer. There is no tone system to encode, no vowel length distinction to memorise, no silent letters inherited from a dead spelling convention. Write a Malay word down and you have very nearly written down how to say it.

Which means this guide is short on rules and long on the two things that actually go wrong: one ambiguous vowel letter, and the English rhythm you bring with you without noticing.

## The alphabet is the one you already have

Standard Malay is written in **Rumi**, the 26-letter Latin alphabet, which is why a beginner can read a Malay sentence aloud on day one — badly, but recognisably. That is a genuine advantage and worth appreciating before we get to the corrections.

You will occasionally meet **Jawi**, the Arabic-derived script with additional letters for Malay sounds. It retains an official role in Brunei, appears in religious and cultural contexts, and turns up on signage in parts of Malaysia. You do not need it to begin, and knowing it exists saves the small shock of encountering it.

A few letters — **v**, **z**, and to a lesser extent **f** — appear almost exclusively in borrowed words. If you see one, you are usually looking at a loan from English, Arabic or elsewhere.

## Vowels: six sounds, and one letter doing two jobs

Standard Malay works with six vowel sounds: the values you would expect for **a**, **i**, **u**, **o**, plus **two** different vowels both written with the letter **e**.

That last point is the single largest pronunciation problem in the language, so it deserves the space.

### The e problem

One **e** is a **schwa** — the neutral, colourless vowel English uses in unstressed syllables. The other is a **clearer front vowel**, roughly the vowel of English *bed*. Ordinary Malay spelling writes both as a plain *e* and gives you no way to tell them apart on the page.

Words where **e** is a schwa:

- **besar** — big
- **sedap** — delicious
- **empat** — four
- **enam** — six

Words where **e** is the clearer vowel:

- **meja** — table
- **teh** — tea

Dictionaries and teaching materials sometimes distinguish the two with a diacritic, but standard writing does not, and you should not expect to see one in the wild. This is the one part of Malay pronunciation where **you genuinely have to hear the word**, and it is the reason a course with audio beats a phrasebook by more than the usual margin.

A useful pattern to notice, though not a law: schwa is very common in first syllables of two-syllable words, which is why *besar*, *sedap*, *beras*, *belajar* and *kereta* all begin the same way. Noticing that will get you most of them.

### Two vowels in a row are two syllables

**air** ("water") is not the English word *air*. It is two syllables — *a-ir*. Likewise **maaf** ("sorry", "excuse me") is *ma-af*, with the two vowels separated rather than run together.

This catches English speakers because English collapses adjacent vowels into diphthongs by reflex. Malay generally does not, outside its three genuine diphthongs.

### The three diphthongs

**ai**, **au** and **oi** are real diphthongs and behave as single vowel sounds. Everything else that looks like a vowel cluster is two syllables.

## Consonants: five rules and you are done

Most Malay consonants are pronounced as an English speaker would guess. These five are not.

**c is "ch".** Always. *cinta*, *cakap*, *cuba* all begin with the sound in English *church* — never a k, never an s. English speakers get this wrong more than any other consonant because English *c* is genuinely unpredictable and the habit is deep.

**j is "j" and y is "y".** *jalan*, *jam*, *ya*. No surprises, but worth stating because learners coming from Spanish, German or French bring different expectations for both letters.

**ng and ny are single sounds.** **ng** is the sound at the end of English *sing*, and crucially Malay allows it at the **start** of a word, which English does not. **ny** is a single palatal sound, roughly the *ny* of *canyon* — as in *nyanyi*, "to sing".

**ng versus ngg.** This is the distinction people miss. **bunga** ("flower") has the plain *ng* sound with no hard g after it. **tangga** ("stairs, ladder") has the *ng* sound **plus** a g. The extra letter is not decoration; it changes the word.

**A final k is a glottal stop.** In native Malay words, a word-final *k* is normally not a released k at all but a glottal stop — the catch in the middle of English *uh-oh*. *tidak*, *budak*, *masak*, *duduk* all end this way. Pronouncing a hard k there is one of the most audible beginner markers, and one of the easiest things to fix in an afternoon.

**A final h is pronounced.** Unlike English, where a final *h* is usually silent or decorative, Malay gives it real breath: *rumah*, *sudah*, *tujuh*.

### The loanword digraphs

Three more digraphs appear mainly in words borrowed from Arabic:

- **sy** — as in *syarikat* ("company"), a *sh* sound
- **kh** — as in *khabar* ("news"), a back-of-the-throat friction rather than a plain k
- **gh** — as in *maghrib*, the voiced counterpart of *kh*

Many speakers simplify *kh* toward a plain k and *gh* toward a plain g in casual speech. Knowing what the spelling is asking for lets you decide rather than guess.

### The letter r

Realisations vary regionally, from a tap to a trill, and it is generally pronounced more distinctly than the *r* of southern British English. This is one of the features that most marks a speaker's origin, and one where matching whoever you are learning from is more sensible than seeking a single "correct" version.

## Rhythm is where the actual work is

Get everything above right and you can still sound unmistakably foreign, because English speakers import a rhythm that Malay does not use.

English is aggressively unequal. Stressed syllables are long and clear; unstressed ones are compressed into schwas. Say *photograph*, *photographer* and *photographic* and you will hear the same vowels move around and change quality entirely.

Malay does not do this. **Stress does not distinguish words**, and syllables get much more even weight. The result is a flatter, steadier rhythm that English speakers instinctively "correct" by adding emphasis somewhere — which is why a learner can pronounce every individual sound correctly and still be hard to follow.

The fix is not a rule you can apply. It is imitation: listen to a phrase, say it back, and specifically resist the urge to lean on one syllable. Recording yourself and comparing is unusually effective here, because rhythm is something you can hear in a recording that you cannot hear while producing it.

This is also why **listening to real dialogue matters more than drilling isolated words**. Rhythm only exists across a phrase.

## The word-final a, and why you will hear two versions

In much of Peninsular Malaysia and in Singapore, a word-final **a** is reduced toward a schwa — so *apa*, *saya*, *nama* and *bila* all end in an indistinct vowel rather than a clear *ah*. Other conventions, including the one used across the strait in Indonesian, keep a fuller *a* in that position.

Neither is wrong. Both are established, and they are among the most reliable cues a listener uses to place a speaker. It is one of several differences worth understanding if you are choosing between the two national standards, and our [beginner's guide to Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/) sets out the rest.

Practical advice: match the convention used where you intend to speak, stay consistent, and recognise the other one when you hear it.

## Ten words to get exactly right

Small list, chosen because each one demonstrates something from above.

| Word | Meaning | What it demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| terima kasih | thank you | even syllable weight |
| selamat pagi | good morning | no stress reduction across four syllables |
| apa khabar | how are you | the kh digraph, and final-a reduction |
| saya | I, me | final a |
| besar | big | e as schwa |
| meja | table | e as the clearer vowel |
| tidak | no, not | final k as a glottal stop |
| air | water | two vowels, two syllables |
| bunga | flower | ng without a following g |
| tangga | stairs | ng plus g |

Ten words that between them cover the whole rule set. If you can say these accurately and evenly, the rest of Malay pronunciation is mostly application.

## How to practise, in order

**Fix the consonant rules first.** They are finite, they are rules rather than habits, and they take a single session. *c* as ch, final *k* as a glottal stop, *ng* versus *ngg*.

**Then work on rhythm, with whole phrases.** Not word lists. Rhythm does not exist in a word list.

**Then collect the e words as you meet them.** Do not try to learn the schwa/clear distinction as a rule. Learn it word by word, from audio, the way you would learn a gender or a tone. It accumulates faster than it sounds.

**Record and compare with a delay.** Listening back immediately, you hear what you meant to say. Listening back the next day, you hear what you actually said.

**Use dictation.** Writing down what you hear forces you to commit to a spelling, and committing to a spelling means committing to which vowel you heard — which is exactly the discrimination you are trying to build.

[Learn Malay - Bahasa Melayu](/apps/learn-malay/) sequences pronunciation as its own track: vowels, consonants, syllable rhythm and the spelling-to-sound patterns together, with guided speaking activities and Malay speech support where your device provides it. Listening practice is built on everyday dialogue with comprehension checks rather than isolated words, and Dictation Mode, Listening Blitz and the missed-questions list bring back whatever you keep getting wrong.

The honest limit: an app can play a contrast, prompt you to produce one, and test whether you recognised it. It cannot hear you the way a fluent speaker can. Pronunciation work in a course is the foundation you bring to a conversation, not a replacement for having one.

## Why this is a good place to start a language

Malay pronunciation is one of the few parts of learning a Southeast Asian language where the effort is small and the payoff is immediate. There is no script to decode, no tone to derive, and no long list of exceptions. A week of deliberate work gets most learners to a point where they are understood without repetition.

That matters more than it sounds, because the languages people abandon are the ones where nothing works for a month. If you want the wider picture of what Malay asks for after the sounds are settled, our [beginner's guide to Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/) covers the affix system — which is where the real difficulty lives — and the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) show what the same first week costs in languages with a script and a tone system to get through first.

title: Malay vs Indonesian: How Close Are They, Really?
metaTitle: Malay vs Indonesian: How Different Are They?
secondaryKeywords: is bahasa melayu the same as bahasa indonesia
which should i learn malay or indonesian

sources.p: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Ask whether Malay and Indonesian are the same language and you will get two confident answers, both partly right. "Basically yes, they're mutually intelligible" is true of a news bulletin. "No, they're clearly different" is true of two teenagers texting. The useful question is not which camp is correct but *where* the two diverge, because that determines what a course in one buys you in the other.

## One ancestor, two standards

Both descend from Malay, the trading language of the Straits and the archipelago. Neither is derived from the other. What separated them was administration.

Indonesian was standardised as the national language of an emerging Indonesian state, on a base of Malay rather than of Javanese — a deliberate choice, since Javanese had far more first-language speakers, and one that made the national language nobody's home dialect and therefore everyone's second one. Malay in the peninsula was standardised separately, under British administration and then in independent Malaysia, and is today maintained by **Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka**. The Indonesian equivalent is **Badan Pengembangan dan Pembinaan Bahasa**. Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia also run a joint language council that coordinates technical terminology across all three, which tells you something about how close the two are and how much work is required to keep them that way.

The tidiest formal statement of the relationship comes from language registration. ISO 639-3 assigns **zsm** to Standard Malay and **ind** to Indonesian, both within a single **Malay macrolanguage**. One family, two standards, each with its own code. That is neither "the same language" nor "different languages" — it is the third thing that most closely related national standards actually are.

Official status follows the same pattern. Malay is the national language of Malaysia, the official language of Brunei, and the national language of Singapore, where it is one of four official languages. Indonesian is the state language of Indonesia and functions as a lingua franca across a country where most people grow up speaking a regional language at home.

## What is genuinely shared

Start here, because it is most of the language and it is why the transfer between them is so cheap.

**The grammar is close to identical for a beginner.** Neither conjugates verbs for tense, person or number. Neither has grammatical gender. Neither has articles. Both build possession by putting the possessor after the thing possessed. Both express time with separate words meaning *already*, *not yet*, *still* and *will*, rather than with verb endings.

**The affix system is shared.** Both build vocabulary families from a root using prefixes, suffixes and circumfixes, and the major affixes are the same ones doing the same jobs. Learn how *me-*, *ber-*, *pe-*, *-an* and *ke-…-an* behave in one and you have learned most of how they behave in the other.

**Core vocabulary is largely shared.** Numbers, family terms, common verbs, basic adjectives, the words for eat, drink, go, come, big, small, good. A beginner's first few hundred words are mostly words that work in both.

**Both are written in the Latin alphabet**, with near-phonemic spelling.

Because of that overlap, the honest advice for anyone choosing is: pick one, learn it properly, and expect the second to be an adjustment rather than a new project.

## Where the divergence actually is

### Loanword layers, and the history behind them

The most systematic difference is where each borrowed its modern vocabulary. Malaysian Malay absorbed a great deal of **English**; Indonesian carries a substantial **Dutch**-derived layer. Both draw on Sanskrit and Arabic from earlier periods, along with Portuguese, Chinese and Tamil.

That single fact produces most of the vocabulary you will notice:

| English | Malaysian Malay | Indonesian |
| --- | --- | --- |
| car | kereta | mobil |
| money | wang | uang |
| shop | kedai | toko |
| office | pejabat | kantor |
| hospital | hospital | rumah sakit |
| police | polis | polisi |
| university | universiti | universitas |
| television | televisyen | televisi |

Look at the last three rows and you can see the mechanism working. Both languages borrowed the same international words, and each adapted them to its own conventions — the Malaysian forms shaped by English spelling and pronunciation, the Indonesian ones by Dutch. *Kantor* comes from Dutch *kantoor*. Neither is a corruption of the other; they arrived by different routes.

### False friends, which are the real hazard

Words you do not know announce themselves. Words that exist in both with different meanings do not.

| Word | In Malaysia | In Indonesia |
| --- | --- | --- |
| kereta | car | carriage; *kereta api* is a train |
| percuma | free of charge | useless, in vain |
| budak | child, kid | slave |
| pejabat | office | official, officeholder |
| boleh | can, be able to | may, be permitted |
| bisa | venom, poison | can, be able to |

The last two rows are worth reading twice, because between them they cover one of the most frequently used ideas in any language. A Malaysian saying *boleh* and an Indonesian saying *bisa* are both saying "can" — and each word exists in the other language meaning something else entirely.

*Percuma* and *budak* are the ones that produce genuine social awkwardness rather than mere confusion, which is a good reason to learn a small list of these deliberately rather than discovering them one at a time.

### Spelling: closer than they used to be

For most of their modern history the two used different Latin orthographies, following British and Dutch conventions respectively. A joint spelling reform in **1972** aligned much of the two systems.

On the Indonesian side that meant replacing Dutch-influenced digraphs: *dj* became *j*, *tj* became *c*, and the capital *Djakarta* became *Jakarta*. On the Malaysian side, English-influenced spellings were adjusted in the other direction, with *ch* becoming *c*.

The result is that the two look considerably more similar in print today than they did before 1972 — and, importantly, more similar in print than they sound aloud. A reader comparing two newspapers will conclude the languages are nearly identical. A listener comparing two conversations will not.

### Pronunciation habits

The most audible difference is the treatment of a word-final **a**. In much of Peninsular Malaysia the final vowel is reduced toward a schwa, so *apa* ends in an indistinct vowel; Indonesian keeps a fuller, clearer *a*. Neither is a mistake. They are two conventions, and this single habit is often enough for a listener to place a speaker within a sentence or two.

Rhythm and intonation differ too, in ways that are hard to write down and easy to hear. This is one of the places where listening to real dialogue does something that reading cannot.

### Register is where it comes apart

This is the point most comparisons miss. The gap between Malay and Indonesian is small in formal registers and large in colloquial ones.

Formal written Indonesian and formal written Malay are close. Colloquial Jakarta Indonesian, with its own pronouns and heavily reduced forms, and colloquial Malaysian speech, with its own particles and English code-switching, are much further apart than the two standards suggest.

So when someone says "they can understand each other", ask which register. A news reader, largely. Two friends joking, much less.

## Difficulty: both are the easy option

For an English speaker, both varieties are unusually approachable by regional standards. The US Foreign Service Institute places **Malay and Indonesian in the same group, Category II**, at approximately **36 weeks of full-time instruction (900 class hours)** for its own students, alongside German, Haitian Creole and Swahili.

For comparison, Category III — Thai, Khmer, Russian, Polish, Vietnamese — runs to roughly 44 weeks, and Category IV, containing Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, Korean and Arabic, runs to 88.

As always, that describes intensive, full-time, small-group classroom training for diplomats — 900 hours across 36 weeks is about 25 class hours a week, before homework. It is not a prediction about app study. What it does say clearly is that FSI's own guidance does not rank one of the two above the other, which is a useful corrective to the folk claim that Indonesian is "the easy one".

## Choosing, and what happens if you switch

**Choose on geography.** Malaysia, Brunei or Singapore points one way. Indonesia points the other.

**Choose on people.** If you are learning because of a family, a partner, colleagues or a community, learn the variety they actually speak. This outranks every other consideration.

**Choose on the material you want.** Films, music, books and social media are not interchangeable between the two, and the body of work you actually want to reach is a legitimate reason to pick.

**Do not try to learn both at once.** They are close enough that the interference is constant and subtle. You will not produce a hybrid that is wrong in obvious ways; you will produce one that is wrong in small ways that native speakers notice immediately and cannot easily explain. Finish a foundation in one first.

If you do switch later, expect the adjustment to be concentrated in exactly the places described above: a vocabulary swap, a false-friend list, a pronunciation habit, and a register you have to rebuild from scratch. The grammar comes with you.

[Learn Malay - Bahasa Melayu](/apps/learn-malay/) teaches **Standard Malay** and is explicit about this distinction: its culture and regional notes explain how Malay is used across different communities and are careful not to treat Indonesian as the same language. The rest of the course covers vocabulary grouped by situation, grammar on Malay terms — word order, pronouns, possession, questions, classifiers, reduplication, passive forms, comparison and the affix system — and pronunciation covering vowels, consonants, syllable rhythm and the spelling-to-sound patterns that make Malay predictable.

## The short version

One historical language, two national standards, maintained by two institutions that also cooperate. Shared grammar, shared affixes, shared core vocabulary, aligned spelling since 1972. Divergent loanword layers, a real set of false friends, different pronunciation habits, and colloquial registers that pull much further apart than the formal ones.

If you have already decided on Malay, our [beginner's guide to Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/) covers what the first month actually asks for, and the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) put that difficulty in context against languages that are considerably less forgiving.

title: Mental Math Practice: The Methods Worth Drilling, and What Practice Actually Buys You
metaTitle: Mental Math Practice App: Methods That Work
secondaryKeywords: how to multiply in your head
body:
There is a version of this article that opens by telling you arithmetic drills will rebuild your brain. This is not that article, because that claim is not one anyone can currently make honestly.

Here is what practice does, stated narrowly enough to be true: it makes you faster and more accurate at the thing you practised. Drill multiplication and your multiplication gets quicker and your error rate falls. Whether that carries over to abilities you did not train is a genuinely contested research question, and any app promising you general intelligence, protection from decline, or transfer to unrelated skills is selling past the evidence.

Narrow is still worth having. Being able to split a bill, sanity-check a spreadsheet, or work out whether a discount is actually a discount without reaching for a phone is a real, daily, slightly embarrassing gap for a lot of adults. That is the thing this fixes.

## Three ideas behind almost every method

Mental arithmetic looks like a bag of unrelated tricks. It is mostly three moves.

1. **Move to a round number, then compensate.** Round numbers are easy; the correction is small.
2. **Break a number apart, then recombine.** The distributive law, used deliberately.
3. **Swap the operation for an easier equivalent.** Halve and double, multiply instead of divide, use an identity.

Everything below is one of those three. Recognising which one you are using is what turns memorised tricks into something you can improvise with.

## Addition and subtraction

### Round and compensate

`47 + 38`. Push 38 up to 40, add, then take the 2 back: 47 + 40 = 87, minus 2 = **85**.

It scales. `486 + 297` becomes 486 + 300 = 786, minus 3 = **783**.

### Subtract by adding up

Borrowing is where mental subtraction falls apart, so avoid it. To do `83 − 47`, count up from 47 instead: 47 + 3 gets you to 50, + 30 gets you to 80, + 3 gets you to 83. Total added: 3 + 30 + 3 = **36**.

This is how shop assistants counted out change before tills did it, and it is faster than the written algorithm because nothing is ever carried.

### Complements from a power of ten

`1000 − 367`. Subtract each digit from 9 and add 1 to the last: 9−3 = 6, 9−6 = 3, 10−7 = 3, giving **633**. No borrowing at any point.

For a number like `2000 − 1486`, do it against 1999 and add one back: 1999 − 1486 = 513, then + 1 = **514**.

## Multiplication

### Decompose

`7 × 68`. Nobody should be attempting that as written. Take it as 7 × 70 minus 7 × 2: 490 − 14 = **476**.

### Halve one side, double the other

The product does not change. `14 × 35` is awkward; halve the 14 and double the 35 and it becomes `7 × 70` = **490**.

### The easy multipliers

| To multiply by | Do this | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | halve, then ×10 | 86 × 5 → 43 × 10 = 430 |
| 25 | ×100, then ÷4 | 36 × 25 → 3600 ÷ 4 = 900 |
| 50 | ×100, then ÷2 | 74 × 50 → 7400 ÷ 2 = 3700 |
| 9 | ×10, then subtract the number | 47 × 9 → 470 − 47 = 423 |
| 99 | ×100, then subtract the number | 63 × 99 → 6300 − 63 = 6237 |

### Multiplying a two-digit number by 11

Split the digits and put their sum in the middle. `43 × 11` → 4, then 4+3 = 7, then 3 → **473**.

The part that gets left out of the version you were taught in a corridor: when the middle sum reaches ten or more, it carries. `87 × 11` → 8, then 8+7 = 15, then 7. The 1 from the 15 carries into the leading digit: 8 + 1 = 9, leaving 5 in the middle. Answer **957**.

Test any shortcut on a carry case before you trust it. That is where the half-remembered versions break.

### Squaring a number that ends in 5

Take the digits before the 5, multiply by the next whole number up, and stick 25 on the end.

`65²` → 6 × 7 = 42, then 25 → **4225**.
`85²` → 8 × 9 = 72, then 25 → **7225**.

### Difference of squares

This is the one that looks like magic and is just algebra. When two numbers sit the same distance either side of a midpoint, their product is the midpoint squared minus the distance squared.

`47 × 53`: midpoint 50, distance 3. So 50² − 3² = 2500 − 9 = **2491**.
`38 × 42`: midpoint 40, distance 2. So 1600 − 4 = **1596**.

The condition matters. Both numbers must be equidistant from a whole-number midpoint, which means they must differ by an even amount. For `47 × 52` the midpoint is 49.5 and the method stops being worth it.

## Percentages

### Anchor on one percent

Find 1% by moving the decimal point two places, then scale. 18% of 250: one percent is 2.5, so eighteen of them is 2.5 × 18 = **45**.

### x% of y equals y% of x

This is the most under-used fact in everyday arithmetic. 4% of 75 looks unpleasant; 75% of 4 is obviously **3**. They are the same number, because both are 0.04 × 75.

Whenever a percentage looks awkward, try flipping it. 16% of 25 becomes 25% of 16 = 4.

### Tips and splits

15% is 10% plus half of 10%. On 62: 6.20 + 3.10 = **9.30**. 20% is 10% doubled. If you can find 10% you can find most of the percentages anyone asks you for out loud.

## Checking your work

### Casting out nines

A two-second check that catches most slips. Reduce each number by summing its digits repeatedly until one digit remains, do the same operation on those reduced values, and compare with the reduced form of your answer.

Say you calculate `384 × 27 = 10,368`.

- 384 → 3+8+4 = 15 → 1+5 = **6**
- 27 → 2+7 = 9 → **0** (nines cast out)
- 6 × 0 = 0
- 10,368 → 1+0+3+6+8 = 18 → **0**

They match, so the answer survives the check. Had you written 10,358, its digits reduce to 8, which does not match 0 — caught immediately.

**Know its blind spots**, because a check you trust incorrectly is worse than no check. Casting out nines cannot see transposed digits: write 10,386 instead of 10,368 and the digit sum is identical, so the test passes on a wrong answer. It is also blind to any error that happens to be a multiple of nine. It tells you when something is definitely wrong, never that something is definitely right.

### Divisibility tests

Useful for simplifying fractions and for spotting whether a division will come out clean.

- **By 3** — digit sum divisible by 3. 4,821 → 4+8+2+1 = 15, so yes (4,821 ÷ 3 = 1,607).
- **By 4** — last two digits divisible by 4. 1,536 → 36, so yes (1,536 ÷ 4 = 384).
- **By 8** — last three digits divisible by 8.
- **By 6** — passes both the 2 and the 3 tests.
- **By 11** — alternate adding and subtracting the digits; if the result is 0 or a multiple of 11, so is the number. 2,915 → 2 − 9 + 1 − 5 = −11, so yes (2,915 ÷ 11 = 265).

### Estimate first, calculate second

Round every number to one significant figure, get an approximate answer, and only then do the real arithmetic. If the two disagree by an order of magnitude, you made a mistake in the second step. This is the habit that catches the decimal-point errors, and those are the expensive ones.

## Turning methods into fluency

Knowing a method and being able to use it under mild pressure are separate skills, and only the second one is useful. The gap between them is closed by repetition, and repetition needs to be short enough that you actually do it.

A few things that make a practice habit hold:

**Daily beats weekly.** Retrieval speed decays between sessions. Six five-minute sessions do more than one thirty-minute session, and they are easier to schedule.

**Alternate speed and accuracy.** Training only for speed teaches you to guess. Training only for accuracy lets you take as long as you like, which does not build fluency. Run both, separately, so you can see which one is limiting you.

**Watch response time, not just score.** Score conflates speed and accuracy. Response time is the cleaner signal of whether the retrieval is getting automatic, and it is the number that moves first.

**Practise your worst operation.** Everyone has one — usually division, sometimes subtraction with borrowing. It is also the one you will avoid unless something schedules it for you.

[Mental Math & Memory Games](/apps/mental-math-memory-games/) is built around that pattern. It covers addition, subtraction, multiplication and division with difficulty that climbs from simple warm-ups to harder rounds, and it varies the pressure deliberately: timed sprints reward speed, accuracy rounds reward getting it right, survival challenges run until you slip, and boss quizzes put a marker at the end of a stretch of work. A daily math challenge gives you a reason to open it on a day you had not planned a session.

Scores, accuracy, streaks, response time and personal bests are all recorded with a history you can look back through, which is what makes progress visible rather than a feeling. Alongside the drills there are techniques for percentages, estimation, number patterns and faster calculation, with games to apply each one straight away. On the memory side, number, grid, sequence and delayed-recall activities change what a session asks of you without changing how long it takes.

Sessions can be two minutes or a long training run, which is the property that makes daily practice realistic. It is free on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases, and it sits in the [education and brain games category](/apps/category/education-brain/) next to our history app — if you want a second habit with a different shape, the [world history timeline guide](/blog/world-history-timeline-guide/) covers how to use that one properly.

## The short version

Mental arithmetic is a small number of ideas reused: round and compensate, decompose and recombine, swap in an easier equivalent. Learn those three and most published "tricks" become things you could have derived.

Check with casting out nines while remembering what it cannot see, estimate before you calculate so decimal errors surface early, and practise in short daily sessions rather than long occasional ones. The payoff is narrow and real — you get quicker and more accurate at arithmetic — and that is enough of a reason.

body:
Most collections of mental arithmetic tricks share two problems: the examples are chosen to make the method look better than it is, and nobody tells you when it stops working. Every method below is worked through with arithmetic you can check line by line, and every one is stated with the case where it fails or becomes slower than the ordinary approach.

## What separates a method from a party trick

A mental arithmetic shortcut is ordinary algebra with the middle steps precomputed. That is the whole story, and it has a practical consequence: every genuine method has a **condition** attached — a range of inputs where it applies and outside which it either stops helping or produces a wrong answer.

The tricks that circulate without their conditions are the ones that get people into trouble. So every method below is stated with the case where it fails, and every example has been worked so you can check it rather than take it on trust.

This article assumes you already have the foundations. Round-and-compensate, complements, the easy multipliers, multiplying by 11, squaring numbers ending in 5, difference of squares, one-percent anchoring and casting out nines are covered in our [guide to mental math training](/blog/mental-math-training-guide/). What follows is the next layer.

## Multiplying numbers near 100

This is the highest-value method most people have never seen. It works when both numbers sit near a round base — 100 is the useful one for everyday arithmetic.

**Both numbers below 100.** Write down how far each falls short.

`97 x 94` — shortfalls of 3 and 6.

1. Cross-subtract: `97 - 6 = 91`. (Taking `94 - 3` gives the same 91, which is a built-in check.)
2. Multiply the shortfalls: `3 x 6 = 18`.
3. Join them: **9,118**.

Verify it the long way if you like: `97 x 90 = 8,730`, `97 x 4 = 388`, total 9,118.

**Squaring is the same move.** `97²` — shortfall 3. So `97 - 3 = 94`, and `3² = 9`, giving **9,409**.

**Both numbers above 100.** Use the excess and add instead of subtract.

`108 x 106` — excesses 8 and 6. `108 + 6 = 114`, and `8 x 6 = 48`, giving **11,448**. Check: `10,800 + 648 = 11,448`.

**The condition, and the case everyone gets wrong.** The second part occupies two digit positions. If the product of the shortfalls reaches 100, it overflows and has to carry.

`88 x 85` — shortfalls 12 and 15. `88 - 15 = 73`. `12 x 15 = 180`. Since 180 exceeds 99, the extra hundred carries: `73 + 1 = 74`, leaving 80. Answer **7,480**. Check: `88 x 80 = 7,040`, plus `88 x 5 = 440`, total 7,480.

That carry is why the method loses its appeal once the numbers drift far from 100. Within roughly ten either side it is very fast; beyond about fifteen you are doing a two-digit multiplication anyway.

**Why it works.** Expanding `(100 - a)(100 - b)` gives `10,000 - 100a - 100b + ab`, which is `100(100 - a - b) + ab`. The first bracket is the cross-subtraction and `ab` is the shortfall product — the algebra is just the binomial expansion with the arithmetic done in advance.

## Same tens digit, units adding to ten

A close relative, and a generalisation of the squaring-numbers-ending-in-5 rule.

When two two-digit numbers share a tens digit and their units digits sum to 10, multiply the tens digit by the next whole number up, then append the product of the units digits.

`43 x 47` — `4 x 5 = 20`, `3 x 7 = 21` → **2,021**. Check: `1,720 + 301 = 2,021`.

`62 x 68` — `6 x 7 = 42`, `2 x 8 = 16` → **4,216**. Check: `4,340 - 124 = 4,216`.

**Condition:** both parts are required. Same tens digit *and* units summing to exactly 10. And the units product needs two digit places, so `61 x 69` gives `42` then `09` → 4,209, not 429. Squaring a number ending in 5 is simply the case where both units digits are 5.

## Squaring an awkward number by shifting to an easy product

The difference-of-squares identity in the [training guide](/blog/mental-math-training-guide/) turns a product into a square. Run it the other way and it turns an awkward square into an easy product plus a small correction: `n² = (n - d)(n + d) + d²`.

Pick `d` to land on a round number.

`43²` → shift down 3 to 40: `40 x 46 = 1,840`, plus `3² = 9` → **1,849**.
`68²` → shift up 2 to 70: `70 x 66 = 4,620`, plus `2² = 4` → **4,624**.

**Condition:** you must *add* the correction when squaring, and the shift is worth it only if it produces a genuinely easy multiplier. If the nearest round number is more than about 5 away, the correction stops being a small number you can hold.

## Division by awkward-looking divisors

Multiplication shortcuts get all the attention; the division versions are used less and are just as fast.

| To divide by | Do this | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | double, then ÷10 | 340 ÷ 5 → 680 ÷ 10 = **68** |
| 2.5 | ×4, then ÷10 | 170 ÷ 2.5 → 680 ÷ 10 = **68** |
| 25 | ×4, then ÷100 | 1,700 ÷ 25 → 6,800 ÷ 100 = **68** |
| 125 | ×8, then ÷1,000 | 3,000 ÷ 125 → 24,000 ÷ 1,000 = **24** |
| 8 | halve three times | 384 ÷ 8 → 192 → 96 → **48** |
| 15 | ÷ 3, then ÷ 5 | 495 ÷ 15 → 165 ÷ 5 = **33** |

Each rests on the same observation: these divisors are factors of powers of ten, so replacing the division with a multiplication and a decimal shift is exact, not approximate.

## Percentages that are really fractions

One-percent anchoring handles anything. But a handful of percentages are exactly simple fractions, and recognising them converts a multiplication into a division you already know.

| Percentage | Fraction | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 12.5% | 1/8 | 12.5% of 248 → 248 ÷ 8 = **31** |
| 37.5% | 3/8 | 37.5% of 96 → 96 ÷ 8 = 12, ×3 = **36** |
| 62.5% | 5/8 | 62.5% of 96 → 12 × 5 = **60** |
| 16⅔% | 1/6 | 1/6 of 342 → **57** |
| 6.25% | 1/16 | 6.25% of 320 → **20** |
| 33⅓% | 1/3 | 1/3 of threefold-friendly numbers |

**Condition:** the fraction route pays off only when the base divides cleanly. 37.5% of 97 is not made easier by eighths; fall back to one-percent anchoring there.

## Percentage changes multiply — this is the important one

More everyday arithmetic goes wrong here than anywhere else in this article.

**Sequential changes do not add.** Start at 100. A 20% fall gives 80. A 20% rise on 80 gives 96, not 100. You are 4% down, because the rise was calculated on a smaller base than the fall.

**Successive discounts do not add either.** "30% off, then a further 20% off" is `0.7 x 0.8 = 0.56` — a 44% total reduction, not 50%.

**Reversing a change means dividing.** If a figure is 130 after a 30% increase, the original is `130 ÷ 1.3 = 100`. If a price is 60 after 25% off, the original is `60 ÷ 0.75 = 80`. Adding 25% to 60 would give 75, and 75 is not the answer.

The mental move is to stop thinking in additions and start thinking in multipliers: down 20% is ×0.8, up 30% is ×1.3, and going backwards means dividing by the multiplier you went forward with.

## Averaging by deviations

To average 87, 92, 79 and 84, do not add them. Anchor at 85 and track only the deviations: `+2, +7, -6, -1`, which sum to `+2`. Divide by 4 for `+0.5`, and add to the anchor: **85.5**.

The numbers you hold in your head are single digits instead of three-digit running totals, which is the entire point. Check: the four values sum to 342, and `342 ÷ 4 = 85.5`.

**Condition:** the values need to cluster. If they are spread across orders of magnitude, the deviations are as big as the numbers and nothing is gained.

## Unit conversions worth memorising

NIST's guidance on SI units gives the exact conversion factors; two of them have unusually convenient mental approximations.

**Miles and kilometres.** One mile is exactly 1.609344 kilometres, following from the international definition of the yard as 0.9144 metre. That ratio sits close to 1.618, which is the limit that consecutive Fibonacci numbers approach — so consecutive Fibonacci numbers convert well enough for conversation:

- 5 miles → about 8 km (exact: 8.05)
- 8 miles → about 13 km (exact: 12.87)
- 13 miles → about 21 km (exact: 20.92)

**Condition:** this is an approximation, not a conversion. It runs roughly half a percent low and should never be used where the exact factor matters.

**Celsius and Fahrenheit.** The exact relation multiplies by 9/5 and adds 32. The common shortcut — double and add 30 — is only exact at 10 °C, and drifts by 0.2 degrees for every degree away from it. At 30 °C it gives 90 °F against a true 86 °F.

The better version costs one extra step and is exact: **double, subtract 10%, add 32.** At 30 °C: `60 - 6 + 32 = 86`. At 20 °C: `40 - 4 + 32 = 68`. Since `2 - 0.2 = 1.8 = 9/5`, this is not an approximation at all.

## Estimating a square root properly

Guessing between the neighbouring perfect squares is the usual advice and it is weak. One extra step makes it good.

Take a guess, divide the target by the guess, and average the two. This is Newton's method specialised to square roots.

**√60**, starting from 8:

- `60 ÷ 8 = 7.5`
- Average of 8 and 7.5 → **7.75**

The true value is approximately 7.7460, so 7.75 is off by about 0.05%. One more pass — `60 ÷ 7.75 ≈ 7.7419`, averaged with 7.75 — gives 7.7460.

**√30**, starting from 5: `30 ÷ 5 = 6`, average → 5.5. Second pass: `30 ÷ 5.5 ≈ 5.4545`, average → **5.4773**, against a true 5.47723.

**Condition:** the averaging step always overshoots on the high side from a low guess and vice versa, so each pass sandwiches the answer. It converges fast, but "fast" still means you are doing a division, and the division is the expensive part.

## Divisibility by 7

The training guide covers tests for 3, 4, 6, 8 and 11. Seven is the gap, and MathWorld lists several tests for it. The usable one: split off the last digit, double it, and subtract that from the number formed by the remaining digits. Repeat until the result is small enough to recognise.

- `371` → `37 - (2 x 1) = 35`. 35 is divisible by 7, so 371 is. (`371 ÷ 7 = 53`.)
- `6,853` → `685 - 6 = 679` → `67 - 18 = 49`. Divisible. (`6,853 ÷ 7 = 979`.)
- `1,073` → `107 - 6 = 101`. Not divisible, so 1,073 is not. (`7 x 153 = 1,071`.)

**Condition:** the test answers yes or no. It does not give you the quotient, so it is for checking whether a fraction will simplify, not for doing the division.

## One pattern worth knowing for its own sake

The decimal expansion of one-seventh is 0.142857 repeating, and every other seventh is the same six digits rotated to a different starting point:

`1/7 = 0.142857…`, `2/7 = 0.285714…`, `3/7 = 0.428571…`, `4/7 = 0.571428…`, `5/7 = 0.714285…`, `6/7 = 0.857142…`

Memorise the cycle once and all six are available. It is a small thing, and it is the kind of structure that makes arithmetic feel less like a set of unrelated procedures.

## Turning any of this into speed

Knowing a method and being fast with it are different states. The gap between them is retrieval: a method you have to reason through costs several seconds, and the same method drilled to automaticity costs a fraction of one. Nothing in this article gets faster by being read again.

That is a training problem, and it responds to short, frequent, mixed practice — the same principles set out in the [training guide](/blog/mental-math-training-guide/). It is also worth understanding the constraint you are working against, which is how little the mind can hold at once while calculating; that is the subject of [working memory and what training can and cannot change](/blog/working-memory-and-training/).

## Where the app fits

[Mental Math & Memory Games](/apps/mental-math-memory-games/) drills addition, subtraction, multiplication and division with difficulty that climbs as you improve, plus timed sprints, accuracy rounds, survival challenges and boss quizzes, and a daily math challenge. It tracks scores, accuracy, streaks, response time, personal bests and history, and includes techniques for percentages, estimation, number patterns and faster calculation.

Response time is the number worth watching. Score mixes speed and accuracy together, but response time is the cleaner signal of whether a method has crossed from reasoning into retrieval.

The app is free with ads. More like it sit under [education and brain training apps](/apps/category/education-brain/), and our other writing on the subject is collected under [education and brain training articles](/blog/category/education-brain/).

## The short version

Learn the base-100 method, learn that percentage changes multiply, and learn the averaging step for square roots. Those three cover more real situations than the rest of the list combined. And for anything you adopt, learn the condition alongside the method — a shortcut applied outside its range is slower than the long way, because you have to do the long way afterwards anyway.

title: Styles Make Fights: How an MMA and Boxing Draft Simulator Decides a Bout
metaTitle: MMA Fight Simulator App: Styles, Drafts and Records
body:
Your best fighter just lost to someone rated below him, and nothing went wrong.

That sentence separates combat sports drafting from every other kind. In a team sport, a better roster is a better roster and the model says so. In a fight, the relationship between two competitors is not a ranking — it is a matchup, and a matchup can invert a ratings advantage. The game is explicit about this: power, defence, cardio, reach, grappling and fight IQ all feed the result, so a stylistic edge can outweigh a ratings edge.

Once you accept that, the entire drafting logic changes.

## The board is not a ladder

Team drafting is fundamentally about coverage: fill each slot with someone suited to it, and do not leave holes. That framework does not transfer here, because there are no slots. What you are covering instead is *matchup space*.

Think about what a ranking actually assumes. It assumes that if A is better than B and B is better than C, then A is better than C. Style-based resolution breaks that assumption on purpose, which is why "styles make fights" is a cliché in the sport rather than a marketing line.
