A grappler who dismantles a striker can be dismantled in turn by a different striker with the tools to keep it standing.

The practical consequence for a drafter is closer to portfolio construction than to team building. A stable made of one archetype is not a strong stable — it is a stable with one predictable weakness repeated several times. When it meets the thing it does not handle, it does not lose one fight. It loses the same fight over and over.

[40-0 MMA & Boxing Fight Draft](/apps/mma-boxing-fight-draft/) gives you a pool that supports the alternative: champions, wrestlers, grapplers and technical boxers, drafted across ratings, records, eras and weight classes. You can build for finishers, for technicians, for grapplers, or for a roster that covers all of it — and the last of those is a strategy, not a compromise.

## Two sports, two simulators

The game does not run one model with a cosmetic switch. Mixed martial arts and boxing are simulated separately, and the difference is not trivial.

### How a mixed martial arts bout resolves

The MMA simulator ends bouts by knockout, technical knockout, submission or decision, weighing striking, wrestling, takedowns, submissions and ground control.

The important structural feature is the number of ways a fight can end. A fighter can be excellent in one phase and vulnerable in another, and because the bout can be decided in any phase, a specialist carries both a high ceiling and a specific exposure. Drafting an outstanding grappler is drafting a fighter whose results depend heavily on whether the fight goes where he wants it.

### How a boxing bout resolves

The boxing simulator adds draws and judges' scorecards, and looks at hand speed, power, defence, footwork and ring control.

Two consequences follow. First, there is a third outcome — a draw is neither a win nor a loss, and in a game built around an unbeaten record, a draw is a different kind of event from a defeat. Second, decisions on scorecards mean that fights which do not end early are resolved on accumulated advantage rather than on a single decisive moment, which rewards a different profile: consistency and control rather than one-shot capability.

The design choice to separate the two is the right one. Collapsing them into a single model would have to discard either submissions or scorecards, and both are load-bearing parts of their sport.

## Eras and weight classes are constraints, not flavour

The pool spans eras, countries and divisions, and it is easy to read that as variety. It is better read as a set of constraints on what your roster can actually do.

Weight class in particular is not a preference. A fighter is only usable in the situations their division allows, which means a stable that is deep in one division and empty in another has a coverage problem regardless of how good the fighters are. When you are drafting for a tournament or a bracket, division depth is a real constraint on your options, and noticing it late is expensive.

Era adds a different texture. Drafting across eras is one of the genuine pleasures of a fictional pool — it is a comparison you can only make in a simulation, because it never happens in reality. It is worth being clear-eyed about that: cross-era matchups are interesting precisely because they are unanswerable outside a model.

## What the simulators assume

Every result the game produces is a model's output, and it is worth stating the boundaries plainly.

The fighters are fictional and generated inside the game. The game is not affiliated with, endorsed by or connected to any real promotion, sanctioning body, event or athlete. No result describes, predicts or relates to any real bout, and nothing in the app is usable as an indication of how a real fight would go. It is not, and is not intended as, guidance about any real-world event.

Inside the model, the assumptions are the ones described above: attributes and styles interact, the interaction can override a ratings gap, and the sport's own rules determine which outcomes are possible. That is a design decision, and it is what makes the drafting worth thinking about. A model where the higher number always won would be a sorting exercise.

The 40-0 record the game is built around — forty fights without a loss — is the target, not the expectation. Getting a stable there is the whole challenge, and falling short is the normal result.

## GM Mode and the ranking system

Beyond drafting, GM Mode runs the business side: signing fighters, managing contracts, and moving contenders toward title shots, with your decisions feeding back into the rankings.

This is where the genre's usual management tensions appear in an unusual form. In a team sport, a roster decision affects a shared outcome. Here, each fighter has their own trajectory, and a matchmaking decision is a resource allocation: the opponent you choose for a contender is simultaneously a risk you are taking with an asset and an opportunity you are creating.

That produces a genuinely different set of questions from team management. Do you move a fighter quickly and accept the exposure, or build carefully and spend time you may not have? Do you protect a valuable record or test it? There is no rule that answers these, which is the point — the [basketball draft and GM guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/) covers what front-office decision-making looks like when the unit is a team instead of an individual, and the contrast is instructive.

## Seven formats

The drafting sits inside Unlimited Fight Draft, Limited Draft, Tournament, VS Computer, Draft Battle Royale, MMA Only Draft and Boxing Only Draft, with a Fighter Explorer, collections, comparisons, quizzes and daily challenges around them.

Three of those are worth calling out for what they teach.

**Single-sport drafts** are the best place to learn. Mixing pools is more interesting and also more complicated, because you are reasoning about two resolution systems at once. Drafting boxing only for a few runs will teach you what the scorecard model rewards far faster than mixed drafting will.

**Limited Draft** removes the ability to keep searching, which converts drafting from a selection problem into a judgement problem. The same distinction shows up in every draft game the studio makes; the [hockey draft guide](/blog/hockey-draft-gm-guide/) works through why the two rulesets test different skills.

**Tournament and Battle Royale** formats punish narrow stables hardest, because a bracket exposes you to a sequence of opponents rather than one. A roster that handles most matchups and none of them spectacularly usually survives a bracket better than a roster of specialists.

The Fighter Explorer and side-by-side comparisons exist for the decision that matters most here: two fighters, similar overall, different profiles. That is the pick where style reasoning either happens or does not.

## A drafting checklist

1. **Ask what your stable currently cannot handle**, not who is best available. That question does the work.
2. **Diversify archetypes deliberately.** Repeating one profile repeats one weakness.
3. **Check division depth before a bracket format**, not during it.
4. **Learn one sport's simulator at a time** using the single-sport drafts.
5. **When two fighters are close, compare profiles rather than totals.** The overall number is exactly the thing that hides the difference that decides the fight.

Drafting under positional constraints instead of style constraints is covered in the [soccer draft XI guide](/blog/soccer-draft-xi-guide/) and the [baseball draft guide](/blog/baseball-draft-gm-guide/). The rest of the studio's drafting and management games are listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: MMA Weight Classes Explained: The Full List and What the Bands Really Mean
metaTitle: MMA Weight Classes Explained: The Unified Rules List
secondaryKeywords: what is catch weight in mma
how many mma weight classes are there

sources.p: Association of Boxing Commissions and Combative Sports
Association of Boxing Commissions and Combative Sports

body:
Weight classes exist for one reason, and it is not fairness in the sporting sense. It is that mass is an advantage no amount of skill reliably cancels, and a sport that lets any two people fight regardless of size is a sport that produces avoidable injuries.

Everything else about the system — the odd gaps between divisions, catch weight, the rules about missing weight — follows from that starting point.

## Where the list actually comes from

There is a published table. The **Unified Rules of Mixed Martial Arts**, maintained by the Association of Boxing Commissions and Combative Sports, set out the divisions and their limits, and state regulators adopt them by reference — Nevada's administrative code for unarmed combat, for instance, points at the unified rules rather than restating them.

That is worth knowing because it means the weight classes are a matter of public record you can check yourself rather than something the sport agrees on informally. It also means promotions do not each invent their own; they select from the published set.

## The full table

| Weight class | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Atomweight | up to and including 105 lbs |
| Straw Weight | over 105 to 115 lbs |
| Flyweight | over 115 to 125 lbs |
| Bantamweight | over 125 to 135 lbs |
| Featherweight | over 135 to 145 lbs |
| Lightweight | over 145 to 155 lbs |
| Super Lightweight | over 155 to 165 lbs |
| Welterweight | over 165 to 170 lbs |
| Super Welterweight | over 170 to 175 lbs |
| Middleweight | over 175 to 185 lbs |
| Super Middleweight | over 185 to 195 lbs |
| Light Heavyweight | over 195 to 205 lbs |
| Cruiserweight | over 205 to 225 lbs |
| Heavyweight | over 225 to 265 lbs |
| Super Heavyweight | over 265 lbs |

Fifteen divisions. Not every promotion or commission runs all of them — the table is the menu of sanctioned divisions, not a claim about what is contested everywhere.

### The bands are not the same size, and that is deliberate

Run the subtraction down the table and a pattern appears:

- Most of the lower and middle divisions step in **10 lb** increments: 115 to 125, 125 to 135, 135 to 145, and so on.
- **Welterweight** (165 to 170) and **Super Welterweight** (170 to 175) are only **5 lbs** wide each.
- **Cruiserweight** spans **20 lbs** (205 to 225).
- **Heavyweight** spans **40 lbs** (225 to 265).
- **Super Heavyweight** has no upper bound at all.

Two forces produce that shape. The first is population: the middle of the table is where most competitors are, so finer divisions are possible and useful there. The second is proportion — five pounds is a meaningful fraction of a 135 lb fighter and a much smaller fraction of a 250 lb one, so equal-sized bands at the top would be splitting hairs while leaving divisions empty.

The practical consequence is that **"same division" means very different things at different ends of the table.** Two heavyweights can legally be forty pounds apart. Two welterweights cannot be more than five.

## Allowances, catch weight and missing weight

Three provisions govern what happens when the neat table meets reality.

**Within a division.** If both fighters weigh in inside the same contracted division, the rules impose no allowance restrictions. They have both made the limit, and that is the end of the matter.

**When somebody misses.** If a fighter misses the contracted weight and the two competitors end up in different weight classes, the rules cap the difference: the heavier opponent shall not exceed five pounds over the lower-weighing fighter. That is the safety backstop, and it is why a badly missed weight can end a bout before it is made rather than merely costing a percentage of a purse.

**Contracted catch weight.** A catch weight bout is one agreed at a figure that is not a standard divisional limit. The rules state there is no weight spread allowance between contracted catch weight fighters so long as both are below the contracted weight, and they explicitly permit commissions to deny a catch weight bout where the differential looks like a safety problem.

Catch weight is often described as a compromise, and structurally that is exactly what it is: a negotiated number, with no division, no ranking and no title attached to it.

## Why the number on the scale is a proxy, not a verdict

Weight is measured once, hours or a day before the fight, and what it is standing in for is frame — height, reach, limb length, muscle mass, the amount of force a body can generate and absorb.

Those things do not track weight perfectly. Two fighters who make the same limit can be built very differently, and the differences that matter in a fight are often the ones the scale does not see:

- **Reach.** Where punches can land from, and whether one fighter can work outside the other's range.
- **Frame and leverage.** Which matters enormously in the grappling exchanges where position is decided by leverage rather than by speed.
- **How the weight was made.** A fighter who cut hard to make a limit and one who walks around near it arrive in different condition regardless of what the scale said.

This is also why a weight class does not settle anything. It equalises one variable so that the others — technique, style, conditioning, decision-making — are what decide the result. That is the whole point of having the table.

## Weight class as a game mechanic

[40-0 MMA & Boxing Fight Draft](/apps/mma-boxing-fight-draft/) builds weight class into the drafting problem directly. You draft across eras and divisions, balancing ratings, records, eras and weight classes, and the simulators settle each bout on style, ratings and weight class rather than on ratings alone.

The genuinely interesting part is that the game models **style advantage**: power, defence, cardio, reach, grappling and fight IQ all feed the result, which means a stylistic edge can outweigh a ratings edge and the higher-rated fighter does not automatically get the nod. That is a defensible design choice, because it is roughly the thing weight classes exist to expose — once size is controlled for, matchups start deciding fights.

Bouts in the mixed martial arts simulator resolve by knockout, technical knockout, submission or decision, weighing striking, wrestling, takedowns, submissions and ground control. Boxing is simulated separately and adds draws and judges' scorecards, which the [boxing scoring guide](/blog/boxing-scoring-explained/) goes through in detail.

Around the drafting sit Unlimited Fight Draft, Limited Draft, Tournament, VS Computer, Draft Battle Royale and single-sport MMA and boxing drafts, plus a Fighter Explorer, collections, side-by-side comparisons, quizzes and daily challenges. GM Mode runs the business side — signing fighters, managing contracts and moving contenders toward title shots, with your decisions feeding the rankings.

### What the simulation is and is not modelling

Worth stating plainly, because combat sports attract this confusion more than most.

The simulators take fictional fighters generated inside the game, apply the game's own internal rules about ratings, styles, divisions and matchups, and return a result. That result describes nothing outside the game. It is not a prediction, not a forecast, not analysis of any real athlete or event, and not guidance of any kind. It is a score on a roster-building puzzle.

The unbeaten record the game is named for is deliberately hard to reach, which is what makes a stable that falls short informative rather than disappointing. And no drafting approach guarantees it — a model with style advantages built in is a model where the obvious roster can lose.

## Quick reference

- Divisions are defined by an **upper limit**; the floor is simply the class below.
- Band widths: mostly **10 lbs**, **5 lbs** at welterweight and super welterweight, **20 lbs** at cruiserweight, **40 lbs** at heavyweight, open above 265.
- **No allowance restrictions** when both fighters make the same contracted division.
- **Five pounds maximum** between fighters who end up in different classes after a missed weight.
- **No spread allowance** for contracted catch weight fighters, and commissions may refuse the bout.
- A professional round is **five minutes** with a **one-minute** rest; bouts run one to five rounds and cannot exceed five rounds or twenty-five minutes.

## Where to read next

The companion piece to this one is [how boxing scoring works](/blog/boxing-scoring-explained/), which covers the 10-point must system and what judges are told to look at. For the drafting side of combat sports specifically, see the [MMA and boxing fight draft guide](/blog/mma-boxing-fight-draft-guide/). If the management layer is what appeals, [career mode versus franchise mode](/blog/career-mode-vs-franchise-mode/) sets out how running a stable differs from playing as one competitor, and [sports GM games without internet](/blog/sports-gm-games-without-internet/) covers playing any of them on a flight.

Everything the studio makes in this genre is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Net Carbs, Explained: What a Nutrition Label Tells You and What It Doesn't
metaTitle: Net Carbs Explained: Total Carbs, Fiber and Labels
secondaryKeywords: do sugar alcohols count as carbs
does fiber count as a carb

sources.p: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service
MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine
MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine
National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
U.S. Departments of Agriculture and Health and Human Services

body:
Put the same tub of yogurt into two different low-carb apps and you can get two different net carb figures. Neither app is malfunctioning. They are applying different conventions to a term that no US regulator has ever defined.

That is the part most explanations skip, and it is the part that actually helps. Once you know what is on a label and what is not, the arithmetic takes about four seconds and you stop being surprised by disagreements.

## What a US Nutrition Facts label actually declares

Under FDA's labeling rules, the carbohydrate portion of the panel is a short list:

| Line on the label | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Total Carbohydrate | Required |
| Dietary Fiber | Required, indented under Total Carbohydrate |
| Total Sugars | Required, indented |
| Includes Added Sugars | Required, indented |
| Sugar Alcohol | Voluntary in most cases |

**"Net carbs" is not on that list.** It is not a nutrient FDA defines for the Nutrition Facts panel, and it is not something a manufacturer is required or permitted to declare as part of it. When a net carb figure appears on the front of a box, it is the brand's own arithmetic printed in its own marketing space — which does not make it wrong, but does mean nobody is checking the method.

The Daily Values used for the percentage column are 275 grams of total carbohydrate and 28 grams of dietary fiber, both based on a 2,000 calorie reference diet. FDA is explicit that this reference diet is a common yardstick for comparing products, not a recommendation matched to your own calorie needs.

### Why fiber sits *inside* total carbohydrate

This trips people up constantly, and there is a concrete regulatory reason for it.

On a US label, total carbohydrate is generally not measured directly. It is calculated **by difference**: the lab measures protein, total fat, moisture and ash, and whatever weight is left over is called carbohydrate. Fiber is part of that leftover weight, so it is structurally inside the total carbohydrate figure rather than sitting next to it.

That single fact explains the entire practice. Fiber is counted in the total, most of it is not digested and absorbed the way starch and sugar are, and so people who care about digestible carbohydrate take it back out again. Net carbs is the name for taking it back out.

## The subtraction, and the two conventions

The arithmetic itself is trivial:

```
net carbs = total carbohydrate − dietary fiber
net carbs = total carbohydrate − dietary fiber − sugar alcohols
```

The first is the conservative version. The second is the convention most commonly used in US low-carb practice, because sugar alcohols are also inside total carbohydrate and are also handled differently by the body from starch and sugar.

As an illustration, take a label reading Total Carbohydrate 23 g, Dietary Fiber 9 g, Sugar Alcohol 6 g. Fiber only gives you 14 g. Fiber plus sugar alcohols gives you 8 g. Same food, same label, same day — a 6 gram gap that came entirely from which line you decided to count.

Neither answer is cheating. What matters is that you know which one you are looking at.

### "Fiber" is not one substance

Since the 2016 label update, dietary fiber on a US label has a specific regulatory meaning: naturally occurring non-digestible carbohydrates that are intrinsic and intact in plants, plus isolated or synthetic non-digestible carbohydrates that FDA has determined have a beneficial physiological effect. Isolated fibers that have not cleared that bar do not get to appear on the Dietary Fiber line.

The practical consequence is that the fiber number on a label is already a filtered figure. Two similar-looking products can declare different fiber amounts partly because of what was added, not only because of what is in the food.

### Sugar alcohols are not one substance either

FDA's labeling regulations do not treat all sugar alcohols as interchangeable. For calorie calculation they assign a specific value to each one: erythritol is assigned 0 calories per gram, mannitol 1.6, maltitol 2.1, xylitol 2.4 and sorbitol 2.6, among others.

Look at that spread and the working rule reveals itself for what it is. Subtracting every gram of every polyol treats erythritol and sorbitol as the same substance, and the regulations that govern the label say they are not. It is a defensible simplification, not a measurement. If you subtract all sugar alcohols in full and your numbers feel optimistic, this is where the optimism is coming from.

### Allulose and monk fruit are not sugar alcohols at all

Worth flagging because low-carb products lean on them heavily. Allulose is a sugar, not a polyol. Monk fruit sweetness comes from mogrosides, a different class of compound again. An app that subtracts erythritol, allulose and monk fruit is applying a broader convention than "total carbs minus fiber minus sugar alcohols" — a defensible one, and a *different* one.

## Why two apps disagree about the same food

Three ordinary reasons, none of them a bug:

1. **Different conventions.** One subtracts fiber only, another subtracts fiber plus polyols, a third also subtracts newer sweeteners.
2. **Different underlying records.** A packaged food's own label and a generic reference entry in a database such as USDA's FoodData Central describe similar foods with different numbers, because one is a specific product and the other is a representative average.
3. **Different starting points after rounding.** This one is underrated, so it gets its own section.

### Rounding is quietly doing a lot of work

FDA's regulations round the carbohydrate figures on a label. Amounts are declared to the nearest gram, an amount below 1 gram may be stated as "less than 1 gram", and an amount below half a gram may be declared as zero.

Read that last clause again with a low-carb pantry in mind. A sauce, a stick of gum, a seasoning packet and a splash of cream can each legitimately declare 0 g and still contribute real carbohydrate to your day. Nothing has been misdeclared. The rounding rule is doing exactly what it was designed to do, and the effect only becomes visible when you eat a lot of small servings.

If you are counting to a tight daily figure, this is the single most common source of the gap between what you logged and what you ate.

## The number is a tool, not a verdict

> Nothing in this article is medical advice, and no carbohydrate figure here is a recommendation for you. Carbohydrate needs vary with age, body composition, activity, pregnancy, medication and medical conditions, and low-carbohydrate eating interacts with some medications in ways that need supervision. Talk to a doctor or a registered dietitian before setting a target you intend to eat to, and especially before changing how you eat while taking prescribed medication.

For orientation only: the National Academies set a Recommended Dietary Allowance for carbohydrate of 130 grams per day for adults, derived from the average minimum amount of glucose used by the brain, and an Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range of 45 to 65 percent of calories. Those are population reference figures, and a low-carbohydrate pattern sits deliberately outside them.

You will also see figures in the region of 20 to 50 grams of carbohydrate a day quoted widely in popular low-carb writing as a range associated with ketosis. Treat that as a commonly repeated convention rather than a clinical threshold: no US federal nutrition authority publishes a carbohydrate cutoff for ketosis, individual responses differ, and the popularity of a number is not evidence for it.

This article makes no claim that any carbohydrate target produces any outcome. Counting net carbs is a measurement practice. Measurement tells you what you did; it does not promise a result.

## Making the arithmetic somebody else's problem

The subtraction is easy once. It is tedious 300 times a week in a supermarket aisle, which is where a dedicated tool earns its place.

[Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb](/apps/keto-diet-tracker/) is built around that specific chore. Fiber and sweeteners including erythritol, allulose and monk fruit come off total carbohydrate automatically as you log, and the app can alert you when a day passes a limit you set yourself. A low-carb food database and barcode scanner cover packaged items, custom foods and recipes cover anything you cook, and a meal planner lets you lay out breakfast, lunch, dinner and desserts in advance.

A built-in calculator turns details you enter — age, height, weight, activity level — into starting fat, protein and net carb figures you are free to change. That is a starting point generated from a formula, not an assessment of you, and it is meant to be overwritten once you know better.

Around the food log sit the other things low-carb eaters tend to record: ketone readings you have taken yourself with blood, urine strips or a breath meter including GKI, an intermittent fasting timer, water, and sodium, potassium and magnesium. The app stores readings you enter; it does not measure anything itself. Charts, body measurements, photo logs and weekly and monthly summaries turn the entries into a record you can look back over.

It is free on Google Play, supported by ads, with no in-app purchases. No account is required and your logs stay on your device rather than on our servers — which also means an uninstall takes the history with it. Other trackers in the [health and nutrition category](/apps/category/health-nutrition/) make different trade-offs. If carbohydrate is not the number you care about, [Protein Diet Tracker](/apps/protein-diet-tracker/) is built around a different one, and [tracking protein instead](/blog/how-to-track-protein-intake/) is a different exercise with the same failure mode, which is friction rather than motivation.

## Practical rules that survive a real week

**Pick a convention and write it down.** Fiber only, or fiber plus polyols. Changing convention mid-month turns your own history into noise.

**Use the label on the package you are holding.** Reformulations happen. A database entry captured two years ago is a guess about today's recipe.

**Check what a carbohydrate line includes before subtracting from it.** Labelling conventions vary between markets, and a package printed for somewhere else may not be built the way a US panel is. If its carbohydrate figure already excludes fiber, subtracting fiber again double-counts.

**Give small servings a floor.** If you routinely eat several things that declare 0 g, count them as something rather than nothing. You will be closer to the truth than the label arithmetic is.

**Read weeks, not days.** A single day is dominated by whatever unusual thing happened in it. Seven ordinary days show you the shape of how you actually eat, which is the only thing worth acting on.

## The short version

Net carbs is a subtraction you perform, not a nutrient anyone measures. US labels give you total carbohydrate, fiber, sugars and added sugars, with sugar alcohol optional, and the total already contains the fiber because it was calculated by difference in the first place.

Two apps can disagree because they use different conventions, different source records, or numbers that were rounded before they ever reached the app. Choose one method, apply it every time, and judge the result as a trend rather than a score — and take the actual dietary decisions to somebody qualified to give them.

title: Protein Sources Compared: Reading a High Protein Foods List Properly
metaTitle: High Protein Foods List: What the Numbers Show
secondaryKeywords: good source of protein label claim

sources.p: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service
National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
U.S. Departments of Agriculture and Health and Human Services
MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine

body:
Every high protein foods list you have ever read was secretly answering one of three questions, and almost none of them said which. Protein per serving, protein per calorie, and protein per unit of money produce three different orderings of the same foods. Chicken breast wins one of them comfortably, lentils win another depending on where you shop, and cheese moves several places between the first two.

Knowing which question you are asking is most of the work. The rest is checking the actual food rather than the category it belongs to.

> This is general information about food composition, not medical or dietary advice, and it is not a plan for any individual. Allergies, medical conditions, medication and pregnancy all change what is appropriate. Talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before making significant changes to how you eat.

## Three lists pretending to be one

**Protein per serving** answers "if I eat this, how many grams did I get?" It is the number that matters when you are trying to hit a daily total, and it is the one most lists show.

**Protein per calorie** answers "how much of this food's energy arrives as protein?" It is the number that matters when total calories are a constraint, and it reorders things sharply. Nuts and cheese carry real protein per serving and considerably more fat alongside it; skinless poultry, white fish, egg whites and non-fat dairy carry protein with comparatively little else.

**Protein per dollar** answers a question no nutrition database can, because it depends on where you shop and what week it is. Eggs, canned fish, dried legumes, tofu and cheaper cuts of meat usually cluster at the efficient end. It is worth thinking about explicitly, because a food you cannot afford consistently is not part of your diet.

A list that does not tell you which axis it sorted on is not wrong so much as unfinished.

## Approximate anchors, and how to treat them

The figures below are rounded, representative values of the kind you will find in USDA's FoodData Central for common preparations. They are here to calibrate your intuition, not to be entered into a log. Cut, brand, cooking method and drained weight all move them, and the entry for the exact food you ate is the one to trust.

**Animal-source foods**

| Food (typical portion) | Approximate protein |
| --- | --- |
| Cooked chicken breast, skinless, 3 oz (85 g) | ~26 g |
| Cooked lean beef, 3 oz | ~22 g |
| Cooked salmon, 3 oz | ~22 g |
| Canned tuna in water, 3 oz drained | ~20 g |
| Plain non-fat Greek yogurt, 170 g container | ~17 g |
| Cottage cheese, ½ cup | ~12 g |
| Cheddar cheese, 1 oz (28 g) | ~7 g |
| Milk, 1 cup | ~8 g |
| Large egg | ~6 g |

**Plant-source foods**

| Food (typical portion) | Approximate protein |
| --- | --- |
| Firm tofu, ½ cup | ~10 g |
| Cooked lentils, ½ cup | ~9 g |
| Cooked black beans, ½ cup | ~7–8 g |
| Cooked pasta, 1 cup | ~8 g |
| Cooked quinoa, 1 cup | ~8 g |
| Peanut butter, 2 tbsp | ~7 g |
| Almonds, 1 oz (28 g) | ~6 g |
| Whole wheat bread, 1 slice | ~4 g |

Two things are worth noticing before the categories start doing your thinking for you.

The first is that the gap between the two tables is smaller per serving than the usual framing suggests, and larger per calorie. Half a cup of lentils and an egg and a half are close on protein; they are not close on carbohydrate, fibre or fat.

The second is that ordinary staples contribute. Bread and pasta are not protein foods, and across a day they still add grams that people forget to count. The unglamorous accumulation is a real part of most totals.

## Protein quality, stated carefully

"Complete protein" is a phrase that does useful work and then keeps going past where the evidence supports it.

The Dietary Reference Intakes identify **nine indispensable amino acids** — histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine — which the body cannot make and must get from food. The report sets a separate reference requirement for each one. Foods differ in how much of each they supply relative to those requirements, which is the real content behind the word "complete".

Two qualifications keep that from turning into folklore.

**The requirement is expressed per day.** The DRI framework sets amino acid requirements as daily amounts. The stricter version of the old advice — that plant proteins must be combined within a single meal — is a stronger claim than the reference framework itself makes.

**Digestibility is part of the picture.** This is not a fringe technicality; it is baked into US labelling. When a percent Daily Value for protein appears on a Nutrition Facts panel, FDA's regulations require it to be calculated from a protein digestibility-corrected amino acid score rather than from the raw gram figure. That is why a label can declare, say, 8 grams of protein and a %DV that does not look like 16 percent of 50 grams: the gram count and the corrected value are answering different questions.

Whether a particular eating pattern meets amino acid requirements for a particular person is exactly the sort of assessment a registered dietitian does and an article cannot.

## What the package is allowed to say

Front-of-pack protein claims are regulated, and the thresholds are simple once you know them. Under FDA's nutrient content claim rules:

- **"High", "rich in", "excellent source of"** — 20 percent or more of the Daily Value per reference serving.
- **"Good source", "contains", "provides"** — 10 to 19 percent of the Daily Value per reference serving.
- **"More", "added", "extra", "plus"** — at least 10 percentage points more of the Daily Value than a reference food.

Against the 50 gram Daily Value for protein, that arithmetic is easy: 20 percent is **10 grams**, and the good-source band runs from **5 grams to 9.5 grams**. A cereal box saying "good source of protein" is telling you it clears 5 grams in a serving as FDA defines that serving — which may be smaller than the amount you pour.

One more quirk. A percent Daily Value for protein is **not required** on most Nutrition Facts panels. Manufacturers declare it when a protein claim is made, or for foods represented for children under four. If you are looking for a %DV against protein and cannot find one, the label is behaving normally. [Reading a Nutrition Facts label properly](/blog/reading-nutrition-labels/) covers the rest of the panel, including the serving-size rules that make claims like this comparable in the first place.

## What travels with the protein

Switching the sources of your protein changes more than the protein.

**Vitamin B12.** The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements notes that vitamin B12 is naturally found in animal foods, and that plant foods contain it only when fortified. That makes B12 a nutrient worth discussing with a clinician for anyone eating largely or entirely plant-based, and one of the clearest examples of why a nutrient-by-nutrient view beats a "protein is protein" view.

**Iron form.** The ODS iron fact sheet distinguishes heme iron, found in meat, poultry and seafood, from non-heme iron, the form found in plant foods and the form used in fortification. The two are absorbed differently, and the difference is large enough that iron intake and iron status are not the same conversation.

**Saturated fat and sodium.** Many convenient protein sources are processed, and processing tends to bring sodium with it. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans discuss these as pattern-level considerations rather than food-by-food rules, and that is the right level to think about them.

**Allergens.** FDA identifies nine major food allergens that must be declared on packaged food labels: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Six of those nine are common protein sources, which is worth remembering before recommending anything to anyone.

## Getting from a list to a total

None of this becomes useful until you know what you actually eat, and estimating from memory is unreliable in a consistent direction — the small, frequent contributors are the ones that vanish.

The mechanics are dull and they work. Log a normal week without changing anything. Weigh the five or six foods you eat most often, once, so you know what your usual portion actually is. Look up the specific entries in FoodData Central for the foods you repeat, and stop looking them up after that. Then read the week rather than the day.

[Protein Diet Tracker](/apps/protein-diet-tracker/) exists for that arithmetic. Meals and snacks go in as you eat them and roll into daily totals for protein, calories, carbohydrates and fat on one screen. Daily goals are yours to set, and the app measures the day against your numbers rather than prescribing them. Workouts and body weight sit in the same record, and progress trends and nutrition history make a week readable instead of a day.

It is free on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases; no account is required and entries stay on your device. If you want the reference figures behind any target before you set one, [how much protein per day](/blog/how-much-protein-per-day/) covers what the RDA, the AMDR and the label Daily Value each actually mean, and the rest of the [health and nutrition category](/apps/category/health-nutrition/) covers the adjacent tools.

## The short version

Ask which list you are reading. Per serving, per calorie and per dollar are three different rankings and only one of them is on the page.

Protein quality is real, the nine indispensable amino acids are the substance behind it, and the DRI framework expresses those requirements per day rather than per plate. Label claims have exact thresholds — 10 grams for "excellent source", 5 grams for "good source" — and a missing %DV for protein is normal rather than suspicious.

And when your protein sources change, check what else changed with them. B12, iron form and sodium do not follow the protein around automatically.

title: Protein Tracking Apps Compared: Database Depth, Paywalls and What You Keep
metaTitle: Best Protein Tracking App: An Honest Comparison

sources.p: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service
MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine

body:
Every protein tracker performs the same arithmetic. It adds grams. Nothing about that step distinguishes one app from another, and no app has a proprietary advantage in addition.

What differs is everything either side of it: how a food gets into the log in the first place, and what you still have a year later. Those two questions are where the real decision lives, and they have very different answers depending on how you eat.

**Disclosure:** this article is published by Reign Creative LLC. We make one of the three apps discussed below — Protein Diet Tracker — so we have a direct commercial interest in you installing it. We have written the comparison to be useful if you install something else instead, and we say plainly below where the other two do things ours does not.

Everything stated here about another company's product was read on that company's own website on **9 August 2026**, and is limited to what we could verify there. Feature packaging and pricing in this category change often. Confirm anything that matters to you with the vendor before you decide.

## Start with how you eat, not with the feature list

Three questions predict your answer better than any feature table.

**Does most of your food come out of a package, or out of a pan?** This is the big one. A barcode is a unique identifier for a manufactured product; it is useless for the chicken thighs you roasted on Sunday. If your week is protein bars, yoghurt pots and ready meals, scanning is a genuine time saving repeated several times a day. If your week is cooking, you are going to be entering foods by hand either way.

**Do you want two numbers or forty?** Some people want protein and calories. Some people want to see iron, B12 and magnesium next to them. These are different products, and an app built for the second is heavier to use than an app built for the first.

**What do you want to still have in a year?** A tracker only becomes interesting once it has months in it. Where those months live — on your device, or on a company's servers behind a subscription — is worth deciding on purpose rather than by accident.

## What each app is built around

### MyFitnessPal

MyFitnessPal's own site describes it as tracking calories in foods along with "macros, vitamins, and other micronutrients," plus weight goals, exercise and water intake. With connected devices it also covers steps, calorie burn and sleep. Its home page additionally names GLP-1 dose and side-effect tracking.

The named tools on that page are Meal Scan (photo recognition), Voice Log, Barcode Scan, an Intermittent Fasting Tracker, an AI Nutrition Coach, and BMR and BMI calculators. Read as a set, that is a product organised around a very large food database and around getting entries into it by as many routes as possible — type, scan, speak, photograph.

For a reader whose diet is heavily branded and packaged, that is the strongest argument in this article, and it is not our app's argument.

### Cronometer

Cronometer's own pages describe tracking food, exercise, biometrics and notes, with macronutrients and micronutrients, water, blood sugar, weight, and sleep and workout data from connected devices. Its features page groups this as Track Food, Track Exercises and Biometrics, Track Any Diet, Meals & Recipes, Reports & Charts, Integrations, Data Security and Accurate Database.

The positioning is nutrient depth. Where MyFitnessPal leads with the number of ways to enter a food, Cronometer leads with the detail of what comes back out. If your reason for tracking is that you want to see whether a restricted diet is leaving gaps in your micronutrients, that emphasis matters.

### Protein Diet Tracker

Ours is the narrow one. [Protein Diet Tracker](/apps/protein-diet-tracker/) rolls meals and snacks into daily totals for protein, carbohydrates, fat and calories on a single screen. It logs workouts and body weight in the same record as the food, so training and intake share one history, and it keeps nutrition history and progress trends so a week can be read as a week. Daily goals are ones you set; the app measures the day against your numbers and does not calculate them for you.

It is free to download on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases. No account is required and entries are stored locally on your device rather than on our servers.

Here is what it does not have, stated as plainly as we can: **no barcode scanner, no large searchable branded-food database, no wearable or device integrations, and no micronutrient breakdown.** It is a fast manual log for people who eat roughly the same things and want the total. If that description does not fit you, one of the other two will serve you better.

## Where the paid line falls

This is the detail most likely to surprise you a month in, because each vendor draws it somewhere different. The table below reports only what each company's own pages stated on 9 August 2026.

| App | What the vendor's own pages place in the free tier | What the vendor's own pages place behind payment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MyFitnessPal | Their Premium page does not enumerate the free tier. | "Ad-free logging experience", "Barcode scan and meal scan", "Voice logging and multi-day logging", "Custom macros and goals", "Intermittent fasting tracker", "Download progress reports", "Priority customer support". A separate Premium+ adds meal planning, recipes and grocery lists. |
| Cronometer | Basic: logging food, exercise, biometrics and notes; barcode scanner; custom foods, meals and recipes; custom macro and micronutrient targets; syncing with apps and devices; reports and charts over a seven-day window. | Gold: Photo Log, Voice Log, Recipe Importer, Fasting Timer, Macro Scheduler, Nutrition Scores, Custom Charts, Crono Coach, ad-free use and unlimited historical data. |
| Protein Diet Tracker | Free to download, ad-supported. Goal setting, daily totals, workout and weight logging, nutrition history and progress trends are in the app. | Optional in-app purchases. |

Two things are worth pulling out of that.

First, **setting your own macro targets is not universally free.** MyFitnessPal lists "Custom macros and goals" under Premium on its Premium page, and its home page repeats the point. Cronometer lists custom macro and micronutrient targets in its free Basic tier. Neither arrangement is wrong; they are different business decisions. But if the whole reason you are tracking is a specific protein target, that difference is not a detail.

Second, **free reporting windows differ.** Cronometer's pricing page describes Basic reports and charts as covering a seven-day window, with unlimited historical data under Gold. If you specifically want to look back over months without paying, that is the sentence to check on their current page.

## The database question, without flannel

A large branded-food database with barcode scanning is a real advantage and we do not have one. It is worth being precise about who it helps.

It helps most if you eat manufactured food, because the entry you scan is the exact product you ate, right down to the brand's own reformulation. It helps least if you cook, because the moment you make a stew you are entering ingredients by hand into whatever app you chose, and a database of two million branded snacks does not shorten that.

There is also a free way to check any food yourself, whichever app you use. USDA's **FoodData Central** is described on its own site as "USDA's comprehensive source of food composition data," it is free to search, and the data are in the public domain under CC0. When you want to know whether an app's entry for a generic food is sensible, that is the reference to compare against.

Our own view, and it is a view rather than a fact: for protein specifically, most people's intake is dominated by a small number of repeated foods. Once those are set up, the size of the database stops mattering and the length of the entry path starts mattering. That is the bet our app makes, and it is a bet that is wrong for plenty of people.

## What happens to the data

Protein Diet Tracker keeps entries locally on your device and requires no account. The honest consequence is symmetrical: there is nothing to sign up for, nothing to cancel and no server-side copy — and if you uninstall or lose the phone, the history is gone with it.

We are not going to characterise how any other company handles your data, because we did not verify that and this article does not include claims we did not verify. What we will say is that the **Data safety** section on any app's Google Play listing states what that app says it collects and shares, and it takes about a minute to read. Do it before you put a year of meals somewhere.

## What none of these apps do

This matters more in nutrition than in most categories, so it is worth stating directly.

- **None of them is a medical or diagnostic tool.** A food log is a record of what you entered. It does not assess your health, and it does not substitute for a doctor or a registered dietitian.
- **None of them can promise an outcome.** No app can guarantee weight loss, muscle gain or any other result, and any marketing that suggests otherwise is selling.
- **None of them determines your target.** MedlinePlus gives a published reference point — the daily recommended intake of protein for healthy adults is 10% to 35% of total calorie needs — and that is a population figure, not a personal prescription. Requirements vary with age, body weight, pregnancy, activity, kidney function and medication. Talk to a qualified healthcare professional before setting a number you intend to eat to.
- **None of them makes an estimate exact.** If you estimate portions, your totals are estimates in every app equally.

## Which one fits which person

**Choose MyFitnessPal if** your diet is largely packaged and branded, you want several ways to get food into the log, and you are comfortable with the paid tier being where several of the headline tools sit.

**Choose Cronometer if** the reason you are tracking is nutrient detail rather than a single macro, you want custom targets and a barcode scanner without paying, and you would use the biometric tracking.

**Choose [Protein Diet Tracker](/apps/protein-diet-tracker/) if** you cook most of what you eat, you want protein and calories rather than a full nutrient panel, you want training and body weight in the same history as the food, and you would rather not have an account at all.

**Choose something else entirely if** you are specifically eating low-carb, where net carb arithmetic is the daily chore rather than protein totals — [Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb](/apps/keto-diet-tracker/) handles that subtraction, and that field has its own set of specialist apps worth comparing separately. The rest of our nutrition tools are listed under [health and nutrition](/apps/category/health-nutrition/).

If you have not tracked before, the mechanics matter more than the choice of app: [how to track protein intake](/blog/how-to-track-protein-intake/) covers the habit itself, and [net carbs, explained](/blog/net-carbs-explained-keto-tracking/) covers why two apps can disagree about the same food.

## How we checked, and a note on names

Every statement above about MyFitnessPal and Cronometer was read on those companies' own websites on 9 August 2026 and is reported as what those pages said. Where a page was ambiguous about which features are free, we said the page was ambiguous rather than guessing. We used no screenshots, icons or brand styling, and we did not test their apps' interfaces or make claims about their speed.

MyFitnessPal, Cronometer and all other product names and trademarks mentioned are the property of their respective owners. Their use here is nominative — for identification of the products being discussed — and does not imply any affiliation, sponsorship, partnership or endorsement in either direction.

title: How to Read a Nutrition Facts Label, Line by Line
metaTitle: How to Read Nutrition Labels: A Line-by-Line Guide
secondaryKeywords: what does percent daily value mean

sources.p: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine

body:
A Nutrition Facts panel looks like a summary of a food. It is closer to a legal document: every line has a defined meaning, a rounding rule and a reason for existing, and several of them mean something narrower than the plain English suggests.

Learning what each line is actually required to say takes one read. After that you stop being misled by the two lines that mislead almost everyone — serving size and percent Daily Value — and you can get an accurate figure off a package in a few seconds.

> This article explains a labelling system, not a diet. Nothing here is medical or dietary advice and no figure on a label is a recommendation for you. Talk to a doctor or registered dietitian about your own intake, especially if you are pregnant, managing a condition or taking medication.

## Start at the top: servings, not portions

The two lines above the black rule govern everything below them, and they are the most commonly misread part of the panel.

**Servings per container** tells you how many label-servings are in the package.

**Serving size** tells you how much one of those is. It is not a recommendation. FDA derives serving sizes from **Reference Amounts Customarily Consumed** — regulated amounts based on what people typically eat in one sitting, published as a table in 21 CFR 101.12. The whole point is comparability: two brands of the same food have to declare their numbers against the same reference amount so you can put them side by side.

Two rules that follow from this are worth knowing because they change what you are looking at:

- A package containing **between one and two** reference servings must be labelled as **a single serving**, because people generally finish it in one sitting.
- Certain packages containing **between two and three** reference servings carry a **dual-column** label, showing the figures both per serving and per package.

So a bottle you drink in one go is usually declared as one serving now, and a container you might split shows you both columns. When neither applies, the arithmetic is yours: two-thirds of a stated serving means two-thirds of every number underneath it.

## Calories, and where they come from

The calorie figure is large on the modern panel because FDA enlarged it deliberately in the 2016 redesign, which also removed the old "Calories from Fat" line.

Calories are not measured in a bomb calorimeter for every product. FDA's regulations permit calculation using specific food factors or the general factors of **4 calories per gram of protein, 4 per gram of total carbohydrate and 9 per gram of fat**, with separate treatment for alcohol and for certain sugar alcohols. That is why the calorie line and the gram lines on a panel are arithmetically related rather than independent measurements — and why a food's calorie count moves when a manufacturer reformulates the grams.

## The nutrient lines, and the rounding underneath them

Below calories, the panel declares nutrients in grams or milligrams, with some nested underneath others.

| Line | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Total Fat | Saturated Fat and *Trans* Fat indented beneath |
| Cholesterol | Milligrams |
| Sodium | Milligrams |
| Total Carbohydrate | Dietary Fiber, Total Sugars and Includes Added Sugars indented beneath |
| Protein | %DV optional in most cases |
| Vitamin D, Calcium, Iron, Potassium | Required since the 2016 update |

Every one of those figures is rounded under 21 CFR 101.9, and the rounding is where quiet inaccuracy lives:

- **Calories** — under 5 may be declared as zero; up to 50, to the nearest 5-calorie increment; above 50, to the nearest 10.
- **Fat** — under 0.5 g may be declared as zero; from 0.5 g to 5 g, to the nearest half gram; above 5 g, to the nearest gram.
- **Sodium** — under 5 mg may be declared as zero; from 5 mg to 140 mg, to the nearest 5 mg; above 140 mg, to the nearest 10 mg.

None of that is a loophole. It exists so labels stay readable and so tiny amounts do not imply false precision. The consequence is real, though: a splash of cream, a spray of oil, a stick of gum and a seasoning packet can each honestly declare 0 g and still contribute to your day. If you count to a tight target, small servings are where your log and your intake quietly diverge — the same effect that makes two apps disagree on [net carbs for the same food](/blog/net-carbs-explained-keto-tracking/).

### Fiber, sugars and added sugars

Dietary fiber and total sugars sit *inside* total carbohydrate rather than beside it, because on a US label total carbohydrate is generally calculated by difference rather than measured directly.

**Includes Added Sugars** is the newest line and the most useful one on many packages. It separates sugars introduced during processing or packaging from those naturally present in the food, which is the distinction that makes a fruit yogurt and a plain one legible next to each other. FDA set the Daily Value for added sugars at **50 grams**, which at 4 calories per gram is 200 calories — 10 percent of a 2,000 calorie reference diet.

## Percent Daily Value: the most useful line, misread constantly

The right-hand column is not "percent of what you need". It is the share of a **Daily Value** that one serving supplies, and Daily Values are reference figures pegged to a 2,000 calorie diet so that products can be compared on one scale. FDA states plainly that this reference diet may not match your own calorie needs.

Used as intended, it is the fastest tool on the panel. FDA's own quick guide is a single sentence worth memorising: **5 percent DV or less is a low amount of that nutrient, and 20 percent DV or more is a high amount.** You can triage a shelf with that rule without doing any arithmetic at all.

The adult Daily Values also turn out to be internally coherent, which is a good sanity check on the whole system:

| Nutrient | Daily Value | As calories, on a 2,000 calorie diet |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total carbohydrate | 275 g | 1,100 cal — 55 percent |
| Total fat | 78 g | 702 cal — about 35 percent |
| Protein | 50 g | 200 cal — 10 percent |
| Saturated fat | 20 g | 180 cal — 9 percent |
| Added sugars | 50 g | 200 cal — 10 percent |

Compare the first three against the National Academies' Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges for adults — 45 to 65 percent of calories from carbohydrate, 20 to 35 percent from fat and 10 to 35 percent from protein — and the Daily Values sit mid-range for carbohydrate, at the top for fat and at the bottom for protein. The label's yardstick was built to be consistent with the reference intakes, not invented separately.

Protein is the exception in one respect: a %DV for protein is **not required** on most panels. It appears when a protein claim is made or for foods represented for children under four, and when it does appear FDA requires it to be corrected for digestibility rather than taken straight from the gram figure. A blank in that cell is normal.

## Below the panel: ingredients, allergens and claims

**The ingredient list** is ordered by weight, most to least. That ordering is often more informative than any single number above it — if a sweetener appears in the first three ingredients, you have learned something the panel expresses less directly.

**The allergen statement.** FDA identifies nine major food allergens that must be declared on packaged foods: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. This is the only part of the package that carries real safety weight for some readers, and it is separate from the nutrition panel entirely.

**Front-of-pack claims** are governed by their own rules. Under FDA's nutrient content claim regulations, terms like "high", "good source", "low", "reduced" and "free" have numeric definitions tied to the Daily Value and the reference serving. "High" or "excellent source" means 20 percent or more of the DV per reference serving; "good source" means 10 to 19 percent. So "excellent source of protein" is a claim about clearing 10 grams against the 50 gram DV, and [what a protein claim is really asserting](/blog/protein-sources-compared/) becomes checkable arithmetic rather than marketing atmosphere.

A claim on the front never tells you more than the panel on the back. It tells you which number the manufacturer wanted you to look at.

## What the label cannot tell you

Worth stating plainly, because label literacy is sometimes oversold.

- **It does not evaluate the food.** Composition is not a verdict, and a panel has no opinion about whether something fits your diet.
- **It is not personalised.** Every percentage is against a 2,000 calorie reference. If your intake is materially different, the percentages are still comparable between products and no longer meaningful as fractions of your day.
- **It is a snapshot of a formulation.** Recipes change. The panel on the package in your hand outranks any database entry captured months ago.
- **It is rounded.** Everything above applies before you add up ten small servings.

## Getting the numbers off the package and into a total

Reading one label well is a skill. Reading four hundred a month is a chore, and that is where a tracker earns its place.

[Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb](/apps/keto-diet-tracker/) is the more label-focused of our two: a barcode scanner and a low-carb food database pull packaged items in, custom foods and recipes cover anything you cook, and fiber and sweeteners such as erythritol, allulose and monk fruit come off total carbohydrate automatically as you log. It can alert you when a day passes a limit you set yourself, and it is free on Google Play, supported by ads, with no in-app purchases.

[Protein Diet Tracker](/apps/protein-diet-tracker/) takes the opposite approach — fast manual entry of meals and snacks rolling into daily protein, calorie, carbohydrate and fat totals, with goals you choose rather than goals it calculates. It is free, contains ads, and offers optional in-app purchases.

Neither stores your logs on our servers or requires an account, which also means an uninstall takes the history with it. The rest of the [health and nutrition category](/apps/category/health-nutrition/) sits alongside them, and if you are setting a target rather than reading a package, [what the published protein reference numbers actually answer](/blog/how-much-protein-per-day/) is the more relevant read.

## The short version

Serving size is a regulated description of what people typically eat, not advice. Percent Daily Value is a comparison scale against a 2,000 calorie reference, and the 5-percent-low, 20-percent-high rule does most of the work. Calories are calculated from the grams using defined factors, and every figure on the panel is rounded before you see it.

Added sugars is the line that earns the redesign. The ingredient list is ordered by weight and often says more than the panel. And the claim on the front of the box is a number with a legal threshold behind it — one you can now check yourself.

title: Russian Cases Explained: Six Jobs, Not Six Tables
metaTitle: Russian Cases Explained for Beginners

sources.p: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Russian cases are usually introduced as six tables of endings, which is roughly like introducing swimming as a table of joint angles. Accurate, complete, and no help at all at the moment you are in the water.

Here is the reframe that makes them tractable: **a case is a job label.** Every noun in a Russian sentence is doing a job — subject, object, recipient, possessor, instrument — and Russian writes that job onto the end of the word. Six cases means six jobs. Learning them is learning what the jobs are and when each applies, and the endings follow from that.

## Russian is not adding information, it is storing it elsewhere

English marks roles by position. *The dog bit the man* and *the man bit the dog* contain the same words and mean opposite things, because English decides who did what from where the words sit.

Russian marks roles on the words. The subject wears a subject ending; the object wears an object ending. Once that is done, the order is free to do something else — emphasis, contrast, what the sentence is about — which is why Russian word order looks alarmingly loose to an English speaker and is in fact carrying meaning English handles with stress and cleft sentences.

**Мама любит папу** and **Папу любит мама** both mean that mum loves dad. *Папу* is wearing the object ending in both, so no reordering can make dad the one doing the loving. What changes is emphasis.

That is the whole system in one example. Cases are not an ornament on top of a language you could otherwise understand; they are where the sentence's structure lives.

## The six, by job

| Case | Russian name | The job it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nominative | именительный | The subject. The dictionary form. |
| Genitive | родительный | Possession, absence, quantity, and a large set of prepositions. |
| Dative | дательный | The recipient — who something is given, said or shown to. |
| Accusative | винительный | The direct object. Also motion toward, with в and на. |
| Instrumental | творительный | The means by which, and accompaniment with с. |
| Prepositional | предложный | Location and topic — only ever after a preposition. |

Read that table as six questions rather than six labels: *who is doing it, whose is it, to whom, what is being acted on, by what means, where or about what.*

## One noun through all six

Concrete beats abstract. **книга** — "book", a feminine noun — through the singular:

| Case | Form | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nominative | книга | Это книга. | This is a book. |
| Genitive | книги | У меня нет книги. | I don't have a book. |
| Dative | книге | — | to/for the book |
| Accusative | книгу | Я читаю книгу. | I'm reading a book. |
| Instrumental | книгой | — | by means of the book |
| Prepositional | книге | Я думаю о книге. | I'm thinking about the book. |

Six forms of one word, and notice that the genitive and prepositional happen to look identical here. That kind of overlap is common, and it is one reason the tables look more intimidating than the system is — you are learning fewer distinct forms than the grid suggests.

Now a masculine noun, **брат** — "brother":

| Case | Form |
| --- | --- |
| Nominative | брат |
| Genitive | брата |
| Dative | брату |
| Accusative | брата |
| Instrumental | братом |
| Prepositional | брате |

Which leads directly to the rule that catches everyone.

## The animacy rule

Look at the masculine table again. The accusative and the genitive are the same: **брата**.

That is not a coincidence and not a shortcut in the table. Russian masculine nouns referring to **people and animals** take the genitive form when they are the direct object. Masculine nouns referring to **things** keep the nominative form instead.

- **Я вижу брата.** — I see my brother. *(animate: accusative copies the genitive)*
- **Я вижу стол.** — I see the table. *(inanimate: accusative copies the nominative)*

This one rule accounts for a large share of the confusion beginners have about "why does this word look like a possessive". It is not a possessive. It is an animate direct object wearing a borrowed form.

## The prepositional case is the honest one

The prepositional gets its name from the only thing it does: it never appears without a preposition. That makes it the easiest case to know you need — if there is no preposition, it is not the prepositional.

It shows up after a small set:

- **в** and **на** for location — *в Москве*, "in Moscow"
- **о** for the topic of thought or speech — *о книге*, "about the book"
- **при**, in a range of senses around presence and attendance

Most courses teach it second or third precisely because of that reliability, and because "I live in…" is a sentence beginners want on day two. **Я живу в Москве.**

## Motion versus location: the highest-value distinction in the system

If you learn one thing from this article, make it this one.

The prepositions **в** and **на** take **two different cases** depending on whether there is movement.

- **Я живу в Москве.** — I live in Moscow. *(prepositional — location)*
- **Я еду в Москву.** — I'm going to Moscow. *(accusative — motion toward)*

And with **на**:

- **Книга на столе.** — The book is on the table. *(prepositional)*
- **Я положил книгу на стол.** — I put the book on the table. *(accusative)*

Same preposition, different case, different meaning. English handles this distinction with different prepositions — *in* versus *into*, *on* versus *onto* — and mostly lets you get away with ignoring it. Russian does not let you ignore it, and the good news is that it is a single, learnable, high-frequency contrast rather than an irregularity.

The general principle worth carrying: **a Russian preposition does not have "a case".** Several govern different cases depending on meaning. Learning "в takes the prepositional" as a flat fact will produce errors within a week.

## What the other cases are actually for

### Genitive: the busiest case in the language

The genitive does more jobs than any other, which is why it repays early attention:

- **Possession.** *Это дом брата* — this is my brother's house.
- **Absence.** After **нет**, the thing that is missing goes into the genitive: *У меня нет книги*.
- **Having.** The ordinary way to say you own something uses **у** plus a genitive: *У меня есть книга*.
- **After many prepositions** — без, для, из, от, до, у, около, после.
- **After numbers.** Два, три and четыре take a genitive singular; пять and above take a genitive plural: *две книги*, *пять книг*. That one is worth knowing exists and worth postponing.

### Dative: the recipient

Who receives, who benefits, who is being spoken to. *Я дал книгу брату* — I gave the book to my brother.

The dative also carries a family of constructions where English uses a subject and Russian does not, most famously age: **Мне двадцать лет** — literally "to me twenty years". Learning to accept that the person is in the dative rather than the nominative is a real conceptual step, and it recurs in expressions about needing, liking, being cold and being allowed.

Prepositions: **к** and **по**.

### Instrumental: by what means, and with whom

- **Я пишу ручкой.** — I write with a pen. *(the means)*
- **Я иду с братом.** — I'm going with my brother. *(accompaniment, with с)*

English uses *with* for both jobs, which is a trap: the instrument takes a bare instrumental with no preposition, and the companion takes **с** plus the instrumental. Saying *с ручкой* for "with a pen" means you are travelling in the pen's company.

The instrumental also appears after **над, под, перед, между**, and in several constructions around what someone is or becomes professionally.

## Why this looks harder than it is

Three things make case learning slower than it needs to be, and all three are avoidable.

**Learning the tables before the sentences.** The tables are a compressed summary of a skill. Reciting endings and choosing an ending mid-sentence are different operations, and only the second one is the goal. Meet each case inside sentences that do something, then look at the table to organise what you already half-know.

**Forgetting that adjectives come along.** Cases are not a noun feature. Adjectives, pronouns, possessives and numerals all agree, so a single case decision propagates across the phrase. Learners who drill nouns alone hit a wall the first time they need to say "in the big house".

**Assuming a preposition has one case.** As above. Several of the most common prepositions govern different cases with different meanings, and в and на are the two you will use most.

There is also a fourth thing, which is not avoidable and is worth naming so you do not take it personally: gender, number and case interact, so a "table" is really a small three-dimensional grid. That is why sequencing matters so much — one case at a time, one gender at a time, in sentences.

## A sequence that works

**Nominative and accusative together.** They let you build a whole sentence — subject, verb, object — on day one. Start with inanimate objects so the animacy rule does not arrive at the same time.

**Then the animacy rule.** Introduced on its own, once you already have accusatives working, rather than as a caveat inside the first lesson.

**Then the prepositional.** Because "I live in", "I work at" and "I'm thinking about" are things you want to say early, and because the case is easy to identify.

**Then motion versus location.** The в/на contrast, taught explicitly as a pair. This is the moment cases stop feeling arbitrary, because you can see the ending doing work no word order could do.

**Then the genitive.** Possession and absence first, prepositions second, numbers much later.

**Then instrumental and dative.** In either order. Both are less urgent than their position in the traditional list suggests.

Two habits make all of it stick faster. First, always learn a noun with its **gender**, because gender determines which pattern the endings follow, and adding it retrospectively is far more expensive. Second, review the cases you have already met while learning new ones — case endings are exactly the kind of material that decays quietly and then fails under speaking pressure.

[Regal - Learn Russian Language](/apps/learn-russian/) is built on that staging: cases, gender, agreement and verb forms are introduced gradually, and the exercises explain why the correct answer is correct rather than only marking it, which is the difference between learning a pattern and memorising an answer. Saved words and missed-question practice pull back what you got wrong, and once the basics are in place there are stories, documents, roleplays, culture lessons and history to read, which is where case endings stop being drills and start being sentences.

## Where cases sit in the wider language

Being straight about this is more useful than reassurance.

The case system is the feature that defines the Russian learning curve, and it is genuinely the thing that takes longest to become automatic. But it is not the hardest thing in the language for most English speakers — **verb aspect** usually is, because there is no English structure to map it onto, whereas cases at least correspond to roles you already understand.

And Russian gives some of it back. There are **no articles** at all, no *a* and no *the*. The present tense of "to be" is normally simply omitted, so a great many sentences are shorter than their English equivalents. Word order is genuinely free, which means you are rarely wrong for arranging a sentence unusually.

For scale, the US Foreign Service Institute places Russian in **Category III**, at approximately **44 weeks of full-time instruction (1,100 class hours)** for its own students — demanding, and a full category below Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, Korean and Arabic. That describes intensive, full-time classroom training for diplomats rather than app study, and it is a relative scale rather than a promise about you.

If Cyrillic is still new, that comes first: our guide to [the Russian alphabet](/blog/learn-russian-cyrillic-beginners-guide/) covers the 33 letters, the false friends and the stress problem, and it is the one part of Russian you can finish this month. For a sense of what other grammars ask by comparison, [Malay](/blog/learn-malay-beginners-guide/) has no cases, no gender and no conjugation at all, and the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) start from the same assumption: no prior study.

title: Salary Cap Basics: How Budget Rules Change a GM Game
metaTitle: Salary Cap Explained: A Guide for GM Games
secondaryKeywords: how contracts work in gm games
body:
Take the cap off a team-building game and it stops being a game. Without a budget, the correct move at every slot is the highest-rated available player, the puzzle solves itself, and there is nothing left to think about after run three.

The cap is the constraint that makes the decisions decisions. Understanding what kind of constraint it is — and what it quietly costs you — is most of the skill in a GM mode.

## What a cap actually is

A salary cap is a ceiling on the **total** a team may commit to player salaries. Not per player, not per position: the sum.

Real competitions adopt caps for two stated reasons — keeping teams competitive with each other, and controlling costs — and the mechanism is the same in a simulation. It removes the option of solving every problem by acquiring the best available answer to it.

The immediate effect is that quality stops being the only axis. Every player now has two numbers, and a pick is only good if the pair is good.

## Hard caps and soft caps produce different rosters

This distinction is worth internalising because it changes the strategy completely, not marginally.

A **hard cap** is absolute. There is no mechanism to exceed it. A roster over the limit is invalid, so your budget is a genuine wall and every unit you spend is permanently unavailable.

A **soft cap** can be exceeded, but only in defined ways — commonly through named exceptions that permit specific transactions, or by paying a penalty on the amount you go over. That penalty structure is usually called a **luxury tax**: rather than blocking the spend, it prices it.

The strategic consequence is direct. Under a hard cap, overspending is impossible, so all your errors are allocation errors. Under a soft cap, overspending is a *decision* — you can buy your way past the constraint if you accept the cost — so your errors are cost-benefit errors instead.

Games use both, and it is worth checking which one you are in before you plan, because a plan that assumes flexibility fails immediately against a wall.

## The vocabulary, defined once

- **Cap space** — the cap minus your current committed salaries. What you can still spend right now.
- **Cap hit** — the amount a single player's contract counts against the cap in a given period. Not always the same as the money actually paid.
- **Dead money** — cap consumed by a player who is no longer on the roster, or otherwise no longer contributing. It buys nothing.
- **Minimum salary** — the floor price of a roster slot. It is the reason your usable budget is smaller than your cap.
- **Luxury tax** — a penalty applied to spending above a threshold, in systems where exceeding the limit is permitted rather than forbidden.
- **Exception** — a defined circumstance under which a soft-cap team may make a signing it otherwise could not.

## Your real budget is smaller than your cap

This is the arithmetic beginners skip, and it is the one that ruins drafts.

Suppose a cap of **100 units**, a **10-player** roster, and a **minimum salary of 2 units**. Ten slots at the minimum costs 20, so only **80 units** are genuinely discretionary. Spend 60 on one player and you are not left with 40 to allocate freely — you are left with 40 that must cover nine slots, of which 18 is already committed as minimums. Your actual remaining freedom is **22 units spread across nine players**.

The habit worth building is to track *discretionary money per remaining slot* rather than raw cap space:

```
(cap space − remaining slots × minimum salary) ÷ remaining slots
```

Watch that number as you draft. When it approaches zero, you have already decided the rest of your roster — you just have not seen it yet.

## The only comparison that matters under a cap
