Rating per unit of money is the obvious metric and it is misleading, because you are never choosing between a player and nothing. You are choosing between a player and the cheapest legal alternative.

Work it with numbers. Say a minimum-salary player at this position rates **60** and costs **2**.

- **Candidate A**: rated 90, costs 30. Improvement over the fallback: 30 rating points, for 28 extra units. That is **30 ÷ 28 ≈ 1.07 rating points per unit spent**.
- **Candidate B**: rated 80, costs 12. Improvement: 20 rating points, for 10 extra units. That is **20 ÷ 10 = 2.0 rating points per unit spent**.

Candidate B is close to twice as efficient, and the gap widens further once you account for what the 18 units you saved can buy elsewhere.

Two honest qualifications. Ratings do not necessarily convert to results in a straight line — the last ten points of quality may matter more than the first ten, in a real sport or in a simulation, and if they do, efficiency arguments understate the case for the expensive player. And efficiency is not the goal; the goal is the best roster you can field. Buying eleven efficient players and no good ones is its own failure mode.

Use the ratio to notice when you are overpaying, not as a rule that decides for you.

## Contract length is a cost you do not see on the sheet

In a single draft, price is the whole story. In a franchise that runs across seasons, **duration** is a second currency.

A long contract does three things at once: it secures a player, it commits money you cannot redeploy, and it removes an option you might want later. The first is why you sign it. The second and third are what you are paying, and they do not appear next to the salary.

This is where dead money comes from. Committing years to a player is a commitment to a future you cannot see, and when it goes wrong the money does not come back — it sits on your cap doing nothing while you try to build around it.

The practical rule that survives contact with actual play: be more willing to overpay in money than in years. An expensive short deal is a mistake you can exit. A cheap long one can be a mistake you carry.

## How this shows up in play

[Basketball Draft GM Franchise](/apps/pro-basketball-draft-gm-mode/) includes **Salary Cap Draft** as one of eight formats, alongside Unlimited, Quick, Blind and Franchise Drafts plus VS Computer, Battle Mode and a Daily Challenge. Running the same board twice — once unconstrained, once under the cap — is the fastest way to feel what a budget does. The rosters will not resemble each other, and the cap roster is usually the more interesting one to defend.

Past draft day, its GM Mode covers **contracts, trades and rotations**, which is where the duration problem becomes real. Trades are also the only tool that genuinely fixes a structural allocation mistake: they convert a surplus you cannot use into coverage you need, at a price.

[20-0 Football Draft & GM Mode](/apps/football-draft-gm-mode/) puts a Salary Cap Draft next to Unlimited, Limited and Playoff formats, and the football roster is the one where cap decisions bite hardest simply because there are more slots to fund. [162-0 Baseball Draft & GM Team](/apps/baseball-draft-gm-team/) includes payroll-focused drafting, and payroll review sits inside its Franchise GM Mode alongside the batting order, rotation and bullpen.

In all three, the currency is fictional and the resulting record is a model's score for how well the roster fits together, not a forecast of anything real.

## A checklist for your next cap draft

1. **Find out whether the cap is hard or soft** before you plan. Everything downstream depends on it.
2. **Subtract the minimums first.** Know your discretionary budget, not your headline budget.
3. **Price each candidate against the cheapest legal alternative**, not against zero.
4. **Recompute money-per-remaining-slot every few picks.** It is an early warning system.
5. **Fund your worst slot before upgrading your best.** A cap punishes weak links harder than it rewards strong ones, because you cannot buy your way out late.
6. **Prefer money over years** when a franchise runs across seasons.

## Related reading

Budget drafting and pick-order drafting are genuinely different skills; [snake draft versus auction draft](/blog/snake-draft-vs-auction-draft/) covers where that split comes from. The valuation reasoning underneath both is in [how fantasy draft strategy works](/blog/how-fantasy-draft-strategy-works/). For what to do with the roster once the money is spent, see [building a balanced basketball roster](/blog/how-to-build-a-balanced-basketball-roster/), and for one game's formats end to end, the [basketball draft simulator guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/).

The full set of management titles is in the [sports GM category](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Snake Draft vs Auction Draft: What Actually Changes
metaTitle: Snake Draft vs Auction Draft: Key Differences
secondaryKeywords: how does a snake draft work
how does an auction draft work
body:
Both formats hand out the same players to the same number of managers, and they produce completely different rosters. The difference is not cosmetic and it is not about pacing. It is that they ration a scarce resource in two incompatible ways, and the skill each one measures barely overlaps with the other.

## The difference stated once, plainly

In a **snake draft**, the scarce resource is **turn order**. Managers pick in sequence, that sequence reverses each round, and you may only take a player nobody has taken yet.

In an **auction draft**, the scarce resource is **money**. Every manager gets an identical notional budget, players are put up one at a time, and each goes to whoever bids highest.

Everything else follows from that one substitution. Which is why the useful question is not "which is better" but "what does each one make impossible".

## Snake drafts: order is the currency

### The reversal, and why it exists

Round one runs 1 through *n* in slot order. Round two runs the same managers in reverse. Round three reverts to the original order, and so on.

With ten managers, that means:

| Slot | Round 1 pick | Round 2 pick | Round 3 pick |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 20 | 21 |
| 5 | 5 | 16 | 25 |
| 10 | 10 | 11 | 30 |

Add the first two picks for each and the totals are 21, 21 and 21. That is the whole design. Without the reversal, the manager at slot 1 would take picks 1, 11 and 21 while slot 10 took 10, 20 and 30, and the gap would widen every round.

Note the asymmetry the reversal creates as a side effect: slot 1 waits nineteen picks between selections, slot 10 waits one. Equal total, very different rhythm.

### What snake drafting rewards

**Reading the board.** Because you cannot choose who is available, most of your skill goes into predicting who *will* be. Recognising that a position is about to dry up and taking it a round early is the core competence.

**Discipline under a clock.** Snake drafts move. The manager who prepared tiers in advance makes better decisions at speed than the one comparing rows in real time.

**Accepting good enough.** You will not get the player you wanted. The format is largely about being unbothered by that.

### What snake drafting takes away

You have no mechanism for wanting something more than someone else. If two managers value the same player, the one picking earlier gets them, full stop. Enthusiasm is not expressible in the format.

That also means every roster in a snake draft ends up structurally similar. Everyone gets one early pick, one late-early pick, and so on down. The spread between the best and worst roster is real but bounded.

## Auction drafts: money is the currency

### How a round works

A player is nominated. Managers bid in increments. Highest bid wins, the amount is deducted from that manager's budget, and the next nomination begins. This repeats until every roster is full.

The critical property: **nobody is out of reach**. If you want the best player in the pool badly enough to spend a third of your budget, you can have them, regardless of where you sit at the table.

### The arithmetic you must hold in your head

Auctions have one hard constraint that beginners break constantly. You must be able to fill every roster slot, so some of your budget is already spoken for.

Your **maximum legal bid** on any player is:

```
remaining budget − (slots left to fill after this one × minimum bid)
```

With a 200-unit budget, 12 roster slots and a 1-unit minimum: your first-player ceiling is 200 − 11 = **189**. After spending 60 on that player, you hold 140 with 11 slots left, so your next ceiling is 140 − 10 = **130**.

That is a ceiling, not a plan. The plan is the second calculation: your **average remaining spend**, which is simply remaining budget divided by remaining slots. Start with 200 and 12 slots and you average 16.7 per slot. Spend 90 on two players and you have 110 for 10 slots, or 11 each. Watching that average fall is how you feel a roster going top-heavy while there is still time to stop it.

### Nomination is a strategic act

Because you nominate players as well as bid on them, you get a tool that does not exist in a snake draft: you can put up a player you do not want, specifically because other managers do, and watch their budgets shrink.

This is legitimate and it is most of what separates experienced auction drafters from new ones. The reflex to nominate your own favourite first is exactly backwards — it invites everyone else to bid you up on the player you least want to lose.

### What auction drafting rewards

**Valuation.** You have to convert "how good is this player" into "how many units is this player worth", for the whole pool, before the format starts charging you for being wrong.

**Patience.** Budgets deplete. The manager who has kept powder dry while others spent can buy well in the last third at prices nobody could pay earlier.

**Structural intent.** You can genuinely decide what shape your roster will be — three expensive players and nine cheap ones, or twelve solid ones — and then execute it. In a snake draft, the shape is largely imposed on you.

### What auction drafting takes away

Time and forgiveness. An auction runs several times longer than the equivalent snake draft, and every manager has to stay engaged the entire way. A single overbid early does not cost you one slot; it lowers the ceiling on every remaining slot for the rest of the draft.

## Side by side

| | Snake | Auction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scarce resource | Pick order | Budget |
| Can you get any player? | No | Yes, at a price |
| Main skill | Reading the board | Valuing the pool |
| Cost of one bad decision | One slot | Every later slot |
| Roster shapes produced | Similar across managers | Highly variable |
| Length | Short | Long |
| Extra strategic tool | None | Nomination |

## So which should you play?

If you are learning to draft, snake. The feedback loop is faster, the decisions are cleaner, and you will run ten drafts in the time one auction takes. Almost everything you learn about tiers, scarcity and replacement value transfers to auctions later.

Choose an auction when the thing you actually want is control over roster shape — when the interesting question to you is *how much is too much for one player*, rather than *who will still be here in two rounds*.

And be honest about the group. Auctions are unforgiving of a table where half the managers have not thought about valuation, because the prices stop meaning anything and the format's whole premise collapses.

## Where our games sit, precisely

It is worth being exact here rather than approximate.

[Basketball Draft GM Franchise](/apps/pro-basketball-draft-gm-mode/) ships eight draft formats: Unlimited Draft, Quick Draft, Blind Draft, Franchise Draft, Salary Cap Draft, VS Computer, Battle Mode and a Daily Challenge. **Salary Cap Draft** is the budget-constrained one. Every pick has a price as well as a rating, and you have to complete a roster inside a limit — which exercises the same valuation muscle an auction demands. It is not an auction: the catalogue describes drafting under a cap, not live bidding against other managers.

[162-0 Baseball Draft & GM Team](/apps/baseball-draft-gm-team/) includes payroll-focused drafting alongside Unlimited Draft, a ten-pick Limited Refresh Draft with no rerolls, VS Computer, Battle Mode, a Daily Challenge and Baseball IQ. Its Franchise GM Mode carries payroll review past draft day.

If you want the auction skill without an auction, cap formats are the closest practice available: they force you to answer "what is this player worth in currency" on every pick, which is the question a snake draft never asks you.

One thing to keep clear in both: the money is a simulation value. In-game salaries, payrolls and budgets have no real-world worth, and the record a simulator returns is a score for how well you built the roster — not a prediction about anything outside the app.

## Further reading

The reasoning that underpins both formats — replacement value, tiers, positional runs — is covered in [how fantasy draft strategy works](/blog/how-fantasy-draft-strategy-works/). If the budget side is what interests you, [salary cap basics for GM games](/blog/salary-cap-basics-for-gm-games/) goes into hard caps, soft caps and why long contracts cost more than their annual figure. For the preparation that makes a fast snake draft survivable, see [what makes a good draft board](/blog/what-makes-a-good-draft-board/), and for one game's formats end to end, the [basketball draft simulator guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/).

More management and drafting titles are listed in the [sports GM category](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Building an XI That Holds Up: A Guide to Soccer Draft Simulators
metaTitle: Soccer Draft Simulator: Building an XI That Holds Up
body:
Soccer is the only sport in this genre where you can play well and get nothing for it.

A basketball or baseball roster that is slightly better than its opponent wins slightly more often. A soccer side that is slightly better than its opponent draws a lot. That third result is why a perfect campaign in this sport reads 38-0-0 rather than 38-0, and why it demands something that "do not lose" does not: you have to convert. A side built to be difficult to beat will produce a long unbeaten run and nowhere near a perfect record.

Everything about drafting an XI follows from that.

## Three outcomes change the shape of a good squad

In a two-outcome sport, defensive solidity and attacking quality are close to interchangeable ways of buying wins. Add draws and they stop being symmetric.

Solidity converts losses into draws. Attacking quality converts draws into wins. Both are worth having, but they buy different things, and a squad that has spent everything on one of them hits a ceiling that more of the same will not raise. This is the specific reason a balanced XI outperforms a lopsided one in [38-0 Football Draft XI Soccer](/apps/soccer-draft-gm-xi/), and it is a genuinely different constraint from the ones the other drafting sports impose.

The practical version: before you start picking, decide roughly where your side sits on that axis, and notice when a pick would push you further in a direction you have already invested in.

## Coverage is not fit

Every draft game asks you to fill each position. This one asks something more specific, because position fit and playing style feed the result alongside the ratings.

The distinction is worth labouring:

- **Coverage** means there is a body in every slot. It is a completeness check, and it is easy.
- **Fit** means each slot holds someone suited to it. It is a judgement, and the simulation reads it.

An XI with full coverage and poor fit looks fine on the team sheet and underperforms in the campaign, which is the most confusing possible failure mode if you do not know fit is being measured. You did everything the interface asked. The result disagreed anyway.

Style adds a second layer on top of fit. Two players can both suit a position and want incompatible things from the players around them. A squad assembled purely by rating tends to accumulate this quietly — several players who each individually make sense and collectively want to play different games.

## Drafting the XI

There is no single correct order, but there is a defensible one, and it comes from thinking about which mistakes are expensive.

### Settle the spine first

The positions that run through the middle of the side — the goalkeeper, the centre of defence, the centre of midfield, the focal point in attack — touch the most situations. A compromise in the spine is a compromise that appears constantly.

Draft these while the board is at its widest. It costs you nothing to solve your most load-bearing positions early, and deferring them is how you end up choosing between two players who neither fit nor appeal.

### Then decide what the wide positions are for

Wide areas are where a squad expresses what it is. This is the point at which the earlier decision about solidity versus conversion becomes a concrete pick rather than an intention: you are either buying more of what you already have or you are balancing it.

If you have built a resilient spine, this is where you buy the goals that turn draws into wins. If your spine is attacking, this is where you make sure the side can defend a lead.

### Finish by checking the squad, not the players

Before you lock the XI, read it as a group rather than a list. Two questions do most of the work:

1. **Is there a position where I settled?** That slot will show up in the campaign.
2. **Do these players want the same things?** A side of individually excellent players with incompatible styles is the classic high-rating, low-result draft.

## The formats change the question

The game runs limited drafts, budget challenges and computer battles alongside the open format, plus tournaments, quizzes, player guessing, season modes and daily challenges.

Budget challenges are the most instructive of these, because a budget converts drafting from ranking into allocation. Without one, the best available player who fits is the pick. With one, a good player at a low price can beat a better player at a high one, and the actual skill is knowing when you are paying for a name rather than a contribution. It is the same lesson the [football draft guide](/blog/football-draft-gm-guide/) covers from the other direction, where budgets expose entire units you underfunded.

Limited formats test something else again: whether you can commit without searching. When you cannot keep looking, each pick has to be made against an internal standard of what "good" means in this run, and building that standard from the first few cards is the skill. Drafters who are excellent when they can search and poor when they cannot are relying on the search to do their judging.

Competitive formats add an opponent's board to the things you are tracking. A pick can now be worth making early purely because losing that player to the other side would cost you twice.

## What the campaign simulation is doing

When the XI is locked and the simulation runs, it plays out a 38-game campaign and reports wins, draws and losses.

That result is a model's output. It is computed from the squad you built — ratings, position fit, playing style, balance — according to the game's own rules. Three clarifications matter:

**It does not describe anything real.** The players are fictional and generated inside the game. The result has no relationship to any real match, club, competition or player, and it is not usable as an indication of any real outcome.

**It is a score for your squad building.** Read it the way you would read the score at the end of a puzzle. The question worth asking is not whether you were unlucky but which decision the result is disagreeing with.

**The perfect record is meant to be hard.** A campaign of 38 wins with no draws and no defeats is the target the game is built around, not the expected reward for a competent draft. Getting close is the normal good outcome.

Because completed runs can be saved and measured against your next attempt, the genuinely useful comparison is your own previous squad rather than any absolute standard. That is the loop the game is designed for: draft, read the result, change one thing, draft again.

## The longer save

Club management extends a single draft into something that runs: formations, squad depth, transfers, contracts, fitness and season progress.

Squad depth is the concept that most changes how you think. A one-off draft is an XI, and an XI is a snapshot. A club is a group that has to keep functioning, and depth is what stops a single problem becoming a structural one. The trade is familiar to anyone who has played a management game — resources spent on depth are resources not spent on the first eleven, and the correct balance depends on how long a horizon you are playing for.

Transfers deserve a specific note, because they are the only tool that fixes a shape problem. If a draft left you strong in one area and thin in another, no amount of good selection repairs it; you have to convert surplus into coverage. That is the same function trades serve in the other sports, covered in the [basketball draft and GM guide](/blog/basketball-draft-gm-guide/).

## Why the quizzes are not filler

Tournaments, quizzes, player guessing and daily challenges sit alongside the drafting, and it is easy to write them off as padding. The knowledge formats are testing the same faculty the draft board needs: reading a set of attributes and forming a fast, accurate judgement about what they will do.

If your drafts keep returning campaigns you did not expect, the gap is usually in that reading rather than in your strategy. Practising it directly is cheaper than practising it 38 games at a time.

## A pre-draft checklist

1. **Decide early whether you are buying solidity or conversion**, and notice when a pick doubles down.
2. **Draft the spine while the board is wide.**
3. **Check fit, not just coverage.** A filled slot and a suited slot are different things.
4. **Read the XI as a group before you lock it.** Incompatible styles are the quiet killer.
5. **After the campaign, change exactly one thing and run it again.** One variable at a time is the only way to learn what the model rewards.

The rest of the studio's drafting and management games — across basketball, football, baseball, hockey and combat sports — are listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Soccer Formations Explained: What the Numbers Actually Decide
metaTitle: Soccer Formations Explained: 4-4-2, 4-3-3 and More
secondaryKeywords: best formation for a weak defence
body:
A formation is not a plan. It is a starting arrangement — where eleven people stand before anything happens — and roughly two seconds into a match it stops describing the picture accurately.

That is not an argument for ignoring it. It is an argument for understanding what it does and does not tell you, because the shape you choose settles a handful of questions permanently and leaves everything else open.

## Reading the notation

The Laws of the Game, published by the International Football Association Board, set a team at eleven players, one of whom is the goalkeeper. Formation notation quietly assumes the keeper and counts the other ten.

The digits run from the defensive end forward. So:

- **4-4-2** — four defenders, four midfielders, two forwards. 4 + 4 + 2 = 10.
- **4-3-3** — four defenders, three midfielders, three forwards. 4 + 3 + 3 = 10.
- **4-2-3-1** — four defenders, two holding midfielders, three attacking midfielders, one striker. 4 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 10.

If a formation you are reading does not sum to ten, someone has either miscounted or included the goalkeeper. That is the entire trick, and once you have it, every shape you have ever seen written down becomes legible.

The extra hyphens in longer notations such as 4-2-3-1 or 4-1-4-1 carry real information: they say that a band has been deliberately split into two lines at different heights. A side listing 4-4-2 and a side listing 4-2-2-2 have the same personnel counts and very different intentions about the space in front of their own defence.

## What a shape actually decides

Formations do not manufacture advantage. There are ten outfield players in every shape, so every square metre you cover in one area is a square metre you have vacated somewhere else. Choosing a formation is choosing which trade you would rather live with.

Four questions get answered the moment you pick one.

**Where does your width come from?** If your wide players are in midfield, they start deep and have distance to cover. If they are forwards, you have width high up the pitch immediately, and your full-backs are exposed to counter-attacks down the same channels.

**How many bodies sit in front of your defence?** One holding midfielder is a single point of failure and frees a player for the attack. Two — a double pivot — is far more secure and costs you a body further forward. This is the most consequential single decision in modern shape-picking.

**How far apart are your lines?** Compact sides are hard to play through and easy to play around; stretched sides are the opposite. Formations with more bands, such as 4-2-3-1, tend to be more compact vertically because each band is smaller.

**Who is your striker's company?** One forward alone against two central defenders spends the match outnumbered, which is fine if your midfield arrives to support and disastrous if it does not. Two forwards occupy both central defenders but leave you a man short in midfield unless somebody else works very hard.

## The common shapes, and what each one buys

| Shape | What it gives you | What you accept |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4-4-2 | Two clear banks of four, simple defensive responsibilities, a strike partnership | Outnumbered in central midfield against three-man midfields |
| 4-3-3 | Width high up the pitch, three-versus-two in midfield, aggressive pressing angles | Full-backs left isolated when possession turns over |
| 4-2-3-1 | A protected defence, a creator between the lines, vertical compactness | A lone striker who is easy to isolate if support is slow |
| 4-1-4-1 | A dense midfield band that is hard to play through | Long distances from the back to the lone forward |
| 3-5-2 | Numbers in midfield, two forwards, wing-backs providing all the width | Enormous physical demand on the wing-backs; wide areas empty if they are caught upfield |
| 3-4-3 | Attacking width and central numbers at the same time | Three defenders facing a counter with very little cover |
| 5-3-2 | A deep, wide defensive block that is genuinely hard to break down | Very little of the pitch when you win the ball back |

Read that table as a set of trades rather than a ranking. There is no row that is simply better than the others, and any guide that hands you one is describing a preference.

## The roles inside the numbers

Two teams can both write **4-3-3** and play almost nothing alike, because the digits say how many and not what kind. The vocabulary worth having:

### The holding midfielder and the double pivot

The player who screens the defence — sometimes called the anchor, sometimes the number six. A single holder allows an extra attacker but has to cover the whole width of the space in front of the back line alone. Two holders share it, cover for each other when one steps out, and make a high defensive line much safer.

### Number eights and number tens

An eight is a midfielder who covers ground box to box; a ten operates between the opposition midfield and defence, in the space defenders do not want to leave and midfielders cannot see. Whether your third midfielder is an eight or a ten changes the character of a 4-3-3 completely, without changing a single digit.

### Full-backs, wing-backs and inverted full-backs

A **full-back** defends the wide area and joins attacks. A **wing-back** in a three-at-the-back shape is really a wide midfielder who is also the last defender on that side — the most demanding running job in the sport. An **inverted full-back** steps into central midfield with the ball instead of overlapping outside, giving you an extra body in the middle at the cost of width on that flank.

### The false nine

A centre-forward who drops away from goal instead of holding position. The idea is that a central defender either follows and leaves a gap in the defensive line, or does not follow and lets an unmarked player receive between the lines. Both outcomes are useful. The cost is that nobody is occupying the defenders, so if your midfielders do not run past the ball, you end up with possession and nowhere to put it.

### The sweeper keeper

A goalkeeper who patrols the space behind a high defensive line, coming off the line to reach balls played in behind before an attacker does.

This is the role that makes aggressive defending viable. Pushing your defence up the pitch compresses the game and wins the ball back higher, but it leaves a large open area between the last defender and the goalkeeper. Somebody has to be responsible for it. A keeper who is comfortable defending that space converts the high line from a gamble into a system; a keeper who is not converts it into a series of one-on-ones.

## The shape you defend in is not the shape you attack in

This is the point at which formation talk usually goes wrong.

The same eleven players hold different positions depending on who has the ball. A side that sets up 4-3-3 may defend as a 4-5-1 with both wide forwards dropping in, and attack as something closer to 2-3-5 with the full-backs high and the holding midfielder alone. Neither description is a lie. They are two frames of the same film.

So when you read that a team "plays 4-3-3", treat it as shorthand for the arrangement at kick-off. The interesting questions are what it becomes in each phase, and whether the players have the legs to make both versions work.

## Choosing a shape for the squad you actually have

The most common mistake is picking a formation you admire and then trying to force players into it.

Work in the other direction. Ask which of your players are genuinely capable of the demanding roles — the wing-back who has to cover a whole flank, the lone holder who has to screen a whole defence, the keeper who has to defend space — and rule out any shape that depends on a role you cannot fill. What is left is your real menu, and a plain shape executed properly beats a fashionable one that leaks.

This is exactly the puzzle [38-0 Football Draft XI Soccer](/apps/soccer-draft-gm-xi/) is built around. Drafting there works across every position on the pitch, weighing position fit and playing style rather than stacking the highest ratings, and position fit, style and squad balance all feed the result. The club management side adds formations, squad depth, transfers, contracts, fitness and season progress for anyone who wants to run a longer save rather than a single draft.

The practical drafting habit that follows: decide the shape before you spend picks, then judge every option by whether it can do the specific job you need in that structure. A high rating in the wrong role is a rating you are not going to collect.

## What the simulation is modelling — and what it is not

When a finished XI goes into the season simulation and comes back with a set of wins, draws and losses across the campaign, that record is the game's own verdict on your squad construction, produced by its internal rules.

It is worth being exact about the limits. The model is weighing roster quality, position fit and balance; it is not reproducing football physics, and it is not describing any real match, club or player. Nothing it returns is a forecast, a prediction or guidance of any kind — it is a score on a squad-building puzzle, which is a more interesting thing for it to be. The perfect unbeaten campaign the game is named for is deliberately hard to reach, so a shortfall is the game working rather than failing.

The useful loop is comparative: change one structural decision, run it again, and see whether the model agrees. That tells you something about your reasoning even though it tells you nothing about football beyond the game.

## Where to read next

If you want to know how the campaign result you get back is assembled into a table, [how soccer league tables work](/blog/how-soccer-league-tables-work/) covers points, goal difference and tie-breaks. If you want the drafting side in more depth, the [soccer draft XI guide](/blog/soccer-draft-xi-guide/) goes through squad construction directly, and the [football positions guide](/blog/football-positions-explained-for-drafting/) shows how the same positional-value thinking looks in a sport with three separate personnel groups. For the practical question of fitting any of this into a commute, see [manager games for short sessions](/blog/best-sports-manager-games-for-short-sessions/).

The full set of drafting and management titles is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Reading Enemy Fire: How to Actually Get Good at a Space Shooter
metaTitle: Space Shooter Arcade Game on Android: A Player's Guide

sources.p: The Strong National Museum of Play

body:
There is a specific moment in an arcade shooter when the screen stops being a threat and becomes a map. The bullets have not thinned out. You have simply started looking at the space between them instead of at the bullets themselves.

Reaching that moment sooner is most of what "getting good" means in this genre, and it is a learnable habit rather than a reflex you either have or you do not. What follows is how the shift happens, and how to stop blaming a game for something that was legible the whole time.

## Density is not difficulty

A pattern that covers three quarters of the screen can be trivially safe if it has one wide, obvious channel running through it. A pattern with a tenth of the bullets can be brutal if every one of them is fast and aimed at exactly where you were standing.

Players read the first as hard and the second as easy, because we judge threat by how much of the screen is covered. Then we die to the sparse one and call it unfair. Understanding why requires splitting projectiles into two categories that ask for opposite responses.

**Aimed shots** are fired at your position at the instant of firing. They are a snapshot of where you *were*. Almost any movement makes them miss, which is why they mainly punish players who stop to line up a shot. Against aimed fire, motion itself is the answer, and it barely matters which direction.

**Fixed patterns** are fired the same way whether you are there or not — spreads, rings, walls, sweeps. Moving does nothing on its own, because the pattern was never about you. What matters is whether you are standing in a gap when it arrives, which makes these a positioning problem with a deadline.

Nearly every real wave mixes both. That is precisely why the two most common pieces of beginner advice — "just keep moving" and "find the safe spot" — each work about half the time and then get you killed.

## What separates a fair pattern from a cheap one

Fairness in this genre is an information problem, not a numbers problem. A pattern is fair when it satisfies three conditions, and it feels like garbage when it breaks any one of them.

1. **It telegraphs.** Something visible tells you what is coming before it arrives, early enough to act on. An emitter rotates, a formation shifts, a boss winds up.
2. **It is consistent.** The same setup produces the same behaviour, so what you learned on your last attempt is still true on this one. Consistency is what converts a death into progress.
3. **The escape route existed beforehand.** There is a survivable path that was already available before the shot was fired — not one that required you to already be somewhere you had no reason to be.

Break the first and the pattern is a surprise. Break the second and learning it is impossible, so every death is noise. Break the third and the game is technically survivable but only for a player who has already memorised it, which is the definition of a cheap shot.

[Space Shooter - Galaxy Arcade](/apps/space-shooter-classic-arcade/) is built on the first two. Projectiles arrive in readable patterns, and movement and timing keep you alive far more reliably than raw firepower does. That is a design stance with a consequence: if you die, the information you needed was almost always on the screen, and the fix is attentional rather than mechanical.

### Watch what is about to fire, not what has already fired

A bullet in flight is settled. It has a direction and a speed, and neither will change. Staring at it gives you nothing you did not already have.

The enemy that has not fired yet is where the useful information lives. Enemy models here move and attack in their own distinct ways, so once you can identify a model by its silhouette, you know roughly what it is going to do before it does it. That is the single largest jump in survivability available to a new player, and it costs nothing but where you point your eyes.

Practically: keep the bullets in peripheral vision and your focus about a third of the screen ahead of your ship, on whatever is arriving next.

### Move in small increments

The beginner instinct under pressure is to sprint for whichever corner looks emptiest. This is wrong twice over.

Corners cut your available escape directions roughly in half, so a pattern that would have been routine in open space becomes a trap. And a long dash crosses far more of the screen than a short adjustment does, which means it intersects more of whatever is in flight. Big movements are how you fly into bullets you had already dodged.

The alternative is to make continuous small adjustments and let the pattern come to you. You are not trying to get to safety; you are trying to already be in the gap that the pattern is about to open.

## Four buttons, four different problems

The ability set is small on purpose, and each button answers a different question.

| Ability | The problem it solves | The common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FIRE | Clearing the fleet in front of you | Trading fire head-on instead of repositioning first |
| ALT | A secondary attack for situations the main weapons handle badly | Forgetting it exists for entire runs |
| Ultimate | A charged answer to a wave or boss that has gone wrong | Hoarding it until the game-over screen |
| Shield | Buying an exit when the screen closes in | Using it as a first response rather than a last one |

The Ultimate deserves a note. Charged resources create a specific psychological trap: the moment you have one, you start waiting for a situation worthy of it, and the situation that finally qualifies is usually the one that just killed you. An ability you never spend is worth exactly nothing. If you are consistently ending runs with a full charge, you are playing more conservatively than the game is asking you to.

The Shield has the opposite failure mode. Because it feels safe, it gets used the instant things look busy — and then it is gone when the screen genuinely closes. Try to move first and shield second. It protects you while it holds, which makes it an escape hatch rather than a permanent state.

## Bosses reward memory over damage

Boss encounters here ask you to learn a pattern rather than out-gun it, and heavy attacks come with openings you have to find. That reframes what a first attempt is for.

Your first run at a new boss is reconnaissance, not a fight. The goal is to survive long enough to see the full rotation of attacks at least once, which means playing far more passively than feels productive. Damage dealt during a losing attempt is not wasted, but information gathered during one is worth more.

The openings are usually at the seams: the moment after a heavy attack finishes, before the next one starts, when the boss is committed and cannot adjust. Find one seam, use only that seam, and add a second one later. Trying to punish every gap at once is how a learnable fight turns back into chaos.

## The upgrade screen is a difficulty dial

Rewards earned during a run go into weapons, unlocked upgrades, ship systems and bonuses you pick yourself, so the ship you launch with keeps changing shape.

The non-obvious point is that damage is a defensive stat. An enemy destroyed early stops producing projectiles, so every point of weapon strength quietly reduces the number of bullets that will ever exist on the screen. Players who think of offence and survivability as a trade-off tend to under-invest in weapons and then wonder why the screen keeps filling up.

That said, upgrades change the slope of the difficulty curve, not the skill required. You cannot buy your way past a pattern you have not learned to read; you can only buy yourself more attempts at reading it.

## Endless Mode asks a different question

The campaign asks whether you can clear what is in front of you. Endless Mode asks how long you can hold, with no finish line and waves that keep escalating.

That distinction matters more than it sounds. When there is something to clear, taking a risk to end a wave faster can pay off. When there is nothing to clear, speed buys you nothing at all, and every risk is pure cost. Endless rewards the most boring possible version of your play: small movements, early ability use, no greed. It is also the honest measure of how much you have actually internalised, because the mode eventually reaches a difficulty no upgrade path carries you through.

## A practice routine that works

Four runs, with one job each. This beats ten runs where you try to do everything at once.

1. **The watching run.** Pick one enemy model and follow only it for a full wave. Learn what its approach looks like before it shoots. Ignore your score.
2. **The spending run.** Deliberately dump ALT and the Ultimate early, before you feel they are warranted. You are recalibrating an instinct that is almost certainly too cautious.
3. **The small-movement run.** Stay away from the edges and forbid yourself any long dash. Expect to die in a place that surprises you.
4. **The changed-build run.** Put your rewards somewhere different from usual and see which waves get easier.

## Where it fits

Space Shooter - Galaxy Arcade is free to download on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases and an Everyone content rating. Runs are short enough for a break and the controls take seconds to learn, which is the arcade bargain: trivial to start, deep enough to keep failing at.

It sits in [Action & Arcade Games](/apps/category/action-arcade/) alongside a game built on the opposite premise — [Zombie Survival: Last Survivor](/apps/zombie-survival-last-survivor/) removes aiming entirely so that movement is the only input, and we wrote about [how its mid-run upgrade choices work](/blog/zombie-survival-roguelike-guide/) separately. If you want something with no reflex requirement at all, [the anime trivia guide](/blog/anime-trivia-quiz-guide/) covers the other end of our catalogue.

The genre has been asking the same question since Taito released Space Invaders in Japan in 1978, designed by Tomohiro Nishikado: not how fast can you shoot, but where are you going to be standing. Almost fifty years of the form later, the answer is still positioning.

title: Spaced Repetition for Language Learning: What the Research Actually Supports
metaTitle: Spaced Repetition for Language Learning: How It Works

sources.p: Classics in the History of Psychology, York University
Psychological Science in the Public Interest

body:
Everyone learning a language runs into the same wall. You study a set of words, you know them, and three weeks later they are gone — not fuzzy, gone. Then you relearn them, and they go again.

Spaced repetition is the standard answer to that problem, and it is a good one. It is also routinely oversold, wrapped in interval numbers presented as scientific findings when they are engineering choices, and applied to material it cannot help with.

This is what the research actually supports, what it does not, and how to get most of the benefit without any algorithm at all.

## It is two findings, not one

"Spaced repetition" is usually treated as a single idea. It is two, and they are worth separating because they give different advice.

### The spacing effect

Hermann Ebbinghaus, working on himself with nonsense syllables in the 1880s, established the basic shape of forgetting: retention of newly learned material drops steeply soon after learning and then more gradually. He also found that relearning was faster than learning, and that repetitions distributed over time were more efficient than the same repetitions packed together.

That second point is the **spacing effect**, and it has held up for well over a century of replication. Given a fixed amount of study time, spreading it across sessions produces better long-term retention than spending it all at once.

The 2013 *Psychological Science in the Public Interest* review of ten common learning techniques rated **distributed practice** as high utility — broadly applicable, well supported, and effective across ages, materials and subjects. It rated highlighting, rereading and summarisation considerably lower.

### The testing effect

The second finding is less intuitive and does more work.

**Retrieving** information from memory is a stronger learning event than **reviewing** it. Trying to recall a word and succeeding strengthens it more than reading the word and its translation together, even though the second feels more productive. The Karpicke and Roediger work published in *Science* in 2008 made the point sharply: repeated retrieval practice produced far better long-term retention than repeated study, while learners' own predictions about which method was working were wrong.

The same 2013 review rated **practice testing** high utility alongside distributed practice. Between them, those two techniques were the only ones in the set to earn that rating.

This is why the format of a review matters as much as its timing. A flashcard you flip before genuinely attempting the answer has been converted from a test into a reread, and it loses most of its value. The pause where you sit there not knowing is not wasted time; it is the mechanism.

## Why cramming feels better and works worse

Cramming produces a very specific illusion. Material seen five times in twenty minutes feels thoroughly known, because it is fluent and immediately available. Spaced review produces the opposite feeling — you keep failing on items you were sure you had learned.

Those feelings are almost exactly inverted from what is actually happening. Fluency in the moment is a poor predictor of retention later, and difficulty during practice often signals that useful work is being done. Researchers at UCLA's Bjork lab describe conditions of this kind as **desirable difficulties**: manipulations that slow learning down and depress performance during practice while improving retention and transfer afterwards.

The practical implication for a language learner is uncomfortable but simple. The study session where you feel competent is often the less useful one. The session where you keep drawing blanks and having to dig is usually the one paying off, provided you are still recovering the answers rather than failing outright.

## What an interval schedule actually is

Here is where most explanations of spaced repetition overreach.

The research supports the **principle**: intervals should expand as an item becomes more secure, and a review is most valuable when recall is effortful but still successful. It does not hand down a table of days. When a system tells you to review at one day, then three, then seven, then twenty-one, those numbers are a design decision built on the principle — a reasonable one, but not a finding.

You should be sceptical of any product presenting its specific intervals as scientifically optimal. What matters, in order:

1. **That you review at all**, more than once, after a gap.
2. **That the gaps widen** rather than staying flat.
3. **That each review is a genuine attempt at recall** before the answer appears.
4. **That items you keep failing come back sooner** than items you keep getting right.

Everything past that is tuning, and the difference between a well-tuned schedule and a roughly sensible one is much smaller than the difference between reviewing and not reviewing.

## Where spaced repetition does nothing for you

This is the part usually left out, and it is the reason a lot of people conclude the method does not work.

**It is a retention tool, not an acquisition tool.** It keeps material you have already understood. It does nothing for material you never understood in the first place. Drilling a grammar point you cannot parse produces a memorised string, not a usable structure — you will recall the card and remain unable to build the sentence.

**It does not produce production ability on its own.** Recognising a word on a card and reaching for it mid-sentence are different skills with different failure modes. Recognition is necessary and not sufficient. This gap is widest in exactly the languages where it hurts most: the Russian case endings covered in our [guide to the Cyrillic alphabet](/blog/learn-russian-cyrillic-beginners-guide/) can be recited from cards long before they can be chosen correctly while speaking, and the tone contrasts in Cantonese behave the same way.

**It does not fix a backlog.** The most common failure mode is not a bad schedule, it is a queue of several hundred overdue reviews that becomes psychologically impossible to face. The cure is preventative: add new material at a rate your future self can service, not at the rate your enthusiasm suggests today.

**It is weakest on things that are not discrete items.** Pronunciation, listening at speed, word boundaries in a script written without spaces, the reflex of choosing the right register — none of these decompose neatly into cards. They need exposure and production, not review.

## Running it without an algorithm

You do not need a specialised system to get most of the benefit. You need three habits.

**Always attempt before revealing.** Whatever the tool — physical cards, an app, a notebook covered with your hand — say or write the answer before checking. If you skip this, you have a reading exercise.

**Widen the gaps on a schedule you can hold.** A workable pattern for a new item is same day, next day, later in the week, the following week, then the following month. Those numbers are a convention rather than a finding, and any similar expanding sequence will do the job. Consistency matters more than precision.

**Sort ruthlessly by what you get wrong.** Time spent on items you already know is close to wasted. Time spent on items you fail repeatedly is where the returns are. If you are tracking nothing else, track your failures.

### Using the review modes in our courses

Worth being precise about what the apps do, because the honest version is less impressive than the marketing version and more useful.

[Learn Cantonese for Beginners](/apps/learn-cantonese/) has seven review modes — Daily Review, Speed Run Review, Mistake Rescue, Listening Blitz, Sentence Builder, Match Blitz and Dictation Mode — all of which draw on material you have already covered, plus a **missed-questions list** that collects what you keep getting wrong. Learn Russian and Learn Cambodian, Speak Khmer keep saved words and missed questions in the same way, and the Khmer course adds flashcards you build and shuffle yourself.

What that gives you is the raw material for spaced review: a record of what you have met and a record of what is not sticking. What it does not give you is a per-item scheduler computing an optimal next review date, and we are not going to claim it does.

So the schedule is yours. In practice that means running Daily Review as the habit, using Mistake Rescue as the priority queue, and deliberately revisiting an old unit after a gap rather than only ever working forward. The mode variety helps for a reason worth naming: reviewing the same word through recognition, through dictation and through sentence building tests different retrieval routes to the same item, which is closer to how you will actually need it than a single card format ever gets.

One design detail matters here more than it looks. There is **no hearts or lives system** in these courses — nothing stops you after a mistake. A review method that depends on you failing frequently is incompatible with a system that punishes failure, and any app that makes errors expensive is quietly teaching you to avoid the difficulty that makes review work.

## A weekly shape that survives contact with real life

Rough, adjustable, and built around the reality that some days you will do almost nothing:

- **Most days:** one short review session first, then new material only if there is time left. Reviews before new content, always. When the two compete, reviews win — new material you never review is wasted effort, while reviews without new material still hold the line.
- **Two or three days a week:** production practice that is not card-shaped. Speaking, dictation, building your own sentences. This is where recognition gets converted into use.
- **Once a week:** deliberately open something from a few weeks back. This is the review your schedule will otherwise never prompt, and it is the one that shows you what has actually stuck.
- **Bad days:** do the review session and nothing else. The habit is the asset.

## What to expect

Honest framing, since this is where a lot of study advice starts making promises.

Spaced repetition will meaningfully reduce how much vocabulary you lose. It will make the second and third encounters with a word cheaper. It will show you clearly which items are weak, which is information you cannot get any other way.

It will not turn recognition into speech by itself, it will not teach you anything you have not first understood, and it will not compress the time a language takes — a point our [guide to the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) makes in a different guise, where knowing every letter still leaves the harder half of the reading job undone.

What it does is stop you paying for the same words twice. Over months, that is a much larger effect than it sounds. If you want to see how the method applies to a specific language's particular sticking points, our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) each have a beginner's guide that names them, and the [Cantonese guide](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/) is the most detailed on the recognition-versus-production gap.

title: Sports GM Games Without Internet: What "Offline" Actually Means
metaTitle: Sports GM Games Without Internet: What to Check
secondaryKeywords: games that work on a plane
body:
You are on a plane, or on a train through a tunnel, or somewhere with two bars that keep pretending to be four. You open a game that worked fine at home and it sits on a loading screen.

The frustrating part is that this was findable in advance. "Offline" just is not one property, and a store page saying so — or not saying so — tells you less than people assume.

## Four things "offline" can mean

Pull them apart and the question becomes answerable.

**1. The core loop.** Can you start the game, play a full session and reach a result with no network at all? This is the one that matters and the one people mean.

**2. Advertising.** Free games funded by ads need a connection to fetch them. A game whose core loop is entirely local can still behave differently offline, because the ad slot has nothing to show.

**3. Accounts and cloud saves.** Some games require sign-in before they will start. Others sign in if they can and shrug if they cannot. A game that needs an account is a game that needs a connection at least once, and often on each cold start.

**4. Live features.** Multiplayer, leaderboards, timed events, live data feeds. These will not work offline in any game, by definition, and how gracefully an app handles their absence varies enormously.

A game can be fully offline in sense 1 and fully online in senses 2, 3 and 4 simultaneously. That is not a contradiction; it is the normal arrangement for free mobile games.

## Why draft-and-simulate is the right genre for this

Some genres fight offline play and some are practically designed for it. Sports management sits firmly in the second group, for reasons worth spelling out.

**There is no opponent to wait for.** A draft is you against a pool of options. A simulation is the game evaluating what you built. Neither needs a second person, which removes the single biggest reason a mobile game needs a server.

**The computation is small and local.** Working out a projected record from a roster is arithmetic on a handful of attributes. There is no reason for it to happen anywhere but on the phone in your hand.

**There is no live data.** A simulator built on fictional players has nothing to sync with. Nobody's form changed overnight, no fixture list moved, no injury report needs fetching. The game is complete the moment it is installed.

**The session has a natural end.** Draft, simulate, read the record, decide whether to run it again. That loop closes, which means an interruption — landing, a tunnel, a stop — costs you a session rather than a save.

Compare that with a game built around live opponents, timed server events or a real-world data feed, and the difference is structural rather than a matter of developer effort.

## The five-minute test

The only genuinely reliable answer for your phone is to check on your phone. This takes about five minutes and works for any app.

1. **Install and open the game once with a connection.** First-run downloads and setup are normal and are not evidence of anything.
2. **Force-close it.** Not just background it — close it properly, so the next launch is a cold start.
3. **Turn on airplane mode.** Confirm Wi-Fi is off too; on many phones airplane mode leaves Wi-Fi available.
4. **Cold start the game and play a complete loop.** For a draft game that means starting a draft, finishing it, and getting a result. Reaching the menu is not the test.
5. **Background the app, wait a minute, and return to it.** Some apps re-check for a connection on resume, which is where a game that seemed offline suddenly is not.
6. **Close it and reopen it again.** Confirm your progress survived.

If all six steps pass, the game works offline for your purposes, whatever any description says. If step 4 or 5 fails, you now know before you are at 30,000 feet.

## What to expect even when it does work

A few side effects are normal rather than faults.

- **Ad slots behave differently.** They may be skipped, may show nothing, or may make an optional reward unavailable until you reconnect. Every sports title the studio publishes is free and ad-supported, so this applies to all of them.
- **Some screens may pause briefly** while a network request times out before the app gives up and carries on.
- **Anything explicitly online is gone.** That is not a bug, it is the definition.
- **Saves are wherever they were.** An app with no account stores progress locally, which is why a long franchise deserves a moment's thought about backup before you commit months to it.

## What we can actually confirm about our own games

We would rather be narrow and correct here than broad and convenient.

**[Basketball Career Sim](/apps/pro-basketball-my-career-sim/) supports offline play and requires no account.** That is stated in the game's own listing and it is the clearest case. It is also a good structural fit for no-signal play, because Live Sim hands you individual possessions — take the shot or move it on, defend alone or call for help, play safe or take the risk — so a session can be as short as one decision.

**162-0 Baseball Draft & GM Team has no online multiplayer and uses no live results** — every record it produces is a projection from the roster you drafted. That tells you the game is not built on other players or on live data, which is a genuine architectural hint. It is not, by itself, the same claim as offline support, and we are not going to present it as one.

**For the rest of the sports catalogue, check the current Google Play listing or run the airplane-mode test above.** Listings change as apps are updated, and a claim in an article written months earlier is worth less than the store page you are looking at now.

That distinction matters more than it might seem. Plenty of guides in this genre assert offline support across a whole list because it sounds helpful. If the assertion is wrong you find out somewhere with no signal, which is precisely the worst place for it.

## The genre fit, using hockey as the example

[84-0 Hockey Draft & GM Manager](/apps/hockey-draft-gm-manager/) is a clean illustration of why this genre suits interrupted time, regardless of what any individual device does on a plane.

A run consists of filling six slots — centre, both wings, two defence positions and a goaltender — plus a coach, and then receiving a projected 84-game record for the lineup you assembled. That is a complete, self-contained session: a problem, a set of decisions, and a verdict. Limited Draft gives you one pass with zero refreshes, which makes a session shorter still, while Unlimited Draft lets you keep comparing until the combination fits.

Behind that sits Franchise GM Mode for organising forwards, defenders and goaltending across multiple seasons, along with quizzes, timed challenges, roster-building tasks and side-by-side player comparisons — all of which are the same shape: small, closed, resumable. The [hockey draft and GM guide](/blog/hockey-draft-gm-guide/) covers the drafting itself, and [line combinations](/blog/hockey-line-combinations-explained/) covers why the six slots are harder than they look.

### What the simulation is doing while you are offline

The projected record is produced by the game's own internal rules acting on players it generated. It is not fetching anything, not comparing you to anyone, and not describing or forecasting any real league, team or athlete. It is a score on a roster puzzle, which is exactly why it does not need a network to produce.

## A short checklist before you fly

- Install and open every game you plan to use **while you still have signal**.
- Run the airplane-mode cold-start test on each one.
- Finish one full session offline, not just the menu.
- Check whether progress survives a close and reopen.
- Assume ads will not appear and that anything labelled online will be unavailable.
- If a save matters, find out where it lives before you rely on it.

Five minutes at the gate beats an hour of a loading screen.

## Where to read next

If time rather than signal is your constraint, [manager games for short sessions](/blog/best-sports-manager-games-for-short-sessions/) covers what makes a management game survive a five-minute window. If you are deciding what kind of sports game you want in the first place, [career mode versus franchise mode](/blog/career-mode-vs-franchise-mode/) sets out the two shapes and who each one suits.

Everything the studio makes in this genre is listed under [sports GM](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: Thai Tones Explained: Five Tones, Four Marks, and Why the Marks Are Not the Answer
metaTitle: Thai Tones Explained: The Five Tones and the Rules
secondaryKeywords: how many tones does thai have

sources.p: Office of the Royal Society, Thailand
U.S. Department of State, Foreign Service Institute

body:
Thai has five tones and four tone marks. That mismatch is not an oversight in the writing system — it is the writing system, and once you understand why the arithmetic does not work, the whole thing becomes learnable rather than arbitrary.

The short version: a Thai tone mark is one input among four. The other three are the consonant you started with, the vowel you used, and how the syllable ends. Beginners who try to learn the four marks and stop are learning a quarter of a rule.

## The five tones

Standard Thai distinguishes **mid**, **low**, **falling**, **high** and **rising**. These are contrastive: change only the tone and you have a different word.

The cleanest demonstration in the language uses four words that every Thai romanisation writes identically as *mai*:

| Thai | Tone | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ไม่ | falling | not |
| ไม้ | high | wood |
| ใหม่ | low | new |
| ไหม | rising | silk; also a question particle |

Four different words. One romanisation. This is why a phrasebook cannot teach you Thai pronunciation, and it is why the script is worth the effort — the spelling of each of those four tells a reader exactly which tone it takes.

A second classic set, this time with a long vowel:

| Thai | Tone | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| เสือ | rising | tiger |
| เสื่อ | low | mat |
| เสื้อ | falling | shirt, clothing |

Same consonant, same vowel, three tones, three unrelated meanings.

## The four inputs

Here is the actual rule, in the order you apply it.

### 1. The class of the initial consonant

Every Thai consonant letter belongs to one of three **tone classes**: mid, high or low. The class is not something you can see from the shape of the letter; it is a property you learn along with the sound.

The inventory splits unevenly:

- **Mid class — 9 letters:** ก จ ฎ ฏ ด ต บ ป อ
- **High class — 11 letters:** ข ฃ ฉ ฐ ถ ผ ฝ ศ ษ ส ห
- **Low class — the remaining 24**

Nine plus eleven is twenty, and the consonant inventory is usually counted at 44, which leaves 24 in the low class. That is why "low class" is the default you can assume when you have not learned a letter's class yet — it is more than half the alphabet.

The mid and high sets are small enough to learn as lists, and doing that early is the highest-value memorisation in the whole script. Everything else is low.

This is also the answer to the question every beginner asks about Thai: why 44 consonant letters for far fewer distinct sounds? Because several letters share a pronunciation and differ only in class, and class changes the tone of the syllable. The apparent redundancy is where a large part of the tone information lives.

### 2. Whether the syllable is live or dead

Thai grammar calls these คำเป็น (live) and คำตาย (dead).

- A **live** syllable ends in a long vowel, or in a nasal or glide sound — the finals written with letters for *m*, *n*, *ng*, *w* and *y*.
- A **dead** syllable ends in a stop — the finals pronounced *p*, *t* or *k* — or in a short vowel with nothing after it.

The test is about how the syllable stops, not about which letters are visible, which is why it has to be learned alongside the vowel system rather than as a separate topic.

### 3. Vowel length

Long or short. This only becomes decisive in one branch of the rules, but it is a genuine distinction in Thai vowels generally, and mishearing it is a common source of beginner errors that have nothing to do with tone.

### 4. The tone mark, if there is one

There are four, and they are written above the initial consonant:

| Mark | Thai name |
| --- | --- |
| ก่ | ไม้เอก (mai ek) |
| ก้ | ไม้โท (mai tho) |
| ก๊ | ไม้ตรี (mai tri) |
| ก๋ | ไม้จัตวา (mai chattawa) |

The ก above is a placeholder consonant so the marks have something to sit on — they never appear alone.

Note the names. They are ordinal: first mark, second mark, third mark, fourth mark. They are not named after tones, because they do not correspond to tones.

## The rules, in two tables

Most Thai words carry no tone mark at all, so start with those.

### Unmarked syllables

| Initial class | Live syllable | Dead syllable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mid | mid tone | low tone |
| High | rising tone | low tone |
| Low | mid tone | short vowel: high tone · long vowel: falling tone |

That single table covers the majority of Thai words you will read. It is worth over-learning.

### Marked syllables

| Initial class | ไม้เอก | ไม้โท | ไม้ตรี | ไม้จัตวา |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mid | low | falling | high | rising |
| High | low | falling | — | — |
| Low | falling | high | — | — |

Look at the first column. **ไม้เอก produces a low tone after a mid or high consonant and a falling tone after a low one.** The same mark, two different tones, decided by a letter written before it. That is the whole reason four marks can serve five tones, and it is the fact that makes "just learn the tone marks" bad advice.

The dashes are also informative: mid-class initials are the only ones that take all four marks. ไม้ตรี and ไม้จัตวา are essentially restricted to mid-class syllables in native Thai vocabulary, which is another reason the nine mid-class letters repay early attention.

## The two workarounds the script built in

Once you see the tables, an obvious gap appears. The low class has 24 letters, and several of its sounds have no high-class counterpart at all — there is no high-class letter for *m*, *n*, *ng*, *l*, *w* or *y*. So how do you write those sounds with a rising tone, which only high-class initials produce unmarked?

Thai solves this with two silent leading consonants.

**Leading ห (ho nam).** Put ห in front of one of those sonorant letters and the pair behaves as a high-class initial. The ห is not pronounced. This is why หมา ("dog") has a rising tone while มา ("to come") has a mid tone — same consonant, same vowel, one silent letter, two words.

Put that beside ม้า ("horse"), which is the same syllable with ไม้โท on a low-class initial, and you get a genuinely useful trio:

| Thai | Tone | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| มา | mid | to come |
| หมา | rising | dog |
| ม้า | high | horse |

**Leading อ (o nam).** A rarer version using อ before ย, which in modern Thai affects a very small closed set of extremely common words: อย่า, อยู่, อย่าง and อยาก. All four take a low tone. Because the set is closed, most courses teach these as four vocabulary items rather than as a rule, which is the sensible approach.

One more structural note: in a genuine consonant cluster, the class of the **first** consonant is what drives the tone. So ปลา ("fish") takes its tone from ป, a mid-class letter, and comes out mid.

## Why this is better news than it sounds

Compare this with how tone works elsewhere. In Cantonese, tone is stored with each word individually and there is nothing in the writing that tells you what it is — which is why [Cantonese tones](/blog/learn-cantonese-beginners-guide/) have to be learned at first exposure, one word at a time, forever.

Thai gives you a machine instead. Once the rules are automatic, you can look at a Thai word you have never encountered and derive its tone from the spelling. That is an enormous long-term advantage, and it converts the script from an obstacle into a tool.

The trade is that the machine takes a few weeks to install. The rules involve holding four things in mind at once, and until they become automatic they feel like arithmetic in the middle of a conversation. This is the stage where learners are most tempted to fall back on romanisation, and it is exactly the wrong moment to do it — the payoff arrives just past the point where the work feels pointless.

## A sequence that works

**Learn each consonant with its class, from the first exposure.** Treat the class as part of the letter, the way you would learn a German noun with its gender. Adding class information to letters you already half-know is much slower than learning them together.

**Memorise the mid and high sets as lists.** Twenty letters. Everything else is low by elimination, and elimination is fast.

**Learn live versus dead alongside the vowels.** The distinction is about syllable endings, so it belongs with vowel and final study rather than in a separate "tones" chapter.

**Derive tones for words you already know by ear.** This is the step most courses skip. Take vocabulary you can already say correctly, work out the tone from the spelling, and check your derivation against what you know. You are verifying the machine on known inputs before trusting it on unknown ones.

**Then read continuous text out loud, badly.** Thai is written without spaces between words, so word boundaries are a separate reading skill, and tone derivation only becomes useful once you can find where a syllable starts.

[Regal - Learn Thai Language](/apps/learn-thai/) is organised around that staging: alphabet practice separates consonants, vowels, tone marks and syllables rather than presenting a full chart on day one, and pronunciation practice handles tones and sounds on their own before longer sentences arrive. Speaking practice asks you to produce the material rather than only recognise it, and dictation is unusually good practice for tone specifically, because writing a word forces you to commit to a spelling, and committing to a spelling means committing to a tone.

Two honest limits. Recognising a tone and producing one are different skills that improve at different rates, and no app can hear you the way a fluent speaker can. And this article describes **Standard Thai**, the variety of education and broadcasting; Northern, Northeastern and Southern varieties have their own tone systems, and what you hear in a market in Chiang Mai or Udon Thani may not match the rules above.

## What to do next

If the script itself is still new, start there rather than here — our guide to [learning the Thai script](/blog/learn-thai-script-beginners-guide/) covers the alphabet, the vowels that wrap around the consonant, and why there are no spaces between words. The tone rules only become usable once the letters are legible, and trying to do both at once is the most common way to stall.

And if you are still choosing a language, the rest of our [language learning apps](/apps/category/language-learning/) include options with no tone system at all.

title: Understanding Probability in Sports Simulations
metaTitle: Sports Simulation Probability, Explained
secondaryKeywords: why does the better team lose

sources.p: National Institute of Standards and Technology

body:
You built the better roster and the record came back worse. This is the most common complaint in the genre and the one with the least interesting answer: that is what probability does. The model was not broken, and you were not cheated.

What is worth your time is knowing how much of a result is your decision and how much is the draw — because until you can separate those, every run teaches you something and half of what it teaches you is wrong.

## A probability is a claim about a distribution

When a model says a team wins 65 percent of the time, it is describing the shape of many possible seasons, not the content of the next one. The 35 percent is not an error term. It is part of the statement.

This trips people up because the interface shows one number and one outcome, so the outcome feels like a verdict on the number. It is not. It is one draw from a distribution the interface never shows you.

The practical version: **a single result cannot confirm or refute a strategy.** It can only be consistent or inconsistent with one, and even a fairly bad strategy produces good runs regularly.

## Season length is doing more work than roster quality

Here is the arithmetic that explains why unbeaten seasons are the hardest thing in the genre. Assume — and this is a deliberate simplification — that a team has a constant probability *p* of winning each game and that games are independent of one another. The chance of winning all *n* games is then *p* raised to the power of *n*.

At **p = 0.9**:

| Season length | Chance of a perfect record | Roughly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 20 games | 0.9²⁰ ≈ 0.1216 | about 12 in 100 |
| 82 games | 0.9⁸² ≈ 0.000177 | about 18 in 100,000 |
| 162 games | 0.9¹⁶² ≈ 0.000000039 | about 1 in 26 million |

Same team. Same quality. The only thing that changed is how many chances the season gave it to lose.

And the sensitivity to *p* is just as sharp. At 162 games, raising the per-game chance from 0.9 to **0.95** takes the perfect-season probability from roughly 1 in 26 million to roughly **1 in 4,000** — still rare, but six thousand times less rare. Small edges compound; so do small vulnerabilities.

Two honest caveats about this calculation. It assumes every game is independent and every opponent identical, which is not how any real sport works and not how a well-built simulator works either. And no actual engine computes a season this way. It is a toy model, and its purpose is to show the *shape* of the relationship between length and rarity, which holds regardless of how much more sophisticated the real model is.

This is also why [162-0 Baseball Draft & GM Team](/apps/baseball-draft-gm-team/) states outright that the perfect 162-0 season is designed to be rare, while [20-0 Football Draft & GM Mode](/apps/football-draft-gm-mode/) can build its whole identity around a 20-game unbeaten run. The two games are asking for very different amounts of luck.

## How wide is "normal"?

Rarity of perfection is one question. The spread of ordinary results is a more useful one.

If a team wins each of *n* games with probability *p*, and the games are independent, the number of wins follows a binomial distribution. Its mean is *n × p* and its standard deviation is the square root of *n × p × (1 − p)*.

For a **162-game** season at **p = 0.6**:

- Mean wins: 162 × 0.6 = **97.2**
- Standard deviation: √(162 × 0.6 × 0.4) = √38.88 ≈ **6.2 wins**

So a team whose true quality is "wins 60 percent of the time" will routinely post anywhere from about 91 to about 103 wins, and will sometimes land outside that. Those look like meaningfully different seasons. They are the same team.

Now the same team over **20 games**:

- Mean wins: 20 × 0.6 = **12**
- Standard deviation: √(20 × 0.6 × 0.4) = √4.8 ≈ **2.2 wins**

Two and a bit wins of standard deviation on a 20-game season is enormous *relative to the season*. Divide the standard deviation by the number of games and you get the spread as a win rate: **6.2 ÷ 162 ≈ 3.8 percentage points** over a long season, versus **2.2 ÷ 20 ≈ 11 percentage points** over a short one.

That single comparison explains a lot about sport and about sims. Long seasons do not make any individual season predictable — the absolute spread actually grows. What they do is make the *rate* more reliable, which is why long competitions sort teams better than short ones and why a short format is a much noisier test of anything.

## What running it again actually buys you

The law of large numbers says the observed average converges toward the true value as the number of trials increases. It does not say results even out, and it makes no promise about any particular run — the widespread belief that a bad streak makes a good one more likely is the exact opposite of what independence means.

For a simulation player, this cashes out as a procedure rather than a philosophy:

1. **Change one thing.** If you alter your drafting approach, your coach and your positional priorities at once, no number of runs will tell you which mattered.
2. **Run both versions repeatedly under the same format.** The format is part of the model; comparing across formats compares two different things.
