body:
This article will not tell you what your ketone reading means. That is deliberate, and it is the most useful thing about it.

What it will do is explain what ketones are, what each type of test physically measures, and why the published sources that describe those tests are careful not to hand out interpretation. Once you understand why they decline, the number in front of you becomes easier to use correctly — as a record, not a verdict.

> This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not written or reviewed by a clinician. Nothing here interprets a reading, diagnoses a condition, or recommends a course of action. If you have symptoms of ketoacidosis, MedlinePlus advises seeking immediate medical help. If you are considering a low-carbohydrate diet, talk to a doctor or registered dietitian first — especially if you have diabetes or take prescribed medication.

## What ketones are

MedlinePlus puts it plainly: ketones are acids your body makes when it breaks down fat for energy.

Normally the cells in your body run on blood glucose, most of which comes from carbohydrate in food. When cells cannot get enough glucose, the body breaks down fat instead, and that process produces ketones. If fat is broken down too fast, ketones can build up in blood and urine, and high ketone levels make blood too acidic — a serious condition called **ketoacidosis**.

Two details in that description do real work later, so it is worth pausing on them.

**The body makes three types of ketone.** MedlinePlus lists beta-hydroxybutyric acid and acetoacetate among the other names for what these tests measure. Different test methods target different molecules, which is why the results are not interchangeable.

**Producing ketones and having ketoacidosis are different states.** Ketones appear whenever fat is being broken down for fuel. Ketoacidosis is what happens when they accumulate to the point of acidifying blood. Confusing the two in either direction is the origin of most bad information on this topic.

## Ketosis and ketoacidosis are not the same thing

This distinction matters enough that it deserves the source's own framing rather than a paraphrase.

MedlinePlus states that people who eat a low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet will have blood ketone levels that are higher but are not high enough to be ketoacidosis, and calls this condition ketosis. It explains that ketosis does not make blood too acidic because the body is able to use the ketones, so they do not build up.

And then it adds the sentence that most low-carb writing leaves out: **it is possible to develop ketoacidosis on a keto diet**, which is why it says to talk with your provider about whether such a diet is safe for you.

**Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)** is the most common form. MedlinePlus describes it as a medical emergency that often develops quickly and can lead to coma and be life-threatening. It affects people with diabetes, most commonly type 1, and is less common with type 2. Ketoacidosis can also arise without diabetes — MedlinePlus lists eating disorders and starvation, long-lasting vomiting or diarrhoea, and alcohol use disorder among the conditions that put a person at risk.

Symptoms of ketoacidosis listed by MedlinePlus include extreme hunger or thirst, urinating much more than usual, dehydration, headache, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, trouble breathing, fatigue, dry skin and mouth, breath with a fruity smell, and muscle stiffness or aches. Untreated, symptoms can become severe quickly, and the guidance is unambiguous: seek immediate medical help.

This article does not, and cannot, help you tell which situation you are in. That is the entire reason the previous paragraph ends the way it does.

## The three ways people measure ketones at home

Each method measures something different, which is the technical reason readings disagree.

**Blood.** A finger-prick sample on a test strip read by a meter. MedlinePlus notes that at-home meters are available that check both glucose and ketones, and that a health care provider can advise which testing approach is right for a given person. Blood meters are regulated as in vitro diagnostic devices, and FDA maintains public material on blood glucose monitoring devices; the instructions that come with a device are part of how it is meant to be used, not an optional extra.

**Urine.** Dip strips, available without a prescription in most pharmacies. MedlinePlus lists the "nitroprusside test" among the other names associated with ketone testing, and reports that results may come back as a specific number or as a **small**, **moderate** or **large** amount. Urine reflects what has been excreted over a period rather than what is circulating right now, so hydration and timing both move the result.

**Breath.** Handheld devices used by some people who track low-carb eating. This is the method with the least public federal consumer guidance behind it, which is itself worth knowing when you compare a breath figure with a blood one.

Because these three approaches target different molecules through different chemistry, a disagreement between them is a normal property of the methods, not a malfunction in any of them.

## What the published sources deliberately will not tell you

Here is the thing you will notice if you go and read the primary sources for yourself: **they do not publish a target range for a person eating low-carb.**

MedlinePlus's material on urine ketone testing says normal results can vary depending on your diet, activity level and other factors, and that because high ketone levels can cause serious health problems, you should talk with your provider about what is normal for you and what your results mean.

That is not an oversight or vagueness. It reflects three things at once: the reading depends on method and timing, the meaningful interpretation depends on your health status and medication, and the same number can be unremarkable in one person and important in another.

You will find "optimal ketosis" ranges quoted confidently across the low-carb internet. Those figures do not come from a US federal health authority, and this article is not going to repeat them as though they did. If you want to know what a specific reading means for you, the person to ask is the one who can see the rest of your chart.

### A normal reading does not clear you

The most important single fact in the MedlinePlus material is easy to skim past. A normal or negative test result usually means your body is not making too many ketones — **but a normal test result does not always rule out DKA**, because the body makes three types of ketone, and in the early stages of DKA only one type may be high, and lab tests often do not measure that type.

That is the sentence that ends any argument about using a home ketone reading as a safety check. It cannot do that job, and the source says so.

## Why your numbers move around

If you do log readings, expect variability, and expect most of it to be uninteresting.

- **Method.** Blood, urine and breath measure different molecules. Comparing across methods is comparing different quantities.
- **Timing.** A morning reading and an evening reading describe different points in a day, and urine in particular lags.
- **Hydration.** Concentration affects a urine strip in ways that have nothing to do with metabolism.
- **Strips and storage.** Test strips have expiry dates and storage conditions, and the manufacturer's instructions exist for a reason.
- **What you did that day.** MedlinePlus explicitly notes that normal results vary with diet and activity.

The correct response to a surprising single reading is generally to note it and to look at the pattern, not to change your eating in response to one data point.

## So what is logging them actually for?

There is a genuine use, and it is narrower than the way ketone tracking is usually sold.

A dated series of readings, recorded consistently and alongside what you ate and when, is **a record you can hand to a clinician**. That is a far more useful thing to bring to an appointment than a recollection. It also lets you notice your own patterns without pretending the numbers grade you.

What it is not: a scoreboard, a measure of effort, evidence that a diet is "working", or a substitute for medical assessment. A higher number is not a better number. There is no achievement encoded in it.

[Keto Diet Tracker: Low Carb](/apps/keto-diet-tracker/) is built with that framing. It has a place to record blood, urine strip and breath meter readings you have taken yourself, including GKI, and it keeps them next to the rest of the day — the food log with net carbs worked out for you, an intermittent fasting timer, water, and sodium, potassium and magnesium. Charts, body measurements, photo logs and weekly and monthly summaries turn the entries into a history you can look back over.

The app stores what you enter. It does not measure anything itself, and it does not interpret a reading. It is free on Google Play, supported by ads, with no in-app purchases; no account is required and your logs stay on your device rather than on our servers, which also means an uninstall takes them with it.

If the surrounding numbers are what you are trying to get straight, [keto macros explained](/blog/keto-macros-explained/) covers the percentage-to-gram arithmetic, [net carbs explained](/blog/net-carbs-explained-keto-tracking/) covers the subtraction that no regulator defines, and [intermittent fasting windows](/blog/intermittent-fasting-windows-explained/) covers the timer that usually sits next to all of this. The rest of the [health and nutrition category](/apps/category/health-nutrition/) covers the adjacent tools.

## The short version

Ketones are acids produced when the body breaks down fat for energy, and there are three of them. Blood, urine and breath tests measure different ones, which is why they disagree.

Nutritional ketosis and ketoacidosis are different states, and diabetic ketoacidosis is a fast-moving medical emergency rather than a stronger version of a diet result. A normal home reading cannot rule it out, because in early DKA the raised ketone type is often the one not being measured.

No US federal health authority publishes a target ketone level for someone eating low-carb, and the reason is that the meaningful interpretation depends on the person rather than the number. Log the readings if they are useful to you. Take the interpretation to someone qualified to give it.

title: What Makes a Good Draft Board
metaTitle: How to Build a Draft Board That Works
primaryKeyword: how to build a draft board
body:
Most people arrive at a draft with a ranked list and call it a board. Then the draft starts, the first four names disappear in ninety seconds, and the list stops answering any question they actually have.

A ranking tells you who is best. A board tells you what to do with the pick in front of you. Those are not the same document, and only one of them survives contact with a live draft.

## The three questions a board has to answer instantly

Everything in board construction serves this. At any moment, without scrolling and without thinking, you should be able to see:

1. **Who is left in the tier I care about**, at each position.
2. **How far the drop is** if that tier empties before my next pick.
3. **Which of my slots is still unfilled**, and how late I can afford to leave it.

If your board cannot answer those three in a glance, it is a reference document, not a decision tool. Fix that before you worry about anything else.

## Build it in five passes

### Pass one: settle the roster structure before you look at a single player

Write down the slots you have to fill and the number of picks you get. The gap between those two numbers is your slack, and it determines how much risk the whole plan can carry.

Say a format gives you fifteen picks and requires twelve filled positions. Three picks are discretionary — you can use them on depth, on upside, or on covering a position twice. Now say the same format requires fourteen filled positions. One pick of slack changes the draft from a strategy exercise into a checklist, and knowing that in advance stops you spending pick four on a luxury you cannot afford.

Football is where this bites hardest, because a team sheet carries a lot of distinct roles and every one of them needs an owner. A plan sized for a handful of slots will not cover it.

### Pass two: rank within positions, never across them

Comparing a lineman's rating to a receiver's rating is comparing two different scales that happen to share an axis. The ratings mean different things because the jobs are different, and the pools have different depths.

So: one column per position, sorted, and no cross-position ranking at this stage. You will get to sequencing in pass four, and you will do it properly there.

### Pass three: cut the tiers at the cliffs

Read down each column and look for where the numbers stop declining gently and fall off. That break is a tier boundary. Everything above it is a band you would be roughly equally content with; everything below is a meaningful downgrade.

The output is deliberately lumpy. A position might have two players in tier one and fifteen in tier three. That shape *is* the analysis:

- **A wide tier** means you can wait. Someone from it will still be there.
- **A narrow tier above a big cliff** means you cannot. If you want anyone from it, this is the pick.
- **A position with no cliffs at all** — a smooth gradient from top to bottom — is one you should almost never spend an early pick on, because the cost of waiting is close to zero.

Finding cliffs is the entire reason preparation beats improvisation. During the draft you are under time pressure and you will not see them.

### Pass four: sequence across positions using scarcity, not preference

Now you compare columns, and the comparison is not "who is better" — it is "which tier will not be there when I come back".

Lay your tiers side by side and ask, for each position: *how many picks until this tier is empty?* You will not know precisely, and you do not need to. You need the ordering. Positions whose top tier is two names deep get taken early. Positions whose useful tier runs fifteen deep get taken from the leftovers.

The uncomfortable implication is that this sometimes tells you to draft a worse player earlier. That is correct, and it is the single most reliable edge in drafting.

### Pass five: write down what you will not do

A short list of pre-commitments, made while calm:

- Positions you will not take before a given round.
- The maximum number of players you will hold at any one position.
- Any player you have decided is not for you, with the reason next to their name.

The reason matters more than the rule. During the draft you will want to break it, and the only defensible ground for breaking it is that the reason no longer applies.

## Running the board while the draft is moving

### Cross off, do not re-rank

When a player goes, strike them. Do not reorder anything. A board that is being continuously rewritten mid-draft is a board you have stopped trusting, and the rewriting eats exactly the seconds you needed for the decision.

### Check the shape every few picks, not every pick

The useful periodic question is not "who is the best available" but "which of my tiers is closest to emptying". That question takes three seconds and it is the one that prevents the classic disaster — arriving at your last four picks with two positions that have nothing left in them at all.

### Deviate only against new information

You will feel the pull to abandon the board at some point in every draft. Apply one test: *can I state in a single sentence what changed?*

Legitimate sentences: "Four managers took that position in a row and the tier is gone." "The cap means I can no longer afford anyone in tier two." "The position I planned to fill last now has fewer players left than I have picks."

Illegitimate sentence: "This one looks good."

### Keep a two-deep view of the danger positions

For any position where a single unfilled slot would sink the roster, know your fallback *before* you need it. Not the best remaining player — the one you would actually accept. Having that name in mind converts a panic pick into a shrug.

## What different rule sets demand from a board

The board-building method does not change across formats. What changes is how finished it has to be when the draft opens.

[20-0 Football Draft & GM Mode](/apps/football-draft-gm-mode/) is a good place to feel that difference, because its formats sit at opposite ends of the spectrum:

- **Unlimited Draft** lets you keep comparing options. Here a board is a convenience — you can do a lot of the thinking live, and this is the format to learn a pool in.
- **Limited Draft** removes refreshes entirely, so every pick has to count. This is where preparation is the whole game. Anything you did not tier in advance, you are guessing at.
- **Salary Cap Draft** adds a price to every name, which means your board needs a second column and your tiers need re-reading in cost terms. A tier-two player at a low price and a tier-one player at a high one are not comparable on quality alone.
- **Playoff Mode** puts the finished roster under pressure, which tends to punish the slot you left thin.

Beyond the drafts themselves the game includes Franchise Mode and GM Mode for the longer organisational decisions, VS Computer, Battle and Tournament for playing a roster against an opponent, a Daily Challenge, and Gridiron IQ tests of how well you read a team sheet. The lineup builder is where the board turns into an actual roster, position by position.

When the season simulator returns a record, treat it as a score for the roster you built rather than a forecast of anything. It is a model evaluating your construction, and reading it as a prediction about the real sport is a category error.

## Five ways boards fail

1. **It is a single list.** One column of names cannot express scarcity, and scarcity is what you are drafting against.
2. **The tiers are cosmetic.** Even bands of five, drawn to look tidy, contain no information at all.
3. **It ignores the format.** A board built for unlimited comparison is not a board for a no-refresh draft.
4. **It has no fallbacks.** Every position needs a name you would settle for, written down while you are calm.
5. **It gets abandoned at pick three.** Usually because it was never checked against the roster structure, so it started giving advice that made no sense.

## The board is also a record

Keep it after the draft. When the season result comes back, the board tells you what you knew at each pick, which is the only way to separate a bad decision from a bad outcome.

Most people improve at drafting by remembering results. Results are noisy. The board is the thing that lets you audit the reasoning instead, and reasoning is the part you can actually change.

## Related reading

The concepts a board encodes — replacement value, tiers, runs — are covered in [how fantasy draft strategy works](/blog/how-fantasy-draft-strategy-works/). If your format prices players instead of ordering them, [salary cap basics](/blog/salary-cap-basics-for-gm-games/) explains what to add to the board, and [snake draft versus auction draft](/blog/snake-draft-vs-auction-draft/) covers how the two allocation systems differ. For the football game specifically, the [football draft simulator guide](/blog/football-draft-gm-guide/) walks through a full run.

Other drafting and management titles are in the [sports GM category](/apps/category/sports-gm/).

title: What Makes a Roguelike? The Definition, the Argument, and a Test That Settles It
metaTitle: What Is a Roguelike? The Definition Explained
body:
Ask what a roguelike is and you will get two answers that both sound authoritative and contradict each other. One describes a turn-based dungeon crawler with a grid and a text display. The other describes a real-time action game with automatic weapons and a level-up screen.

Neither person is wrong. The word is doing two jobs — naming a specific game from 1980 and naming everything descended from it — and almost every argument about the term is really an argument about which job it is doing at that moment.

## The game the word points at

**Rogue** was written around 1980 by Michael Toy and Glenn Wichman, with Ken Arnold later contributing the display work, and it spread through university Unix systems. It presented a dungeon drawn in text characters, generated fresh each time you played, explored one turn at a time. Items were unidentified until you used them. And when your character died, that was the end — no reloading, no saved state to return to.

Those four properties were not conceived as a genre manifesto. They were sensible answers to the constraints of the machine and the sensibilities of the people writing it. Random generation meant the authors did not have to hand-design content and could not spoil their own game. Permadeath meant the save file could not be abused, which on a shared timesharing system was a practical concern as much as an artistic one.

What nobody anticipated is that the combination would turn out to be one of the most durable structures in game design, and that it would still be generating new commercial genres four decades later.

## Why the definition became a fight

Through the 1980s and 1990s a family of games grew directly out of Rogue — **NetHack** from 1987, and later Angband, ADOM and their descendants — each vastly more complex than the original and each recognisably the same kind of thing.

The label itself came later than the games. It settled during the early 1990s out of Usenet discussions among players trying to name what they were all playing, and the term stuck largely for lack of a better one rather than because anyone was pleased with it.

That is the origin of the problem. A name chosen by committee, retroactively, for a family defined by resemblance to one specific game, was never going to hold up when the family got large.

By the mid-2000s, developers were building games that clearly inherited the structure while discarding the surface — real-time instead of turn-based, graphical instead of text, and often much shorter. Traditional players objected that these were not roguelikes. Action players objected that the objection was pedantry. In 2008 a group of developers met in Berlin and tried to write it down.

## The Berlin Interpretation, in full

The result lists **nine high-value factors** and **six low-value factors**. The high-value ones carry more weight; the low-value ones are common to canonical roguelikes but not decisive.

| High-value factors | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Random environment generation | The world is generated per run, explicitly to increase replayability |
| Permadeath | Death ends the character; you start a new run rather than reload |
| Turn-based | Each action takes one turn, with no time pressure on the decision |
| Grid-based | The world is a grid of tiles, and everything occupies one |
| Non-modal | Every action happens in the same world state, with no separate combat screen |
| Complexity | Enough interacting systems that a problem has multiple valid solutions |
| Resource management | Limited supplies force you to keep choosing what to use and when |
| Hack'n'slash | Killing large numbers of enemies is a core activity |
| Exploration and discovery | Unidentified items and unknown layouts require exploring, not just executing |

| Low-value factors | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Single player character | One avatar, and the world does not continue without them |
| Monsters are similar to players | Enemies obey broadly the same rules you do |
| Tactical challenge | Early deaths are expected; the game must be learned |
| ASCII display | The traditional text grid |
| Dungeons | Rooms and corridors rather than open terrain |
| Numbers | Character statistics shown to the player openly |

### What the list is actually for

The most important thing about the Berlin Interpretation is stated by its own authors and ignored by almost everyone who cites it: it is a **scale, not a border**. A game is measured by how many factors it exhibits and how strongly, producing a judgement about how roguelike it is rather than a verdict on whether it is one.

Read that way, most of the arguing evaporates. A real-time action game with procedural levels and permadeath scores on some factors and not others. That is a description, not a rejection.

Read the other way — as a checklist you must pass — the definition immediately excludes most of the games that made the word popular, which is a good sign you are using it wrong.

It is also worth noticing what the list quietly reveals. Six of the nine high-value factors describe *decision quality*: complexity, resource management, exploration, non-modality, turn-based play, tactical challenge from the low-value list. Only two describe structure. The definition is mostly an argument that a roguelike is a game about making informed choices with incomplete information, and the dungeon is a delivery mechanism.

## Roguelike, roguelite, and what a loss costs

The modern split is cleaner than the historical argument, because it hangs on a single question: **when you lose, does anything survive?**

A strict roguelike sends you back to exactly where you started. Your knowledge improves; nothing else does. The next run is materially identical in difficulty to the last one, and every gain is in your head.

A **roguelite** keeps something. Currency banked between runs, characters unlocked, upgrades that persist, new items added to the pool for future attempts. Losing still ends the run, but it leaves a deposit. The term spread through developers describing their own work rather than through critics — Rogue Legacy notably billed itself as a genealogical rogue-lite — and it caught on because it named something players could feel.

Some writers proposed less loaded alternatives, "procedural death labyrinth" among them, on the reasonable grounds that naming an entire genre after one 1980 game is odd. None of them stuck. Roguelike and roguelite won, and the language is not going to be tidied up now.

The trade between them is real and worth understanding as a player:

- **Strict** keeps every run honest. Nothing between you and the game except what you have learned. It also means a bad losing streak feels like pure loss.
- **Lite** guarantees forward motion, which makes a losing run tolerable and keeps people playing. It also risks turning difficulty into a waiting game, where the answer to a wall is not "learn it" but "grind past it."

Neither is better. But the second one has a failure mode worth watching for, because a game where persistence solves everything is not really asking you to make decisions any more.

## The modern family tree

The structure has been grafted onto almost every genre, and it is more useful to think in branches than in a single label.

**Traditional roguelikes.** Turn-based, grid-based, deeply systemic. NetHack and its descendants, plus modern entries in the same tradition. The Berlin Interpretation describes these precisely, because they are what it was written about.

**Action roguelikes.** Real-time combat, procedural stages, permadeath, usually a meta-progression layer. The Binding of Isaac, released in 2011 by Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl, is the clearest bridge — an action game whose item interactions produce the combinatorial strangeness of a traditional roguelike. Spelunky, from Derek Yu, did something similar with a platformer.

**Run-based strategy.** FTL: Faster Than Light, released by Subset Games in 2012, applied the structure to a ship management game where the interesting decisions are logistical rather than tactical.

**Deck-builders.** Cards as the upgrade pool. Each run assembles a deck out of what you were offered, and the deck is the build.

**Horde survival.** The newest large branch, which arrived in the early 2020s: dozens or hundreds of enemies, weapons that fire automatically, level-ups delivered mid-fight as a choice between upgrades, and a run measured in minutes rather than hours. It strips the structure back to its minimum — random offers, exclusive choices, one life — and removes almost everything else.

## A test that beats the argument

If you want to know whether a given game has the structure that makes any of this worth caring about, ignore the store page and ask three questions.

**1. Do runs differ in a way that changes your decisions?** Not "is the layout different" — different scenery is cosmetic. The test is whether what you were offered this run makes you play differently from last run. If the answer is no, the randomness is decoration.

**2. Does losing actually cost the run?** If you can retry from a checkpoint, the decisions you made before it were provisional, and provisional decisions do not carry weight. Permadeath is not there to punish you. It is there to make your choices mean something while you are making them.

**3. Do the choices exclude each other?** This is the one that matters most and the one most often missing. If you can eventually take every upgrade, you do not have a decision system, you have a delivery schedule. The genre's engine is the thing you had to turn down.

A game answering yes to all three has the structure, whatever it calls itself. A game answering no to the third has a randomised campaign, which can be perfectly good and is a different thing.

## Where a phone horde survival game lands

[Zombie Survival: Last Survivor](/apps/zombie-survival-last-survivor/) is on the horde survival branch, and it is a useful case for applying the test rather than the label.

What the game actually does: your weapons fire on their own while you move, experience collected during a stage levels you up in the middle of the fight, and each level hands you a choice between weapon boosts, damage increases, survival upgrades or a special ability. Those stack into a build over the run. Enemy types behave differently and bosses arrive with their own attack patterns, across stages of dark streets, infected zones and abandoned areas.

Against the three questions: the offers differ, so runs diverge; the build is assembled inside the run, so what you take is what you have; and taking one upgrade at a level-up means not taking the others at that level-up. That is the engine, intact, in a game with no grid, no turns and no text display. Against the Berlin Interpretation it would score poorly on half the high-value factors and strongly on the rest — which is exactly what a scale is for. [The build guide](/blog/zombie-survival-roguelike-guide/) goes into how to actually make those choices well.

For contrast, [Space Shooter - Galaxy Arcade](/apps/space-shooter-classic-arcade/) sits on the other side of the persistence question: rewards earned during a run go into weapons, unlocked upgrades, ship systems and bonuses you choose yourself, so the ship carries forward between attempts. Same shelf, opposite answer to "what does a loss leave behind." Both are in [Action & Arcade Games](/apps/category/action-arcade/), and both are free to download on Google Play with ads.

The games named in this article belong to their respective developers and publishers. Reign Creative LLC is an independent studio and has no connection to any of them.

## The short version

Roguelike names a 1980 dungeon crawler and everything that inherited its shape, and both meanings are in active use. The Berlin Interpretation is the best-known attempt to write the definition down, and it works properly only when you use it as a scale rather than a gate.

The distinction that actually matters to a player is not turn-based versus real-time. It is whether the run is self-contained, whether losing it costs something, and whether the choices inside it exclude each other. Get those three and you have the genre. Miss the third and you have a randomised campaign with a difficulty curve.

title: What Is Working Memory, and Can Training Actually Change It?
metaTitle: What Is Working Memory? And Can It Be Trained?

sources.p: Current Directions in Psychological Science, via PubMed Central (PMC2864034)
Perspectives on Psychological Science, via PubMed
Psychological Science in the Public Interest, via PubMed
National Institute on Aging, National Institutes of Health

body:
This is an article about working memory written by a company that sells a memory game, which is a reason to be sceptical of it. So here is the conclusion first: the evidence that training improves the trained task is decent, the evidence that it improves anything else is genuinely disputed among competent researchers, and we make no claims of the second kind about our app. The rest of this explains what working memory is and why that dispute exists.

## The thing you are using right now

Read this sentence, and by the time you reach the end of it you are still holding the beginning. That holding is working memory: the capacity to keep information in an accessible state while you actively do something with it.

Nelson Cowan puts the functional case plainly in his review of the topic — cognitive tasks can only be completed if there is sufficient ability to hold information as it is being processed. Multiplying 47 by 6 in your head requires holding a partial product while you compute the next one. Following an argument requires holding the premises while you evaluate the conclusion. When the holding fails, the task fails, regardless of whether you understood the method.

That makes working memory an obvious target for training, and it is why an entire commercial category exists around it. What follows is an honest account of what is known, what is disputed, and what we will not claim.

## How small the capacity actually is

The number most people have heard is seven. In a famous 1956 paper, described by Cowan as humorously complaining about being persecuted by an integer, George Miller reported that people can repeat back a list of no more than about seven randomly ordered meaningful items or chunks.

Later work produced smaller figures. Cowan argues that beneath the task-dependent surface there is a more constant underlying mechanism: a central memory store limited to roughly **3 to 5 meaningful items** in young adults. He notes that young adults recall only 3 or 4 longer verbal chunks.

The gap between the two figures is not a contradiction so much as a difference in what is being measured. Performance on a given task can be inflated by strategies — rehearsing, grouping, using long-term knowledge — layered on top of the core store. Strip those away and the underlying capacity looks smaller.

The practical reading of this is uncomfortable and useful: whatever you thought you could juggle, it is probably fewer than that.

## The unit is the chunk

The limit is not counted in letters, digits or words. It is counted in **chunks** — units that have become meaningful as wholes.

The sequence `1 4 9 2 1 7 7 6 2 0 0 1` is twelve digits, which is far past anyone's limit. Read as `1492 1776 2001` it is three chunks, which is comfortably inside it. The digits did not change. The chunking did.

This has two consequences worth carrying around:

**Expertise looks like capacity but is not.** A chess player who reconstructs a board position after a glance is not holding more than you can. They are holding fewer, larger units, because years of exposure turned configurations into single meaningful things. Their raw capacity is ordinary.

**Chunking is trainable in a way that raw capacity may not be.** Building the units is a knowledge process, and knowledge accumulates. This is the honest mechanism behind most impressive-looking memory feats, and it is domain-specific by construction — chunks built for chess do nothing for phone numbers.

## Near transfer, far transfer, and where the argument is

Two terms make the entire research literature legible.

**Near transfer** is improvement on the trained task and on tasks that closely resemble it. Practise a digit-span task and get better at digit span, or at a similar span task.

**Far transfer** is improvement on genuinely different abilities — reasoning, reading comprehension, arithmetic, intelligence test scores, performance at work or school.

Near transfer is comparatively well supported. Far transfer is the disputed territory, and it is also, not coincidentally, what marketing implicitly promises. "Train your brain" is a far-transfer claim wearing a near-transfer claim's clothes.

## What the meta-analyses found — including the one that disagrees

This section deliberately presents both sides, because the field genuinely contains both.

**Melby-Lervåg and Hulme, 2013, in *Developmental Psychology*.** A meta-analytic review of 23 studies with 30 group comparisons, spanning clinical samples and typically developing children and adults. The programs produced reliable short-term improvements in working memory skills. For verbal working memory those near-transfer effects were not sustained at follow-up; for visuospatial working memory limited evidence suggested they might be. On generalisation, the authors reported no convincing evidence of transfer to other skills — nonverbal and verbal ability, inhibitory processes in attention, word decoding, and arithmetic. Their conclusion was that the programs produce short-term, specific training effects that do not generalise.

**Melby-Lervåg, Redick and Hulme, 2016, in *Perspectives on Psychological Science*.** A much larger review: 87 publications with 145 experimental comparisons. Immediately after training there were reliable improvements on measures of intermediate transfer — verbal and visuospatial working memory. On far transfer measures (nonverbal ability, verbal ability, word decoding, reading comprehension, arithmetic) there was no convincing evidence of reliable improvement **when working memory training was compared with a treated control condition**. Two further findings from that paper matter. First, the degree of improvement on working memory measures was not related to the magnitude of far-transfer effects — which undercuts the proposed causal chain. Second, their publication bias analysis concluded there was no evidential value from the studies using treated controls.

**Au and colleagues, 2015, in *Psychonomic Bulletin & Review*.** This is the meta-analysis on the other side, and it should not be left out. Focusing specifically on n-back training and fluid intelligence outcomes, in healthy participants aged 18 to 50 with a control group, the authors included 20 studies and found **a small but significant positive effect of n-back training on improving fluid intelligence**. They concluded that short-term cognitive training on the order of weeks can produce beneficial effects on important cognitive functions as measured by laboratory tests. The paper attracted published commentary in the same journal the following year — itself a signal of how contested the result was.

**Simons and colleagues, 2016, in *Psychological Science in the Public Interest*.** Rather than adding another effect size, this review asks why the field disagrees. Its framing is striking: in 2014 an international group of more than 70 scientists published a consensus statement holding that brain games do not provide a scientifically grounded way to improve cognitive functioning or stave off cognitive decline. Months later a group of 133 scientists and practitioners countered that the literature was replete with demonstrations of benefit. The review sets out and justifies a set of best practices for brain-training interventions, then evaluates the published peer-reviewed intervention studies cited on the websites of leading brain-training companies against those standards.

## Why reasonable people reach opposite conclusions

The disagreement is mostly methodological, and the reasons are worth knowing because they apply well beyond this topic.

- **Active versus passive controls.** If the comparison group does nothing, any improvement in the training group may reflect attention, expectation, or simply doing something. Melby-Lervåg and colleagues' 2016 null result for far transfer is specifically the result *against treated controls* — which is the harder and more informative comparison.
- **Expectancy.** Participants who know they are in a brain-training study expect to improve. That expectation can move performance on outcome tests by itself.
- **Outcome measures that resemble the training.** If the "far transfer" test shares structure with the trained task, an apparent generalisation may be near transfer in disguise.
- **Publication bias.** Positive results are more likely to be published. Melby-Lervåg and colleagues' bias analysis is a direct engagement with this, and their conclusion about evidential value is not a minor caveat.
- **Different inclusion criteria.** Au and colleagues restricted their analysis to one training paradigm in one age band; the broader reviews cast wider. Meta-analyses of different question sets can both be competently executed and still disagree.

## What regulators and health agencies have said

Two data points sit outside the academic literature and are directly relevant to how these products are marketed.

In January 2016 the Federal Trade Commission announced that the creators and marketers of the Lumosity brain-training program had agreed to settle charges alleging that they deceived consumers with unfounded claims. Lumos Labs paid $2 million in redress and was required to notify subscribers and provide an easy way to cancel auto-renewal. The FTC's complaint described claims that training would improve performance on everyday tasks, in school, at work and in athletics; delay age-related cognitive decline and protect against mild cognitive impairment, dementia and Alzheimer's disease; and reduce cognitive impairment associated with a list of health conditions — and that scientific studies proved these benefits. In the words of the Bureau of Consumer Protection's then-director, Jessica Rich, "Lumosity simply did not have the science to back up its ads."

The National Institute on Aging takes a similar line for consumers. Its guidance on cognitive health notes that cognitive training designed to improve specific cognitive skills appears to have benefits for maintaining cognitive health in older adults, citing the ACTIVE randomised controlled trial, in which participants trained in reasoning and speed of processing experienced less decline over ten years than the memory and control groups. But it follows that directly with a warning: "Beware of claims that playing certain computer and online games can improve your memory and thinking. There currently is not enough evidence available to suggest that commercially available computer-based brain-training applications have the same impact on cognitive abilities as the ACTIVE study training."

That distinction — between a structured research protocol and a commercial app — is the one most marketing quietly elides.

## What we will not claim about our app

Stated explicitly, because the absence of a claim is easy to miss:

- We do not claim [Mental Math & Memory Games](/apps/mental-math-memory-games/) makes anyone smarter.
- We do not claim it raises IQ or fluid intelligence.
- We do not claim it prevents, delays or protects against cognitive decline, dementia or any medical condition.
- We do not claim it improves performance at work, at school or in any activity other than the ones it drills.
- We do not claim any therapeutic benefit for any condition.

If you see any of those claims attached to any brain-training product, the FTC action above is the relevant precedent for how seriously to take them.

## What the app actually does

[Mental Math & Memory Games](/apps/mental-math-memory-games/) drills addition, subtraction, multiplication and division with difficulty that climbs as you improve, alongside number, grid, sequence and delayed-recall memory games. It includes timed sprints, accuracy rounds, survival challenges, boss quizzes and a daily math challenge, and it tracks scores, accuracy, streaks, response time, personal bests and history. It also covers techniques for percentages, estimation, number patterns and faster calculation.

Those are claims about practice and measurement. Getting faster at arithmetic through arithmetic practice is the near-transfer effect the evidence reasonably supports, and it is a worthwhile thing on its own terms — mental arithmetic is genuinely useful, and being fluent at it is genuinely convenient. It just is not a claim about your brain.

The app is free with ads. More in this area sits under [education and brain training apps](/apps/category/education-brain/), with our other writing collected under [education and brain training articles](/blog/category/education-brain/).

## The practical takeaways

If you want to be more effective at tasks that stress working memory, the evidence points less towards training capacity and more towards not needing as much of it:

- **Build chunks in the domain you care about.** This is knowledge work, it is domain-specific, and it is the mechanism behind most of what looks like superior memory.
- **Automate the sub-steps.** A method you have to reason through occupies working memory; a method you retrieve does not. This is exactly why drilling arithmetic facts helps with multi-step arithmetic, and it is the honest case for practice. Our [mental math training guide](/blog/mental-math-training-guide/) and [the methods worth learning next](/blog/mental-math-tricks-that-work/) both work on this principle.
- **Externalise.** Writing down an intermediate result is not cheating; it is removing a load the system was never built to carry.
- **Reduce interference.** Capacity that small is easily disrupted. Interruptions cost more than they appear to.

## The honest summary

Working memory is real, it is small, and it constrains a great deal of thinking. Whether it can be trained in a way that transfers beyond the trained tasks is a live scientific dispute, with substantial meta-analytic evidence on the sceptical side, a smaller positive result on the other, and a detailed review explaining why competent researchers reading the same literature reached opposite conclusions.

Anyone telling you that question is settled — in either direction — is telling you more than the literature does.

title: How to Actually Learn Something From a World History Timeline App
metaTitle: Interactive World History Timeline App: A Guide
secondaryKeywords: how to check a historical date

sources.p: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration
Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars
Lillian Goldman Law Library, Yale Law School

body:
Most people finish school able to name a few dozen historical events and unable to place any of them next to each other. Ask when printing reached Europe relative to the fall of Constantinople, or which came first between the Haitian Revolution and the abolition of the British slave trade, and the answer is usually a shrug — not because the facts were never taught, but because they were taught as isolated units with nothing holding them together.

That gap is exactly what a chronology tool is for. It is also worth being precise about what it cannot fix.

## What a timeline is good at

Three things, and they are worth having.

**Relative position.** Knowing that something happened *while* something else was happening is a different kind of knowledge from knowing its date. It is what lets you notice that the same decades produced unrelated-looking developments on separate continents, and that is where most interesting questions start.

**Breadth without commitment.** You can pass through two hundred years of a region you know nothing about in ten minutes and come out with a rough shape. That shape is low resolution and it is not worthless — it tells you where to read properly later.

**Repetition that does not feel like revision.** Chronological order is a natural retrieval cue. Ordering, matching and recall exercises built on a timeline hit the same material from several angles, which is how sequences get retained.

### What it is not

A timeline app is not a historian, a textbook, or a source. It gives you compressed summaries with the argument removed, and the argument is where most of the actual history lives. It will not teach you historiography — how interpretations formed, competed and changed — and it cannot show you the evidence a claim rests on.

Use it as a map. Nobody learns a city from a map, but everybody who knows a city can read one.

## Three layers you should keep separate

Almost every confusion about history comes from collapsing these into one. Here they are with worked examples.

### 1. What the documents record

The engrossed parchment of the United States Declaration of Independence is held by the National Archives. The Second Continental Congress adopted the text on 4 July 1776, ordered it engrossed on parchment on 19 July, and delegates began signing that parchment on 2 August 1776 — John Hancock first. Not everyone who eventually signed was in the room that day; 56 signatures were added in total. The National Archives states all of this plainly, and it quietly dismantles the familiar image of a single room signing on Independence Day.

That is documentary. It rests on a physical object you can go and look at.

### 2. What historians infer

Why the colonies broke with Britain is a different kind of question. Taxation, representation, imperial debt after the Seven Years' War, land policy west of the Appalachians, Enlightenment political theory, slavery and the interests of particular colonial elites all appear in serious accounts, weighted differently by different historians.

None of that is invented, and none of it is settled the way a date is settled. It is inference from evidence, and reasonable specialists disagree about the weighting. When you meet a confident single-cause explanation of a revolution, you are reading a summary of an argument, not the argument.

### 3. What the popular story has smoothed

The Rosetta Stone is a useful case. The documented part: it carries a decree issued at Memphis in 196 BC, inscribed in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Ancient Greek; it was found in 1799 during the French campaign in Egypt; it has been in the British Museum since the early nineteenth century, where you can look up its catalogue entry today.

The popular story compresses everything after that into one name and one moment. The reality was a contested, incremental decipherment: Thomas Young made real progress on the Demotic text and on identifying royal names in cartouches, and Jean-François Champollion's breakthrough in the 1820s built on and went far beyond it, with an argument about priority that the two men's supporters were still conducting long afterwards. Who "deserves credit" is interpretation. That the stone bears three scripts is fact.

A third example makes the point in the modern period. That the Berlin Wall's crossings opened on the night of 9 November 1989 is documented in exhaustive detail. *Why* it opened that night — a mishandled press conference, sustained mass protest, the economic condition of the GDR, changes in Soviet policy, or the interaction of all of them — is a live historical argument, and the declassified diplomatic record that feeds it is publicly readable in archives like the Wilson Center's.

> Rule of thumb: dates, texts, objects and inscriptions are the floor. Causes, motives, significance and credit are the building. An app can hand you the floor. It cannot hand you the building, and you should be suspicious of anything that pretends to.

## Why dates are slipperier than they look

If two sources give you different dates, the disagreement is usually about convention rather than about facts.

### Calendars changed under people's feet

The Gregorian calendar was introduced in 1582, but adoption was staggered across centuries and jurisdictions. Britain and its colonies switched in 1752, dropping eleven days to realign — so British documents from before that switch are dated in a different system from contemporaneous documents elsewhere in Europe. Archives handle this with "Old Style" and "New Style" notation, and The National Archives publishes guidance on reading dates in records from that period.

The clearest illustration is Russia's. The revolution known as the October Revolution began on 25 October 1917 by the Julian calendar then in use, which is 7 November by the Gregorian calendar adopted in 1918. Both dates are correct. Neither source is wrong. The event has two dates because the country changed calendars afterwards, and the name stuck to the old one.

### There is no year zero

In the conventional era numbering, 1 BC is followed immediately by AD 1. There is no year zero between them, which is why intervals spanning the boundary are one year shorter than subtraction suggests. Astronomers use a different numbering that does include a year zero, precisely because the standard convention makes arithmetic awkward — the U.S. Naval Observatory's astronomical applications material covers the distinction.

BCE/CE and BC/AD number years identically; they differ only in the label. A source switching notation has not changed any dates.

### "Circa" is doing real work

Dates for the ancient world often rest on chains of synchronisation — regnal years, king lists, dated astronomical observations, stratigraphy, radiocarbon ranges — each with its own uncertainty. When a timeline shows a clean number for something four thousand years old, that number is the midpoint of a scholarly range, and the range is the honest form. This is not a flaw in the app; it is a property of the evidence.

## Getting real value out of the app

[World History Timeline Sim](/apps/world-history-timeline-sim/) covers more than 2,000 major events and lets you browse them by year, era, region, country or category, with a world history map showing where things happened. The chronological browse is the part that does the work described above, and it is worth using deliberately rather than at random.

**Pick one century and read it across regions.** The default instinct is to follow a single country forward. Reversing that — fixing a period and moving sideways across the map — is where the relationships show up.

**Use Time Travel Mode for structure, not for answers.** It drops you into a turning point with its historical context and what actually happened, offers realistic options with their trade-offs, then plays out consequences and a Butterfly Effect Score. The genuine value is in being forced to articulate what a decision depended on. The value is *not* the outcome it generates, which is designed narrative. Nobody knows what would have happened, and anyone who says otherwise is writing fiction — enjoyable fiction, and it belongs in the "what if" column rather than the "what happened" column. There are over 2,000 of these scenarios, plus a Rewrite History Campaign that works through the eras and a Daily Time Jump that drops you somewhere unplanned.

**Treat Civilization Survival Mode as a model, not a claim.** Steering a famous civilization through food shortages, invasion risk, trade collapse, disease, political instability, climate stress and diplomacy is a good way to internalise that pre-modern states were constrained by logistics and harvests far more than by intentions. It is a simplification with a small number of variables, and simplifications teach by leaving things out.

**Close the loop with the recall tools.** Daily quizzes, flashcards, word search, crosswords, timeline ordering, matching games and map challenges exist because exposure is not retention. Timeline ordering in particular is the exercise most directly aimed at the skill this whole article is about. Timeline Detective works backwards from clues to causes, History Boss Battles and the What-If Tournament put markers at the end of a stretch of work, and there is a museum of artifacts to unlock as you go.

The app is free on Google Play, supported by ads, with optional in-app purchases. It sits in the [education and brain games category](/apps/category/education-brain/) alongside our arithmetic training app; if you want a second short daily habit that is measurable in a way history is not, the [mental math methods guide](/blog/mental-math-training-guide/) covers that side.

## How to check something a history app told you

If a claim matters — you are quoting it, arguing with it, or putting it in an assignment — check it. These are free, institutional, and take about a minute each.

| Source | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| U.S. National Archives | American founding documents and federal records |
| The National Archives, UK | British state records, dating conventions, research guides |
| Library of Congress digital collections | Newspapers, photographs, manuscripts, maps |
| The British Museum collection | Objects, inscriptions, provenance and dating |
| Wilson Center Digital Archive | Declassified twentieth-century diplomatic documents |
| Yale's Avalon Project | Full texts of treaties, charters and legal documents |
| UNESCO World Heritage List | Sites, with descriptions and dating from nomination files |

Two habits make these useful. First, look for the document rather than a description of the document — most of these will show you the actual text or object. Second, notice when a museum or archive hedges. Institutional language like "attributed to", "probably", or "traditionally dated" is not evasion; it is the honest state of the evidence, and it is the tone a summary strips out.

We try to hold this page to the same standard. What we will and will not assert, and how the claims here get sourced, is set out in our [editorial policy](/editorial-policy/).

## The short version

Chronology is scaffolding. It is worth building deliberately, and a timeline app is an efficient way to build it — breadth, relative position, and enough repetition that the sequence sticks.

What it hands you is compressed and stripped of argument, so keep the layers apart: documents and dates are one thing, historians' inferences are another, and the tidy popular version is a third. When a date looks wrong, suspect the calendar before you suspect the source. And when something is worth repeating, spend the minute it takes to find the document behind it.

title: The Upgrade You Don't Take: How Roguelike Survival Runs Stay Interesting
metaTitle: Zombie Survival Roguelike for Android: Build Guide
secondaryKeywords: zombie game no in app purchases
body:
You are eleven minutes into a run, the screen is more undead than street, and the game stops to ask you a question. Take the weapon boost or the survivability. Two seconds of quiet, one decision, and then the horde comes back.

That pause is the entire genre. Everything around it — the zombies, the stages, the automatic weapons — exists to make that two seconds matter.

## The genre's real invention was the interruption

Roguelikes take their name from *Rogue*, a 1980 dungeon crawler, though the label itself was settled much later: the term emerged around 1993 out of Usenet newsgroups where players argued about what to call this family of games and eventually landed on "roguelike" as, in the community's own framing, the least bad option available. In 2008 a gathering of developers in Berlin produced the nearest thing the genre has to a definition, identifying nine high-value factors of a canonical roguelike. Two of them get quoted constantly: random level generation, described explicitly as a way to increase replayability, and permadeath, where a character's death means starting over rather than reloading.

Those two factors are usually presented as the reason roguelikes are replayable. They are not, quite. Randomness by itself produces variety without meaning — a slot machine is extremely random and nobody replays it for the decisions. Permadeath by itself just raises the cost of losing.

What actually generates replay value is the thing those two mechanics enable: **choices that permanently exclude each other**. Because the run cannot be reloaded, taking one upgrade means never having the other one this time. Because the layout differs, you cannot pre-plan your way around the decision. The result is that a game with a modest list of upgrades produces a very large number of genuinely distinct runs, and the variety lives in the shape of your build rather than in the content of the game.

Modern horde-survival games stripped this idea down to its core and put it on a timer. [Zombie Survival: Last Survivor](/apps/zombie-survival-last-survivor/) sits squarely in that lineage: experience collected during a stage promotes you mid-battle and hands you an upgrade choice on the spot, and because you are picking under pressure rather than at a leisurely menu, no two runs come out the same shape.

## Opportunity cost is the actual mechanic

Ask a player what their favourite upgrade is and you will get an answer about damage numbers. Ask what made their best run work and you will get an answer about a decision they made at level four that changed everything after it. The second answer is the one that describes the game.

Here is the trap that catches most people. Faced with weapon boosts, damage increases, survival upgrades and special abilities, the instinct is to keep everything roughly level — a bit more damage, then a bit more survivability, then something that sounded interesting. It feels prudent. It is the most reliable way to have a mediocre run.

The reason is that the pressure rises faster than a balanced build does. Spreading upgrades thinly means every one of your capabilities stays just barely adequate, and "just barely adequate" has a shelf life measured in stages. A build that does one thing to an absurd degree outruns the curve for longer, because the curve is steep and only a steep answer keeps pace with it.

> The practical rule: after the first two or three level-ups, ask what your run is *about*. Then take the option that makes that answer more true, and decline the option that would make it merely broader.

This is also why the choices need to hurt. An upgrade system where you eventually collect everything is not a decision system, it is a delivery schedule. The moment you can have it all, the interesting question — what am I willing to go without? — disappears, and with it most of the reason to start a second run.

### When to break your own rule

Commitment is a heuristic, not a law. Two situations justify abandoning your plan mid-run.

The first is a genuine gap. If nothing you have taken addresses the thing that is currently killing you, specialising further just makes you better at surviving a problem you do not have. The second is a special ability that changes the category of what you can do rather than the size of a number. Anything that alters how you handle a situation is worth more than an incremental boost to a situation you were already handling.

## Movement is the only input, which is not the same as easy

Your survivor shoots automatically. That single design decision is often mistaken for the game playing itself, and it is closer to the opposite.

When you remove aiming, you remove the thing that absorbs a player's attention and hides their positional mistakes. What is left is one continuous decision — where am I, and where am I drifting — evaluated dozens of times a second against a field that is actively closing. It is a smaller input space and a harder one to be good at, because there is nowhere to put the blame.

Three things decide it.

**The gap behind you.** New players watch what is in front. The horde in front is visible, slow to reach you, and mostly harmless as long as you are moving away from it. The run ends when the swarm you were outpacing quietly closes the space you were planning to retreat into. Look behind more often than feels necessary.

**Distance from the fast ones.** Different undead behave differently, and the quick ones do not care about the plan that worked on the slow ones. Any decision that would be fine against a shambling mass can be fatal when something in that mass is faster than your drift.

**Never the middle.** Being surrounded is not a state you enter suddenly; it is the last frame of a process that started when you cut a corner too tight ten seconds earlier. Staying out of the middle of the horde means avoiding the geometry that produces it, not escaping it once it exists.

Power-ups are worth collecting, but they are best treated as a reason to take a route you would have taken anyway. Detouring into a bad position for a pickup is one of the most common ways an otherwise good run dies.

## Bosses are a pattern problem

Boss fights bring their own attack patterns, and they are less about raw damage than about spotting the openings.

That flips how you should approach a first encounter. Your build is not going to change between now and the end of this fight, so the only variable you control is how well you read the rotation. Spend the opening exchange doing nothing ambitious: watch what the heavy attacks look like as they begin, and note where the fight goes quiet. The quiet is the opening.

If a boss beats you, the useful post-mortem is rarely "I needed more damage." More often it is that you were in the wrong half of the arena when a heavy attack started, which is a positioning answer to a positioning question.

## What a lost run is actually worth

The stages run through dark streets, infected zones and abandoned areas, each with its own enemy types and rising pressure. Losing somewhere in there is the normal outcome, and the genre is built around that being fine.

The test of whether a run was wasted is simple: can you name the decision that ended it? Not the moment — the decision. "I got surrounded" is a moment. "I took the fourth small bonus instead of committing" is a decision, and it is the kind of thing you can act on next time.

Runs where you cannot answer that question usually mean you were playing on autopilot, which is the one genuine risk of a game this easy to control. If three runs in a row blur together, stop and make one deliberate change, even a bad one. A run that tests something is more valuable than a run that repeats something.

## Five habits that push runs deeper

1. **Drift, do not dash.** Constant small movement keeps escape routes open. Sprinting commits you to a direction the horde can plan around.
2. **Decide your build early and out loud.** Naming your plan at level three makes every later choice faster, which matters when the game is not waiting for you.
3. **Check behind you on a schedule.** Not when it feels dangerous — on a rhythm, because the moment it feels dangerous is already late.
4. **Treat pickups as opportunistic.** Route through them, never toward them.
5. **Change one thing per run.** Isolate variables and you learn something; change everything and you learn nothing.

## The practical details

Zombie Survival: Last Survivor is free to download on Google Play, supported by ads, with no in-app purchases and an Everyone content rating. Controls are simple enough to explain in a sentence, and runs stretch or shrink to fit whatever time you have.

It lives in [Action & Arcade Games](/apps/category/action-arcade/) next to [Space Shooter - Galaxy Arcade](/apps/space-shooter-classic-arcade/), which takes an almost opposite position — four abilities you spend manually, patterns you learn by sight, and rewards that go into the ship between runs. If you want the reflex-driven half of the argument, the [space shooter guide](/blog/space-shooter-arcade-guide/) covers how to read enemy fire. For something with no time pressure whatsoever, [the anime coloring guide](/blog/anime-coloring-app-guide/) is the other end of the shelf.

The genre's oldest lesson still holds: the run you remember is not the one where you got lucky with the offers. It is the one where you turned something down and it worked.
